summary: The appellant was a dealer in food articles for the year 1962. He was a dealer for the sale of food articles for sale to the public. He was prosecuted for an offence under section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955. The appellant was convicted and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of one year and to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000/- and in default to undergo rigorous rigorous imprisonment for one year. The appellant filed an appeal to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant then filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court for a writ of certiorari quashing the order of the High Court and for a writ in the nature of mandamus directing the State of Delhi to pay the amount of Rs. 2,000/- as fine. The High court held that the appellant was guilty of an offence under Section 7 of the Act and sentenced him to undergo rigorous Imprisonment for a period one year and a fine of 1,000/-. The High Court held that the offence was not established by the prosecution and the High Court was wrong in its conclusion that the article of food was unfit for human consumption. The High, Court also held that the article was not adulterated and the appellant was liable to undergo rigorous sentence of one year. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the High Court had erred in its conclusion on the ground that the article in question was not adulterated. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts were right in their conclusion that the appellant had not established by any satisfactory evidence that the Lal mirchi powder was adulterated. [775 H] 2. The High. Court was wrong. The appellant had not been convicted for an offence punishable under section 7. The High-Court was wrong in holding that the appellant could not be convicted for an act of an offence punishable by section 7. [776 H] 3. The High Curt was wrong in taking the view that the article which was not adulterated was not adulterated because the article was unfit for consumption. [778 H] 4. The appellant could not have been convicted for the offence of an offence of an attempt to commit an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term of one year or upwards. [779 H] 5. The appellant is not guilty of an act of commission punishable under section 8. The appellant has not been convicted of an offence which is punishable by section 8. [780 H] 6. The appellant cannot be convicted for the act of an attempt or preparation for human consumption unless it is proved that the offence is punishable by law. [782 H] 7. The appellant can be convicted for a breach of the provisions of section 7 of Act. [785 H] 8. The HighCourt was wrong. [786 H] JUDGMENT: CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Criminal Appeal No. 9 of 1972. Appeal by Special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 14th July, 1972 of the Delhi High Court in Criminal Appeal No 9 of 1972 and Criminal Appeal No 10 of 1972. S. T. Desai, S. K. Bagga and S. K Gupta for the Appellant. S. K Jain and S. P. Nayar for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by RAY, J. This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment of the High court of Delhi dated 14th July 1972. The appellant, who was convicted by the trial court for an offence of attempt to commit murder, was convicted for an attempt to murder, and sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for life. The appellant challenged his conviction and sentence on the ground of his conviction under section 7 and sentence of rigorous imprisonment for six months. The appellant contended that the offence of attempt was not punishable under section 3 of the Act. The High (Court) was wrong in relying on the decision of this Court in [The State of Delhi vs. The State of Delhi] , referred to above.

The appellant was a tenant of a shop in the village. He was a tenant in the shop. He was in possession of a shop. He filed a suit for eviction against the appellant. The trial court held that the appellant was a "dealer" within the meaning of the Act and that he was an agriculturist. The trial Court held that the lease deeds were not genuine and that the appellant had not produced any receipts of payment of lease money and he was an agricultural labourer. The trial Judge held that the provisions of the Act were not attracted and that the presumption under paragraph 3(2) of the order could not be drawn against the appellant and that the finding of the trial court was confirmed. The appellant filed a revision petition to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the revision petition. The appellant then filed a revision application before this Court. The appellant contended that the provisions contained in section 49 of the Act did not apply to him and that the provisions in the Act were inapplicable to him. The High court held that in the present case the appellant was an agriculturist and it was not possible to find out whether he was an agriculturists. The High. Court held that in view of the provisions contained under section 49 of Act, the presumption under section 3(2)(a) could not be raised against the appellant as he was an Agricultural labourer. The High, Court held that there was no evidence to show that the appellant is an agriculturist. In the present case, the appellant was not an agriculturist. He was an agriculturist, and therefore, the presumption was not drawn against him. The appellant was an agricultural labour. The High Curt held that the presumption was rebutted by the evidence of one witness on oath. The High' Court held that it was not necessary to prove that the appellant has been an agriculturist. It was further held that the High Court was not justified in holding that the provisions were not attracted. The High 'Court held that the Act was inapplicable to the appellant. In the result, the appeal was allowed and the order of the High Court is set aside.

The appellant was a tenant of a shop in the premises in suit. The respondent filed a suit for eviction of the appellant from the shop in suit on the ground of arrears of rent. The appellant contended that the respondent was a tenant from month to month under the provisions of section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. The trial judge held that the respondent had a right to receive rent from the defendant and that the defendant was a tenant under the provisions, Transfer of Property (Amendment) Act, 1929. The trial court held that the defendant had a right of tenancy under the provisions. Transfer of Property Rules, 1955, and that the respondent could not be said to be a tenant from the month to month. The trial Judge held that the tenant was a tenant in the shop in the suit and that the tenant had a right under the provisions and the provisions of the Transfer Act. The respondent appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the tenancy of the appellant was one from month to months under section 106, Transfer of property Act and that the appellant was a monthly tenant under section 106 of Transfer of Property. The High court held that by the provisions of Section 106, Transfer and Transfer of Property, Act, the respondent was not a tenant from a month to month and that the tenancy was one from months to month under section 106. The High, Court further held that the appellant had a right in the property to receive rent for one year only from the date of the suit and the suit was not barred by time. The High. Court further held, that the respondent did not have a right to get the rent from the appellant as he was a monthly tenancy under section 106 and that the trial judge was right in holding that the respondent became a monthly tenant from month-to-month under section 106 Transfer of Property and that the High Court was right in the view that the respondent would be entitled to receive rent only from the month of the suit. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts have not given any finding on the question of arrears of tenancy. [557 D] 2. The respondent was a monthly lessee under the provisions in section 106 of TP Act. The appellant was a statutory tenant under the Act. The tenancy was one for one year and the respondent was paying rent for one month. [558 D] 3. The respondent had a statutory right to receive the rent from a tenant under section 116 of the Transferof Property Act. [559 F] 4. The respondent could not have been said to be tenant from month and could not be held to be a monthly tenant. [560 D] 5. The respondent having a right to obtain the rent from month tomonth under section 116, the respondent could be said to have a right of a tenancy under section 116. [566 D] 6. The respondent being a statutory tenant could not be treated as a tenant from year to month under Section 106 of the TP Act. [546 D] 7. The respondent is a statutory tenant. [546 F] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 15 of 1971. Appeal by Special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 9th July, 1971 of the High Court of Calcutta in Appeal from Order No. 8 of 1971. S. T. Desai, S. K. Bagchi, S. N. Mukherjee, S. P. Nayar and S. K Patel, for the appellant. S. K Jain, for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. The appellant is a statutory tenancy under the [Transfer of Property Act]. The respondent was the tenant under the appellant. The respondent instituted a suit for possession of the shop in question on the ground that the appellant is a monthly tenant and that the suit was filed by the respondent for possession of that shop.

The appellant, a resident of Bombay, was assessed to income tax by the Income Tax Officer, Bombay, for the assessment year 1964 65, on the ground that the income tax authorities had failed to furnish the information asked for by the appellant in the assessment proceedings. The appellant filed a return of income for the assessment years 1964 65, 65 and 66 on the ground of failure to furnish the required information. The Income Tax Officer rejected the return filed by the appellant and assessed the income tax payable by the appellant. The appellant preferred an appeal to the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, which allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the Income Tax officer. The appellant then filed a writ petition in the High Court of Bombay. The High Court held that the Income Tax Act, 1961 was not applicable to the case of the appellant and that the Income tax authorities had no jurisdiction to summon the production of the relevant documents. The High court held that the appellant had not furnished the required information in the assessment proceeding and that the order of assessment was not passed by the Income tax Officer in accordance with the provisions of Section 138(1)(b) of the Act. The appellant, therefore, filed a writ appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The provisions of Section 139 of the Act are not applicable to cases where the information etc. as contemplated by the Section is called for by any person, other than a court. [675 H] 2.1 The High Court was in error in holding that the Income-tax Officer had no jurisdiction under Section 138 of the Act to summon the relevant documents in a case pending before the court when the court, by a judicial order, requires the production of such documents. [682 H] 2 2.2 The High Court, therefore, fell in error in quashing the order of reassessment. [683 H] 2:2. The High Courts of Bombay and Bombay had no jurisdiction in the matter of summoning the production of documents in a court of law. [684 H] 2] 2.3 The High Court fell in error by holding that the order passed by the Commissioner under Section 138(l)(b) was not passed in accordance with law. [650 D] 2.4 The High Court erred in quashing the proceedings. [650 A] 2.5 The High Court had no jurisdiction. [650 B] 2.6 The High Court could not be said to have jurisdiction under Section 139 of The Act. The High Curt was in error by quashing the order passed under Section 138 (l)(b). [650 D D] 2:3. The HighCourt fell in error of law in quashing the proceeding. [650 E] 2:4. The High-Court fell in the error of law by holding that in the case of a proceeding pending before the Court, the Income Tax authorities had no authority to summon the material in the assessment case. [650 F] 2:5. The High.Court fell in a wrong view of law by not quashing the order under Section 138. [650 G] 2:6. The High,Court fell in wrong view of the law by holding the order of an Income Tax Officer in the case before it was not passed. [650 H] 2.:7. The High' Court fell in the wrong view of fact. [650 C] 2:7. The order of the High Court was not passed on the basis of the provisions of the Act and the Income Tax Department had no jurisdiction, therefore, the order of Income Tax Officer was not passed under Section 139(1)(a) of the Income-Tax Act, 1961. [650D] 2:8. The High 'Court fell in its error of law. The High T.C.A. was not competent to quash the order of re-assessment. [650E] 2:9. The High: Court fell in wrong of law.

The gift was made by a grandfather to his minor grandsons. The father of the minor was a minor. The father was a minor and the father was a young man. The father died in the year 1955. The father filed a suit for partition and separate possession of the property. The father claimed that the father was entitled to the property and that the father had no right to dispose of the property by sale. The father also claimed that the property was gifted to his minor grandson and that the gift was valid. The father, however, filed a suit in the Court of the Munsif, who decreed the suit. The father then filed a second appeal before the High Court. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the decree of the trial court. The High court held that the father of the father was not entitled to dispose of any thing given to his wife, and that the son was not entitled under Muhammadan law to dispose of his property by sale and that the sale was valid. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the father could not have made the gift on behalf of his minor grandson, and that in the absence of any evidence to the contrary, the gift was invalid. HELD: (1) The gift was valid and the father had the right to dispose the property by gift. The gift was invalid and the father could dispose of the same. [557 D] (2) The gift in question was valid and it was not invalid. The gift in favour of the minor son was valid. [558 E] (3) The father was not a minor and was not entitled in law to dispose the land by sale. [559 F] (4) The father had no power to make the gift on his behalf. The gift is valid and the gift is valid. [546 F] (5) The gift is invalid. The father had the power to make gift on behalf the minor son. The gift could not be made by a son. The father could not make the gift. [546 G] (6) The gift made by a father to his minor son was invalid. The son was not a major. The gift made was valid. There could be no question of making the gift on the part of the father. [546 H] (7) The gift could be made by the father only if he was a minor, and not otherwise. [546 D] (8) The gift being valid, the father could make the gift only if he had the power of making the gifted property. [546 E] (9) The gift did not create any interest in the property. [547 F] (10) The gift deed was valid. It was not invalid and the gift was not valid. [547 G] (11) The gift by a father was valid. If the father had made the gift, the father was bound to make the transfer. [547 H] (12) The gift had been made on behalf of a minor. [547 A] (13) The gift, therefore, was valid. But the gift was made on behalf the father. The gift did create a valid gift. [547 D] (14) The gift cannot be made by any one else. The gift deed is valid. The gift cannot therefore be made by another person. [547 E] (15) The gift must be valid. [548 G] (16) The gift has been made on the basis of the gift deed. The gift has to be made by an individual. [548 F] (16)(a) The gift does not create any right in the property by a father. [548 A] (b) The gift of a minor is valid. If a minor is a minor, the father is bound to make a gift on behalf and in the name of the minor. [548 B] (c) The gift can be made by one person only.

The respondent, a religious institution, was established by the appellant, and the respondent was appointed as a manager of the said institution. The appellant was appointed as the manager of the institution. The respondent was appointed to manage the affairs of the institution and to administer the affairs of that institution. The management of the institution was taken over by the Government. The appellant filed a suit in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Tiruvannamalai, for a declaration that the respondent temple was a public temple and for a declaration to that effect. The respondent claimed that the temple was a private temple and was not a public temple. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondent was a public religious institution and that the respondent had not established a public temple in the suit land. The respondent filed an appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that the respondent is a public religious Institution and that the appellant was not a private temple. The High court held that the appellant had established a public religious endowment in the suit property and that the suit was not maintainable. The High Curt also held that the suit filed by the respondent was not maintainable and that the High Court was in error in holding that the appellant is a public temple within the meaning of the Act. The High. Court further held that the question whether the respondent temple is a public or private temple was not a question of fact and the High Court held, therefore, that the appellant has not established a prima facie case in the suit. The High, Court further held, that the respondent has not established any public religious endowment within the meaning ofs. 76(1) of the Act and that the question of public religious endowment was not a matter of fact. The High 'Court further held that in the suit filed in the Court the respondent had failed to establish a prima facie relationship between the appellant and the respondent. The High' Court further held "it is clear that the respondent cannot be said to be a public religious or a private temple within the definition of the Act". The High Court further held: "The question whether the appellant is an public religious or private temple is a question of law and the High court has not determined whether the appellant has established a public public religious endowment or not. The question whether the temple is a private temple or not is a question which is a question in terms of a percentage of the income. The question of public trust is a matter of law and in the light of the facts and circumstances of the case, the High Court has proceeded to consider the question whether there is a prima facie relation between the appellant temple and the respondent temple. The question is whether the appellant was a public institution within the meaning s. 76(2) of the Indian Act. The question was whether the appellant had establish a public religious trust in the suit premises. The High Courts have held that the issue of public religious trust is a question arising out of the facts of the case and the High Courts have not determined whether there is any public religious or public religious institution in the suit properties. The High courts have not determined the question whether in the suit, the appellant has establish a public temple or not. In the circumstances, the High Courts were not right in holding that there is a relationship between the respondent temple and the appellant. The High-Court has not determined the issue of Public religious endowment. The HighCourt has not decided the question whether it is a question involved in the suit and that the issue is a question involving a public religious Endowment. The High -Court has not considered the question whether a public religious endowments are a matter of record. The High |Court has not dealt with the question whether any public religious endowments have been established in the suit lands. The High|Court has not given any finding on the question whether such a question is a question relating to public religious endowment. In the result, the appeal is allowed and the judgment and decree of the High Court are set aside.

The appellant was a member of the Orissa High Court. He was appointed as a Judge of the High Court of Orissa. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he was guilty of contempt of the High court. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of dismissal. The High Court dismissed the petition. The appellant then filed a writ appeal in this Court. The appellant contended that the order of the High. Court was not an order initiating contempt proceedings and that the High Court was not competent to pass an order under section 19 of the Act. The High court held that the order passed by the High Court in the exercise of its jurisdiction under section 19 was an order passed by a High Court in exercise of its inherent jurisdiction. The appellant, therefore, filed a writ application in the High court for quashing the order of his dismissal. The appellant also filed a writ in the High. court for quashing of the order of punishment. The High. Court dismissed the writ petition. The High, Court held that the appellant was guilty of the contempt of the Court and was, therefore, not entitled to the protection of section 19 of Act. The appellant's writ petition was dismissed. The appellant thereafter filed a writ. in the High' court. The High' Court held that in the absence of an order of the Court, the order of suspension was not an ex parte order. The appellant was, therefore. not entitled to any relief. The appellant accordingly filed a writ-petition in the High 'Court. The High ' Court held that an order of suspension passed by a high Court in exercise o the inherent jurisdiction of the High' Court under section 19 is an order of a High Court and not an order of an appellate Court. The High-Court held that the High-Court was competent to pass a decree for contempt against the appellant. The appellant thereupon filed a writ of certiorari. The appellant did not press the question whether the order of a high Court passed in exercise of the inherent jurisdiction under section19 was an order initiating the proceeding for contempt. The High Curt held that the writ petition was not maintainable. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: (1) The order of the high Court dismissing the writ petition in limine was an order of discharge passed by a higher Court. The order of discharge was not an interlocutory order. The order was an interlocutory order and not an interlocutory one. [523 G] (2) The order passed by an appellate Court in exercise or an inherent jurisdiction of a High' Court is an order passed in exercise o' the inherent jurisdiction. [524 G] (3) The order dismissing the writ application in limine was not an appealable order. The High Courts inherent jurisdiction under article 226 of the Constitution is an inherent jurisdiction. It is an order which is an order initiating a proceeding for contempt and not an an order of any higher Court. [526 G] (4) The order was passed by the Court in exercise, of its inherent powers. The order passed in the exercise or an order of this Court was an order in exercise of inherent jurisdiction. An order of the higher Court is an interlocutory order, and not an intermediate order. [527 G] (5) The order is an order in the exercise o' any inherent jurisdiction of this Court. [506 G] (6) The order dated April 5, 1975 was an order under the provisions of section 19. The order dated May 5, 1975 is an order under sections 19 and 20. [528 G] (7) The order under section 20 is an order made by a higher court. [529 G] (8) The order does not amount to an order initiating proceedings for contempt. [530 G] (9) The order in the nature of an order passed under section 19 does not amount an order initiating proceeding for contempt unless an order of Court.

The appellant was prosecuted for an offence under section 6 (1 A) of the Act, and was convicted by the trial court and sentenced to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000/-. The trial court convicted the appellant under section 6(1 A) and sentenced him to pay a sum of Rs. 500/- and a fine of rupees 500/-. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. The appellant filed an appeal to this Court. The appellant contended that section 6 (2) of the , Act, and section 6 (3) of the, Act, were not applicable to the case and that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of section 6 (4) of the said Act. The High Court held that section 6(2) of Act XVII of 1933 was not applicable to a case of a former Act, and that the provisions of section 6(3) of Act XVIII of 1933 were not applicable. The High court held that section 5 of the Act was not applicable in the case of a later Act, and, therefore, the appellant was entitled to the benefits of section 6 of the Act. The appellant, therefore, filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court. The High, Court held that the appellant had not established that section 6 of Act XVIII was applicable to the facts of the case. The appellant then filed a petition for special leave to appeal to this court. The appellant also filed a petition to this Court for special leave. The appellant did not file any petition for special Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court held that in the absence of a specific provision in the Act, the provisions of the Act were not applicable and, therefore. the appellant was liable to pay the amount of Rs. 2,000/- and Rs. 500/respectively. The appellant was, therefore, entitled to the relief claimed in the petition. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The appellant is not entitled to any relief under section 6 of this Act. [775 H] 2. The provisions of section 5 of Act XVIII were not applicable in a case of an earlier Act. The provisions in the Act were applicable to the present case. [776 H] 3. The provisions contained in section 6(4) of Act XIX of 1933 were applicable to a later Act. The words "the provisions of section 4 of the Act" were not used in the Act. [750 H] 4. The provisions relating to the offences under the Act were made applicable to the cases of the former Act. The Act was not in force at the time of the commencement of the Act but was in force at that time. [750 A] 5. The provisions made in the Act are not applicable to cases of a former statute. The provisions regarding the offences under section 6 are not applicable in cases of a later enactment. [750 B] 6. The provisions under section 6 were not applicable when the offence was committed by the appellant. [750 D] 7. The provisions for the offences under sections 6 and 6 were not in force when the offence is committed by the person concerned. [750 G] 8. The provisions as to the offences mentioned in section 6 are applicable to cases where the offence was not committed by the accused. [750 F] 9. The provisions referred to in section 6 of that Act are not attracted to cases of the latter Act. [751 G] 10. The provisions mentioned in section 5 of this Act are not in force in the case. [751 H] 11. The provisions are not applicable when a previous Act is repealed. [751 A] 11. Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, applies to the present Act. [75 H] 12. The provisions, of section 6, are not applicable where the provisions of a previous Act are not applied to cases of an earlier enactment.

The appellant, who was the owner of the property, purchased the property in execution of a decree passed by the court in the year 1940. The appellant purchased the property from the said property on July 26, 1940. The said property was purchased by the appellant in the year 1942. The said purchase was made in the year 1943. The appellant filed a suit for possession of the property in the year 1944. The said suit was decreed by the trial court. The appellant preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant then filed a second appeal to this Court. The question that arose for consideration was whether the appellant was entitled to the benefit of clause (e) of section 36(2) of the Bengal Money Lenders Act, and if so, whether the appellant is entitled to the relief of restoration of possession. HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that the appellant was not entitled to the protection of clause (b) of section36(2). [675 H] (ii) The High court was right in observing that the appellant had not been in possession of the properties sold in the year 1941. The appellant was not in possession of any of the properties in the year 1945. The appellant had not acquired any right which could be protected under clause (c) of section 35 of the Bengal Act. [675 B] (iii) The High Courts were right in holding the appellant to be the purchaser of the property from July 26, 1941. [676 H] (iv) The High courts were right in observing in the judgment that the appellant could not be held to be the purchasers of the property sold in the years 1942 and 1942. [678 H] (v) The High Curt was right in taking the view that the appellant is not entitled to any relief under clause (b). [678 B] (vi) The High,Court was right in directing restoration of possession to the appellant. [679 H] (vii) The High. Court was right. [680 H] (viii) The High-Court was right. The appellant could not claim the benefit of the clause (e). [682 H] (ix) The High' Court was right, in holding that in the absence of a valid sale deed, the appellant was a purchaser of the properties from the said date. [682 B] (x) The High 'Court was right, and the appellant was also entitled to the reliefs claimed by him. [683 H] (xi) The HighCourt was right and the appellant is also entitled to relief under clause(e) of [section 36(2)] of the Bengal Finance Act, and the High Court was also right in holding, that the appellant cannot be held to have acquired any right under clause (e), of section 35(2). The High Court also was right in giving relief under clause 5 of the said section. [690 H] (xii) The High Turt has not given any direction for restoration of possession of the said property to the appellant and the appellant has not been able to establish that the appellant has acquired any right in the said property. [691 H] (xiii) The High F.C.I. was right in not granting the relief of possession to judgment debtors. [692 H] (xiv) The High [Court] was right in granting the relief under clause 15 of the said sub section. [650 H] (xv) The High L.R.C. was right. (xvi) The High R.C.A. was right, (xvii) The High H.C.C. had no jurisdiction to restore possession to the decree-holder. [693 H] (xviii) The High P.C.R. was right and was rightly not granted. [694 H] (xix) The High O.I.C.

The appellant, a minor, filed a suit for partition and separate possession of the property in suit and for recovery of possession of the same. The appellant filed a written statement and contended that the suit was not maintainable. The trial court held that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of section 146 of the Code of Civil Procedure and that the appellant could not be permitted to take advantage of section 146(1) of the Code. The trial Court held that the suit filed by the appellant was not maintainable and that the respondent was not a transferee of the decree. The trial Judge held that the respondent could not be allowed to take advantage under the provisions of section 146 (1) of Code of Civil procedure. The appellant preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that section 146(2) of the code of Civil Procedure was not applicable to the case and that the trial court was right in holding that the respondent had not established his title as a transferee of decree. The High court further held that the trial Court was right in taking the view that the respondent did not establish his title as transferee of the property after the transfer. The High, Court further held that section 147(2) was not applicable in the case. The High. Court further held, that the respondent cannot be permitted to raise the plea of the appellant that the respondent should be permitted to be impleaded as a transferee in writing within the meaning of Order XXI, rule 16 of the Code and that the High Court was right. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts have not been right in holding otherwise. [557D] 2. The respondent cannot be allowed to raise the contention that the appellant is not a transferee in possession of the decree and that the question of title was not a question of title in the eye of law. [558F] 3. The High C Court was right when it held that the provisions of Order XXI were not applicable to a case where the respondent was a transferee of a decree. [559F] 4. The respondent was not entitled to be permitted to file an application for execution of the decree passed in favour of the appellant. [560F] 5. The respondent could not claim to be a transferee of an interest in the decree after the transfer of the decree, which was subsequently obtained. [566F] 6. The respondent is not a transferor of the decree but he is a transferee of his decree. [546F] 7. The respondent can be permitted to withdraw the decree by an assignment in writing within a period of three months from the date of the decree or within such further period as the Court may allow. [546G] 8. The respondent has not established his right to be a purchaser of the decree after it is passed and that the Court has no jurisdiction to execute the decree. [548G] 9. The respondent had not proved his title as the transferee of the judgment-debtor. [548F] 10. The respondent did not prove his title as purchaser of the property. [548B] 11. The respondent having not proved his possession as a transferee, the appellant could be permitted to recover possession of the premises after it was passed. [548D] 12. The respondent being a transferee of possession of a decree, he could not be said to be a ' transferee of the original decree. [549F] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 15 of 1972. Appeal by Special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 14th May, 1972 of the Allahabad High Court in Second Appeal No. 11 of 1972. S. T. Desai, S. K. Bagga, S. N. Andley, for the appellant. S. S. Khanduja, for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by RAY, J.

The respondent was a registered dealer in the goods and was assessed to sales tax under the Sales Tax Act. The respondent purchased the goods from the appellant and sold them to the customers. The appellant sold the goods to the customers and the customers were paid the sales tax. The respondent paid the sales-tax on the sales of the goods. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court for quashing the assessment order and for a direction to the appellant to pay sales tax. It was contended that the contract was a composite contract and the contract was one for sale of the goods and the sale of the materials was not a pure works contract. The High Court held that the contract did not constitute a composite contract. The respondent contended that the contracts were not contracts for sale of goods and were not incidental to the execution of the contract. The Court held that in the circumstances of the case the contract was not a composite contract but a composite contract, and the contract did, and the respondent was not a dealer. The High court held that the contracts in question were composite contracts and the respondent could not claim the amount agreed to be paid to it. The High. Court held that it was only upon the "fixing" of the window leaves and labour were involved in the making and fixing, but the contract was composite contract. In the present case, the contract was for sale of windows and the respondent had agreed to supply the windows to the customers, and the appellant was liable to pay sales-tax. The High, Court held that there was a contract for sale of a building contract and the respondent did not supply the windows and the windows. The High' Court held that as the respondent had not supplied the windows and labour, the contract did. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts were right in holding that the contract in question was a composite one and the respondent is a dealer. [557 H] 2. The contract was one composite contract and not a composite one. The contract did not create a separate contract. The contract in question did not constitute composite contract. [558 H] 3. The contract is a composite contract; it is a composite one, and the property in the goods passes under the terms of the contract and the services rendered in connection with the installation are under a separate contract and the goods are not incidental to it. [559 H] 4. The contract does not constitute a contract for the sale of a goods. The contract must be a composite contract as distinguished from a composite contract for the supply of the goods for consideration. [560 H] 5. The contract for sale is a composite transaction. The contract provides for a composite contract which is a composite and separate contract. [546 H] 6. The contract cannot be a composite one; it is only upon the work and labour. The contract also does not constitute composite contracts. [546 G] 7. The contract of sale is a separate contract; it does not constitute an indivisible contract. [548 G] 8. The contract has to be a composite and composite contract. It is a composite document. The contract falls within the composite contract. There is no contract for sale. [548 H] 9. The contract involves a composite contract consisting of two parts. The contract contains a composite contract containing composite contract. A composite contract containing a composite contract is a separate and independent contract. [547 H] 10. The contract may be composite one. [548 A] 11. The contract, in the instant case, is composite one. There is a composite agreement for the supply and service of the windows and other fittings. The contract ends and ends. [548 D] 12. The contract between the parties is a composite composite contract.

The appellant was prosecuted for the offence of cheating under section 420 read with section 511 Indian Penal Code read with section 120B Indian Penal Code. The appellant was prosecuted by the Presidency Magistrate, Calcutta for the offence under section 420 Indian Penal Code and section 120B of the Indian Penal Code for cheating. The appellant pleaded not guilty. The trial court convicted him and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year and to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000/- and in default of payment of fine to undergo rigorous rigorous imprisonment for six months. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. The appellant filed an appeal before the High Court. The High court dismissed the appeal. The appellant then filed a revision petition in the High Court which was allowed by the High Court on the ground that the appellant was not a party to any conspiracy to defraud or cheat the complainant. The High Curt also held that the appellant had not been able to prove that he was a party to the conspiracy. The High. Court held that the prosecution had failed to prove that Raj Kumar Agarwalla was a party of any conspiracy to cheat the complainant and that the appellant did not commit any offence. The High, Court also held that there was no evidence to show that Raj Kumar respondent was a party or that Raj Kumar was a party in any conspiracy to cheating the complainant. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in quashing the charge against the appellant. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts in exercise of their revisional jurisdiction under section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, should not interfere with the judgment of the High Court unless it is shown that the High court was in error of law in interfering with the judgment. [675 H] 2. The High courts in exercise of the revisional jurisdiction under the Code of criminal procedure are invested with the power to interfere with the order of the High court in exercise of its revisional jurisdiction. The High 'Court in exercise of revisional jurisdiction under [section 439] of the Code can interfere with the findings of the trial court only if it is shown to be perverse. [682 H] 3. The High-Court in exercise its revisional jurisdiction under s. 439 of the Criminal Procedure Code can interfere where the High Court is satisfied that the case was made out against the accused. [683 H] 4. The High' Court in exercise of jurisdiction under s 439 of the code of Criminal Procedure can interfere with an order of acquittal. [684 H] 5. The High -Court in exercise under s. 435 of the Code could not interfere with an acquittal. The High [Court in exercise thereof could not interfere in the exercise of its jurisdiction under s.. 439 of the [Code of Criminal Procedure]. [682 B] 6. The High--Court in exercise, of its revisional Jurisdiction under s.438 of the Code, can interfere with findings of the Trial Court only if it was shown to be so perverse. [650 D] 7. The High "Court in exercise Of the revisional jurisdiction can interfere with a finding of fact only if it can interfere with " the judgment of a High Court in exercise thereof. [650 H] 8. The High (Court) in exercise of powers under s. 438 of the Code cannot interfere with the finding of the trial Court only if the High Court could interfere with the trial court. [650 A] 9. The High: Court in exercise under the revisional jurisdiction could interfere with findings in exercise of power under s. 437 of the Code. [650 B] 10. The High COurt was not justified in interfering with an order under s. 438 of the code. [650 G] 11. The High Co-operative Court in exercise,of the revisional jurisdiction, could not interfere. [650 C] JUDGMENT: CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Criminal Appeal No. 9 of 1971.

The petitioner was a railway servant. He was a railway employee. He was employed as a conductor in the Railway. He was issued a charge sheet under Rule 14 of the Railway Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1968. He was dismissed from service by the order dated August 30, 1981. He filed a writ petition in the High Court of Patna challenging the order of dismissal. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The petitioner filed a writ appeal against the order of the High Court. The High court allowed the writ petition and quashed the order of termination. The petitioner challenged the order of his dismissal by filing a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution. The High, Court allowed the writ petitions and quashed the orders of dismissal. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the order of removal was not passed in accordance with the provisions of the Railway Rules and the Rules and, therefore, the order of compulsory retirement was not justified. HELD: (i) The order of dismissal was passed in accordance to the provisions of Rule 14 of Railway Servants (Conduct) Rules, 1966. The order of compulsory superannuation was passed in violation of the provisions of Article 311 of the Constitution and the order of punishment was not justified in law. [775 H] (ii) The order was passed in contravention of the provisions contained in Article 311 of Constitution. [776 H] (iii) The order passed by the High Court was not justified and the order was not justified on the ground that the petitioner was guilty of misconduct. [778 H] (iv) The order is not justified on any ground. The order was not passed by the competent authority. The order is passed in violation to the provisions contained therein. [779 H] (v) The order in question was passed in breach of the provisions in Article 311. [780 H] (vi) The order dated August 29, 1981 was passed in compliance with the provisions contained under Article 311 of constitution. [782 H] (vii) The order did not suffer from any infirmity. [785 H] (viii) The order does not suffer from the vice of arbitrariness. [786 H] (ix) The order has been passed in violation with the provisions in the Constitution. [750 H] (x) The order cannot be sustained on the ground of violation of the principles of natural justice. [750 A] (xi) The order being in violation of Article 311, the order is not sustainable on the ground as it is not justified. [750 B] (xii) The order suffers from the vice that it was passed in consonance with the provisions. [750 D] (xiii) The order having been passed in breach to the provisions in [Article 311] is not justified in the facts and circumstances of the case. [750 G] (xiv) The order, therefore, is not justified and it is not sustainable. [750 E] (xv) The order can be passed in breach with the provisions as contained in Article 14 of the Constitution, [750 A G] (xvi) The order could be passed in violation thereof. [750 F] (xvii) The order must be passed in accordance, with the provisions, contained in Article 77 of the Constitution [750 A-B] (xviii) The order should be passed in conformity with the provisions [Article 311]. [750 B-C] (xix) The order may be passed in contravention to the provisions [Articles 14] and 311 of the constitution [750 A.B] (xx) The order shall be passed in consonance to the provisions. The order shall not be passed in the manner laid down in Article 311 [750 A.] (xxi) The order under Article 311 is not passed in breach.

The plaintiff, who was the Manager of the temple, was the Manager in the year 1896. He was appointed as a Manager in the temple. He was paid a sum of Rs. 1,000/- per annum. He was also paid a sum Rs. 1 lakh per annum. The plaintiff was appointed as Manager in the Temple. He was given a charge of the temple on the basis of the income from Telibandha to the Gharu Khata. The plaintiff filed a suit for declaration that the defendant was the Manager and the trustee of the temple. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the defendant had not established the dedication of the village to the temple. On appeal, the High Court held that the plaintiff was not entitled to succeed, and dismissed the appeal. The plaintiff then filed a second appeal before the High Court. The High Court held, inter alia, that the plaintiff had not established that the defendant in the suit was the Manager or trustee of the village and that the plaintiff could not be allowed to take the plea that the defendant did not have the benefit of the trust. The High court further held that the defendant could not be permitted to take the ground that the plaintiff did not have any right to succeed, that the defendant, having failed to establish that the defendant is the Manager or the trustee of a temple, the High court held that the High Court was not justified in holding that the plaintiff failed to establish the dedication of Telibandha in favour of the temple and that the High court was not justified to hold that the plaintiff is entitled to succeed. The High, Court further held that in view of the finding that the plaintiff has not established that he was the Manager, the High. Court held that by the mere fact that the plaintiff does not have the right to succeed in the suit, the High 'Court was not justified. The High. Court further held, that the High.Court was not right in holding that in view the finding that there was no dedication of the suit land to the temple, the plaintiff was entitled to succeed and the High Court's decision was not justified on the basis that the plaintiff's case was that the defendant should be allowed to raise the plea that he was not the Manager or a trustee of the suit. The High' Court further held in the case of the plaintiff that the plaintiff having failed to prove that the defendant has the benefit of his own trust, the High' Court was not right. The High 'Court further held that there was a finding that the defendant failed to establish his dedication to the temple and the plaintiff was also entitled to succeed in his suit. The plaintiff's appeal was, therefore, allowed. The High C.A. No. 8 of 1976 has been filed by the plaintiff. The plaintiff has filed this appeal by special leave. The plaintiff is a retired employee of the temple in the year 1959. He was a Manager of the Temple. The plaintiff had been appointed as Manager of the said temple. The plaintiff, therefore, was entitled to the benefit of s. 5 of the Act. The High-Court held that the suit was not maintainable. The HighCourt further held, inter-alia, that the suit is not maintainable. In the result, the appeal was allowed and the suit was dismissed. Hence, this appeal by the plaintiff-appellant. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The plaintiff-appellant was not entitled for the benefit of S. 5 of Act. The plaintiff could not have been allowed to take a ground that the defendant-respondent was the Manager. [775 H] 2. The plaintiff having failed in the suit he was not entitled, to succeed. [776 H] 3. The plaintiff cannot be allowed to claim the benefit of section 5 of the Limitation Act. [778 H] 4. The plaintiff must be deemed to have established his right to succeed. He must establish the same.

The appellants were convicted by the Trial Court for contempt of court for disobeying the order of the High Court passed in a contempt proceeding. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court of Allahabad challenging the order of conviction and sentence passed by the Trial Judge. The High Court quashed the order of sentence passed by a learned Single Judge of the Allahabad High Court and directed the appellants to pay a sum of Rs. 1,000/- to the respondent. The appellants challenged the order of their conviction and sentence by filing a writ petition before the High Court. The High court quashed the order and directed the sentences to run concurrently. The appellants then filed a writ appeal before this Court. The appellants contended that the High Court was in error in quashing the order of punishment passed by the learned Single Judge. The appellants also contended that the order of dismissal passed by the High Court is not in accordance with the provisions of the [U.P. High Court's Act, 1952] and the Rules framed thereunder. The High Courts held that the order passed by the District Judge was in accordance with law and the order of confirmation of sentence passed in the appeal was not in accordance to the provisions of law. The High. Court held that the appellants were guilty of contempt of court and sentenced them to pay a fine of Rs. 500/- each. The High' Court held that there was no contempt of court. The High 'Court further held that the High 'Court was not competent to pass any order of punishment under the Act. The appellants' appeal was dismissed. The appellants thereafter filed a writ application in the High' Court. The learned Single Judge dismissed the writ petition. The appellants preferred a Letters Patent Appeal before the Division Bench. The Division Bench allowed the appeal and set aside the order of acquittal passed by the trial court. The appellants have come up in appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The High-Court was not justified in quashing the orders of the Trial Court. The order of the District Judge is not in consonance with the provisions contained in the [U P. High Court]'s Act, 1952. [775 H] 2. The High Curt was not justified under the provisions of Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The order passed by a District Judge was not in consonance to the provisions contained therein. [776 H] 3. The order was passed by the Additional District Judge. The order is not in conformity with the provisions. [778 H] 4. The order does not in any way affect the rights of the appellants. The order cannot be passed in breach of the provisions of any statute. [779 H] 5. The order should be passed in accordance with Section 115 of Code of Civil procedure. [780 H] 6. The order must be passed in conformity with law. [782 H] 7. The order being in accordance with provisions of law, the order of a District Judge is in accordance with [Section 115] of the Code. Appeal by Special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 14th July, 1973 of the Allahabad, Allahabad High Court in C.M.P. No. 11 of 1973. S.K. Bagga, S.K Srivastava, S.P. Singh, R.K. Garg, S.C. Agarwal, S.N. Srivastava, S K Srivastava, S P Singh, S.B.

The appellant, a registered society, was incorporated under the provisions of the [Indian Companies Act, 1913] (hereinafter referred to as the 'Act') and was registered as a society under the provisions thereof. The appellant was a registered society under the Act. The society was registered under the provisions contained in the Act. On the basis of the resolution of the society, the Registrar of the society passed an order on the application of the society under Section 15 of the Act. In the appeal filed by the society, it was contended that the order of the Registrar was erroneous and without jurisdiction. The High Court held that the order passed by the Registrar was not in accordance with the provisions of Section 15 of Act and the order was not in conformity with the principles of natural justice. The High court held that the Registrar had no jurisdiction to pass an order under Section 15. The High, Court held that in the absence of any provision in the Act, the order passed under Section 15 was in conformity with Section 15 of that Act. The High. Court further held that the provisions of section 15 of the said Act were not applicable to the society and the order passed was in conformity to the principles of justice and fair play. The High Curt, however, held that the appellant was not entitled to get the custody of the award from the custody of his court to take back the award from him. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court. The High' Court held that since the order passed in the appeal was in conformity of the principles of law, the order was in conformity. The High 'Court further held that in view of the provisions of [section 15] of the Act, it was not necessary to consider the question of limitation. The High-Court further held, that the order was erroneous and the order of registration was in conformity, with the principles laid down in section 15 of Act. The appellant, therefore, filed a writ appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The order passed by a court in the absence, of any provision, is in conformity with section 15 of that act. [557F] 2. The order of the High Court was erroneous and in conformity with law. [558F] 3. The order was in accordance with law. The order dated 24th of June, 1985 was in conformity and in conformity. [559F] 4. The order under Section15 was in conformity or in conformity with [section 15 of the Arbitration Act, 1940]. [557G] 5. The order is in conformity or not in conformity. It is not necessary to discuss the ratio of A the decision of the Full Bench of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in M. The appeal is allowed and the order dated 24.6.1985 passed by the High Court is set aside. [560G] 6. The order in appeal was erroneous and no opportunity was given to the appellant to file a counter to the writ petition. [566G] 7. The order impugned in the writ petition was in conformity/in conformity with the provisions contained therein. [567G] 8. The order cannot be sustained and is set aside and the writ petition is allowed. [568G] 9. The order made by the High court is set aside, but in the circumstances of the case, the order is set aside with costs.

The respondent, a firm, was a registered dealer in the business of manufacturing and selling cotton and cotton. The respondent was a partner in a firm. The firm was assessed to tax under the provisions of the [Indian Income Tax Act, 1922] (hereinafter referred to as the Act). The respondent filed a return of income for the assessment year 1948-49 in respect of the assessment year 1949-50. The respondent claimed that the income of the firm was exempt from tax under section 13(1)(e) of the Act. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order. On further appeal, the Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals) held that the income was exempt from the tax under section 10 of the Act and that the respondent was entitled to claim that the income should be assessed under the provisions for the assessment years 1949-50 and 1949-50, and that the income must be assessed under section 13 of the Act, and that in the instant case the respondent was not entitled to claim the benefit of the exemption under section 13 (1)(e). The respondent appealed to the Appellate Assistant commissioner. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the respondent had not claimed the benefit of section 13(l)(e) and that the Income Tax Officer was not entitled, in law, to claim the exemption under the Act. On further appeals, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Appellate Assistant. The respondent then filed a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that the Income tax Officer was not competent to assess the respondent under section 13 and that the order of assessment was not liable to be set aside. The High court held that the order passed by the Appellate Assistant was not a valid order and that the appeal was liable to be dismissed with costs. The respondent filed an appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that the Income-tax Officer was competent to assess a person under section 13. [775 H] (2) The respondent was not a registered dealer and was not entitled under section 13 to claim the benefits of the Act as he was not entitled. [776 H] (3) The respondent had not filed any return of income under section 13, and therefore, the order of eviction passed by the Income Tax officer was not liable for interference. [778 H] (4) The respondent could not be allowed to claim the relief under section 13 as he was a registered registered dealer. [779 H] (5) The respondent did not file any return of the income of his income. [780 H] (6) The respondent is not entitled to the benefit of Section 13. [750 H] (7) The respondent has not filed any income tax return and the order of cancellation of the registration is not liable to the same. [750 A] (8) The respondent cannot be allowed to say that the income is exempt from tax. [750 B] (8)(a) The respondent does not have a right to claim the refund of the tax under the Act and the order passed is not liable for the refund. [750 D] (b) The respondent having not filed any returns of income under the Act, the order passed under section 13 is not liable under section 13 because the respondent has not claimed the exemption under [section 13] and that the application for the relief under [section 11] was not maintainable. [750 F] (c) The respondent, therefore, was not entitled for the relief of refund under section 13 since the respondent was a registered firm. [750 G] (d) The respondent being a registered dealer was not entitled as he was entitled to the relief under the Act as the respondent was only a registered dealer. The respondent cannot claim the relief of exemption under section 10.

The respondent was appointed as a Head Master of a school in the State of Maharashtra. He was appointed as Head Master of the school on the basis of a written examination held by the Board. He was promoted as Head Master on the basis that he was a teacher in a school. He was also promoted as Head master on the basis on the basis, that he was appointed as head master on the recommendation of the Board. The respondent was appointed to the post of Head Master on a temporary basis on the recommendation made by the Board on the basis thereof. The respondent challenged the order of his appointment as Head Master by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court quashed the order of the Education Standing Committee and directed the Board to hold a fresh examination for the post of head master. The High court held that the respondent was not a teacher in the school and that he was not a candidate in the examination conducted by the Board and that the finding of the Education standing Committee that the respondent had used unfair means at the examination was not correct. The High. Court held that the finding recorded by the Education Standing committee that the respondent did not have the knowledge of the physical and mental condition of the students was not correct and that the findings recorded by the School Committee were not based on any evidence or evidence. The High, Court held that in the absence of any evidence or any evidence or material to the contrary, the finding recorded against the respondent was illegal. The High Curt also held that the findings of the Education Committee that the finding was based on no evidence or evidence were not based upon any evidence or were based on any material or evidence. In the result, the High Court quashed and set aside the order of termination of the respondent as well as the order of dismissal passed by the respondent. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court which was allowed by the impugned judgment. The High' Court held that since the finding recorded in the enquiry was not based on evidence or was based on any such evidence, the finding was illegal. In the present appeal, it is contended that the finding that the finding is illegal is not based on the evidence or is based on any other evidence or evidence and that the High Court was in error in quashing the order of punishment. The respondent contended that the findings were not based either on evidence or were not based by evidence. The respondent also contended that the High court was in error by holding that the finding in the enquiry is not based upon evidence or was not based upon the evidence. The learned counsel for the respondent contended that in the present case the finding recorded is not based either upon any evidence nor is it based on any of the evidence. In support of the contention, the learned counsel for respondent relied upon the decision of this Court in [State of U.P. vs Ram Chandra] , referred to.

The prosecution case was that the appellants were prosecuted for the offence of criminal misconduct by the prosecution. The prosecution case was as follows: The appellants were prosecuted under section 5(1) read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. The prosecution alleged that the appellants had given a bribe to Madan Lal and that the appellants gave him a bribe of Rs. 100/- to Madan Lal. The prosecution also alleged that the appellant Madan Lal gave him a sum of Rs. 200/- to Madan lal and that the appellant gave him a receipt for the same. The prosecution further alleged that the money was given to Madan Lal by Madan Lal and the appellant gave a receipt for that amount. The prosecution examined the witnesses and also produced the evidence of the witnesses. The trial court held that the prosecution had proved that the appellants did not give the bribe to Madan lal. The High Court, however, reversed the finding of the trial court and convicted the appellants. The High court held that in view of the evidence of Labhu Ram, the prosecution case was not proved beyond reasonable doubt. The High Curt also held that the evidence of PW 1 was not sufficient to prove that the appellants made a bribe to the complainant. The HighCourt further held that the appellants could not be convicted under section 5 (1) readwith section 5(3) of the Act. The High. Court also held that in the absence of any evidence to prove that he was a public servant, the presumption under section 5 of the Act was not attracted. The High, Court also held, that the evidence showed that the appellants knew that the bribe was given to the complainant and that the complainant was a public Servant and that the presumption under Section 5(1)(d) of the said Act was not rebutted. The High' Court also held in the case of Madan Lal that the evidence was not sufficient for proving that the appellants paid the bribe to the respondent. The High 'Court also held that there was no evidence to prove the fact that the appellants accepted the bribe. The High-Court also held in favour of the appellants. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the High Court was wrong in holding that the evidence given by the witnesses was not sufficient. The High Courts held that the presumption of the appellants under section 5 was not rebutted by the evidence of DW 1. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High T Court was wrong. The evidence of the witness was not sufficient and the presumption under [section 5(1)] was not rebutted and the presumption was not rebutted in the case. [523 D] 2. The presumption under section 6 was not rebutted or rebutted by the other appellants. The presumption was not raised by the appellants in the case and the High Court rightly held that the accused were not guilty of the offence under section 5. [524 D] 3. The presumption of the accused under section 5 is not rebutted by any evidence. The presumption is not rebutted in a case of this nature. [526 D] 4. The presumption in the case under section 5 cannot be rebutted by the accused. [527 D] 5. The presumption contemplated by section 5 is a presumption of law. The presumption must be rebutted by evidence. [528 D] 6. The presumption as to the offence under [section 6] is not rebutted. [529 D] 7. The presumption that the appellants have accepted the bribe is not rebutted and that the accused are not guilty of any offence under section 161 of the Indian Penal Code. [530 D] 8. The presumption arising under section 5 will be rebutted by other evidence. [506 G] JUDGMENT: CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Criminal Appeal No. 11 of 1966. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated the 9th July, 1966 of the Bombay High Court in Criminal Appeal No.. 11 of 1966 arising out of the judgment and Order dated the 9.7.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956, was incorporated in the year 1956, and the appellant was a partner in the firm of the respondent. The respondent, a partnership firm, was incorporated on September 16, 1957, and the respondent was a partner of the firm. The appellant was a member of the joint family of which the respondent was the partner. The respondent was a member at the time when the contract of guarantee was entered into. The appellant filed a suit against the respondent for recovery of the amount due to the respondent. During the pendency of the suit, the respondent filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 1,50,000/- on the ground that the appellant had not taken any benefit of the guarantee given by the respondent. On the pleadings of the parties, the trial court held that the appellant was not entitled to the decree for recovery of money and that the respondent was not entitled for the decree for the recovery of the said amount. The respondent filed an appeal against the decree and the High Court reversed the decree and dismissed the suit. The appellant preferred a second appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The appellant is not entitled to any relief under the provisions of the Act. [775 H] 2. The appellant has not taken any advantage of the guarantee of the respondent given by the appellant. The respondent has not taken the benefit of the security given by the principal debtor. [776 H] 3. The appellant had taken the benefit under the guarantee given to the respondent by the respondent and the surety was not entitled, therefore, to the decree. [778 H] 4. The appellant could not be allowed to take advantage of the security offered by the respondent which itself may be a consideration for the surety offering his personal guarantee. [779 H] 5. The appellant cannot be allowed to claim restitution. The surety is entitled to restitution. [780 H] 6. The appellant being a member of a joint family of the respondent, he is entitled to the benefit of Section 141 of the Act and the surety is entitled for restitution. [750 H] 7. The appellant having taken the benefit by the security given to the appellant, the respondent cannot be allowed restitution. [751 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 15 of 1977. Appeal by Special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 14th May, 1977 of the High Court of Judicature at Bombay in First Appeal No. 8 of 1977. S. T. Desai, S. S. Khanduja, S. N. Andley, for the appellant. S. S., Khanduja, for the respondent. S. N.. Khanduja, M. S. K. Sastri, S. K., T. H. K. Khanna, for the respondents. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by RAY, J. This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment of the High court of Bombay dated 14th May 1977. The appellant, a member of his joint family, was a member in the joint family. The respondent is a partner at the time of the contract of the guarantee. The respondent had taken the advantage of the surety offered to the respondent and had not taken the advantage under the guarantee. It is not disputed that the appellant has taken the benefit thereunder. The appellant did not take any benefit under the surety offered by the principal creditor. The appellant also did not take the benefit of his surety offering his own personal guarantee. The appellant's case is that the surety offered the personal guarantee by the respondent, was not taken by the principal-debtor. The appellant contends that the surety was entitled to the benefits of the guarantee under the guarantee and the surety offered his personal guarantee and the respondent is entitled to take the benefit under that guarantee. The Act was passed by the Legislature of Madras on the basis of the Hindu Law of the community. The Hindu law of succession was adopted by the Hindu law of the community as a whole and the Hindu law was adopted by a Hindu law of inheritance. The Hindu Law of succession was, however, adopted by the Hindus. The Hindu system of inheritance was adopted by Hindus in the family of the Hindu law. The Hindu laws of succession were adopted by the members of the family. The Hindu family was governed by the Hindu Law. The Hindu community was governed by Hindu law. Under the Hindu law, the Hindu law in general not only in matters of succession and inheritance but also in matters of their property including the Hindu concept of coparcenary and joint family, the right of a son in the property held by his father, a right expressly saved by section 3 of the Act. The Act was passed to provide for the division of the property held in the family by the members in the family. Section 3 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, provided that all Cutchi Memons, including the joint family property, were subject to the provisions of section 3, to the provisions in section 3, and the Hindu Law was adopted by Hindu law of descent. The Act provided that all cutchi Memons would in matters of descent be governed by the Mahomedan law. The Act also provided that all Patchi Memons in the family would in matters in which they were governed by the Muslim law, be governed by Muslim law. The provisions of the Act were not inconsistent with the provisions of the Mahomedan law and were not inconsistent therewith. The Act did not provide for the distribution of the property by survivorship. The Act, therefore, provided that the provisions of Hindu law in the matter of distribution of property by survivorship and the right of the son in it by birth in the property holding by his father were saved by section 4 of the Act and the Act was not inconsistent with that section. The Act had not provided for the division and division of the properties held by the father. The Act made no provision for the division or division of the joint family properties by metes and bounds. The Act only provided for the distribution and division of property by metes and fiefs. The Act does not provide for division of the income of the joint Hindu family by metes and shares. The Act provides for the division by metes and partitions of the joint property by metes & bounds. The provisions in the Act were inconsistent with the Mahomedan law, and were not consistent with the Mahomedan Law. The Act is not inconsistent with section 3 of Act. The provisions were not inconsistent. The Act has not provided for division of property. The Act cannot be inconsistent with the Muslim law.

The appellants are engaged in the manufacture of cotton fabrics. They are engaged in manufacture of cotton yarn. They are manufacturing cotton fabrics. The appellants are manufacturing cotton yarn. The appellants manufacture cotton fabrics. In the year 1965, they filed a declaration under rule 9 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944, declaring the goods in question as yarn. The declaration was filed by the appellants on the basis that they were manufacturing cotton fabrics and were manufacturing cotton yarn in the same manner as they were manufacturing the cotton fabrics. On the basis of the declaration, the appellants were manufacturing cotton fabric. The appellants filed a declaration on the basis of rule 9(1) of the Central excise Rules, 1944. The appellants were manufacturing the yarn in question. The appellants also filed a declaration in respect of the goods produced at an intermediate stage and consumed or utilised in the continuous process of manufacture of the end product. The appellants claimed that they were entitled to the benefit of the said rule. The Assistant Collector of Central Excise, who adjudicated the case, held that the appellants were not liable to pay excise duty on the yarn manufactured by them. On appeal, the Collector of Central excise, Bombay, held that they were not liable for payment of excise duty. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that the goods produced by the appellants were goods manufactured in the factory of the appellants and, therefore, the appellants are not liable to payment of excise. The Tribunal held that in the instant case, the appellants have not produced any specification by the Collector of the place of manufacture or production of the goods at an intermediate stages of an integrated process. The appellants have not filed any declaration under rule9(1) in respect of goods produced at the intermediate stage and, therefore the Assistant Collector was not competent to make the assessment. The Tribunal also held that the appellant was not liable to be paid any excise duty. The Tribunal further held that the provisions of the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944, were applicable to the goods produced in the factory. The Tribunal, therefore, held that as the appellants were required to pay excise duties on the yarn produced by the appellant, they were not entitled to the exemption under the said rule and, therefore they are not liable for paying any excise duty on yarn. The Tribunal accordingly, held that in view of the provisions of rule 9 of Central Excise Rules 1944, the appellants should be paid excise duty on their yarn. The present appeal is filed by the Revenue.

The appellant filed a suit for eviction of the tenant from the suit premises on the ground that the landlord had filed a scheme for the purpose of providing transport facilities in the area and that the scheme was duly published in the official Gazette. The scheme was published in the gazette on the date of the publication of the scheme under section 68C of the Act. The scheme under section68C of the said Act was published in a newspaper on the same day. The scheme, inter alia, provided for the preparation of a scheme for providing transport facilities for the persons who had filed the scheme. The scheme provided for the manner in which objections or representations could be filed and to appear before the Hearing Authority. The scheme had been duly published in accordance with section 68C(1) of the Act and on such publication the scheme was published. The scheme as published in the Gazette was published in accordance wit h the scheme. After the scheme was finally published in the Official Gazette, the scheme was re-constituted under section 68D of the Act by an order made under section 68 D of the Act on the same date. The scheme in the present case was published in terms of section 68D(1) and the scheme was approved by the State Government. The scheme published in the prescribed manner was published in two newspapers on the same dates. The scheme did not contain any provision for the preparation and publication of the schemes. The scheme having been duly published, the scheme could not be rejected at the threshold under order 7 rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The High Court was, therefore, in error in refusing to stay the further proceedings in the suit. The High Curt was, therefore. in error in interfering with the orders of the High Court. The appeal is allowed.

The appellant was the tenant of a building in the premises in question. The landlord filed a suit for eviction of the tenant on the ground of demolition and reconstruction. The assessee, a resident of U.K. was a resident of the State of U.P. The assessee was assessed to income tax on the income of the Indian Company. The Income Tax Officer, on the basis of the accounts of the Indian company, assessed the assessee to income tax. The assessee filed an appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner allowed the appeal and held that the assessee was not maintaining its accounts on mercantile basis and that the assessee had not maintained any particular method of accounting regularly in respect of the said royalty amount. The Appellate Tribunal, on further appeal, held that the method of accounting adopted by the assessee was in accordance with the provisions of Section 145 of the Act and that the said method of accounting was not relevant. The Tribunal held that the amount was not a payment or receipt, but was a payment made by the assessee in U.K., and that the amount of royalty was not a receipt by the assessee. The Tribunal, however, held that in the circumstances of the case, the assessee was entitled to the benefit of Section 5(2) of the Act. The Tribunal also held that the said amount was not an income by the assessee but was a receipt by it. The Tribunal accordingly allowed the appeal of the assessee and held that it was not a revenue receipt. The assessee then filed a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that the Tribunal was not justified in holding that the assessee did not maintain any particular method or accounting regularly in the accounts of its Indian company. The High court held that the question whether the assessee was maintaining its accounts or not was a question of fact and the Tribunal was right in holding that it was a receipt in U. K. and not a receipt. The High. Court also held that in view of the provisions of sub section (2) of Section 145, the assessee is not entitled to the relief under Section 5(1) of the said Act. The High, Court also held, that the assessee is entitled to the benefits of Section 5 of the Act, and that the question of law referred to the High Court was not a question of law. The High C.A. No. 23 of 1967 filed by the assessee is allowed and the order of the Tribunal is set aside.
