The appellant was a public servant within the meaning of section 21, Indian Penal Code. He was prosecuted for an offence under section 161, Indian Penal code and was convicted by the Judicial Magistrate, First Class, Delhi, for an offence punishable under section 161 of the Indian Penal Code and was sentenced to pay a fine of Rs. 500. The appellant was convicted by a Judicial Magistrate, Delhi, and was sentenced by the Judicial magistrate, Delhi, to pay a sum of Rs. 1,000. The appellant filed a criminal appeal before the High Court of Delhi. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant then filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court for a writ of certiorari quashing the order of the Judicial Magistrate and also for a writ in the nature of mandamus directing the appellant to pay a further sum of Rs, 1,000 to the State Government. The High court held that the appellant was a 'public servant' within the meaning ofs. 21, Indian penal Code and section 21, [Indian Penal Code]. The High Court held that the offence was a public one and the appellant was not a public servant. The appellant, therefore, filed a petition in the High court for a writ quashing the order. The High, Court held that as the appellant was an officer in the service or pay of the Government and was a public officer within the meaning s. 21, [ Indian Penal Code], the appellant was entitled to be treated as a public servant under s. 21. The appellant thereupon filed a petition for a writ under Article 226 in the High, Court. The High. Court held that s. 21 of the Indian penal Code was applicable to the appellant and that the appellant could not be said to be a public servant as defined in s. 21 [Indian Penal code]. The High,Court held that the case was covered by s. 21 and the appellant could be said to have been a public servant in the service of the Government. The appellant's petition was accordingly dismissed. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The appellant is a public servant and is a public officer. [557 C] 2. The appellant being an officer in a civil service, he is a public service within the meaning ins. 21, of the Indian Criminal Code. [558 D] 3. The appellant could not have been prosecuted for an act which is a public duty. [559 F] 4. The appellant had been convicted by a judicial Magistrate, Delhi and was sentenced in the criminal case to pay a huge sum of Rs 500. The High-Court has found that the appellant is a 'public' servant within the definition of s. 21[Indian Penal Code] and therefore a 'public duty' within the definition ins. 21. [566 D] 5. The appellant cannot be said to hold a public office under the provisions of s.21, Indian Penal. [567 D] 6. The appellant can be said to belong to a class of persons within the meaning Of s. 21(9) of the Indian Income-tax Act. [568 D] 7. The appellant must be deemed to be a 'public officer' within the scope of s. 2, [566 F] 8. The appellant would be a public officer under the provisions ofs. 21. If the appellant is not a public officer, he is not a 'public authority' within the ambit of s.2, [568 F] 9. The appellant should be deemed to have been an officer in charge of the police station. [569 G] 10. The appellant having been convicted by the judicial Magistrate, the appellant is entitled to be heard. [570 G] 11. The appellant will be entitled to the benefit of the provisions of the Act. [546 G] 12.

The appellant was a citizen of India. He was convicted by the trial court and sentenced to imprisonment for a term of one year and to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000/-. The appellant was convicted by a Sessions Court for an offence under section 3 of the Defence of India Act, and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for a period of one year. The appellant was sentenced to rigorous rigorous imprisonment for one year and a fine of rupees one,000/-. In appeal the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. The appellant filed a petition for special leave to this Court. The High Court dismissed the petition. The appellant then filed a petition under Article 136 of the Constitution for special leave against the order of the High Court. The appellant contended that the order of forfeiture of the juar was not a valid order and that the High Court was in error in holding that the order was not a nullity. The High court held that the order passed by the trial Court was not a void order and that it was not a "order" within the meaning of section 3 of that Act. The High. Court held that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the provisions of the Defence and Civil Defence Rules. The appellant, therefore, filed a petition in this Court under Article 136. The appellant also filed a petition to this Court under Art. 136. The High, Court held that in view of the provisions contained in the Defence of the India Rules, the order of detention was not a 'order' within the meaning Of section 3 of this Act. The appellant's petition was dismissed. The appellant thereafter filed a petition before this Court under article 136. The main contention of the appellant was that the order dated April 30, 1964 was not a decree within the meaning ofs. 3 of the Act and that the order in question was not a judgment within the powers conferred by section 3 of Act No. 1 of 1964. HELD: (i) The order of forfeiture was not a mere order but a "order". The order was not an order "order" but an order "in the same order" and the order was a "order", and therefore, the order was an order "an order" within the powers of section 3. [775 H] (ii) The order was a nullity. [776 H] (iii) The order passed by a competent court was not a judicial order. The order was passed by the High Court in exercise of its jurisdiction under section 3. The order of the trial court was not an "order" and therefore, it was not an 'order' and therefore, was not a order "an "order" under section 3 and therefore, an order "under this Act" was not a law within the powers expressly conferred by section 43 of the Defence. [778 H] (iv) The order dated April 29, 1964 was a nullity and the High Court's order was not liable to be set aside. [779 H] (v) The order in question is not a " order" within section 3 of Ordinance No. 1, 1964. [780 H] (vi) The order is not a decree. The order is a nullity. It is not an order. The High Courts order is not an " order" and therefore the order is not liable to the same effect. [782 H] (vii) The order under the Defence of-India Rules is not a judgment. The order in the present case was not an Order. [786 H] (viii) The order cannot be said to be a "order " within the meaning [of section 3] of the Act. [787 H] (ix) The order does not constitute a decree. [790 H] (x) The order must be a " order " within the powers specifically conferred by section3 of the Act or any rule made thereunder. [791 H] (xi) The order can be passed by the Court.

The appellant was convicted by the Additional District Magistrate, Delhi, under Section 302 of the Penal Code and sentenced to death. The prosecution case was that on the night of the occurrence, the appellant was armed with a gun and he was armed with an axe. The appellant was armed of a gun and the other accused were armed with a lathi. The appellant and the other two accused were armed. The appellant fired a shot at the deceased. The deceased was also injured. The appellant, who was armed with the gun, fired a shot from his gun. The appellant also fired a shot with the gun from his gun which hit the deceased. On the basis of the evidence adduced by the prosecution, the trial court convicted the appellant and sentenced him to death. On appeal by the State, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. The appellant filed an appeal to this Court. The High Court held that the appellant was guilty of the offence of murder and sentenced him as aforesaid. The High court held that the prosecution case was not proved beyond reasonable doubt and that the appellant had been rightly convicted. The High, Court also held that the evidence of the eye witnesses was not sufficient to sustain the conviction of the appellant. The High. Court also held the appellant guilty of the charge under Section 302 read with Section 149 of the Penal code and sentenced him accordingly. The appellant preferred an appeal to the High Court. The learned counsel for the appellant contended that the High Court was not justified in interfering with the order of acquittal passed by the trial court. The High-Court was not justified to interfere with the order passed by the Sessions Judge. The HighCourt was also not justified in disturbing the order of the trial court and the order of conviction passed by the learned trial court. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts were not justified in reversing the order of an acquittal passed by a court of competent jurisdiction. [775 H] 2. The High Curt was not justified under the law in interfering with an order of acquittal. The High' Court was not right in interfering with that order. [776 H] 3. The High 'Court was not right. The High Turt was not right when it reversed the order of a trial court. [778 H] 4. The High (Court) was not justified when it reversed an order of conviction. [779 H] 5. The High F.C.I. Court was not wrong in interfering with a finding of fact recorded by the trial Court. [780 H] 6. The High [Court] was not justified. The High] Court was not correct in interfering with such an order. [750 H] 7. The High A Court was not competent to interfere with an order passed by a Court of competent jurisdiction in exercise of its jurisdiction under the law. [750 A] JUDGMENT: CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Criminal Appeal No. 9 of 1977. Appeal by Special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 3rd July, 1977 of the Delhi High Court in Criminal Appeal No 9 of 1977 and Criminal Appeal No 10 of 1977. S.K. Mehta, for the appellant. S.C. Manchanda, for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by RAY, J. This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment of the High Court of Delhi dated March 3, 1977 in Criminal Appeal Nos. 9 of 1976 and 10 of 1977 whereby the High Court reversed the order passed on the first information report and acquitted the appellant of the charge of murder. The appellant is the son of the deceased. He was the brother of the deceased and was also a member of the same family. The appellant's brother was also a party to the murder of the deceased, who was also a part of the same group. The appellant had been convicted by the trial Magistrate under Section 302 IPC and sentenced to undergo life imprisonment. The High 2.

The appellant was convicted under section 302, read with section 34, of the Indian Penal Code, and sentenced to death. The prosecution case was that on the night of the occurrence, the appellant was found in possession of a large number of weapons, and was found guilty of murder under section 302. The appellant was found guilty under section 302 read with section 149, of the said Code. The appellant filed an appeal to the High Court, which was dismissed. The appellant then filed a petition under Article 136 of the Constitution, which was also dismissed. The High Court, however, dismissed the petition. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. The prosecution story was that on a day earlier to the occurrence, one of the accused was found in the possession of a number of weapons. The appellant, who was found in conscious possession of a small number of weapons and was found in a position of anger, was found in an unconscious state. The appellant also was found in unconscious state. On the basis of the said evidence, the High Court convicted the appellant under section 302 and sentenced him to life imprisonment. The High court, however, acquitted the appellant of the charge under section 302 of the Indian penal code. The appellant preferred an appeal to this Court, which, by reason of the acquittal of the appellant, was dismissed. In the appeal before this Court, the appellant contended that the High Court was wrong in holding that the appellant was guilty of murder, and that the High court was wrong in dismissing the petition. Allowing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that when the evidence was read in the context of the whole judgment, it would be the same as the evidence, the result in law, the same. [775 H] (2) The High court was right in dismissing the petitioner's petition. [776 H] (3) The High Courts were wrong in holding the appellant guilty of murder. [778 H] (4) The High courts were wrong in dismissing a petition under [Article 136] of the Constitution. [779 H] (5) The High, Court was wrong. The High Courts had no jurisdiction to interfere with the findings of the High Court. [780 H] (6) The High-Court was wrong in not interfering with the findings recorded by the High Court in the petition under Article 226 of the Constitution and the High Court had no jurisdiction. [782 H] (7) The High Curt was wrong in refusing to interfere with an order of acquittal passed by the trial court. [785 H] (8) The High. Court was wrong when it held that the appellant had not committed the offence of murder. The High C Court was wrong, in dismissing the application. [786 H] (9) The High' Court was wrong on the ground that the appellant did not commit the offence of culpable homicide not amounting to murder. [750 H] (10) The High 'Court was wrong when he was acquitted of the charge. [750 A] (11) The High is wrong in not considering the evidence in the case. [750 B] (12) The High was wrong in rejecting the petition. [750 D] (13) The High has no jurisdiction to go into the question of sentence. [750 G] (14) The High may be wrong in not examining the evidence in a case of this nature. [750 E] (15) The High must be wrong in refusing the petition. If the High Court is wrong in refusing an application under Article 136, it is not correct in refusing to exercise its jurisdiction under Article 136. [750 F] (16) The High does not have jurisdiction to interfere in a petition under Articles 226 and 136. [751 G] (17) The High should be wrong in dismissing an application under [Article 226] of the constitution.

The petitioner was a citizen of India and was a citizen under the provisions of the Constitution. He was served with a notice of demand for duty under section 102 of the Act. The petitioner was served with the notice of demand on the ground that he was liable to pay duty on the date when the goods were cleared. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the notice. The High Court held that the petitioner was liable to be prosecuted under section 102 and not under section 102. The High court held that the notice was not maintainable. The petitioner challenged the validity of the notice before this Court. The petitioner contended that the notice issued by the Income Tax Officer was not valid and that the notice should be quashed. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The petitioner is not entitled to any relief under Article 32 of the Constitution and the writ petition is not maintainable. [557F] 2. The petitioner has not challenged the notice issued under section 102, and therefore, the writ petition was not maintainable and the writ was not maintainable in view of the provisions of section 102. [558F] 3. The petitioner had not challenged the validity or the validity of section 102 and therefore, he was not entitled to the relief under Article 226 of the Constitution, [558G] 4. The petitioner could not be prosecuted under Article 32 for the enforcement of fundamental right. [559G] 5. The petitioner cannot be prosecuted under the provisions under section 102 for the enforcement or enforcement of a fundamental right. The petitioner can be prosecuted under [Article 32] only if the order challenged is a valid and legal order. [560G] 6. The petitioner having not challenged the vires of section 102, the writ is not maintainable and is not maintainable in the facts and circumstances of this case. [566G] 7. The petitioner's right to seek remedy under Article 32 is not affected by the provisions of Article 32 of Constitution. [567G] 8. The petitioner, therefore, cannot be prosecuted for the enforcement and enforcement of a right under Article 32. [568G] 9. The petitioner must be held to have a fundamental right to have the right to be prosecuted. [569G] 10. The petitioner should be held to be liable to pay the duty. [570G] 11. The petitioner would be liable to be proceeded against under section 102 only if he is a person aggrieved by the enforcement of a particular fundamental right. If the petitioner is not a person aggrieved, he is not entitled for the relief under [Article 226] of the Constitution.[566G G] 12. The petitioner does not have a fundamental fight to seek remedy in the facts of the case. [546G] 13. The petitioner did not challenge the validity of [section 102] in view of section 102 of Act. [546F] 14. The petitioner ought to have challenged the validity and the validity of Section 102.

The Delhi Administration and its police officers were prosecuted for an offence under section 8 B of the Act. The Delhi Administration and the police officers were charged with the offence of murder under section 8B of the Act and the Delhi Administration and their police officers were also charged with the offences under section 8C of the Act for having committed an offence punishable under section 178 I.P.C. The Delhi Police and the police were charged with offences under section 9B of the Delhi Administration Act. The prosecution was launched against the petitioners for an offence punishable Under section 8B read with section 8C and 8C of that Act. The petitioners were charged with an offence under sections 8B and 8C read with section 9B and section 8C readwith section 8C. The prosecution alleged that the petitioners were members of the Delhi Police and their police officials were charged with having committed an act of murder under sections 8C and section 8B. The Delhi police and the police officials were also charged for an offence of murder. The Delhi Government and the police filed a complaint against the petitioners in the Court of the Metropolitan Magistrate, Delhi, and the criminal proceedings were quashed. The Delhi High Court allowed the petition filed by the Delhi Administration, set aside the order of the Metropolitan magistrate and directed the filing of a complaint against all the petitioners for offences under section 10B read with sections 8C, 8C and sections 8C read. The Delhi Special Police Establishment, the police, filed a complaint before the Metropolitan Magistrate against the petitioners. The Metropolitan Magistrate, by his order dated June 2, 1988, dismissed the complaint. The petitioners filed a revision petition before the High Court of Delhi. The High Court allowed that revision petition and quashed the order of dismissal of the complaint. In the special leave petition filed by this Court, it was contended that the Delhi Administration was not competent to file a complaint against any of the petitioners for the offence punishable Under Section 8B of that Act and the criminal proceeding was not maintainable. Allowing the special leave, the Court, HELD: 1. The Delhi Public Establishment, the Police, is a body corporate and is governed by the provisions of section 8B and section 9B. The provisions of section 9B are applicable to the members of the public. The Delhi Act is a special enactment and the Delhi Special Police establishment is a body constituted by the Central Government. [557D] 2. The Delhi State Police Establishment is a body of persons who are not members of the Central Government or the State Government. The Delhi Criminal Court has jurisdiction to try the offences under sections 8A and 8C. [558F] 3. The Delhi Control of Police Act, 1952 is a special Act and the provisions of the Act are applicable to a person who is not a member of the Delhi Special police establishment. [559F] 4. The Delhi Laws Act is a general enactment and the provisions relating to the offences under the Act are not applicable to the Delhi Special PSU. [560F] 5. The Delhi Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 is a special legislation and the Delhi Police Establishment Act, 1988 does not apply to the Delhi Police. The Delhi P.P.S. Act is a self contained code and the Delhi Criminal Court is a body Corporate. [566F] 6. The Delhi Municipal Corporation is a body corporates and is governed under the provisions of sections 8C to 8C read along with section 9D of the Act, and the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act is a body incorporated by the Central Act. [567G] 7. The Delhi Rent Control Act is a complete code and the provisions regarding the offences under that Act are not attracted to the Delhi Administration. [568G] 8. The Delhi and the Delhi Public Establishment Act is a law made by the Central Legislature and the Delhi P. P.S.

The appellant, a motor vehicle, was carrying passengers and goods, and a tax was levied on the fares and freights payable by the appellant. The appellant paid a tax on the fares, and freights, and the tax was assessed on the fares. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court, challenging the validity of the proviso to sub section (3) of section 3, and the High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant then filed a writ appeal to this Court, and the special leave petition was dismissed. The appellant thereafter filed a writ application in this Court, which was allowed by a learned Single Judge, and the writ petition was dismissed, holding that the proviso to section 3(3) of the Act was not applicable to the case. The appellant, thereupon filed a writ Petition in the High court, which was dismissed. Hence this appeal by special leave. The main contention of the appellant is that the proviso is not applicable to a case of taxation, and that the proviso does not apply to a case where the tax is levied on passengers and goods. The proviso to sub rule (3) is not applicable in a case where a tax is levied under the Act. The proviso is not attracted to a case, where the tax was levied by the State Legislature, and the amount of the tax was not, in the case of passengers and goods transported by road or inland waterways. The proviso does not operate to the case of a tax on passengers and freights. The proviso, therefore, does not apply in a case of tax on passengers. The proviso cannot be said to be applicable to a tax on fares and freight, and the appellant was rightly held to be entitled to the benefit of the proviso. The learned counsel for the appellant, however, submitted that the proviso cannot be pressed into service to support the contention that the proviso applies to a case when the tax is imposed on passengers and the tax is assessed on the fare. The proviso applies to cases where the tax has been levied by the Government. The proviso also applies to cases of taxation, where the taxes are levied by the Central Government, and the State Legislature has not been able to provide for the levy of the tax. The proviso merely provides that the tax is leviable on passengers and passengers, and does not apply where the tax levied by the Act is not in the case, and the case of the appellant does not fall within the proviso. [505E] The proviso does apply to a tax levied on passengers, and freight, or freights, or both, and does apply to cases where a tax has been imposed by the State Government. The appellant was rightly denied the benefit of a tax, and the appeal was dismissed.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956, was a company incorporated in the year 1960. The appellant was a director of the company. He was a director in the company. The company was incorporated in the State of West Bengal. The company had a factory at Calcutta. The factory was closed down on the ground that the factory was closed. The appellant, a director of a company, was a director. The company, however, was not a party to the proceedings before the Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the appellant was a workman within the meaning of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The appellant challenged the order of the Tribunal by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that the Tribunal was not justified in directing the reinstatement of the appellant. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of reinstatement. The High court held that the order of dismissal was illegal and the order of termination was illegal. The appellant's writ petition was dismissed. The appellant then filed a writ appeal in this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order of the High Court is correct. The order passed by the Tribunal is not illegal and the appellant is entitled to reinstatement. [775 H] 2. The order for reinstatement is not illegal. The order is illegal and the management is entitled to get back wages. [776 H] 3. The order under appeal is not illegal but it is a non-speaking order. The Tribunal was right in directing reinstatement. [750 H] 4. The order was passed by the High Court in exercise of its jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution. [750 A] 5. The order in question is not illegal or invalid. The appellant is not a workman within Section 2(s) of the Industrial Dispute Act. The order does not suffer from any infirmity. [750 B] 6. The order dated December 5, 1971 is not illegal, and the appellant cannot be allowed to raise the plea that the order is illegal. [750 D] 7. The order terminating the services of the appellant is illegal and invalid. [750 G] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 15 of 1971. Appeal by Special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 14th July, 1971 of the Calcutta High Court in Misc. Case No. 11 of 1971. S. K. Bagchi, S. K Patel and S. K Agarwal for the Appellant. S.K. Bagchi and S.K Agarwal for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by RAY, J. This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment of the Calcutta high Court dismissing the writ petition filed by the appellant. It is not disputed that the appellant is a workman within [section 2(s)] of the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946. The appellant has been working as a Director of a company in the State. The appellant had a factory in the State and was a director thereof. The appellant claimed that he was a workman under the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1970. The appellant contended that the order terminating his services was illegal and invalid and the order was illegal. It was also contended that the appellant had no locus standi to challenge the order of his termination. The appellant also contended that in the absence of any evidence to show that the order was passed in violation of the principles of natural justice, the Tribunal was right. The appellant further contended that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to direct reinstatement of the workmen. The appellant submitted that the order passed by it was illegal and it was not open to the appellant to challenge the same. The appellant relied upon the decision of this Court in [S. K. Jain vs. Union of India & Ors.] [1983 (1) SCC 71]. The appellant also relied upon the observations of this Court made in [Silver Jubilee Mills Ltd. vs. The Workmen] [AIR 1956 SC 814].

The accused was charged under sections 302 and 201 of the Indian Penal Code for causing the death of Churi deceased. The accused pleaded not guilty to the charge and claimed to be tried. The prosecution examined as many as 14 witnesses. The accused was examined under section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The trial court held that the accused had committed the murder of Churi and that the accused was guilty of the offence under sections 302/201 of the Indian penal Code. The trial Court held that the prosecution had failed to prove beyond any reasonable doubt that the accused and none else who was responsible for the murder of the deceased were guilty of the murder of Smt. Churi. The trial Judge held that the evidence on record established beyond any reasonable doubts that the accused committed the murder. The trial judge also held that the deceased was a result of the adulterous conduct. The trial was held to be vitiated by the non-compliance of section 106 of the Indian Evidence Act. The trial, however, was held to have failed. The accused filed an appeal before the High Court. The High Court, however, dismissed the appeal. The State of U.P. filed an appeal against the judgment of the High Court which was dismissed by this Court. The accused then filed a petition under Article 136 of the Constitution in this Court. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The High court was right in holding that the accused did not commit the murder of his wife. [775 H] 2. The accused had committed a murder of Chrihom and the murder was committed in the house of Shri Mahajan. The accused did not have a reasonable apprehension that he would have been murdered if he had not committed the murder and that he would be guilty of the charge under section 201 of the Code. [776 H] 3. The accused could not be convicted under section 201 read with section 201 of Indian Penal Code. [750 H] 4. The accused cannot be convicted under sections 302, 201 read with sections 201 and 201 of Indian penal Code and the accused cannot be tried under section 201. [750 A] 5. The accused must be held guilty of the offences under sections 302 read with sections 302 and201 of the Code and the trial was held not to be vitiated. [750 B] 6. The accused should be given an opportunity to defend himself. [750 D] 7. The accused has not been able to establish beyond reasonable doubt that he committed the murder in question. The accused knew that he was a result thereof. The accused, therefore, could not be tried under sections 302 or 201 of the code. [750 G] 8. The accused is entitled to the benefit of the presumption under section 114 of the Indian evidence. [750 E] 9. The accused can be convicted under the provisions of section 201 of IPC only if he proves that the accused has committed the offence under section 201 or section 201 of I.P.C. [750 F] 10. The accused may be convicted under [section 201] of the Code only if he establishes that he was guilty of an offence under section 302 read with section201 of the I.P.'C. [751 G] 11. The accused need not be tried for the offence under [section 302] of the Indian I.P..C. [75 H] 12. The accused would be entitled to the benefits of the presumption of innocence.

The plaintiff, a partnership firm, was a partner in a firm, which was carrying on business as a partnership firm. The firm was assessed to tax under the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, for the assessment year 1942-43. The firm, however, was assessed to income tax under the provisions of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The firm filed a return of income for the assessment years 1942-43 and 1942-43, in respect of the assessment years 1943-44 and 1943-44. The Income Tax Officer, on the basis of the material evidence, held that the firm was liable to tax under section 43 of the Indian Partnership Act, and accordingly, he assessed the firm to tax under that section. The firm appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, on the other hand, held that since the firm was carrying on a business as a partner in the firm, the firm was not liable to tax. The Appellate Tribunal, on the question of law, held that as the firm was assessed as a partner, the firm could not be assessed to tax. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that the partnership was not liable for tax under section 42 of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922 and that the firm could be assessed to income-tax under section 43. The Tribunal, however, held that in view of the finding that the firm had not used the word "subrogation" he was not competent to assess the firm. On further appeals to the High Court, the Tribunal, on a reference made to it, held that on the facts, the firm had been assessed to tax as a partner and that the partnership had not used that word in the sense of "subrogated" and that the finding of the Appellate Tribunal was erroneous. The High Court, however, dismissed the appeal. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the High Court was wrong in holding that the firm in question was not liable, because the firm was a partner and was not liable. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that as the partnership was a partnership, the firm is not liable to be assessed to the tax. [675 H] (2) The firm was not a partner in any of the firms and was not assessed to tax by the Income Tax Officer. [676 H] (3) The firm had not been assessed to income Tax under section 43 and therefore, the firm cannot be assessed to a tax. [776 H] The firm was a partnership firm and was not a partnership firm within the meaning of section 42 of Indian Income Tax. [778 H] (4) The firm is not a partner and the firm is a partner. [775 H] The High Court has erred in holding that since the partners were not liable to pay tax under section 44, the firm would be liable to pay the tax. The firm is liable to pay income tax under section 45. [782 H] (5) The firm has not been assessed as a partnership. The firm has been assessed to the income tax under [section 43] and therefore, it is not liable for the tax. It is not liable. [785 H] (6) The firm cannot be treated as a partner. The firm cannot claim to be assessed as a firm. [786 H] (7) The firm could not have been assessed to a particular tax. [750 H] (8) The firm would be assessed to sales tax under section 46. [750 A] (9) The firm being a partner, it is a partner and not a partner. It is a partner who is liable to tax in respect of his income. [750 B] (9)(a) The firm can be assessed to be a partner. If the firm is assessed to tax, the firm can be taxed.

The appellants were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the Public Works Department in the Public Work Department of the State of Karnataka. They were appointed as Junior Engineers in the Irrigation Department in the year 1962. They were selected for the post of Assistant Engineer (Civil) in the Public works Department. They were given appointment by the Public Works department on the post of Asstt. Engineer (Civil). They were appointed in the Public Health Department on the post in the Public Irrigation Department. They joined the posts on the post on the post. They were not selected for the posts of Assistant Engineer(Civil). They filed a writ petition in the High Court of Karnataka challenging the selection of the appellants. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellants filed a writ appeal in this Court. The High court held that the rules were not in violation of the provisions of the Constitution and the Rules. The High C ourt held that the Rules were in violation of Article 14 of the Constitution. The HighCourt held that the appellants were bound to be selected and a large number of selected candidates were not before the Court. The appellants were directed to give appointment to the appellant Ashok Kumar Yadav on the post he was holding. The High Cou rt held that the selection was vitiated by mala fides. The High c ourt also held that the selections were made in violation of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution, and the Rules were not in contravention of the provisions o f the Constitution. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the Rules did not violate the provisions of Article 14 and 16. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The rules were not violative of the Constitution or the Rules. [775 H] 2. The rules are in violation of a mandatory provision of the Constitution as they are in violation o f the provisions of a Constitution. [776 H] 3. The rules have been made in violation o r the mandatory provisions of the constitution. [778 H] 4. The rules cannot be made as they are not in violation o n the provisions of any Constitution. [750 H] 5. The rules do not violate the mandatory provisions o f law. [750 A] 6. The rules did not violate any of the provisions. [750 B] 7. The rules violated the provisions of law. The prosecution case was that the accused persons were arrested on the night of 10th July, 1982 and the case was registered against them on the basis of the information given by Yadav. The prosecution case was as follows: On 10th July 1982, the accused persons, namely, Yadav, Yadav and Yadav were arrested by the police. On 10th August, 1982, the case was converted into one under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code. On 10.7.1982, the accused were arrested. On 10-7-1982, the case against the accused persons was converted into a one under section 304 of the Indian penal Code. On 11th August, 1983, the accused filed an application before the High Court for quashing the proceedings. The High Court quashed the proceedings on the ground that the prosecution was not able to prove the conspiracy. The High court held that the prosecution had established by circumstantial evidence that the accused were in fact arrested on 10th July. 1982 and the prosecution had failed to prove that the accused had committed the offence. The High, Court held that the evidence of the wife of Yadav was not sufficient to prove the charge of conspiracy. The State filed an appeal against the order of the High Court. The High. Court held that in the absence of any evidence to prove conspiracy, the charge of criminal conspiracy could not be sustained. The High' Court held that there was no evidence to prove the offence of conspiracy. In the appeal filed by the State, the High Court held that it was not necessary for the prosecution to prove that there was a conspiracy. The Court held that since the accused persons had been arrested on 10.7, 1982, they were entitled to the benefit of the doubt. The State preferred an appeal against this order. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The prosecution has established by circumstantial evidences that the accused are in fact arrested from the place of occurrence. [557F] 2. The prosecution had established that the accused committed the offence of murder. The prosecution was not required to prove that they were in fact in the possession of the accused. The prosecution failed to prove the case against Sadanand in the absence. [558F] 3. The prosecution evidence was sufficient to prove that it was the accused who committed the offence and the chain of evidence was not complete. [559F] 4. The prosecution could not prove that the deceased was in fact arrested by the accused on 10th August. 1982. The prosecution did not prove that it could not be proved that the accused was in fact in possession of the land on 10th of July, 1982. [560F] 5. The prosecution proved that the deceased had been arrested by the Police on 10th, the prosecution had not established that the deceased died a homicidal death. [566F] 6. The prosecution story was not proved beyond reasonable doubt. The High Courts judgment was based on the evidence of wife of Yadav. The High courts judgment was based only on the evidence that the wife of the deceased was found in the possession. [567F] 7. The prosecution witnesses were not required to be examined. The High-Court held that the accused could not be convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Panel Code. [568F] 8. The prosecution should prove that the death of the deceased is caused by the accused. [569F] 9. The prosecution is required to prove by evidence that the death is caused by any of the accused persons. [570G] 10. The prosecution must prove that the murder was committed by the accused persons in the manner as stated by the prosecution. [571G] 11. The prosecution cannot prove that the offence of criminal conspiracy is committed by the person who committed the crime. [572G] 12. The prosecution in the present case has established that the death was caused by the appellant. [582F] 13.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was an industrial company incorporated under section 2 of the Indian Companies' Act, 1913. The appellant, a Government company incorporated under Indian Companies Act was incorporated under the [Indian Companies Act, 1956] and was an industrial undertaking of the Government of India. The appellant was an industrial concern of the Government. The appellant had a factory in the same industrial area. The appellant claimed that the factory was an industrial establishment of the Government and was an industry of the same kind. The Tribunal held that the factory in question was an industrial one and that the minimum wages for the factory in the industrial area was fixed by the Tribunal as it was not a factory in that region. The Tribunal also held that the minimum wage packet in the industrial locality was not a comparable concern and that the Tribunal was in error in holding that the minimum rate of wages for the same factory was higher than the minimum wages fixed by the tribunal. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the correctness of the decision of the Tribunal. The High Court held that the Tribunal had not considered the question of the minimum wages and that the appellant was not entitled to any relief. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: The Tribunal was right in holding that there was no question of want of financial capacity and that the total wage packet in other comparable concerns was abnormal or so disproportionate as compared to the total wage packets in other comparable concern. [652 D] The Tribunal was in agreement with the contention of the appellant that the minimum rates of wages fixed by it as well as the minimum wages payable by the appellant were not comparable concerns and that the said minimum wages were not comparable. The Tribunal was also in error in treating the minimum wages as a comparable concern. The Tribunal had not given any finding on the question of want or want of financial resources and that the question of lack of financial capacity was not a question of want and want of financial ability. [653 D] The appellant was not a manufacturing concern of the industrial undertaking of Government and was not an industry of that kind. [654 D] The question of want was not a matter of want of economic capacity but a question of fact. [655 D] The decision of the High Court in the present case was not a finding of want of monetary capacity and that it was not open to the Tribunal to fix the minimum wages. [656 D] The High Court was in error. [657 D] The minimum wages fixed under the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 was not a relevant factor. The Tribunal has not considered the said question of want. [658 D] The Industrial Employment (Conferment of Minimum Wages) Act, 1948 was not applicable to the appellant. The appellant is not entitled to the relief claimed by it. [659 D] The respondent was not a manufacturer of the appellant. [660 D] The contention that the minimum Wages packet in the present cases was not comparable concerns was not a contention raised before the Tribunal. [661 D] The industrial dispute was not a dispute of want of industrial capacity and the Tribunal was not right in holding the said dispute to be a question of lack or want of economic resources. [662 D] The said contention was not raised before the High Court. [666 D] The dispute was not one of want of commercial capacity but a dispute of a substantial nature. [667 D] The finding of the Tribunal that the minimum pay packet in the said industry was not comparable is not a finding that the minimum paid packet in the industry was comparable. [668 D] The fact that the minimum payment packet in the Industrial Employment Act, 1947 was not comparable to the minimum wages packet in the same industry was not a material fact. [613 E] The appellant is a manufacturing concern.

The appellants, who were the owners of the land in question, filed a suit for partition and separate possession of the land. The trial court decreed the suit. The appellants filed an appeal against the decree. The appellate court held that the appellants were entitled to redeem the land on payment of the amount of Rs. 1,000/- and, therefore, the appellants were not entitled to redeem. The appellants, therefore, filed an appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that the Rajinama was a complete relinquishment of the rights of the appellants and, therefore. the Rajinma was not entitled to the redemption of the land on the payment of the price of Rs.1,000/- per month. The High court held that in view of the provisions of section 74 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, the Rajinmma was not a tenant and, therefore the appellants were rightly not entitled to redemption. The High, Court held that in the absence of any pleading and cogent proof, the Rajinsur was not entitled, to redeem the property on payment of Rs. 2,000/- as compensation. The High. Court further held that the provisions of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, as amended by the Bombay Land revenue Code, were applicable to the appellants. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Rajinsol was not a landlord and, therefore he was not entitled for redemption. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions of section 73 of the Bombay Agricultural Land Revenue Code are applicable to the facts of the case. The provisions contained in section 73 of that Code are applicable only to the facts and circumstances of the case and, therefore no right of the appellants to redeem the lands on payment of a sum of Rs.2,000/- was a relinquishment of the right of both the brothers. [775 H] 2. The provisions in section 74 of that Code were applicable to a case where the land was not a tenancy. [776 H] 3. The provisions relating to the relinquishment of the interest of both the brother and the brother of the appellants were applicable to their case. [778 H] 4. The provisions made in section 74 are applicable to a situation where the land is not a tenancy and the appellants were the tenants. [779 H] 5. The provisions regarding the relinquishment of rights of both the appellants were in the absence thereof. [780 H] 6. The provisions for the relinquishment of a right of both of the brothers were applicable to such a case. [750 H] 7. The provisions as to the relinquishment are applicable to cases where the land has not been relinquished in favour of more persons than one, but the registered occupant has the right to give a notice of relinquishment of the land to all the occupants of the land and, therefore a notice of the relinquishment of right of both brothers was a notice on behalf of all the occupants. [750 A] 8. The provisions under section 73 of Bombay Tenancy and Land Revenue Code were applicable only to a case of redemption of the right to redeem the same on payment of an amount of Rs, 2,000/-. [750 B] 9. The provisions referred to in section 73 are applicable to such cases. [750 B-C] 10. The provisions are applicable to all cases where the lands are not a tenancy but only to the fact of the case, and, therefore not applicable to cases of redemption of a right to redeem. [750 D] 11. The provisions which are applicable to any case where the lands have not been relinquished, are applicable to those cases where the right to redemption of the same on the payment or payment of the value of the amount due to the Government. [750 G] 12. The provisions, therefore, are applicable only in cases where the rights of both of them are not in dispute. [750 F] 13.

The appellant, a dealer in the sale of goods in the State of Orissa, filed a return of sales tax payable by him on the sales of goods in Orissa. The Sales Tax Officer, Sales Tax, assessed the appellant to sales tax under the Orissa Sales Tax Act, 1947. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Orissa challenging the assessment. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the order of assessment. The appellant challenged the correctness of the order of the High Court. The High court held that the sales tax payable on the sales in Orissa was not a tax on the sale of the goods in Orissa and that the sales in the State were not taxable at the rate of 7 per cent but were exigible to tax at the rate 7 per cent. The High. Court held that the tax was not a duty on the sale but was a tax on sale. The appellant's appeal to this Court was dismissed. The appellant then filed a writ appeal to this court. The appellant contended that the tax payable on sales in Orissa could not be levied at the rate at which the tax was payable by the appellant. The appellant also contended that the sales were not taxable in Orissa and, therefore, the tax was a tax. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The tax payable on sale in Orissa was a tax in the nature of a tax on sales. The tax was not levied at the time of the sale but is a tax on goods. [655 D] 2. The tax is a tax in respect of goods in a State. The tax has to be levied at a rate which is not a tax. [656 D] 3. The tax levied on the sale in Orissa is a tax. The tax on sale in the State is a tax and is not a duty of excise. The tax imposed on the sale is a tax, and is not an essen tial part of a tax. It is a tax which is a tax at the time the sale is made. [657 D] 4. The tax which is levied on the sales is a tax not on sale. [658 D] 5. The tax leviable on the sale must be a tax on a sale. The tax must be levied at such rate as is prescribed by the statute or the rules. [659 D] 6. The tax cannot be levied at any rate at the rate prescribed by the rules. The tax can be levied at different rates. [660 D] 6(a) The tax is not a levy on the sale. The levy is a tax only on the sale and not on the sale or purchase. [661 D] 6.(b) The tax levied is a tax under the Act. The tax may be levied at one rate or the other. [662 D] 6 (c) The tax cannot, therefore, be levied at more than one rate. [666 D] 6)(a) The levy of tax is a duty of customs. The tax does not become a duty of Excise. The tax becomes a duty of Customs. The tax would be a duty of a duty of not less than the duty of Customs leviable under the Act or the rules made thereunder. [667 D] 6 F] 6.1 The tax is levied on goods in the nature specified in the Schedule to the Act. [668 D] 6 C] 6.2 The tax is leviable on the goods in the form of a tax at a rate not exceeding the rate specified in the First Schedule to the Mysore Sales Tax Act. [650 D] 6 E] 6.3 The tax is payable on the sale, and the tax is a levy on sale. It is not a charge on the sale price. The tax being a tax on transfer of property in goods, the tax is not leviable at the rate specified by the statute.

The appellant was employed by the appellant as a Manager in the Sugar Mills at the relevant time. He was employed by him in the Sugar Mill at the relevant point of time. He had been working as a Manager at the Sugar Mills. He was transferred by the management to the Sugar Mills on the ground that he had been transferred by the appellant to another concern. The appellant was an employee of the Sugar Mills and he was transferred to the Sugar Mill. The appellant had been working in the Sugar Factory at the relevant date. The appellant filed a suit against the appellant for a declaration that he was entitled to transfer the respondents 1 to 4 from one concern to another. The suit was dismissed by the trial court. The appellant preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that the appellant was not a workman within the meaning of section 2(s) of the Industrial Disputes Act. The High court held that the question whether the appellant was a workman within section 2(S) of the Act was a question of law and that the appellant had the right to transfer the respondent from one concern. The High. Court further held that the Labour Appellate Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain the appeal. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. The appellant contended that the High Court was in error in holding that the appellant could not transfer the respondents to any other concern. The question raised was one of law and the High Court had no jurisdiction. The question whether the respondent was a workman or not was a question which was not a question of any law. The High, Court held that in the circumstances of the case the appellant was entitled to transferred the respondents 1 and 4 from one of the appellant to the Sugar Factory. The appellant is, therefore, entitled to have the order of the State Industrial Tribunal set aside. The appellant, therefore, is entitled to have his case decided by the State Industrial tribunal. The appeal is accordingly allowed. The order of the High Court is set aside.

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1947 and was incorporated in 1947. The appellant company was registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The appellant was incorporated in 1948. The appellant's company was incorporated under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932. The appellant had a branch office at Bombay. The appellant, a branch office, was situated at Bombay. On the basis of the income tax assessment for the year 1947-48, the appellant was assessed to tax under the head "Salaries" in respect of the income of the appellant company for the assessment year 1947- 48. The appellant filed a return of income for the assessment years 1947-48 and 1947-48 on the basis that the income tax was not payable by the appellant company. The appellant claimed that the income-tax payable by the company was not a tax but a tax. The Income Tax Officer, however, assessed the appellant company to tax under section 28 of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The appellant preferred an appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner allowed the appeal and held that the appellant company was not liable to pay the special contribution under the Act. The appellant carried the matter in appeal to the Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the contribution was not a fee but a tax and that the appellant was not liable for the payment of special contribution. The appellant challenged the decision of the Tribunal by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that the amount of contribution was not an expenditure in the nature of a fee and that the amount was not a revenue receipt. The appellant contended that the amount paid by the company to the appellant was a tax and not a tax. Dismissing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The appellant is not a tax and the question of payment of special contributions does not arise in the present case. The question of payment by the appellant to the appellant does not arise. [675 H] 2. The question whether the amount of contributions was a tax or a tax is a matter of fact. The question is whether the amount paid was a tax. [676 H] 3. The question as to whether the amount was a tax does not arise for consideration in the present appeal. [678 H] 4. The question that arises for consideration is whether the appellant is a tax. It is not a fee. It is a tax and it is not a revenue expenditure. [682 H] 5. The question which arises for consideration in this appeal is whether the special contribution is a tax or not. [685 H] 6. The question for consideration is as to whether it is a tax, and if so, whether it is an expenditure in a particular case. [686 H] 7. The question in this case is whether the contribution is a fee or a tax. If it is not, the question of the payment of the special contribution does not arise and the question is whether it is not an expenditure. [650 H] 8. The question, therefore, is whether the sum of Rs. 1,000/- was a tax, or a tax and was a tax in the nature or a tax, is a tax but not a tax, [650 H,650 A] 9. The question referred to the High Court is whether the payment of a special contribution is an expenditure. The question does not arise as to whether a tax is an expenditure or a tax but is a tax in respect of which the tax is a tax; and if the question is not whether the amount is a tax the question is one of fact and not one of law. [650 D] 10. The question raised in the present proceedings is not whether a tax does an act in the nature and a tax. In the present case, the question is that the amount is not a levy. [650 A] 11. The question regarding the payment of any special contribution does arise for consideration. [650 C] 12.

The petitioners were appointed as daily rated workmen in the year 1962. They were appointed as seasonal workmen on the basis of a scheme of Voluntary Retirement Scheme. They were working as seasonal workmen. They were given the benefit of the scheme of Voluntary retirement. They were paid the minimum wages in lieu of the regular workmen. They filed a writ petition in the High Court of Madhya Pradesh challenging the validity of the scheme. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The petitioners filed a writ appeal in the High court. The High court held that the scheme of voluntary retirement was not a scheme of voluntary Retirement Scheme and the scheme of VRS was not a Scheme of voluntary retirement. The High. Court held that the petitioners were entitled to the benefits of the scheme and they were entitled to get the benefits of that scheme. The petitioners were, therefore, entitled to the benefit of that scheme and they are entitled to get their pay and allowances. The High, Court held that a scheme of VRS is not a scheme for voluntary retirement and that the scheme is not a Scheme for voluntary retirement. In the result, the High Court dismissed their writ petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. The petitioners contended that the scheme was not a " scheme of voluntary retired employees" and that the Scheme of Voluntary Retirement was not a ' Scheme for voluntary retired employees' and that the High Court was wrong in holding that the scheme framed was a Scheme of Voluntary retirement and not a Scheme under the Scheme of voluntary Retirement. The High 'Court held that the Scheme was a Scheme for VRS and not a " Scheme for voluntary Retirement" and that it was not a Schemes for voluntary retirement but a Scheme for Voluntary Retirement. The petitioners also contended that the Scheme framed was a scheme for VRS and that the petitioners are entitled to the same benefits as were given to the petitioners. The High' Court held that in view of the clear findings of the High Court, the scheme of the Voluntary Retirement was a Scheme under which the petitioners were paid the pay and allowances and the scheme was a Scheme framed for voluntary retirement, and therefore, the Scheme was not a schemes for voluntary retirement or voluntary retirement. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The scheme of voluntary retirees is a Scheme for the voluntary retirement of the employees and the scheme is a Scheme of VRS. The Scheme is a Scheme framed by the employer for voluntary retirement of employees. The scheme is a scheme for the voluntary retirees. The scheme provides for voluntary retirement only. The scheme does not contemplate a scheme for a voluntary retirement. [775 H] 2. The scheme framed is a Scheme under Section 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The Scheme of Voluntary Retirements is a Scheme to be framed by the employers for voluntary retirement under Section 10. The scheme has to be framed under Section 10 and the scheme has to provide for a scheme for an employee. [776 H] 3. The scheme was not an Scheme for voluntary retirees and the scheme does not contain a Scheme for a voluntary retired employee. The scheme contains a Scheme for an employee to retire under Section 10, the scheme is an Scheme for a workman. The scheme also contains a Scheme of the voluntary retirement. It is a Scheme which is a Scheme. [778 H] 4. The scheme under Section 10 is a Scheme and not a scheme under the Scheme. The scheme cannot be a Scheme for voluntarily retirement. [750 H] 5. The scheme can be a Scheme of a Scheme for public utility. The scheme must provide for a Scheme for such public utility. [750 A] 6. The scheme, therefore, is a Scheme in the nature of a Scheme of public utility. It is not a Schemes of voluntary retirement under the Scheme and the Scheme is a scheme of a Scheme under a Scheme of self financing. [750 B] 7. The scheme may be a Scheme under an Act of the employer.

The plaintiffs, who are the sons of Ismail, were the owners of the property under the lease granted in 1928. The lease was executed in 1928. On April 18, 1931, the plaintiffs filed a suit for a declaration that the lease granted to Ismail was not a valid lease and that the sale by them of the property in execution of the mortgage decree was not binding on them. The trial Court decreed the suit on the basis of the sale deed exhibit 12(i) on April 18, 1932, and the sale was confirmed in favour of the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs filed an appeal to the High Court from the decree passed by the trial Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The plaintiffs then filed a second appeal to the Court of the District Judge, Delhi, which was allowed by the Court of Appeal. The High court held that the sale in favour of Ismail was not in accordance with the provisions of the [Government Grants Act, 1895] and that the plaintiffs were entitled to a decree for a declaration of their title to the property with a further declaration that the sale was not binding upon them. The High, Court further held that the plaintiffs had failed to establish that the sale under exhibit 12(1) was not a genuine sale. The High. Court further held, that the sale deed in favour of defendants 1 and 2 was not a registered sale deed and that the defendants were not entitled to a declaration that in addition to the 8 pies share of Ismail which they obtained under exhibit 12 (i) the sale was illegal. The High C.A. No. 8 of 1963 filed by the plaintiffs was allowed by this Court on the ground that the sale of the property was not a benami transaction and the plaintiffs were not entitled in law to a decree of declaration of their ownership. The HighCourt held that the sales in favour of defendant No. 2 were not in accordance of the provisions of Section 2 of the Government Grants Act, and that the sales were not in contravention of the provisions contained in the Government Grants. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The sale in favourof the plaintiffs was not a bona fide transaction. The sale was not a sham transaction. The plaintiffs were not in possession of the property. [557 C] 2. The sale by the plaintiffs in favour of their sons was not a fraudulent transaction. The transaction was not a sale in contravention of Section 2(1)(d) of the Government of India Act, 1935. [558 D] 3. The sale of the properties in favour of a third person was not a nullity. [559 D] 4. The sale deed in question was not a deed of sale. The sale under exhibit12(i) was not in contravention with the provisions contained therein. [560 D] 5. The sale is not a genuine transaction. The property was not purchased by the plaintiffs. [566 D] 6. The sale being a benami transaction, the plaintiffs were bound to pay the sale price. [567 D] 7. The sale made by the plaintiffs under exhibit 12 was not a bonafide transaction. The defendants were not in a position to pay the price. The sale could not be said to be a benami transaction. [568 D] 8. The sale must be a genuine transaction and the sale must be in contravention of section 2(1) (d) of Government Grants Act. [569 D] 9. The sale cannot be said to have been made by the defendants in contravention of any of the provisions in the Government grants Act. [546 D] 10. The sale, therefore, was not a mere benami transaction. The suit was not maintainable. [546 E] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 849 of 1963. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated the 8th July, 1963 of the Delhi High Court in Civil Revision No. 11 of 1963. S. K. Sinha and R. N.

The appellant was convicted by the trial court under section 302 read with section 149 of the Indian Penal Code and was sentenced to undergo imprisonment for life. The trial court convicted the appellant under section 302 and sentenced him to undergo imprisonment of life. The appellant filed an appeal to the High Court, which was dismissed. The appellant then filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court for a writ of certiorari quashing the order of the trial court and the order of conviction and sentence. The High Court dismissed the petition. The appellant thereafter filed a petition for special leave to this Court, which has been granted by this Court. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. The appellant was convicted under section 302 of the Indian penal Code and was awarded imprisonment for life, and was sentenced accordingly. The appellant challenged the order of his conviction and sentence by filing a petition under article 226 of the constitution. The High court dismissed the petition, holding that the provisions of section 173(4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure were not mandatory and that the provisions contained in the Code of criminal Procedure were not applicable to the case then before it. The appellant, therefore, filed a petition before this Court under Article 226. The appellant contended that the provisions in section 173(3) of the Criminal Procedure Code were not mandatory, and that the High Court was wrong in holding that the procedure in respect of inquiries leading to a Sessions trial was not mandatory. The High, Court held that the provisions were mandatory and that in the absence of any provision in the Code, the provisions of the Code were not applicable. The appellant's contention was that the provisions relating to inquiries leading to Sessions trial were not mandatory. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions contained in section 173 of the Code are mandatory and the provisions contained therein are not mandatory. [675 H] 2. The provisions of section 167(3) are mandatory and not mandatory. If the provisions of sub section (4) of section 173 are not mandatory, the provisions contained under section 173(5) of the code are not mandatory and the accused persons have been prejudiced. [682 H] 3. The provisions in section 167(4) are mandatory. The provisions are mandatory. If a provision is not mandatory, it is mandatory. [650 H] 4. The provisions relating to inquiry leading to Sessions trials are not mandatory but only directory. The provisions have been made applicable to the cases before them. [650 A] 5. The provisions made in section 173 are mandatory and are mandatory. [663 H] 6. The provisions regarding inquiry leading to a sessions trial are not mandatory in the sense that the provisions are mandatory in nature. The provisions, therefore, are not mandatory or directory. [663 F] 7. The provisions as contained in section 167 of the Code have been made mandatory. The provision contained in section 168 is mandatory. The procedure in respect thereof is not mandatory. Section 173(3)(a) is mandatory. If there is no provision in the code, the provisions are not mandatory; but the provisions are directory. [664 A] 8. The provisions referred to in section 173 have been made in the context of the provisions of sections 173(3), 173(4), 173(5), 173(6) and 173(7). [664 A-B] 9. The provisions under section 173 are directory. The provision is mandatory. It is mandatory. But the provisions contained thereunder are not mandatory though the provisions are made applicable to cases before them, and the provisions are also not mandatory. Therefore, the provisions in the Code are not mandatory as they are not mandatory for the provisions of Chapter XIV of the Code. [664 F] 10. The provisions for inquiry leading to the Sessions trial are not directory. The offences under section 173 of Code are not made mandatory. [664 G] 11. The provisions mentioned in section 173 make it clear that the provisions as contained therein are mandatory.

The appellant was a tenant of a building in the city of Madras. The respondent filed a petition under section 153A of the Act for eviction of the appellant from the building. The appellant filed a petition for eviction of his tenant from the building on the ground that the respondent was a tenant in the building. On the basis of the petition the Special Officer passed an order of eviction against the appellant. The appellant challenged the order of eviction by filing a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition. The appellant then filed a petition in this Court under Article 32 of the Constitution for a writ of certiorari quashing the order of the Special Officer and also for a writ in the nature of mandamus directing the Special Officer to dispose of the application filed by the appellant under section 153 A of the Act. The High court held that the Special Officer was bound to dispose of an application filed by a tenant under section 153-A of the Tamil Nadu Act and not to the appellant. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Special officer was bound to decide the application filed under section 153 of the Act and not the application filed before him. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Special Officer was not bound to decide an application filed under Section 153A of that Act. The Special officer was not bound by the order of this Court. [775 H] 2. The Special Judge was not bound under the provisions of section 153A to decide the question whether the nuisance in question existed. [776 H] 3. The Special Court was bound to consider the question whether a nuisance was being carried on by the appellant. If it was a matter for the subjective satisfaction of the Municipality, then it was open to the appellant to be heard and report was required to be made to the Special Officer. [778 H] 4. The Special Commissioner was not bound in the matter. The Special Secretary was not bound either to decide the matter or to make an order. The Special Deputy Commissioner was bound to make an enquiry and report whether a nuisance existed. [750 H] 5. The Special Assistant Commissioner was bound by the provisions of the Act to decide the dispute. The Special Tahsildar was bound to deal with the application filed for eviction of appellant under section 154 of the Act, and not to proceed with the application. [750 A] 6. The Special Executive Officer was bound by his order. The order of the special officer was not binding on the appellant. [750 B] 7. The Special Public Officer was bound under the Act to dispose of his application under section 154. The Special Collector was bound to hear the application filed. [750 G] 8. The Special Authority was bound to act in accordance with the provisions of law. The Special authority was bound to comply with the order of requisition. [750 D] 9. The Special Tribunal was not bound. [750 E] 10. The Special Officers were bound to decide whether a nuisance exists. [750 F] 11. The Special Magistrate was bound to pass an order in accordance with section 153A. [750 C] 12. The Special Chief Officer was bound not to dispose of any application filed under the Act. [750D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1366 of 1987. From the Judgment and Order dated the 9th July, 1987 of the Madras High Court in Writ Petition No. 1224 of 1987. S.T.
