Venugopal, S.C. Jain, K.R. Venugopal, K.S. Venugopal, V.

The appellant was a railway servant. He was prosecuted for an offence under section 3 of the Indian Railway Act, 1890. The appellant was prosecuted for the offence under section 4 of the Indian Railways Act, 1890, for having purchased the property of a railway administration. The trial court held that the articles seized were railway stores within the meaning of section 2 of the Act. The appellant filed an appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that the article seized was railway stores within that meaning and that the articles were not railway stores within section 2 of that Act. The High court held that in view of the provisions of section 2, the articles seized could not be said to be railway stores within Section 2 of the said Act. The State of Orissa filed an appeal against the order of the High Court in this Court. The appellant contended that the articles in question were not railway property within the meaning ofs. 2 of the Indian Act and as such the question of punishment under section 3 did not arise. The High. Court held that in the absence of any averment to the effect that the articles are railway stores within s. 2 of that act, the question of sentence under section 3 could not be sustained. The High, Court held that as the articles were seized from the possession of a railway, the question whether the articles were railway stores or not did not arise and as the articles seized had not been used for the construction, operation or maintenance of a railway. The High' Court held that it was not necessary to prove that the articles which were seized were railway property within section 2. The High 'Court held that the appellant was guilty of the offence under s. 3 of the Act and as the article seized were railway properties within the meaning s. 2. The appellant, therefore, filed an appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions of section 3 of Act are not applicable to the case. The provisions in the Act are not attracted to the case and the question of conviction under section 3 does not arise. [775 H] 2. The provisions contained in section 2 of Act are applicable to the facts of the case before us. [776 H] 3. The provisions relating to the offence of theft and theft of goods are not applicable in the case of theft or theft of goods. The provisions are not applicable. [778 H] 4. The provisions regarding the offence of stolen property are not applicable and as the goods were seized from a person who was not a railway property within Section 2, the question as to whether the articles seized are railway property within s.2 does not arise and the question whether they are railway property or not does not arise in this case. [779 H] 5. The provisions for punishment under section 4 are not applicable when the articles seized form a railway property. The provisions under section 2 are not applicable where the articles seized from the person of a railway servant are railway property. [780 H] 6. The provisions made in the Act do not apply to the facts before us. The provisions as to the offence under the Act are applicable only to the facts and circumstances of the case. [750 H] 7. The provisions referred to in section 2 are applicable to cases where the articles are seized from a railway. [750 A] 8. The provisions mentioned in section 2 do not apply where the articles were found to be railway property within [section 2] of the Act, and as the provisions of the Act are inapplicable to the facts. [750 B] 9. The provisions which are not applicable are not applicable if the articles seized under section 3 are railway property and the provisions of [section 2], therefore, apply to the case before the courts. [750 G] 10. The provisions [in the Act] are not applicable as the provisions are not attracted. [750 D] 11. The provisions, therefore, are not applicable for the offence of railway property.

The appellants were inducted as tenants in the demised premises on the basis of a lease deed dated 30.6.1965. The appellants were inducted in the demised shop on the basis that they were tenants in the said premises. The appellants continued to remain in possession as tenants till the date of the suit as statutory tenants. The appellants filed a suit for eviction against the respondent on the ground of non-payment of rent. The respondent filed a written statement and contended that the appellants were tenants in respect of the suit premises and that they were not tenants in the suit premises. The trial court held that the appellants had become the statutory tenants by virtue of the provisions of the Act and accordingly, the suit was decreed. The appellants preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that the provisions of Section 13(1)(a) of the Act were not applicable to the facts of the case and that the appellants could not be evicted from the suit premises on the ground that the appellants continued to be in possession as statutory tenants and tenancy rights in respect of commercial premises were heritable. The High court held that in view of the provisions contained in Section 13(2) of the Rent Act, the appellants were not entitled to get the protection of the Act. The appellants then filed a second appeal to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court held that in the case of bona fide requirement of the appellants, the protection afforded to the tenant under the Act was not available to the appellants. The Supreme court held that Section 13(3) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 was not applicable to a case of bona fides. The Supreme (1) [1965] 1 S.C.R. 869. Court held that Section13(3) was not applicable in the facts of this case. The appellants thereafter filed a second suit for eviction on the ground under Section 13(4) of the said Act. The High Courts held that the protection afforded by the Act was available to the tenants only in the case where the appellants continued in possession as tenant. The appellants also filed a second application for eviction on that ground. The High courts held that the appellant was not entitled to remain in occupation as statutory tenants in the premises. The High (1) A.I.R. 1965 S.C, 869. (2) [1965) 1 S. C.R. 969. (3) [19651 S.C R. 869, 869, (4) [19652 S.C C.R, 869] referred to above. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The protection afforded to a tenant under the provisions of section 13(1) (a) of Tamil Nadu Buildings Lease and Rent Control Act, 1960 is not available to a tenant who continued to remain as tenant after the termination of the tenancy. [675 H] 2. The protection given to the tenant by the Act is not available in the facts and circumstances of this case and the protection afforded is not available under the Act. [676 H] 3. The protection under the Act is available to the tenant only in the cases where the appellants continue to be in occupation as tenant. [678 H] 4. The protection of the provisions under the Act cannot be extended to the facts and the circumstances of the case. The protection is available to a person who continues to be in the occupation of the premises as tenant. If the appellants continued as tenants after the termination, the protection under the provisions is available to them. [691 H] 5. The protection provided by the Act cannot extend to the facts as stated in the case. [692 H] 6. The protection extended to the tenants under the Act does not extend to the case of the appellants. [693 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 869 of 1987.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956, was incorporated in the year 1956. The company was incorporated under the provisions of the Companies Act. The company had a capital of Rs. 1,50,000. The company paid a sum of Rs. 2,50,00,000 to the Government. The company also paid a sum to the Government on the basis of the capital of the company. The company then applied to the Government for a certificate of the Industrial Tribunal under section 66 of the Electricity Act, 1948. The Tribunal held that the interest on the loans advanced by the company to the Government was a statutory liability and that the interest was not deductible in computing the profits. The Tribunal also held that the interests on the loans were not deductible in the computation of the profits. On appeal by the appellant, the Tribunal held that interest on loans advanced by it to the Government could not be deducted in computing the profit. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that the Tribunal was right in holding that the interest paid to the Government by the company was a statutory obligation and was a definite proportion and it was a definite share capital. The appellant, therefore, filed a writ appeal to this Court. The appellant contended that the interest should be deducted in the computation for the purpose of computing the profits and that the Tribunal should have allowed the interest on loans. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Tribunal was right. The interest on loans was not deductible under the statute. The interest paid to Government by the appellant was a statutory duty and was a specific proportion of the interest paid by the company. [532E] 2. The interest is a statutory liability. The interest must be paid in the manner laid down in the statute. [533F] 3. The interest should be calculated on the basis that the interest is a definite proportion. [534F] 4. The interest payable by the company is a definite share. The interest has to be calculated in the manner provided in the statute and it is a definite percentage. [535G] 5. The interest cannot be deducted in calculating the profits. It is a definite contribution to the depreciation reserve. [536F] 6. The interest was not a definite proportion but a definite proportion of the amount of the interest. The interest could not be calculated in calculating the profit. [537F] 7. The interest can be deducted in computation of the profit. It is not a definite share of the interest which is a definite part. [538F] 8. The interest which is not deductible in computation of profits is a definite amount. The interest may be deducted in arriving at the profits. [539F] 9. The interest does not become deductible in computing profits. The interest will have to be calculated on that basis. [540G] 10. The interest shall be paid in accordance with the provisions of section 64 of the Electricity Supply Act, 1948 and the rules made thereunder. [541G] 11. The interest under the Electricity Supply act, 1948 is a definite and definite proportion. The interest in the case of the company is not a specific proportion. [546G] 12. The interest of the company cannot be deducted. [546F] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1566 of 1967. Appeal by Special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 9th July, 1967 of the Kerala High Court in Writ Appeal No. 8 of 1967. S. T. Desai, S. T.. Desai and S. S. Khanduja, for the appellant. S.T. Desai, R. N. Sachthey and S. P. Nayar, for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Sikri, J. This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment and order of the High Court of Kerala dated September 9, 1967.

The appellant was married to one of the respondents, who was married to the appellant on 5.5.1971. The appellant was married with the respondent on 5.6.1971. After the marriage, the appellant was living with her husband in the house of the respondent. The respondent filed a petition under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for maintenance. The appellant filed a petition for maintenance under section 125, Code of Criminal procedure, praying for maintenance. During the pendency of the petition, the appellant filed an application for maintenance under Section 125, Code, of Criminal Procedure, praying for the maintenance of her husband. The said application was dismissed by the trial court. The appellant preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant then filed a petition to the High court for a direction to the respondent to pay maintenance to the appellant. The High court dismissed the petition. The appellant thereafter filed a petition in the High Court for a direction that the respondent should pay maintenance to her. The High, Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant was not a "person" within the meaning of the aforesaid provision. The appellant, therefore, filed a petition before the High Court under Article 227 of the Constitution. The High. Court dismissed the writ petition. The respondent then filed a writ petition in the Delhi High Court. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts in India have consistently taken the view that the provisions of the Code are not applicable to the case. [775 H] 2. The provisions of the [Code of Criminal Procedure] are applicable to the cases under the Code of 1973. The provisions contained in the Code of 1898 are applicable to cases under the said Code. [776 H] 3. The provisions in the Code are applicable to all cases under the [Code] of Criminal Procedure. The provisions relating to the maintenance of the wife and the husband, therefore, are applicable to such cases. [778 H] 4. The provisions regarding maintenance of wife and husband, therefore. are applicable to a case under the said section. [779 H] 5. The provisions made in the Code relating to the custody of the wife, the husband, are applicable only to cases under section 125. [780 H] 6. The provisions for maintenance of wife, therefore, apply to cases under sections 125 and 125. [750 H] 7. The provisions under the Code are in addition to and not in derogation of the provisions of any other law. [750 A] 8. The provisions as contained in the [Code], are applicable to proceedings under the said Act. The provisions are applicable to those proceedings. [750 B] 9. The provisions referred to in the said section are applicable to pending proceedings under the Code. [750 D] 10. The provisions, contained in the said sections, are applicable in the case of a case under section 125 and section 125. The provisions therein are applicable to an application filed under section 125 to the proceedings under the Act. [750 G] 11. The provisions to the effect that the provisions contained in section 125 are applicable to any case under the Code, are applicable not only to cases where the husband is a "person", but also to cases where a husband is a 'person' within the meaning ofs. 125. [751 H] 12. The provisions with regard to the maintenance and the provisions of section 125 are not applicable in the cases under section 126. [751 G] 13. The provisions mentioned in the said sub section are applicable only in cases under the provisions of sections 125 and 126. [750 F] 14. The provisions which are applicable to matrimonial proceedings under the provisions contained therein are applicable only when the husband is living with the wife. [751 A] 15. The provisions that are applicable to divorce proceedings under the Indian Divorce Act, 1869, are applicable. [751 B] 15.

The plaintiff filed a suit for the eviction of the defendant from the land in question on the ground that the defendant was in possession of the land as a tenant. The trial court held that the defendant had not proved that he was in possession as a tenant and that the plaintiff was in possession. The trial Court held that the plaintiff had not proved his possession as a licensee and that the defendant could not be evicted from the land. The trial Judge held that the suit was not maintainable and that the suit filed by the plaintiff was not maintainable. The defendant filed an appeal against the judgment and decree of the trial court. The appellate court held that as the plaintiff had failed to prove his possession as tenant, the suit was maintainable. The plaintiff filed an appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that as a tenant the plaintiff was entitled to the protection of the Rent Control Act. The High court held that in view of the provisions of the Rent Act the plaintiff was a licensee and the suit was liable to be dismissed. The plaintiff has filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The plaintiff was in occupation of the land in dispute as a tenant as a tenant under the State Government. The plaintiff had not pleaded that he was a licensee. The plaintiff could not be said to be in possession as tenant. [652 D] 2. The plaintiff having failed to prove that he was not in possession as an licensee, the suit filed was not maintainable in the eye of law. [653 D] 3. The plaintiff is not a licensee. He is not a tenant. He is a licensee. [654 D] 4. The plaintiff cannot be said to have proved his possession. The plaintiff must prove his possession. [655 D] 5. The plaintiff in the suit filed for the Parade Ground and the land in Rasala Lines is not shown to be that of the Municipality. The plaintiff did not claim that he was the licensee. The suit was not filed by the Municipality. [656 D] 6. The plaintiff being in possession as licensee, the plaintiff was bound to pay the Revenue from the date of the suit till the date of filing of the suit. [657 D] 7. The plaintiff, having failed to establish his possession as licensee cannot be said that he was entitled to possession. [613 D] 8. The plaintiff can be said to hold the land as licensee only on the basis that the plaintiff is in possession as the licensee. [613 E] 9. The plaintiff does not claim that the defendant is in possession. [625 G] 10. The plaintiff's possession as a lessee is not a licence. The plaintiff continues to be in the possession as a trespasser. [658 D] 11. The plaintiff who is in possession of land as a licensee cannot be evicted from it. [659 D] 12. The plaintiff should prove his possession in the suit. The plaintiff need not prove his possession on the basis of the title to the land. [660 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 864 of 1987. Khanduja and S.K Srivastava for the Appellant. S.K Jain, S.M. Jain, S K Jain and S.N Sharma for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by K.J. Shah, J. This appeal by special Leave is directed against the judgment of the Bombay, High Court, dated 10th May 1952, in Second Appeal, No. 11/1952, whereby the High Court has dismissed the appeal filed by the appellant.

The appellant was a public servant within the meaning of section 21 of the Indian Penal Code. He was prosecuted for an offence under section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The appellant was convicted by the Special Judge, Delhi, for an offence punishable under section 5 of the Prevention Of Corruption Act, and sentenced to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000. The appellant filed an appeal to the High Court of Bombay. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant then filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution in this Court. The appellant contended that the High Court was wrong in holding that the appellant was an officer of the Government and was not a public servant. The appellant also contended that the order of the High Court setting aside the order of conviction was illegal and that the High court was wrong in quashing the order of sentence. The appellant further contended that the appellant had been convicted by the trial Court under section 5 (1) (d) of Act II of 1947 and was, therefore, not a public officer within the meaning ofs. 21 of the Act. The High court rejected the contention. The appellant, therefore, filed a petition in this Court under Article 226. The appellant urged that the High Courts of Bombay and Bombay had erred in holding that a public servant was not an officer of Government and was, in fact, a public servant and was therefore, not 'an officer ' of the Government. The appellant submitted that the High courts of Bombay and the Bombay High Court had erred in quashing the conviction of the appellant. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts of Punjab and Haryana and the Gujarat High Court had rightly held that the appellant is an officer of a Government and was a public officer. [652 D] 2. The appellant had been rightly convicted under section 5 and was, accordingly, not a 'public servant' within the meaning Of section 21 of Indian Penal Code and was, consequently, not a person 'an officer' within the definition of section 21. [653 D] 3. The appellant could not be said to be an officer 'an officer of the government' within the ambit of section 21, Indian Penal Code because he was not an 'officer' within the purview of section 21 and was, thus, not a "public servant" within the meaning o section 21. The appellant's case was rightly rejected by the High Court. [654 D] 4. The appellant is an 'officer'. [654 E] 5. The appellant has been rightly convicted by the High Courts. [655 G] 6. The appellant cannot be said to have been an officer 'a public servant' within section 21 of Act II, Indian Penal code. [656 H] 7. The appellant having been convicted under section5(1)(a) of Act I of 1947, he was not a ' public servant' as defined in section 21 of that Act. [657 H] 8. The appellant did not hold any office of profit under the Government. [658 H] 9. The appellant being an officer of government, he was, therefore not a public authority within the meaning s. 21 of Act I, Indian Penal. [659 H] 10. The appellant must be held to be an 'officer ' within the meaning ins. 21 of Indian Evidence Act. [650 H] 11. The appellant would be an officer of an officer 'in the service or pay of the Government' within the scope of section 21 or section 21 of this Act. [643 H] 12. The appellant should be held to have been a public servant as defined in s. 21. [643 D] JUDGMENT: CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Criminal Appeal No. 11 of 1972. Appeal by Special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 14th July, 1972 of the Bombay High court in Criminal Appeal No, 11 of 1972 and Criminal Appeal No..

The Respondent was a tenant of a shop in the premises in dispute. He was a tenant in the premises. He was assessed to the rent of the said shop by the Rent Controller, Patiala, on the ground that the Respondent was a defaulter in payment of rent for the period from 1.4.1941 to 31.3.1941. The Respondent filed a suit for eviction of the Respondent from the said shop on the ground of nonpayment of rent for a period of more than six months. The Respondent contested the suit. The Rent Controller decreed the suit on the ground, inter alia, that the Respondent had failed to pay the rent for the said period and that the Respondent is liable to pay the same. The Respondent then filed a suit in the Court of the District Judge, Patiala, for a declaration that the Respondent has been in arrears of rent for more than six years and that the Appellant was liable to pay rent for the aforesaid period. The Respondent also prayed for a decree for eviction. The Respondent resisted the suit. He pleaded that the Respondent being a defaulter in paying the rent for a continuous period of more and that the notice of demand was not served on him. The Trial Court decreed the suit. On an appeal by the Respondent, the District Judge reversed the decree and decreed the suit in favour of the Respondent. The Respondent thereafter filed a second appeal before the High Court. The High Court allowed the second appeal and set aside the decree passed by the Trial Court. The Respondent preferred a second appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The Respondent was a statutory tenant in the suit premises. The Respondent had not paid the rent for six months. He was liable to be evicted from the said premises. [557D] 2. The Respondent is a defaulter in the payment of rent. The Respondent has not paid the arrears of rent. [558F] 3. The Respondent being a statutory tenant, he was liable to make payment of rent in accordance with the provisions of the said Act. [559F] 4. The Respondent having failed to pay rent within the period of six months, the suit was rightly decreed. [560F] 5. The Respondent could not be evicted from his shop on the grounds of nonpayment or nonpayment of the rent for more and that he was liable for eviction. [566F] 6. The Respondent, having failed to make payment for six months, was liable to deposit the rent for three months. [567F] 7. The Respondent cannot be said to be a defaulter in depositing the rent for two months. The Appellant was liable for payment of rent only for six months and not for six months as contended by the Respondent. [568F] 8. The Respondent did not pay the rent within the stipulated period of six month. The Respondent paid the rent in accordance therewith. [569F] 9. The Respondent continued to pay the arrears of the rent in arrears for six months only. The Respondent failed to pay arrears of rent within the specified period. [570F] 10. The Respondent's contention that the Respondent did not make payment for the period of more, was not correct. The Respondent himself was a defaulter. The Respondent defaulted in payment of the rent. [500F] 11. The Respondent must be held to be a tenant in arrears of the amount of rent for six month. [571F] 12. The Respondent should be held to have been in arrears for more than three months. The High court was wrong in holding that the Respondent should be deemed to be a defaulting tenant. [572F] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 2944 of 1980. From the Judgment and Order dated the 9th July, 1980 of the Punjab and Haryana High Court in Civil Revision No. 2945 of 1980. S.K. Jain, S.K Jain and R.K.

The respondent filed a return of his income assessed on the basis of the valuation made by the Special Deputy Collector. The respondent claimed that the value of the lands acquired by him was Rs. 1,000/- per acre and that the value was fixed by the Special Assistant Collector as the value of his lands at Rs. 1.000/- per cent. The respondent also claimed that the valuation of the lands was Rs. 2,000/-per cent. The Special Deputy Collector, however, rejected the claim of the respondent and held that the value fixed by the special Deputy Collector was not correct. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Special Deputy Commissioner. The High Court held that the valuation made in the year 1972 was not correct and that the valuation was not correct in view of the enhanced compensation awarded by the Special Collector. The High court held that the Special Deputy collector was not justified in rejecting the claim of compensation on the basis that the valuation for the lands was not correct as the value was determined by the Special officer as the value fixed for the lands on the date of the death of the deceased. The High. Court further held that the respondent was entitled to the benefit of the enhanced amount of compensation as he had not acquired the lands in the year of the death. The High, Court held that in the absence of any evidence to the contrary, the value of lands was not a mistake apparent from the record and, therefore, the respondent was not entitled to the enhanced amount. The respondent then filed a writ appeal in the High court. The High' Court held that when the value of land was fixed by a special Deputy Collector as the proper valuation he was bound to adopt that evaluation as his own estimate of the value of such lands. The High 'Court held that the assessment made by the special officer was not correct, and, therefore. the enhanced compensation was not a case of change of opinion on his part as regards the correct valuation of the land. The High Curt also held that the claim of enhanced compensation was a case of a change of opinion as regards the value of a land which was not a change of the opinion. The High-Court further held that in view of Section 59 of the Act, the respondent had no objection to the enhanced compensation fixed by the Civil Court. The High: Court held that since the respondent had accepted the value of her lands as determined by the special authority, the respondent is not entitled to any enhanced amount of the compensation. The High 2. The respondent, therefore, filed a writ application in the High' Court challenging the validity of the order of assessment. The High |Court held that in a case of this nature, the respondent could not be said to have adopted the valuation made for the lands which he wanted to enhance by relying upon the valuation made on the basis thereof. The HighCourt held that since in the absence thereof, the respondent would be entitled to the benefits of enhanced compensation as he was not entitled thereto, the respondent cannot be said to be entitled to any enhancement of the value. The respondent thereupon filed a writ. The High,.Court held that as the respondent had not acquired any land in the year 1971, the enhanced compensation should be deemed to have been fixed by the civil court. The respondent thereafter filed a writ in the High. Court challenging the correctness of the order passed by the Special Officer. The High T.A.D. Court held that as in the absenceof any evidence to that effect, the respondent's claim for enhanced compensation was rightly rejected. The Hight Court held that there was no evidence to the effect that the respondent had acquired the land in the years 1971 and 1971. The High R.A. D. Court held, that the respondent's case was not covered by the provisions of Section 59(b) of the Act. The High L.A. Appeal was, therefore, dismissed. The respondent's writ petition in this Court was also dismissed.

The appellant was a member of the Bombay Cooperative Bank Ltd. and was elected as a Director of the Bank. The appellant was elected as Director of the said Bank. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court of Bombay challenging the validity of the notice of the Deputy Registrar dated 21.10.1986. The High Court held that the appellant was a defaulter and his seat was deemed to be vacant. The High court held that the disqualification on the ground of default was not a disqualification under section 78(1) of the Act and that the disqualification was not a result of any default. The High, Court held that section 78(2) of the said Act was not attracted and the disqualification on account of default was a disqualification under the Act. The appellant filed a writ appeal against the judgment of the High Court. The High. Court held that there was no default in the payment of any instalment of the loan and section 78(3) was not attracted. The High' Court held that in the absence of any default in the repayment of any instalment, the disqualification on that ground was not a bar to the election of the appellant. The appellant's appeal was dismissed. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1.1 The disqualification on account (a) of the appellant was not a default in the payments of any instalment or loan granted to him; (b) the disqualification on this ground was not an offence under section 78 of the Act. [501 G] 1.2 The disqualification on the basis of default in the repay of any instalment was not a defect in the election of a Director. The disqualification on that account was not a condition precedent to the election. [502 G] 1:3. The disqualification under section78(1) was not a mere irregularity in the payment or default of any instalment. [503 G] 1.:3. The appellant having ceased to be a defaulter, his seat was vacant. The disqualification was a disqualification for being a member of a committee. [504 G] 1.(a) The disqualification on this account was not an act of a defaulter but a defect in his election. [506 G] 1.] 1.4. The disqualification of the appellant on account of his default in the making of any instalment in the payment, of any instalment thereof, was not a nullity. [505 G] 1.'b] The disqualification on a ground of default in payment of any instalments of any instalment is not a disqualification. [506 G] 1.[507 G] 1] 1.5. The disqualification is not a mere defect in the payment. [507 G B] 1.6. The disqualification for being elected as a director is not a defect of a nature which is not a condition of the election. The disqualification has to be a defect in a vacancy in the office of the Director. [508 G] 1\4. The appellant had ceased to be an officer of the Bank and his seat became vacant. [509 G] 1'B] 1.7. The disqualification as a result of the disqualification on a finding that the appellant had committed default in the performance of any of the obligations under the contract of the Bank, was a defect in service. [510 G] 1[510 G B] 2.1. The disqualification in the present case was not a continuing offence. [511 G] 1I] 1.8. The disqualification could not be a disqualification for a period of more than six months. [512 G] 2.2. The disqualification, therefore, was not an individual act of a person who was a defaulter. [514 G] 2:1. The appellant could not be disqualified for being a director of the Bank on the ground that he had committed default. [515 G] 2] 2.3.

The respondent was appointed as a Sugar Inspector in the State of Maharashtra. He was promoted as a Sugar Supervisor in the year 1962. He was served with a charge sheet dated October 16, 1962, and he was served with the order of punishment of reduction of pension by 50 per cent. The respondent was served with an order of punishment on October 16, 1963. The respondent challenged the order of reduction of his pension by the State Government by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court quashed the order of the State Government and directed the State Government to reconsider the question of reduction of the pension of the respondent. The State Government preferred an appeal to this Court. The Court held that the order of reducing the pension was not in accordance with the Rules and the State Government was not competent to reduce the pension. The Court further held that the State Government had no authority to initiate any proceedings against the respondent for reduction of pension. The High court held that the respondent was entitled to the benefit of the order of penalty of reduction of 50 per cent of his pension. The State of Maharashtra preferred an appeal against the order of this Court. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The order of reduction passed by the State of Bombay was not in conformity with the Rules. [775 H] 2. The order passed by the Collector of Kolhapur was not in consonance with the Rules but was in accordance with Rules 188 and 189 of the Rules. The order was passed by the Government in exercise of the powers conferred by Rule 189 of the rules. The order dated October 16. 1982 was passed by a competent authority. The order did not suffer from any infirmity. [776 H] 3. The order reducing the pension by 50% was passed by an authority competent to do so. The order is not in accordance to the Rules. Rule 189 of Chapter IX of the Rules provides that the order passed by a Government servant shall be in accordance with Rule 188. The order has to be passed by the competent authority. [778 H] 4. The order imposing the penalty of reduction in pension by 50 percent was passed by exercising the powers conferred on the State Government under Rule 189 of Rules 188 and 190 of the Rules and was in accordance to Rules 188 and 188 of the Rules.[778 H; 780 A] 5. The order enhancing the pension was passed by way of punishment and the order was passed in accordance with law. [780 H] 6. The order in question was passed by virtue of the powers vested in the State Government. The order does not suffer from the vice of any infirmity. The order being in accordance with rules 188 and 189, the order of imposition of penalty of removal from service was not in contravention of the Rules but is in accordance with provisions of Rule 188 of the rules.[778 G] 7. The order having been passed by the authority competent to impose the penalty of removal of the respondent was not in the prescribed form, the order was not in violation of the Rules, and the order of compulsory retirement was not in compliance with the provisions of Rule 189 of Part IX of the rules, [778 G-H] 8. The order under appeal was not in terms of the Rules; the order was in accordance of the Rules [778 A] 9. [779 H] 10. The order for reduction of the petitioner's pension was passed in exercise of powers conferred by the Rules. It was not in breach of the Rules or the order was contrary to the Rules.[878 G] 11. The order cannot be sustained in law. [878 G- H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1342 of 1987. From the Judgment and Order dated the 9th July, 1987 of the Bombay High Court in Writ Petition No. 8 of 1987. S.V. Gupte, S.K. Mehta, R.K. Jain, R.N.

The appellant was a tenant of a shop in the premises in dispute. The respondent filed a suit for eviction of the appellant from the shop in dispute on the ground that the appellant was a landlord and that the respondent was a tenant. The appellant filed a suit against the respondent for eviction on the ground of non-payment of rent. The respondent contended that the appellant had not complied with the mandatory provisions of the Act and that the order passed by the District Magistrate was without notice to the respondent and was, therefore, illegal. The trial court held that the appellant could not move the Commissioner under section 3 (3) of the Act for permission to bring a suit against him. The appellant was directed to file a suit for possession against the respondent. The appellant preferred an appeal to the District Court. The District Court held that the provisions of the [Act and the Rules were not applicable to the case and that the provisions contained in the Act were not applicable. The District Judge, however, held that the order of the District Magistrate granting permission to the appellant to bring a civil suit against the appellant was illegal and as such, a nullity. The District court, however, allowed the appeal and set aside the order passed in the suit. The appellant then filed a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that in the absence of a notice to the appellant, the order passed under section 3(3) was not valid. The appellant, therefore, filed a writ appeal in this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High court was in error in holding that the provisions in the Act and the Rules are not applicable to cases where the procedure prescribed by the Act and Rules were not in force. [775 H] 2. The provisions contained in section 3 (4) of the General Clauses Act, 1897, are not applicable in the case of orders passed under the Act. The provisions of the General clauses Act are not applicable. [776 H] 3. The provisions in the General Clauses Acts are not applicable as they are not applicable for the purpose of determining the scope of the provisions of any of the provisions. [778 H] 4. The provisions made in the Act are not in the nature of a procedural provision. The provisions are not applicable when the procedure prescribed in the Act or the Rules is not in force or is not in existence. [779 H] 5. The provisions relating to the jurisdiction of the Commissioner under the Act are applicable to the cases where the irregularity or illegality bad been committed by the District Officer in granting or refusing to grant permission to the petitioner to bring a Civil suit against the petitioner. [780 H] 6. The provisions as contained in the General clauses Acts are not in any way applicable to the facts of the case. The provisions regarding the jurisdiction of a Commissioner under the General clauses are not applicable and the provisions contained therein are not applicable, as they are in the nature not applicable to a case where the procedure is not in the Act. [782 H] 7. The provisions referred to in the Act have to be read in the context of the provisions contained under the Act and rules. [785 H] 8. The provisions under the Act have not been made applicable to cases of serious illegality in granting permission to bring civil suit against a tenant. [786 H] 9. The provisions for the jurisdiction of an Commissioner under the provisions of a special Act are not attracted. The provisions have to be construed in the light of the provisions in that behalf. [787 H] 10. The provisions, as contained in section 4 of the Act, are not in force for the purpose for which they are not in existence and are not applicable if they are in force. The provisions contain a provision for the jurisdiction and the procedure to be followed in the case. [790 H] 11.

The respondent filed a complaint under section 7 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, against the appellant, alleging that he was a member of the Punjab Public Service Commission and that he was falsely implicated into the charge of assault on the respondent. The trial was held by the learned Judge of the High Court. The appellant was convicted by the trial Court and sentenced to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000/- and in default to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one month. The respondent filed an appeal before the High Court and the High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant filed a revision petition before this Court. The High Court dismissed his appeal. The respondent then filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the High court. The High court dismissed the writ petition. The respondent thereafter filed a writ appeal before this Court which was allowed by a learned Single Judge of the Punjab and Haryana High Court by his judgment and order dated April 14, 1983. The High, Court held that the respondent was guilty of misconduct and accordingly, sentenced him to pay a sum of Rs. 2,000/- as fine. The respondent challenged the order of conviction and sentence by filing a writ petition before this court. The learned Single Judge dismissed the writ appeal. The High. Court held that there was no evidence to prove the charges against the respondent and that the charge of misbehaviour was not proved. The High' Court held that it was not open to the respondent to prove the charge of misconduct. The High 'Court further held that the evidence of the witnesses who were examined by the respondent was not sufficient to prove the guilt of the respondent. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in holding that the respondent had been falsely implicated into a charge of assault. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts have given concurrent findings of fact that the respondent is guilty of misconduct. [775 H] 2. The High-Court has not given any finding on the question of charge of misbehaviour. The High Curt has not given a finding on the said question. [776 H] 3. The HighCourt has not recorded any finding on any of the issues which the parties have led before it. The High -Court has not considered the evidence on the record and has not given its finding on the same. [778 H] 4. The High T.A.C. has not given the finding on the charge of misbehavior. [779 H] 5. The High Couit Court has not given an finding on the other issues which the respondent has not led before it and the High court has not given finding on the remaining issues. [780 H] 6. The High courts have given concurrent finding of fact that there was a breach of the conditions of the service of the respondent and the High Curt was not justified in interfering with the order of sentence. [782 H] 7. The High F.A.R. has not been given any finding. The High A Court has not recorded a finding on any issue which the parties had led before it, that the respondent has been guilty of misconduct or that he has been guilty by the appellant. [786 H] 8. The High [Court] has not given findings on the other points which the respondent had not led before the High court and the High [Court has not assigned any finding on those points. [787 H] 9. The High LC has not given reasons for the finding of the learned Judge. [790 H] 10. The High R.C.A. has not recorded findings on any of issues which the appellant has not led. [791 H] 11. The High H.C.R. is not a Court of competent jurisdiction. [792 H] 12. The High COurt has not recorded finding on any issues which the Court has not considered.

The temple was dedicated to the public for the worship of a family idol. The temple was installed in the temple. The members of the public were allowed to worship in the temple and the temple was installed by the members of the family. The members were entitled to worship at the temple. In the year 1962, the temple was constructed by the members and the members of that family were given a share in the income of the temple. On the death of the members of a family, the temple became a public temple. The temple is a private one. The members and the family were entitled to the benefit of the temple and they were entitled to be given the benefit of worship at the Temple. The temple, therefore, became a public one. The temple became a private one and the members and members of the community were allowed to perform the worship of the temple by members of the private parties. The temple being a private one, the members of it were entitled to take over the management. The temple also became a public endowment. The members belonging to the public were entitled to have the management of the temple, but they chose not to do so. The High Court, therefore, held that the endowment was of a private nature and the temple being a public one, the provisions of the Act were not applicable. The High court held that the provisions of Section 15 of the Act did not apply to the temple and that the temple was a private one as defined in the Act. The High, Court held that the temple being an ancient one, the public were not entitled to worship in a temple. The High. Court also held that the members of public were entitled, as of right, to worship at any of the religious places. The High 'Court held that the property was not a public one and that the provisions in Section 15 of Act were not attracted. The High' Court held that in the absence of any provision in the Act, the provisions in the Act were applicable to the temple. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts were right in holding that the provisions contained in Section 15 were not applicable to the temples. [535 H] 2. The provisions of Section 16 of the Act are not applicable to a temple. Section 16 of Act is not applicable to temples. The provisions in the statute are applicable to the institutions. [536 H] 3. The provisions contained in the Act are applicable to a private temple. The provisions are applicable to an institution. The provisions relating to the management of a temple are applicable to such institutions. [506 H] 4. The provisions made in Section 15 are not applicable in a private temple and the provisions in Sections 15 and 16 of the act are not applicable. [537 H] 5. The provisions regarding the management of an institution are applicable to private temples. The members or the members of such private temples are entitled to take the management. [538 H] 6. The provisions as contained in Section 16 of act are not attracted to a private temples. [506 G] 7. The provisions under Section 15 are applicable to temples and not to private temples and the provisions of Sections 15 and 17 are not applicable for the temple. [539 H] 8. The provisions for the management of private temples are applicable to institutions. The provisions that are applicable to religious places are not applicable when the provisions are not applicable and the provisions are applicable. [506 A] 9. The provisions referred to in Section 15 have to be read in the context of Section 15 and Section 17 of the Act. [540 H] 10. The provisions have to be applied to the institutions and not to the private temples. Section 15 is not applicable. Section 15 does not apply to a private institution. [541 H] 11. The provisions which are applicable to public temples are not applicable where the provisions are made applicable to private institutions. [504 H] 12.

The appellant was a member of the Indian Air Force. He was appointed as a member of a civil service of the Union of India. He was promoted as a member in the Indian Air force. He was given a pension of Rs. 500 per month. He was paid a pension of a sum of Rs. 200 per month. The appellant was paid a sum of rupees 500 per month on November 1, 1952. He was also paid a sum equivalent to the pension of Rs, 200 per month on December 1, 1952, and was paid a further sum of rupees 200 per month by way of pension. The appellant filed a suit in the court of the 1st Additional District Judge, Jabalpur, for a declaration that the order dated July 19, 1948 was a valid order and was not a valid order. The suit was decreed by the trial court. The appellant preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that the order of the 1 st Additional District Judge was a valid one and was not an order of assignment. The High court further held that the appellant was not a party to the pending appeal and that the order was not a nullity. The High. Court further held that there was no transfer of the decree, or of the claim which was the subject matter of the pending appeal as the borrower was the owner and the lender was only authorised to act as his agent. The High, Court further held, that the order passed by the 1st Addl. District Judge was not a decree within the meaning of s. 2(1)(c) of the Code of Civil Procedure. The High Courl also held that the decree passed by the trial Court was not a judgment within the meaning ofs. 2(2) of the CPC. The High' Court further held in the case that the order in the suit was not a "judgment" within the meaning s. 2 (1)(c). The High Court further held the order was a nullity. In the result, the High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court HELD: 1. The order of the High Court is not a decree. The order passed by it is a decree. [557 G] 2. The order was not an interlocutory order. The order is a decree passed by a competent court. The order does not create an assignment of the money or a right in the fund. The order has to be a decree within. the meaning of the expression "judgment" in s. 2. [558 G] 3. The order dated July 20, 1948 was not an "order" within the contemplation of s.2. The order did not create an assignable assignment of the funds. The order clearly shows that the order is a "decree". [558 H] 4. The order in the present case was not an 'order' within the meaning o[s. 2(i)(c) and was not one of the orders of assignment. [559 H] 5. The order under appeal was not an award. The order could not be executed. The order became an order of the court. [560 H] 6. The order made by the 1 st Addl. District Magistrate was not an appealable order. The High Courts order was not one passed by the District Judge. [566 H] 7. The order cannot be executed. [567 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1320 of 1966. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated the 14th July, 1966 of the Allahabad High Court in Civil Misc. Writ No. 1123 of 1965. S. K. Sinha and R. H. Dhebar, for the appellant. S. P. Sinha and S. K Srivastava, for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Hegde, J.

The appellant was a member of the Indian Income tax Appellate Tribunal, Madras, who was a member in the Indian Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, Bangalore. The appellant was assessed to income tax under the Income tax Act, 1961, on the income of Rs. 27,948/ by the Income tax Officer, on the ground that the income of the assessee was exempt from tax under section 17(3) (ii). The Income tax Officer rejected the claim of the assessee that the income was exempt from income tax under section 16(3) of the Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, allowed the claim of exemption and held that the income from house property was exempt from the tax under section 15(3) and section 17(1)(iv). The appellant filed an appeal to the Income tax Appellate Appellate Tribunal, which was allowed by the Tribunal. The appellant then filed a writ petition in the High Court of Madras. The High Court held that the Income tax officer was not justified in rejecting the claim of deduction of the income from the house property. The appellant filed a writ appeal to this Court. The appellant contended that the income in question was exempt from payment of tax under section 10(1) (iv) of the Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1962, and that the income tax officer was justified in rejecting that claim. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High court was right in holding that the income-tax officer was justified on the ground of exemption from tax under the Act. [675 B] 2. The income tax officer is not justified in refusing to accept the claim of benefit of exemption under section 17 (3) (i) of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922. [682 C] 3. The income-tax authority was justified in refusing the claim of relief under section 10 (1) (iii) of the 1922 Act. [650 D] 4. The income in question is exempt from tax. The income is exempt from income-tax under section 15 of the Act and section 17 (1) is not a condition precedent to the exercise of the power under section 17. [650 E] 5. The income of the appellant is exempt from the income tax under sections 15 and 17. [685 F] 6. The income from house properties is exempt from payment to income tax. The Income tax officer is justified in refusing relief under section 17 of the Act on the ground, that the income is exempt under section 15. [686 G] 7. The income under the head "Profits in lieu of salary" is exempt from liability under section 15 and section 17. The income, therefore, is exempt from taxation under section 15, and section 17 is not a bar to the exercise by the Income Tax Officer of the power to refuse to accept the plea of benefit of the exemption under section 15 or section 17. Section 17(3)(ii) is not an exemption provision. [691 G] 8. The income was exempt under section 17 and section 17 was not a condition of exemption under the Act and the income was not exempt from tax by reason of the exemption. [692 G] 9. The income being exempt from tax, the income is not exempt from taxation. [693 G] 10. The income must be exempt from tax and the income must be assessed under section 15 as well as section 17. If the income is exempted from tax under sections 16 and 17, the income must also be assessed under sections 15, 17 and 17. The Income Tax Officer is not justified on the basis of the income. [694 H] 11. The income has to be assessed under the head 'Profits in lieu or in addition to any other income'. [694 A] 12. The income cannot be assessed under any other head. [695 B] 13. The income can be assessed under [section 15] as well as under section 17 as well as [695 H] 14.

The Act was passed by the State Legislature in exercise of the powers conferred by article 48 of the Constitution. The Act was passed to provide for the regulation of the slaughter of cows and calves of cows and for the control of the slaughter and for the regulation and control of the use of the said cows and calts. The Act provided for the regulation, control and regulation of the use and maintenance of the said bulls and calts and for the protection of the animals and the regulation of use and maintenance thereof. The Act also provided for the control and regulation by the State Government of the use or maintenance of the bulls and calves and for the prevention of the spread of the said animals. The Act imposed a duty on the State Government to take measures for the protection and improvement of the animals. The State Government passed a resolution on the basis of which the Act was passed. The Act, however, was amended by the Act. The Act came into force on April 1, 1967. The Act received the assent of the President on April 1. 1967. The State Legislature passed the Act in the year 1967. The Bill was passed in the year 1968. The Act had been passed in the middle of the year 1967 and the Act was amended in the year 1969. The Act in the meantime was passed in order to provide for regulation, control, regulation and control by the State. The Act provides for the regulation control and regulation and is in force in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The Act is not in force in so far as it prohibits the slaughter of the cows of all ages and calves, of cows, male and female, but it is a law in force in Uttar Pradesh. Section 2 of the Act provides for regulation and control. The Act has been passed in order that the slaughter of a cows of all age and calves should be carried on in accordance with the provisions of the Act. Section 3 provides for the control by the Government of the slaughter, of the animals of all ages, calves and cows, male or female, and the regulation and maintenance of use and custody thereof. The State has also made provision for the regulation by the Government. The Act does not provide for the control or regulation by the state. The Act cannot be challenged on the ground that it is not in the interest of the general public. The Act seeks to regulate the slaughter of animals of all age, calves, and cows, female and female, and to regulate the use and custody of the said animal. The Act further provides for the regulations by the State and the regulation by Government. The State is also entitled to regulate the exercise of the right of the State to regulate the health and welfare of the animals in the State.

The respondent was appointed as a workman in the Office of the Company on January 1, 1957. He was appointed as an Assistant Manager in the Office, Mains Department, Stores, Power House, Nagpur, and was confirmed in the post of Assistant Manager in a post carrying a scale of pay of Rs. 400-600. On January 1, 1958, the respondent was appointed in the Office as an Assistant Engineer in the Office. On January 2, 1958, he was appointed as Assistant Engineer in a post in the Office and was confirmed on January 3, 1958. The suit was dismissed by the trial Court. On appeal, the High Court held that the Standing Order No. (e) of the Company was not applicable to the respondent and that the respondent was not an employee of the Company. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The Standing Orders in the present case were not applicable in the respondent's case. The Standing Orders were not applicable as they were not in force at the time of the respondent's appointment. [775 H] (ii) The Standing Order No.(e) of a workman was not applicable in a case where the respondent was a workman. [776 H] (iii) The Standing order in question was not applicable as the respondent was an employee of a Company. [778 H] (iv) The Standing orders in question were in force at Nagpur and were not applicable. [779 H] (v) The Standing Counsel for the respondent was right in his submission that the Standing order in the present matter was not applicable. (e) was not applicable because the respondent was employed in the Office in question as an Assistant. [782 H] (vii) The Standing Instructions in question were applicable to the Respondent and his service was terminated in accordance with Standing Order No.[778 H].

The appellant, a Company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was incorporated in the year 1962. The Company was incorporated in 1962. The appellant, a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956, was incorporated on April 1, 1962. The company was incorporated in 1963. The Company had a share capital of Rs. 1,00,000/- and the balance sheet of the Company was prepared for the Company in respect of all its units. The Company, however, did not pay any bonus to the employees of all the units on the basis of consolidated profit and loss account. The Company filed a writ petition in the High Court of Delhi challenging the validity of the Act. The High Court held that the Act was not applicable to the Company and that the Act did not apply to the Company. The High court held that the provisions of section 16(1) of the Act were not applicable to all the units of the Company. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Act is not applicable to a company, and that the provisions contained in section 16(2) of the said Act are not applicable to an establishment of a Company. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Act is not a law applicable to an industry, but is a law applicable in the case of an establishment. [652 F] 2. The Act does not apply to an establishment which is a separate establishment. The Act applies to the establishment of a company. The Act provides for a consolidated balance sheet for the Company and the balance sheets for the Company are prepared for the company in respect of the whole of the paid up capital or out of loans taken by the Head Office. [653 G] 3. The Act was not a law in force in the State of Delhi. The Act did not provide for any separate profit and loss. [654 G] 4. The Act has to be read in the light of the provisions contained therein. The Act, therefore, does not apply in the case where the Act is applicable to an establishments of a Company, and the Act does not provide for a separate profit and Loss. [655 G] 5. The Act cannot be applied to an establishment where no separate profit and losses are worked out and the bonus is paid in any year to the employees. [656 G] 6. The Act also does not apply. The Act only provides for a separate fund for the separate profit and the loss of the establishment. [613 G] 7. The Act makes no provision for separate profit and, therefore, the Act does apply to an establishments. [613 H] 8. The Act in the case is not applicable in the present case. The Act merely provides for a general balance sheet for each company. The provisions contained in the Act are not in the nature of a law in the State. [613 A] 9. The Act contains a comprehensive provision for separate profits and loss of the company. The object of the Act is to provide for separate profit. [613 C] 10. The Act clearly provides for separate profit for each company and the Act provides for separate profits. [613 D] 11. The Act lays down a separate fund to be called the "Capital Fund" and the Act also provides for separate fund for separate profit or loss of the Company for each company, and the Income Tax Act, 1961, does not provide any separate fund for each company for separate profit, and the provisions contained under section 16(4) of the Income Tax, 1961, do not apply to any establishment. [625 G] 12. The Act deals with separate profit and gains of the company and does not provide separate profit and gain. [657 G] 13. The Act further provides for separate accounts and separate profit and profit and loss accounts. [658 G] 14. The Act prescribes separate profit and/or loss account for each company in respect to each company.

The levy of cess on the sale of goods produced in the State of Uttar Pradesh was challenged by the respondents on the ground that the levy of cess was not on the sale or consumption of goods produced within the State of U.P. and that the levy was not on sale or consumption within the State. The High Court held that the levy in question was not on manufacture of goods but on the sale and consumption of goods. The High court held that the cess was not leviable on the sale by the State of UP and that the cess could not be levied on the sale. The High. Court held that in the case of sale of goods the levy was on the sale but the levy was in the nature of a tax on sale or purchase of goods. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The levy in question is not on the manufacture of goods. It is not on manufacture. The levy is not on sale but on the consumption of goods and the levy is not for the purpose of consumption. [775 H] 2. The levy of cess is not on consumption of goods but is on the sale thereof. The levy was not for the sale of the goods produced within a State. The levy did not fall within the ambit of Entry 15 of Schedule I of the Cess Act. [776 H] 3. The levy under the Cess Act was not on consumption but on the manufacture and it was not on production of goods. [778 H] 4. The levy imposed by the Act was not for consumption within the meaning of Entry 15. [779 H] 5. The levy could not be imposed on the sale in the State. [780 H] 6. The levy being in the nature and in the nature which is not a tax on the sale, the levy was a tax on consumption. [750 H] 7. The levy does not fall within Entry 15 of the Schedule I. The levy cannot be levied on sale or use of goods. In the case of manufacture of goods, the levy is on the manufacture or production of goods and not on the production of goods within the State.[750 H] 8. The levy therefore was not on a sale but on a sale. [750 A] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 15 of 1972. Appeal by Special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 9th July, 1972 of the Allahabad High Court in Civil Misc. Writ No. 879 of 1972. S.K. Mehta, S.K Jain and S.K Gupta for the Appellant. S.C. Manchanda, S.N. Prasad, S.P. Gupta, S.C Gupta, S, K. Jain and S, K Jain for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by RAY, J. This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment of the Allahabad Court dismissing the writ petition filed by the appellant. The appellant is a company registered under the [U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950] (hereinafter referred to as the 'Act'). The appellant is engaged in the manufacture of fabrics and the manufacture of cotton fabrics. The appellant was manufacturing cotton fabrics in the State and was paying cess on the sales of the said goods. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Allahabad challenging the levy of the cess. The High, Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant has filed this appeal by special Leave. The appellant contends that the levy is in the nature, of tax on the sales in the State, and is not on a sales tax. The levy, according to the appellant, is on the sales. The levy has been made on the sale which is not on an activity of the industry. The levy falls within the ambit and scope of Entry 15 in the Schedule I of Cess Act. The levy can be imposed on a sale or purchase.

The appellant, a tenant of a building, owned by the respondent, filed a petition under Section 10(3) (a) (iii) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, for eviction of the tenant on the ground of his requirement for a business which he was carrying on in the other portion of the same building. The respondent filed a petition for eviction of his tenant on the grounds of his requirement under Section 10 (3) (b) (iii). The Rent Controller held that the respondent was a tenant of the building and that the tenant was not a 'business' within the meaning of the Act. The tenant filed an appeal to the District Court. The District Court held that the tenant had a right to be evicted from the building and the tenant was entitled to be evicted. The District Judge, however, held that the appellant was a 'business ' within the meaning in Section 10(1) (a)(iii) of Andhra Pradesh Buildings Lease, Rent and eviction Act, 1960. The District court, however, allowed the petition and directed the eviction of the appellant. The High Court held that in the context of the Act, the word 'business' was used in Section 10 (1) (b)(iii) and not in the context in which the word ' business' was used. The High court held that the word ' Business' in Section 10 was not a "business" within the meaning, of the Act and that the appellant had a right under Section 10 to be evicted on the ground that the practice of law was 'business'. The High Court accordingly allowed the petition. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts have erred in law in holding that the practice in question was 'business' and that the practice was 'business ' in the sense of a 'business'. [775 H] 2. The expression 'business' in Section 2(i)(iii) is not a " business " within the meaning. [775 G] 3. The word 'business ' is a term of wide import. It is a term used in the sense in which it is used in the context. It is not a term of the nature of a "business". It is a word of wide import and it is not a word of the nature which is used in a statute. [776 H] 4. The word "business" in Section 10 is not a mere matter of convenience. It is used in connection with the business of a person. [778 H] 5. The word business' in Section 3(1)(iii) means the business of the person. [750 H] 6. The word is not a generic term. It is an inclusive definition. It is also not a term in the context which is used for the purpose of the Act in Section 10. [750 A] 7. The word in the context is not a 'stamp' or 'business' or 'dry' or 'deficiency' or 'unfair trade practice' or 'cruelty' or 'stamp-procurement' or 'admitment' or 'resulting' or 'excessive' or 'undue' or 'relative' or 'attempting' or "unfair trade practices" or "cruelty" or "un unfair trade practice" or "admitment" or "resulting" or "excessive or unfair trade practice or "untilue" or "relative" or "attempting" or 'un unfair trade practices or unfair or deceptive practice or unfair or unfair or restrictive trade practice or unfair trade practices" [750 B] 8. The word `business' in the context means the business or profession. [750 C] 9. The word has a wider meaning.

The respondent was a partner of the appellant. The appellant was a partner in a firm of the respondent. The respondent was a firm of which the appellant was a member. The firm was a partnership firm. The respondent paid a sum of Rs. 4,00,000 to the appellant. On the basis of the agreement between the parties, the respondent became the creditor of the firm. The appellant paid a sum Rs. 4 lakhs to the respondent on November 30, 1942. The respondent filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 1,00,00,100. The appellant contended that the suit was barred by limitation. The trial court held that the suit filed by the respondent was barred by time. The trial Court held that the appellant was entitled to a decree for Rs. 1.00,00.000. The appellant filed an appeal against the decree. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant then filed a second appeal before this Court. The High court held that there was a demand for a part of the amount in the year 1943 and therefore limitation would start from that date. The High. Court held that there must be an unqualified demand for the whole sum before the limitation can be said to be a case of deposit and the appellant was therefore entitled to a sum of money. The High, Court further held that the respondent was a defaulter and therefore limitation was not applicable. The High Curt also held that there were two conditions in the agreement between them. The High 'Court held that there could be no question of an unqualified demand in the year of 1943 because the appellant was not a party to the transaction between the appellant and the respondent. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that there was no demand for a sum of rupees 4,00.00.000 by the respondent and therefore limitation could start from that day. Allowing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that there was an unqualified demand of a part of Rs.4,00, 000 by the appellant for the obvious reason that there was demand in the month of October, 1943. [775 H] (2) The High C Court was right. The High Courts were right in holding otherwise. [776 H] (3) The High Courts had no jurisdiction to interfere with the decree of the trial court. [778 H] (4) The High court was right in taking the view that there was only a demand for the part of the sum in the year 1944. The High courts were right in taking a view that there must have been an unqualified demand. [779 H] (5) The High. Courts were right. [780 H] (6) The High,Court was right in not interfering with the decree passed by the trial court on the ground that there was acceptance of the amount by the respondent. [782 H] (7) The High-Court was right. [750 H] (8) The High' Court was right, and the appeal was dismissed. [750 A] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 14 of 1972. Appeal by Special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 10th July, 1972 of the Calcutta High Court in Appeal from Original Order No. 1 of 1972. S. T. Desai, S. K. Bagchi and S. K Patel, for the appellant. S. K Jain, for the respondent. S. S. Khanduja, for the intervener. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. The appellant is a firm carrying on business in the name and style of M/s. Hindustan Lever Ltd. and the respondent is a firm. The firm is a partnership firm and the respondent was the partner of the firm and the appellant is the partner of M/S. Hindustan Levers Ltd. The respondent is a partner of M.L.A. The respondent has a branch office at Calcutta.

The petitioner was arrested on the basis of a criminal case registered against him under the Customs Act. The petitioner was arrested and produced before the Magistrate on the 27th of February, 1986. The petitioner filed an application for bail before the Magistrate. The Magistrate rejected the bail application on the ground that the petitioner was in custody and that he was in detention. The petitioner moved the High Court of Delhi in a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The petitioner then filed a writ petition in this Court. The petitioner contended that the detention order was vitiated by non-application of mind. The High court held that the detention was not warranted. The petitioner's detention was therefore illegal. The petitioner challenged the order of detention by filing a writ petition. Allowing the petition, HELD: 1. The detention order was not vitiated by non application of mind. [775 H] 2. The detention was not in accordance with law. [776 H] 3. The detention is not vitiated by any non application of the principle that a detention order can be passed for detention of a person in custody. [778 H] 4. The detention of a detenu is not illegal merely because he is in detention. [779 H] 5. The detention in jail is not illegal. The detention cannot be made in jail. The detention can be made in the custody of the court. [780 H] 6. The detention under the National Security Act is not illegal if the detention is not in accordance to law. [750 H] 7. The detention does not amount to an order of detention. The detention, therefore, is not illegal unless it is shown that the detention is necessary. [750 A] 8. The detention must be in accordance with the law. [751 H] 9. The detention being in accordance with a law, the detention is illegal. [751 A] 9. In the instant case, the petitioner was arrested in the jail on the 27.02.1986. The petitioner could not be detained for a period of more than six months. The detention could be made in anticipation of the detention. [751 B] 10. The petitioner is entitled to be released on bail. [751 D] 11. The detention for a period longer than six months is illegal. The order of detention is illegal if it is not in conformity with law. The detention has to be in accordance to the law. The order is illegal if the period of six months is not completed. [751 G] 12. The detention itself is illegal if there is no satisfaction of the detaining authority that the detention of the petitioner is necessary. The detention would be illegal if it was not in conformity to law. The petitioner cannot be detained in the custody. [751 E] 13. The detention orders are illegal if they are not in accordance. [751 F] 14. The detention and the order of the detention is bad. [751 C] 15. The detention on the ground of non-application is illegal if not illegal. [751 D] 15. In the facts of the present case, the detention order is illegal. It is not in the interest of the petitioner to continue the detention. The order was passed on the 27-02-1986. The detention did not amount to the order of his detention. [753 H] 16. The detention by itself is illegal. If the detention is held to be illegal, the detention would be invalid if it is shown to be illegal if the order is not in consonance with law. If the order is illegal, the detenu is entitled to have his detention quashed. [751A] 17. The detention as such is illegal if he is in custody. The detention may be made in accordance with Section 3 of the Act. [751B] 18. The detention Order is illegal if no satisfaction of a detaining authority that it is necessary to detain the petitioner in the interest.

The petitioners were appointed as casual labourers in the Telecom Department of the Government of India in the year 1962. They were appointed as daily wages casual labourers in 1964. They were engaged as casual labourers on daily wages in the year 1964. They worked for more than six months in the Telecom. Department. They were paid wages at the rates equivalent to the minimum of the pay scale of semi skilled labour in the corresponding cadres but without any increments with effect from 5th of February, 1986 on which date the first of the above two petitioners were working. They were not being regularly employed. They were, therefore, not entitled to the same privileges which the regular employees were enjoying. They were also not being regularly appointed. They were being paid wages at a rate equivalent to the basic pay in the pay scale applicable to the regular employees. They were denied the benefit of the revised pay scale. The respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The petitioners filed a Special Leave Petition in this Court. The petitioners contended that the respondents were not entitled to any benefit of the revision of pay scale. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The petitioners were not entitled for the same privileges as were being paid to the regular workers in the Department. [535E] 2. The petitioners belong to the category of casual labour and are not being regularly working. They are not being regular employees for the purpose of absorption in the Posts and Telegraphs Department. They are being paid wages in accordance with the job content of corresponding regular posts in the corresponding cadre but without any increment with effect from the 5th of the above mentioned two petitioners. [536F] 3. The petitioners are not entitled to get the same privileges. They are, therefore, entitled to the benefits of the revised scale of pay. [537F] 4. The petitioners cannot be denied the same privileges in accordance with law. [538F] 5. The petitioners have been working as casual labourers for more than one year in the Telecom department. They are entitled to the benefit of revised pay scale as was granted to the regular workmen in the Telecom, Department. [546F] 6. The petitioners, who are working as casual labour, are not being paid the same privileges, which the regular workmen are enjoying. [546G] 7. The petitioners' claim for the same benefits as were being granted to the casual labourers in their respective posts is not tenable. [546H] 8. The petitioners do not belong to the categories of casual labour. They are only entitled to the revised pay scales. [546A] 9. The petitioners can be denied the benefits of revised pay scales only on the ground that they belong to the class of labour. [546B] 10. The petitioners could not be denied the benefit under the revised pay Scales. [546C] 11. The petitioners should be treated as regular employees for all purposes. [546D] 12.
