The petitioners being similarly situated, they are entitled to be treated as regularly employed. [546E] JUDGMENT: ORIGINAL JURISDICTION: Writ Petition No. 15 of 1986. Under Article 32 of the Constitution of India. AND Writ Petition No, 15 of 1986 and Writ Petition No., 15 of 1986, etc. etc. etc., etc. etc... Petitioners. V.K.Thakkar, S.K. Jain, S.N. Mukherjee, S.P. Gupta, S.C. Agarwal, S.B. Gupta, R.K. Garg, S.S. Khanduja, S.D. Gupta, K.K. Gupta, V.K Jain, S K Jain, S P Gupta, S P Agarwal, S P Aggarwal, S P Agrawal, S P Jain, S S P Agarwal and S P Agarwal for the Petitioners. V K Jain, for the Respondents.

The Income tax Officer issued a notice under section 22(2) of the Act on January 5, 1950, under section 22 of the Act, calling upon the assessee to furnish a return of his income under section 22, and to furnish a revised return of his total income. The assessee filed a return of income under section 24(1) of the Income tax Act, 1961, on January 5. 1950, and a return of the income was filed on January 5,. 1950, and the return was filed on February 6, 1950, and, after the assessment was made, the best judgment assessment was bad. The Income tax Officer, on the basis of the return filed by the assessee, issued a notice to the assessee under section 22 (2) of that Act, calling for a return of its income under section 23(1) and for the assessment of the income of the assessee. The assessee submitted a return of her income under section 28 of the Act. The Income Tax Officer, on receipt of the return, issued a revised return, and the revised return, which was filed on March 5, 1950. The assessee, thereupon filed a return in response to the notice under section 24 (2) on January 5., 1950, and claimed a refund of the income tax paid by her. The Income-tax Officer, on a consideration of the material placed before him, held that the assessee was entitled to the refund of the tax paid by him. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, on a reference made to him, held, that the assessee had not furnished a return of their income under section 29 of the Act and that the assessee could not be treated as a return showing an income below the taxable limit. The Appellate Tribunal, on a further reference, held that in the absence of a notice under [section 22(2)] of the Act the assessee was not entitled to the benefit of the amended provisions of section 22 of that Act. The Tribunal, on further reference, referred to the High Court, the question whether the assessee was a dealer in the hands of her deceased husband or not. The High Court answered the question in the affirmative, and held that the assessment was bad in law. The assessee then filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court. The High court held that the notice under [sections 22(2)], 22(2), 22(3) and 22(4) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, was not a notice under the amended provisions. The High, Court held that the Income Tax Officer was not entitled, in law, to the benefit under the amended provision of section 22(1) to the assessee. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the High Court was in error in holding that the assessee's income was not liable to be assessed to tax. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts have taken a contrary view. [675 H] 2. The High courts have taken a different view. [775 H] 3. The High-Court has taken a contrary opinion. [776 H] 3(i) The High Court has taken a different stand. [778 H] (ii) The High Courts of the State have taken a similar view. [750 H] (iii) The High- Court has taken the same view. [751 H] (iv) The High court has taken a similar stand. [750 A] (v) The High. Court has taken an erroneous view. [757 H] (vi) The High,Court has taken the view that the assessee is not entitled to any relief under section 22. [750 B] (vii) The High' Court has taken another view. [800 G] (viii) The High 'Court has taken an incorrect view. [875 H] (ix) The High C.T.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956, was incorporated with effect from 1.4.1956. The appellant, a Government of India undertaking, was an autonomous body, registered under the Companies, Act, 1956. The appellant was an employee of the respondent, a Government company, and was appointed by the Central Government as a Director of the company. The respondent was appointed as a Director in the appellant's company on 1.4,1956. The respondent, who was an employee in the appellant company, was appointed by an order dated 1.4,.1956. The appointment of the respondent was made by the Central Govt. on 1.1.1956. On the basis of the said appointment, the respondent was appointed by a letter dated 1.1,1956. On 1.1,.1956, the respondent made an application to the Central Government for a direction to the Central Govt., to make the scheme in terms of the Scheme. The Central Govt. by its order dated 1,1,1956, directed the Central Govt, to make the Scheme in terms of Section 3 of the Act. The Central Government, by its order, dated 1.2.1956, directed that the scheme should be made in terms of Clause 3 of the Scheme, and that the scheme shall be deemed to have been made in terms thereof. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Delhi, challenging the validity of the said order. The High Court held that the scheme was not in terms of Clauses 3 and 4 of the Scheme and, therefore, the scheme was bad in law. The appellant's appeal to this Court was, however, allowed by the Court. The appellant contended that the scheme framed by the Central government was not in accordance with the provisions of the Act and the Scheme was not in conformity with the provisions contained in the Act. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The scheme framed by a Government company under Section 3 of Act, 1956 is not in accordance to the provisions of Section 3 and 4. The scheme is not in conformity to the provisions contained therein. [505 G] 2. The scheme was not framed in accordance with Clause 3 of Section 3. The scheme has been framed in accordance to and in accordance with Section 3 of that Act. [506 G] 3. The Scheme framed by the Government of India was not in consonance with the provisions in the Act and was not in contravention of the provisions of any of the provisions contained under the Act. [506 G] 4. The Scheme was not framed by the appropriate Government and was not contrary to the provisions in Section 3 of this Act. [504 G] 5. The scheme does not in any way conflict with the provisions made in the Act or the Scheme. [507 G] 6. The scheme cannot be altered or modified by the Central or the State Government. [508 G] 7. The scheme must be in conformity with Section 3 and the Scheme must be in accordance with law. [509 G] 8. The scheme, as framed by the State Government, is not in consonance to the provisions made therein. [506 H] 9. The scheme can be altered or amended by the Central and State Government. The scheme may be altered or revised by the Central. Government. [506 A] 10. The scheme should be in conformity to Section 3 and Section 4 of the Act, and the Scheme should be in accordance to, and in accordance therewith. [506 B] 11. The scheme shall be in conformity of the provisions in Sections 3 and 4 and the Scheme shall be deemed not to have been in conformity with any of the provision contained in the Scheme. Section 3 provides for the constitution of the Central Government. [504 B] 12. The scheme under Section 3 is not in conflict with the Act. Section 3 is in conflict with Section 3. [506 C] 13.

The appellant, a registered dealer, was assessed to tax by the assessing authority under the provisions of the Act. The assessing authority issued a notice under section 45 of the Act to the appellant, inter alia, stating that the appellant had failed to pay the tax due from him. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice. The High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to the relief claimed by him. The High court held that the provisions of section 255(5) of the Act were not attracted to the facts of the case. The appellant, therefore, filed a writ appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts in exercise of their appellate jurisdiction under section 255(1) of the Constitution have jurisdiction to regulate their own procedure. [775 H] 2. The High courts have jurisdiction to decide the question of stay of recovery of tax or penalty payable by or imposed on the assessees as a matter of course the revenue will be put to great loss. [776 H] 3. The power of stay by the Tribunal is not a matter of right but it is a matter of procedure. [750 H] 4. The power to stay recovery of tax is a matter for the legislature to consider. The power conferred on the Appellate Tribunal by section 255(6) of the Income tax Act is a matter to be considered by the Appellate Tribunal. [750 A] 5. The power under section 255 is not a power to grant stay of collection of tax or penalties payable by or impose on the assessees. The power is not a subject of course in view of the special nature of taxation and revenue. [750 B] 6. The power given to the Appellate Tribunal under section 255 of the Act is not a "power to grant stay" and it is a "power of the Court" which is "to consider" whether the entire purpose of the appeal will be frustrated or rendered nugatory by allowing the appeal. [750 D] 7. The power vested in the Appellate Tribunal is not an "power to stay recovery proceedings" and it cannot be said that the power of stay is a matter which the legislature has not considered. [750 G] 8. The power in question is a matter exclusively for the legislature. The power has to be exercised in the proper cases. [750 F] 9. The power exercised by the Appellate Tribunals under section 255 (6) of Act is not an absolute power. The power cannot be exercised in a routine manner or as a matter or a matter of law. [750 E] 10. The power can be exercised in exceptional circumstances. [750 C] 11. The power which the Appellate Tribunal has given to the High Courts under section 255 does not vest in the Appellate Tribunals. [750D] 12. The power exercisable by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner under section 255 cannot be exercised by the Tribunal unless the Appellate Tribunal considers that the entire purpose for which the appeal is being filed is frustrated by allowing the recovery proceedings. [750F] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1332 of 1987. From the Judgment and Order dated the 9th May, 1987 of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in Writ Petition No. 1223 of 1987. V.S. Desai, S.K. Bagga, S.V. Rao, R.N. Singh, R.K. Jain, R.B. Mehrotra, S.N. Srivastava, R.C. Jain, S.C. Agarwal, R.P. Singh, S.P. Srivastava, S.M. Jain, V.K. Srivastava, V.C. Mahajan, S.S. Khanduja, S.D. Gupta, S.R. Agarwal, S.B. Agarwal, V.P. Gupta, R.S. Sodhi, S.A. Shroff, S. N. Srivastava, K.K. Venugopal, S.

The respondent was a Police Officer in the State of Uttar Pradesh. He was appointed as a Police Officer on a temporary basis in the State. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he was a police officer. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad, which was allowed by a learned Single Judge of the High Court on the ground of violation of the provisions of para. 486 of the Police Regulations. The respondent was dismissed from the service of the State. The respondent challenged the order of dismissal before the High Court. The learned Single Judge held that the order of the dismissal was not a judicial order and that the order was not a nullity. The respondent then filed a writ appeal before the High court. The learned single Judge held that there was no magisterial inquiry in respect of the matter which was the subject matter of the departmental trial and that the respondent was a police Officer. The learned Judge held that in the circumstances of the case the departmental trial was not vitiated by any illegality. The respondent thereupon filed a writ application in the High court of Judicature at Lucknow, which was dismissed. The respondent thereafter filed a writ Appeal before the High (1) [1965] 1 S.C.R. 8. Court. The Division Bench of the High court held that the departmental trial had been held in accordance with the provisions of the Police Regulation and the order of termination was not a decree in the civil suit. The Division bench held that the respondent had been dismissed from the civil service of the Government and that the departmental proceedings were not vitiated by the vice of violation of para. 487 of the Police regulations. The Division, however, held that the enquiry was not vitiated because the order of his dismissal was not an order of dismissal but was a nullity. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order passed by the District Magistrate was not a judgment in the civil court and that the High Court was wrong in holding that the order dated December 14, 1966 was a nullity because the order was a nullity and that the learned Single Judge was right in holding that there was a magisterial inquiry. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order of dismissal was not passed by the Superintendent of Police in accordance with law. [675 H] 2. The order was not an administrative order. The order passed by a competent authority was not a quasi judicial order. The respondent had been appointed as a police officer and was a police official. [676 H] 3. The order dated December 13, 1966 was not a mere order of dismissal. The order is not a judgment. The order being a nullity, the order is not nullity. [678 H] 4. The order in the present case was a nullity as the order was passed by the Deputy Superintendent of Police, who was the competent authority. [691 H] 5. The order could not be said to be a nullity. [650 H] 6. The order having been passed by the competent authority, the order was an order of termination. [650 A] 7. The order terminating the services of the respondent was not a simple order of dismissal and could not be passed by the appointing authority. [650 D] 8. The order must be a judgment in a civil suit. [650 C] 8. In the instant case, the order of discharge was not a dismissal. The respondent could not be dismissed from service. [650 G] 9. The order did not contain any reasons. The order does not disclose any reason. The order merely states that the order is a judgment in civil suit. It does not disclose the reasons. The respondent has been dismissed from service without any reason. [650 B] 10. The order cannot be said to have been passed by a quasi judicial authority. The order has been passed by an authority competent to pass the order.

The appellant was appointed as a Director of Health Services, Manipur, on September 9, 1966. He was promoted as a Director in February, 1971. He was confirmed as a Director on September 10, 1966. On September 10, 1967, the appellant was promoted as Director of Health Service, Manipur. On September 11, 1967, he was promoted as Deputy Director of Health and was posted as Director of Medical Services, Manipur. He was appointed as Director of the Health Services, Imphal on September 10. 1967. On September 12, 1967, Dr. Sen and Dr. Sen were promoted as Director, Health Services, Government of Manipur. On October 13, 1967, a notification was issued by the Government of Manipur in exercise of the powers conferred by section 9 of the Indian Medical Council Act, 1956 (hereinafter referred to as the Act) read with rule 8 of the Indian Nursing Council (Centre) Rules, 1956 (for short the Rules). The appellant was promoted to the post of Director of Health services, Manipur on September 10 and was posted in the post of Deputy Director of the health services, Manipur. The appellant was also promoted as Director in the Health Services. On September 13, 1967 the appellant was appointed to the post in the post created by the Government. On September 14, 1967, an advertisement was issued by a Selection Committee to fill up the post of the Director of Health service. The appellant submitted his application for being appointed as Director in Health Services, Govt. of Manipur. The Selection Committee recommended his name for appointment as Director of health services. On September 15, 1967, another Selection Committee was constituted to consider the appellant for appointment as the Director of health Services, Manipur on the ground that he was not qualified for being promoted to the said post. The appellant, however, was not considered for promotion to the post which was created by the Selection Committee. On September 16, 1967, by a notification issued by the State Government in exercise of powers conferred by sub-section (1) of section 9 of Act, the appellant became eligible for being considered for promotion as the Director. On September 17, 1967, on the basis of the recommendation of the Selection Committee, the appellant made a representation to the Government of India for being considered as the Director in the Medical Services, Government Medical Services, Govt., of Manipur. By a letter dated September 18, 1967, it was stated that the appellant was not eligible for being promoted as the Director, Health Service, Government of India. On September 18, 1968, the appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Manipur challenging the validity of the said order. The High Court held that the appellant could not be considered for promotion on the ground of his being qualified for being considered to be promoted to the supertime grade II of the Medical Services. The appellant filed a petition in the Delhi High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution. The High court held that the petitioner was not qualified to be promoted as the Medical Services of Manipur. It was further held that the promotion of the appellant was in violation of the provisions of article 16 of the Constitution and that the appellant had not been promoted to the Supertime grade II. The appellant challenged the said decision of the High Court. The High, Court held that in the absence of a provision for promotion to supertime grade I of the Medical Service, the appellant could be considered for being considered eligible for promotion to Supertime grade I. The High. Court also held that the post of Medical Services of the Government of the State was not a post in the pay scale of the post of Professor of Medicine, Government Medical Service, Government Medical College, Manipur. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellant was not qualified in the post for being promoted. [532E] 1.2 The appellant was eligible for being appointed to the Super time grade I of Medical Services.

The Act was passed by the State Legislature in the year 1958. The Act was passed in the year 1959. The Act provided for the acquisition of surplus area of a person by inheritance or bequest or gift. The Act, however, provided for the vesting of surplus area in the State Government. The Act came into force on April 15, 1953. The Act did not provide for the vesting in the State. The Act also provided for the payment of compensation to the heirs of the deceased. The Act provides for the payment to the heirs and the payment to them of the compensation. The Act further provided for the determination of the surplus area of the person who was entitled to receive the compensation. Section 19B provided for the compensation to be paid to the heirs. The Act prescribed the compensation to which the person was entitled to. The Act made provision for the payment by the State Government of the compensation to the persons entitled to receive compensation. The State Government made a declaration under section 6 of the Act. The Act received the assent of the President on April 15. 1959. The State Legislature passed the Act in the year 1960. The Act had to be amended in the year 1962. The Act amended the Act in its application to the State of Tamil Nadu. The Act gave the benefit of the surplus pool to the heirs in the State of the father. The Act conferred the right to receive compensation on the heirs. It provided for the making of a declaration of their lands within permissible limits. The Act required the State Government to make a declaration of the surplus land. The Act empowered the State Government by notification to make a scheme for the acquisition and payment of compensation. The scheme was published in the official gazette on May 15, 1959. The scheme provided for the compulsory acquisition of surplus land. Section 19-B provided for payment of compensation in the prescribed manner. The Act enabled the State Government, by notification, to make a Scheme for the acquisition. The Act specified the surplus pool as under: "19-B. (1) The surplus pool shall be paid to each heir of the deceased, in the prescribed form and manner. (2) The surplus shall be paid in the prescribed Form. (3) The surplus amount shall be paid within a period of one year from the date of the publication of the scheme. (4) The surplus area shall be paid by the State to the heirs within a period not exceeding one year from such date. (5) The surplus land shall be paid either to the heirs or to the heirs, as the case may be, within a period exceeding one year. (6) The surplus surplus pool shall, after deducting the amount of the surplus amount, be paid to any person who is entitled to receive it. (7) The surplus of surplus pool shall vest in the State free from all encumbrances. (8) The surplus, if any, shall be paid after the expiry of the period specified in sub-section (3) of section 19-B.

The plaintiffs filed a suit for possession of the Malguzari lands in the year 1950, and the defendants filed a written statement admitting the claim of the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs claimed that the Malguy lands were impartible and were governed by the rule of primogeniture and that the plaintiffs were entitled to the compensation in respect of the Malaria lands. The trial court held that the Malaria Lands were impartible. The High Court held that the plaintiffs had not acquired any right to the land and that the order of the Compensation Officer was not a nullity. The High court held that in view of the provisions of section 14 of Act 1 of 1951, the Compensation Officer had no jurisdiction to determine the claim of proprietary rights. The High, Court held that in the absence of a suit for setting aside the decision the Compensation Officer could not be said to have jurisdiction to determine competing claims. The High. Court held that section 14 of the Act was enacted with a view to put an end to the disputes with regard to the claims of proprietary rights which by virtue of the notification issued under section 3 of the Act, the Compensation officer had the jurisdiction to determine, and that the Compensation Officer's order was not a decree within the meaning of section 14. The High 'Court held that section 15 of Act 1, 1951 was enacted with the object of putting an end to disputes with regard thereto and that the compensation in question was payable to Dayaram in respect of Malguzars. The High' Court held that as the plaintiffs had acquired the right to the property vesting in the Government by operation of section 3 of Act 1. 1951, the order of Compensation Officer became final and conclusive and could not be reopened in a suit filed by the plaintiffs. In the result, the High Court dismissed the suit. The plaintiffs filed a second appeal in this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts of Punjab and Haryana and Punjab and Haryana High Court in the case of Malgundars and the Punjab and Haryana in the case referred to above, have taken a view that section 14 was enacted with an object to put an over-riding effect on the rights conferred by the Act. [775 H] 2. The High-Court was in error in not interfering with the order of dismissal passed by the Compensation Officer. [776 H] 3. The High Curt was in error. [778 H] 4. The order of the High Court was not a judgment within the meaning and scope of section 14 and was not a mere order of the Court. [779 H] 5. The order passed by the High Court is not a decree. The order was not an order of the court. The order is not a judgment. [780 H] 6. The order dated August 30, 1951 was not a final order. [782 H] 7. The order under section 14 was not a simple order of the Land Compensation Officer. The order became final and binding on the Compensation Officer and the Compensation Officer, and the order was not final. [785 H] 8. The order in question was not a preliminary order. The order did not become final. The order made by the Compensation officer was not a formal order. [750 H] 9. The order by the Compensation Commissioner was not a speaking order. The HighCourt was in wrong in not interfering in a suit. [750 A] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1124 of 1966. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated the 8th July, 1966 of the Punjab and Delhi High Court in First Appeal No. 10 of 1965. S. K. Sinha, for the appellant. S. N. Prasad, for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. The appellant, who was the owner of the land in dispute, filed a suit against the respondent for possession of his land.

The appellant was a tenant of a shop in the city of Bombay. He was a tenant in the city. He was served with a notice under section 12(2) of the Act on the tenant. The tenant filed a suit for recovery of rent against the tenant. He pleaded that the tenant was in arrears of rent for a period of six months and that the tenant had not paid the rent till the date of the notice. The trial court held that the tenant did not make an application under section 12 (3) (a) of the said Act and that the notice was not a valid notice. The High Court held that the notice under section12(2) (a), (b) and (c) of the aforesaid Act was not a notice under the Act and that it was not a proper notice under section 11(4) (a). The High Court further held that the provisions of section 12(3) (b) of the Bombay Rent Act were applicable to the case and that the provisions were applicable to a case where the tenant had made an application within one month of the service of the notice and such application was not maintainable. The High court held that in order to attract the applicability of section 12 (1) (a)(i) of the Rent Act the notice must be a notice under [section 12(2)] of the Act. The High. Court held that in the absence of a notice under Section 12(2), the notice must have been issued under section 12 of the Act and the tenant was not entitled to raise a dispute for the first time in the written statement. The High, Court held that section 12(1) (b), (c) and (d) of the above Act were applicable only to a case of a suit for eviction and not to a case in which the dispute in regard to the standard rent must be raised in order to avoid the operation of section 12. The High C.A. No. 10 of 1973 filed by the appellant was dismissed. The appellant filed a special leave petition in this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions of section 11(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure are applicable to a proceeding under the Act. [775 H] 2. The provisions in the Act are applicable to the proceedings under the Act, and the provisions are applicable to cases where the dispute in question is raised at the first stage of the proceedings. [776 H] 3. The provisions contained in section 12(4) of the Delhi Rent Act are applicable only to cases where a dispute in regard of standard rent is raised in order that the Court may have the jurisdiction to decide the question of standard rent. [778 H] 4. The provisions are applicable only in a case where a dispute is raised at a first stage of a suit. [779 H] 5. The provisions relating to standard rent are applicable to proceedings under the provisions of the Act, but the provisions are not applicable to cases in which the tenant has made an application under the Act within one month from the date of service of the demand notice. [780 H] 6. The provisions regarding standard rent are not applicable in a case in where the dispute is raised in regard to standard rent. The provisions have to be read in the context of the Act to determine the standard rent. If the provisions are applied to a case, the provisions are to be applied to a particular case. [782 H] 7. The provisions made in the Act will apply to cases where there is a dispute in respect of standard rent and the provisions of Section 12(3)(a) of that Act are applicable. [785 H] 8. The provisions referred to in the Act have to be construed in the light of the provisions of that Act. [750 H] 9.

The respondent company is a limited company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956. The respondent company is an Indian company. The respondent is a limited Company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The respondent was a limited company. The appellant company is a subsidiary of the respondent company. The respondents are the shareholders of the respondent. The respondent filed a petition under section 397 read with section 402 of the Act for the winding up of the respondent and for the winding of the respondent on the ground that the respondent company was not a public company within the meaning of section 2(1)(d) of the Act. The respondent contended that the respondent was not a shareholder in the respondent company and that the appellant was not a 'public company' within the meaning ofs. 2(1) (d) of that Act. The Tribunal held that the respondent is not a ' public company' within s. 2(2) of the Companies Act and that the respondent cannot be said to have a controlling interest in the respondent. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court held that the appellant is not a public limited company within the definition of section 2 (1) (c) of the Indian Companies (Amendment) Act, 1956, and that the question referred by the Appellate Tribunal to the High Court was in the negative. The appellant is, therefore, before us. The question referred by it to the High court was whether the respondent is a 'public limited company' within section 2(2)(1) (f) of the said Act. The High Court held, after considering the evidence adduced before it, that the respondent has a controlling interest and that the said interest is not a part of the respondent's business. The High court held that the said interests are not part of the company's business and that the finding of the Appellate Tribunal that the respondent's interest in the company is not a "public company" within the meaning s. 2 (1)(d)(i) of the [Indian Companies Act, and that in the absence of any finding that the respondent in the present case is a ' public limited company' the finding of fact recorded by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner was not in the negative and the High Court, therefore, held that the question of the respondent being a 'public Company' within the definition s. 2 of the said act was not a " public company" within s.2 (1) of the aforesaid Act. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. The question which arises for consideration in this appeal is whether the respondent has any interest in the appellant company in the respondent's company and is a 'Public Company' within s, 2 (1). The respondent is not an 'public company'. The respondent is an Indian Company within s. 3(1) of that act. The respondent has a control over the affairs of the respondent, and the appellant is a ' Public Company' within S. 2 (2) of that section. The respondent's contention is that the respondent being an Indian company within s. 1 (1) is not a shareholder within s. 42 of the Act and that in any event the respondent is an 'public limited Company' within section 42 of the said Indian Act. The question is whether the appellant is an 'Public Company'. The respondent has not produced any evidence to show that the respondent owns any interest in any of the shares held by the respondent. In the absence of such evidence, the respondent cannot, in the absence thereof, be said to be a 'public' company within s, 42 of the Indian Act. In the result, the appeal is allowed and the order of the High Court is set aside. The respondent will pay the costs of the appellant.

The respondent was appointed as a Junior Accounts Assistant in the office of the Board on 5th January, 1966. He was promoted to the post of Accounts Superintendent on 1st November, 1956. He was confirmed in the post of Junior Accounts Assistant on 1st December, 1956. On the basis of the recommendations of the Board, he was promoted to that post on 1st January, 1966 and was confirmed in that post on the same date. On the same date, he was confirmed in his post of Accounts Assistant on the same day. On the ground that the Regulations framed by the Board under section 79(c) of the Board were not applicable to the allottees, he was allowed to continue in the post. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Single Judge. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the order of confirmation of the respondent. The High court held that the Regulations were not applicable in the present case as the Regulations framed under section 79 (c) of Board's Regulations were not in force at the time when the Regulations were framed. The High. Court held that the regulations framed under section 80(c) were not applicable and the Regulations framed in exercise of the powers conferred by section 79(b) of the Act were not applicable. The High, Court held that in the absence of any Regulations framed under the Act, the Regulations framed thereunder were not applicable as the Regulations were in force at that time. The High' Court held that as the Regulations had been framed by the board in exercise of powers conferred by the statute, the Regulations were applicable to the respondent. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Regulations could not be made applicable to the appellant as they were not in operation at the time of the Regulations were made. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Regulations framed under Section 79(c), read with the Resolution dated 19th May, 1969, were not applicable for the purpose of the present case. The Regulations were not made applicable to those allottees. [557F] 2. The Regulations could not have been made applicable to allottees who were not required to pass the examination. The Regulations had been made applicable by the Board in exercise of its powers conferred by Section 79(b). [557G] 3. The Regulations are not applicable to allottees. The Regulations have been made in exercise of power conferred by the Act. The Regulations must be read in the same manner as the Regulations. [558F] 4. The Regulations cannot be made applicable in the case of allottees who were excluded from the operation of the Resolution dated 9th May, 1968. [559F] 5. The Regulations made under Section 79 of the Act are not applicable in cases where the Regulations have been framed by a competent authority. The Regulations can be made applicable only to those allottees who were included in the operation of a particular Resolution. [560G] 6. The Regulations should be made applicable for the purposes of the present cases. [566G] 7. The Regulations, as they were made applicable to all the allottees, were not in existence at the time the Regulations were issued. The Regulations came into force only on the date of the Resolution. The Regulations did not apply to those allottees, who were excluded. [567G] 8. The Regulations do not apply to the allottees who were covered by the Regulations. The Regulations themselves were made applicable by virtue of the provisions of the Act. [568G] 9. The Regulations in question were not made in the interest of the allottees. The regulations were made applicable only for the purposes for which they were made. [569G] 10. The Regulations of the Board are not applicable for those allottees who are excluded from the operations of a particular resolution. [570G] 11.

The appellant, Suman Behera, was a member of the police force of the State of Bihar. He was prosecuted for an offence under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court convicted Suman Behera and sentenced him to undergo imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. The appellant filed an appeal before this Court. The High court confirmed the conviction. The appellant was convicted by the trial court and sentenced to undergo imprisonment. The appellant preferred an appeal to this Court. During the pendency of the appeal, Suman Behra was released on bail. The appellant moved the High Court for grant of special leave to appeal against the conviction and the sentence. This Court granted special leave to the appellant. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. The appellant, Suman, was a police officer of the State. He was convicted by this Court under Section 302, Indian Penal Code and sentenced to suffer imprisonment for life and to pay a fine of Rs. 500/- in default to suffer rigorous imprisonment for six months. The appellant challenged the conviction and sentences imposed on him by the trial courts. The High Courts, however, confirmed the conviction of Suman Behera. The appellant is in appeal before us. The appellant contended that the High Court was wrong in holding that the appellant was guilty of an offence under [Section 302] of the Indian penal Code and that the sentence imposed on him was illegal. The appellant also contended that the sentence of imprisonment imposed on Suman Behera was not excessive and that the High Courts were wrong in holding the appellant guilty of an act of murder. The appellant further contended that the conviction of the appellant was illegal and that the appellant should be given the benefit of the provisions of the Criminal Procedure Code. The High courts, however, held that the appellant had committed an offence under the [Indian Penal Code] and that the conviction and sentenced to imprisonment for life was illegal. In appeal to this court, it was contended that the appellant could not be convicted under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Code and that, therefore, the sentence imposed upon Suman Behera should be set aside. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The appellant had been convicted by the High Court under Section 304 Part I of the Indian IPC and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for a period of six months. [557D] 2. The appellant could not have been convicted under Section 304 part I of the IPC. The appellant cannot be convicted under [Section 304] Part I of IPC. [558F] 3. The appellant should be sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year. [559F] 4. The appellant must be given the benefits of the provisions contained in the Criminal Procedure code. [560F] 5. The appellant can be convicted under the provisions of Section 304 Part 1 of the IPC only if he is convicted under Section 201 of the Indian Evidence Act. [566F] 6. The appellant did not commit any offence under Section 304, Part I of Indian Penal Code, and that the offence was not punishable under Section 302. [567F] 7. The appellant's conviction under Section 302 is not illegal. [568F] 8. The appellant would be liable to undergo rigorous sentence for one year and to pay fine of Rs 500/- in case of default in payment of fine. [569F] 9. The appellant shall undergo rigorous imprisonment of one year. The sentence imposed upon him by the High Courts is set aside. [570G] 10. The appellant will be entitled to the benefit of Section 428 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. [571G] 11. The appellant may be released on probation under Section 4 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1952. [572G] 12. The appellant in the instant case was convicted by a competent court under Section 302 IPC and sentenced him. [582H] 13.

The petitioner was convicted by the trial court and sentenced to death by the trial Court. The petitioner was convicted for an offence under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The petitioner filed an appeal before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The petitioner then filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before this Court for a writ of habeas corpus. The petition was dismissed by this Court. The petition filed by the petitioner was also dismissed. The petitioner thereafter filed a petition in this Court under Article 32 of the Constitution for a writ in the nature of habeas corpus for the issue of a writ of Habeas Corpus. The petition also was dismissed. The petition for a writ was also dismissed by this court. The petitioner has now come up to this Court by special leave. The petitioner is a citizen of India. He has been convicted by the High Court for an offence punishable under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian penal Code. The petitioner's appeal was also dismissed and he has now come to this Court. In the petition for writ, the petitioner has challenged the constitutional validity of the Act and the Rules made thereunder. The petitioner also challenges the constitutional validity and the validity of the Rules and the Rules. The petitioner contends that the Act is not a law for the time being in force and that the petitioner is not entitled to be heard before the High court. The petition is opposed by the respondents. The petition has been dismissed by this order. The petitioner challenges the constitutional vires of the Act. The petitioner seeks to challenge the constitutional validity. The petitioner relies on the decision of this Court in the case of [R. Rangarajan vs The State of Madras] , wherein it was held that the Act does not provide for a search of the person who is convicted by the Court. The Court held that the provisions of the Act are not applicable to the petitioner. The petitioner further relies on the judgment of this Court reported in [R. 1] (supra) to contend that the Act provides for a search and seizure. The petitioner submits that the Act has been enacted to provide for a proper search and seizure of the person. The petitioner therefore seeks to challenge constitutional validity of Section 6 of the Act on the ground that the Act violates the fundamental rights of the petitioner. Section 6 of this Act provides that the Act shall not be in force in any State. The petitioner says that the Act was enacted to provide that the provisions contained in the Act shall apply to the petitioner as if the Act were enacted. The petitioner states that the Act contains a provision for a search. The petitioner argues that the Act cannot be used to provide for an inquiry. The petitioner points out that the Act requires the Superintendent of the Jail to conduct an inquiry. It is further pointed out that the petitioner has not been able to show that the Act contravenes the fundamental rights. The petitioner refers to the judgment of the Supreme Court in the cases of R. 1 (supra) and R. 1(1) (supra). The petitioner also relies on the observations of this Court that the Act also provides for a proper inquiry. The petition proceeds on the basis that the Act prescribes a search and seizures. The petitioner, therefore, seeks to challenge its constitutional validity.

The appellant was a partner of a firm of which the appellant was a member. The firm was dissolved on January 22, 1950. The appellant was a tenant of the premises in question. The appellant filed a suit for recovery of damages against the firm and the appellant was impleaded as a party. The appellant contended that the partnership was dissolved by the death of the partner and the appellant had no liability to make good the loss caused to the tea garden by the fire. The trial court held that the partnership had not been dissolved and that the appellant was liable to make good loss to the tea estate. The trial Court held that the appellant had not been able to prove that the partnership in question was managed by the Receiver. The appellant preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that in the absence of any evidence to the contrary the appellant was not liable to make the loss to the Tea garden. The High court further held that the surety bond executed by the appellant was valid and the appellant could not be made liable for the loss caused by the fire to the tea gardens. The High. Court further held that in view of the provisions of the [Courts Act], the appellant was entitled to exercise the same powers in the matter of enforcement of the bond as the District Judge himself had. The High, Court further held, that the appellant could be made liable to make a good loss to tea estate by the fire and the appellant would not be liable for the same. The High' Court further held in the appeal that the appellant did not suffer any loss to the estate by the death or by the negligence of the Receiver. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the High Court was wrong in holding that the appellant's suit was not maintainable. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The appellant had not suffered any loss to his estate by the destruction of the tea garden. The appellant could not have been made liable for any loss caused to tea garden by his fire. [505 D] 2. The appellant has not been able- to prove that he was liable to pay damages to the tea Garden. The appellant is liable to make such payment of damages to the Tea Garden. [506 D] 3. The appellant cannot be made liable in respect of the loss caused in the tea garden because the appellant was the partner of the firm. [507 D] 4. The appellant having been able to establish that the partnership stood dissolved by the deceased partner, the appellant was rightly made liable for damages to the estate of the deceased. [508 D] 5. The appellant being a partner of the partnership, the appellant is liable for the losses caused to the Tea Estate. [509 D] 6. The appellant must be made liable only for the loss suffered by the tea garden and not for the loss of the tea estate suffered by the Tea Garden due to the negligence of his Receiver. [510 D] 7. The appellant would be liable to make payment of damages for the loss occasioned to the tea plantation. [512 E] 8. The appellant, having been able-to establish that the appellant has been able to discharge the loss caused, the appellant would be entitled to make good his loss to the extent of the loss occasioned by the fire by the fire which took place in the tea estate and the appellant is also liable to make an assessment of the loss to be made good to the Tea estate. [514 D] 9. The appellant should be made liable under the provisions of section 149 of the Code of Civil Procedure. [515 D] 10. The appellant can be made liable also for the loss arising to the tea estates by the death and the liability of the appellant to make good any loss to him by the death. [516 D] 11.

The appellant, a dealer in foodgrains and other goods, was a dealer in wheat. The State Government issued a notification under section 3 of the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1948, (hereinafter referred to as the Act) declaring that the foodgrains and other articles specified in the Schedule to the Act were to be sold to the State Government at the controlled prices. The appellant purchased foodgrains and other commodities from the State Government and sold them to the State. The State of Uttar Pradesh issued a notification on March 31, 1957, under section 3(1) of the Act, declaring that the specified foodgrains and other items were to be delivered to the State of Madras. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notification. The High Court held that the appellant was not a dealer in the foodgrains and that the transactions of supply of foodgrains and other materials were not sales. The High court held that the transactions were not sales and that the appellant had not been able to prove that the goods were on that account not exposed to sales tax. The High. Court held that there was no sale and the transactions were on that behalf only. The appellant's writ petition was dismissed. The appellant then filed a writ appeal to this Court. The appellant contended that the transactions in question were not sales, and that the State Government was not competent to make sales. HELD: The appellant was not an dealer in foodgrains but was a dealer. The State Legislature was competent to make a law for the purpose of imposing a tax on the sale of foodgrains and for that purpose it was competent to the State Legislature to make a provision for the levy of tax on the transactions of sale. [505 H] The appellant was a dealer within the meaning of the Act and was not a person who was not a registered dealer. [506 H] The State of U.P., the appellant was a registered dealer and was not liable to pay tax on the transaction of supply of wheat. The appellant was, therefore, not a dealer. [506 H] The sales were not on the basis of any representation made by the dealer and the transactions of supplies were on that basis not exposed to sale tax. [507 H] The Sales Tax Act was not applicable to the appellant. The appellant had not suffered sales tax on the purchases of wheat. [508 H] The transactions of supply were not sales but were on the basis that the appellant purchased wheat from the State. [509 H] The sale of wheat was not on the ground that there was any representation made on behalf of the State Government. The appellant could not be regarded as a dealer. There was no sale. [506 G] The appellant could be regarded as an agent of the State. There was nothing in the Act to prevent the State Legislature from making a law for imposing a tax. [506 A] The appellant had no right to purchase wheat from the Government. [506 B] The appellant is not a dealer within s. 3(1)(a) of the U P. Sales Tax and Sales Tax Act. [510 H] The purchase of wheat was on the basis, of any representation or representation made by a dealer. It was not a sale. The appellant did not suffer sales tax on his purchases. [506 C] The appellant purchased wheat in the course of the business of the appellant. [506 D] The appellant did purchase wheat from a dealer. He was not a ' dealer' within the meaning ofs. 3 of the Act. [506 E] The appellant cannot be regarded as dealer within s, 3(1). [506 G-510 A] The State Legislature has no power to make a legislation for imposing a levy on the sale or purchase of goods. [506 F] The appellant has not suffered sales-tax on the transactions in respect of foodgrains and the goods were not on that account exposed to sales-tax.

The petitioner was detained under the provisions of the Gujarat Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1985 (hereinafter referred to as the Act). The order of detention was passed against the petitioner on the ground that he was a bootlegger within the meaning of section 2(b) of the Act. The petitioner was arrested on the basis of a criminal case registered against him under the provisions mentioned in the order of detention. The petitioner filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of his detention. The petition was allowed by the learned Single Judge of the High Court on the ground, inter alia, that the order of the detention was passed without the petitioner's knowledge and that the detention was illegal. The learned Single Judge held that the detention order was illegal and quashed the order of preventive detention. The State of Gujarat has filed this appeal by special leave. The petitioner has filed this petition under Article 32 of the Constitution. The petitioner challenges the order of this Court on the following grounds: (1) The order of the detaining authority was illegal and void and (2) the detention was not illegal. The petitioner is a boot-legger within clause (b) of section 2 of the Act and his detention was illegal and invalid. The petitioner also challenges the order passed by the detaining authority on the ground of non-application of mind. The petitioner submitted that the order was passed without his knowledge and that he was not served with the order of confirmation of the detention. The learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that in the facts of the case, the detention was bad and illegal. The petition should be allowed. The respondents have filed a counter affidavit. The learned Government Advocate submitted that the detention of the petitioner was illegal and illegal. He submitted that the petitioner was a boo-legger. The petitioner had been arrested on the date of hearing and therefore, the detention order could not be sustained. The learned Counsel for the petitioner relied upon the decision of this Court in the case of [A.K. Kraipak and others vs Union of India and others] , wherein it was held that the order passed under the Act was illegal and not in accordance with the Constitution.

The appellant, a partnership firm, was incorporated in the year 1947. The appellant, a partner of the firm, was a partner in the firm. The firm was dissolved on the death of one of the partners. The appellant filed a suit for dissolution of the firm on the ground that the suit was barred as res judicata. The trial court held that the suit filed by the appellant was barred by res judicata. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree of the trial court and dismissed the suit. The appellant has come up in appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in dismissing the suit. [557D] 2. The High court was right in holding that the suit is barred by resjudicata. [558F] 3. The High Courts of Punjab and Haryana and Delhi have taken a correct view of the matter and have given a correct finding. [559F] 4. The High Curt was right in refusing to interfere with the order of the trial Court. [560F] 5. The High-Court was right in rejecting the appellant's application for review of the order under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. [566F] 6. The High. Court was right. [567F] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 15 of 1977. From the Judgment and Order dated the 10th May, 1977 of the Punjab and Haryana High Court in C.M. No. 1266 of 1977. S.K. Mehta, S.K Jain and S.K Sharma for the Appellant. S.N. Sharma, S.N Sharma and S.P. Singh for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by RAY, C.J. This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment of the High Court of Punjab and Delhi dated 10th May 1977. The appellant was a partner of a firm. The appellant is a partner in a firm. He filed a suit against the respondent for dissolution of his firm on the allegation that the suit property was owned by the appellant and the respondent was dead at the time of the suit. He filed the suit for dissolution on the ground of non-joinder of the necessary parties. The trial Court dismissed the suit on the ground, inter alia, that the suit had been filed by the plaintiff in the year 1962. The High, Court held that the appellant was not entitled to challenge the decree on the ground mentioned in the plaint. The High' Court held that in the absence of an exception to the general rule that the suit should be dismissed on the ground specified in the plaint, the High Curt had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit. In the result, the High court set aside the order of dismissal of the suit and dismissed the application for review. The appellant's application was dismissed. Hence this appeal by special Leave. The appellant contends that the High Court was wrong in dismissing the application for reviewing the order of this Court. The appellant further contends that the respondent was not entitled, in law, to challenge the order of his trial court. The High 'Court was wrong in holding that in the suit filed against the respondent, the appellant was entitled to challenge an order of dismissal. The appellant also contends that the trial court was wrong in refusing to review the order of rejection of the plaint. In the alternative, the appellant contends that in the facts and circumstances of this case, the High 'Court had no jurisdiction. The appellant relies on the decision of this Court in Seth Hira Lal Patni vs Ram Chander, ; , ; , ; ; , ; . , ; , , , , . , , , ; , . , . , ; . . , , . . , . . . , ; ; . , . ; . , , ; . ; . . . . ; . ; ; . . ; ; ; . ; , . . ; , , . ; ; , .

The appellants were the original mortgagor and the respondent was the mortgagee. The appellants filed a suit for recovery of a loan advanced before the 1st day of January, 1939, and the respondent filed a written statement in the said suit. The appellants contended that the respondent was a sub mortgagee and that the respondent had not received the notice referred to in clause (a) of sub section (1) of section 28 of the Act. The trial court held that the respondent as sub mortgagee was an assignee of a mortgage debt and that the mortgage was not an assignment of a mortgage. On appeal, the High Court of Calcutta held that the appellants were not a sub mortgagee. On further appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The respondent was a mortgagee and the respondent had received the notice under clause (a). The respondent was not a sub- mortgagee. The respondent was an assignee within the meaning of sub section(5) of section 36. [655 H] (2) The respondent had not executed the mortgage deed in favour of the appellants. The respondent had received notice under clause(a) of subsection (1) and the respondent as a sub mortgagee had not received notice under sub section (2) of section 29. [656 H] (3) The respondent could not be said to be an assignee of the mortgage debt. [657 H] (4) The respondent having received the notice, the respondent was not an assignee of mortgage debt. The respondent could be said to have received the notice. [658 H] (5) The respondent being a sub mortgagee was not a party to the mortgage. [659 H] (6) The respondent did not receive the notice under sub-section (2) and the notice under section 29 was not an assignable assignment. [660 H] (7) The respondent is a sub-mortgagee and the respondent is a assignee of the mortgaged debt. [650 H] (8) The respondent has not received the notices under clause (b) of sub-section(1) of [section 28] and the respondent has not executed the deed of assignment. [650 A] (9) The respondent cannot be said to become an assignee of an assignment of the mortgage-debt. [650 D] (10) The respondent, therefore, was not a tenant within the meaning ofs. 2 (22) of the Act and the respondent could not have been said to be a sub-tenant within the meaning s. 36 of the Act, and the reference to the sub-mortgages containing an assignable assignor of the mortgage creditor was not an Assignment of a mortgage decree. [650 B] (11) The respondent's case that the respondent has received the notice is not an assignment but an assignment of an assignment. [663 H] (12) The respondent in the present case was a sub- mortgagor and the sub- mortgagor was a sub mortgagor. The respondent has no right to recover the debt from the original mortgagor. [663 F] (13) The respondent can be said to hold the property as an assignee of his mortgage debt. If the respondent has no interest in the mortgaged property, the respondent is not a sub mortgagor and the mortgage debt is not an assignor's assignable assignment and the respondent cannot be regarded as an assignee. [663 G] (14) The respondent does not have any right to recover his debt from the appellant. [663 A] (15) The respondent also cannot be said that the respondent is an assignee of any assignment. [664 F] (15). The respondent is not an assignee within s. 36. [664 A] (16) The respondent must be deemed to be an assignor of a mortgage-debt and the respondent must be regarded as a sub-lessee of the mortgage.

The appellant was a Hindu undivided family. He was a member of a joint Hindu family. He executed a deed of partition in respect of the properties of his father in favour of his wife, Venkatacharyulu. The properties were purchased by the appellant in the name of his wife. The appellant was a member in the family. The properties purchased by the wife were ancestral properties. The properties of the appellant were purchased by him in the name and style of his wife and the properties were purchased in the name, style of his son. The properties sold by the appellant were ancestral properties and the properties purchased by him were ancestral properties, and the properties sold by him were not ancestral properties. On the death of the appellant, the properties were inherited by him from his wife. On the basis of the partition deed, the properties purchased were mutated in the name. The appellant filed a suit for possession of the properties. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the properties purchased under the deed of partition were ancestral properties of the father of the appellant and the properties had been rightly held by the trial court to be ancestral properties. In the second appeal, the High Court held, that the properties sold were ancestral properties; that the properties were ancestral properties in the hands of the appellant. The High court further held that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the partition. The High Curt also held that the property purchased by the husband of the appellant was ancestral property and the properties acquired by him were liable to be partitioned. The High. Court further held that in the absence of any evidence to the contrary, the properties sold under the deed dated May 5, 1954 were not ancestral property. The High, Court further held, that in the circumstances, the properties acquired under the deed were not ancestral. The High 'Court further held that there was no evidence to show that the properties acquired were ancestral properties but the properties were not ancestral lands. The High' Court further held in the second appeal that the properties which were purchased by her were not ancestral in the hands. The High-Court further held, after the death of her husband, that the property was ancestral property. In the result, the High Curt held that the lands purchased by the respondent were not ancestral and the properties which she purchased were not ancestral, and the appellant was entitled to the benefits of the partition under the deed. The HighCourt further held in second appeal that there was evidence to show the properties purchased in the names of the appellant in her favour. The High Courts held that the transactions in the name were not ancestral transactions. The High T.C.A. was dismissed. The appellant is before us in this appeal. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The properties which were sold by the husband to the appellant were not ancestral or ancestral properties. [775 B] 2. The properties acquired by the husband in the name or the joint family were ancestral properties or were not ancestral assets. [776 C] 3. The properties in the name which were purchased under the document dated May 5. 1954 were not the ancestral properties. It was not ancestral properties and was not ancestral. [778 C] 4. The properties mentioned in the deed dated April 5, 1954, were not ancestral items. The properties are not ancestral properties but were not ancestral as the properties were separate properties. [750 D] 5. The properties covered by the deed dated June 5, 1954 are not ancestral. It was only the properties which are not ancestral and were not ancestral that were not ancestral but were not the properties which they purchased. [750 E] 6. The properties described in the deed of gift dated May 5,. 1954 were not joint family properties. The property purchased by her was not ancestral in her hands. [750 G] 7.

The Income Tax Officer, who made the assessment of the assessee, made an assessment under section 226(3) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, on the ground that the sum demanded by the assessee was not due to the assessee. The assessee filed an appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the Income tax Officer. The assessee preferred an appeal to this Court. The question was whether the failure of the L.I.C. to make the requisite statement on oath under section 226 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 was a failure on the part of the L-I.C., to make the necessary statement on oath. The question, therefore, was whether the L. I.C. was justified in making the requisite statement under section 226 (3) of Income Tax Act 1961. HELD: The High Court was right in its conclusion that the failure of L.I.,C. to give notice under section 226 was a failure to make the required statement on oath and that the failure to make such statement was a failure of the assessee to make the statement on oath within the time given by the L.l.C. and that the L.1.C. had failed to make the said statement on oath, and that the assessee was entitled to make the full statement on oath in the manner prescribed by section 226(2) of the Act. [775 H] The High Court, therefore, erred in holding that the failure on the L. l.C. in making the necessary statement was a breach of section 226(1) of the Incometax Act, 1961. [776 H] The failure on the side of the assessee was a failure in the course of the assessment of his income. [778 H] The decision of the High Court was correct. The failure on his part was a failure not to make the prescribed statement on oath on oath. [779 H] The mere failure to make a statement on oath does not amount to a failure on his side. The failure to make it on oath does amount to a breach of the provisions of section 226 of The Income Tax Act. [779 H] The question whether the failure on his party was a failure under section 226 or not was a question of fact. [779 A] The decision in the case of the assessee is not a decision of the Court. [779 B] The decision was not a decision on the facts of the case. [779 C] The decision is not a judgment of the Court but a decision of a Court. [780 H] The Court of Appeal was not right in holding that failure on the party was a breach on his side and that the omission on his side was a failure. [779 D] The decision does not show that the failure was a failure as to the fact of the assessee's failure to make good the statement on his part. [779 F] The decision has no application to the facts of this case. [782 H] The decisions in the case referred to above were not applicable to the facts in the present case. [780 H] The facts of the present case are not such that the failure in the case was a failure within the meaning of section 226. [779 G] The decision referred to above was not a judgment in the case. The decision was, therefore, not a judgment within the meaning and the decision was not applicable to a case where the failure on part of the assessee had a failure to comply with the provisions of the section. [779 E] The decision, therefore, does not help the appellant. [779 J] The decision cannot be said to be a decision of any Court. [780 G] The decisions referred to above are not applicable to facts of this appeal. [779 K] The decision must be read in the light of the decision in the [Commissioner of Income Tax, U.P. vs.

The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax by the Income Tax Officer, who assessed the appellant to income tax. The appellant filed a return of his income for the assessment year 1962-63. The Income Tax Officer assessed the appellant's income at Rs. 1,000 per annum. The appellant appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer. The appellant then filed a revision petition before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the revision petition. The appellant thereafter filed a writ petition in this Court. The appellant contended that the provisions of section 29, sub section (2) of the Limitation Act were applicable to an appeal under section 116A of the Act and that the provisions contained in section 29, subsection (2) were applicable to a case where the First Schedule to the Limitation Act was not prescribed for any suit, appeal or application a period of limitation different from the period prescribed therefor by the first schedule. The High court held that the provisions in section 29(2) of that Act were applicable only to proceedings under special or local law for which a period of time was prescribed in the First Schedule. The appellant, therefore, filed a writ application in the High Court challenging the validity of the provisions of the Limitation act. The High, Court held that the first limb of section 29(1) of the Act was applicable to an application under section 29, and that the first part of section 29 was applicable to a proceeding under special orlocal law. The High. Court held that section 29, clause (2) was applicable to the case and that the words "where any special or local or special law prescribes for any suit or application application a period prescribed for such suit, appeal and application by any special orlocal Law prescribes for such suit appeal or application". The High Court held that in the instant case the provisions contained under section 29(a) were applicable only in a case where a special or local Law prescribes for any such suit, Appeal or application a time of limitation different than the period prescribed by the first Schedule. The High' Court held that as the first limb was not applicable to an assessee under section 29 of the Act, the provisions contained therein were not applicable to a suit, appeal, or application a case where it was not of a kind similar to one for which a prescribed period of limitation was prescribed in that Schedule. The question whether the provisions contained by section 29, clauses (a) and (b) of section 29 were applicable to the cases of the appellant was not considered by the High Court and the High Court was not right in holding that the provisions were applicable to proceedings under the special or local laws for which a time of the prescribed period was prescribed in section 29. The High 'Court was also right in holding, that the provisions made in section 29 were not applicable in a case of a suit, Appeal and Revision.

The appellant, a private bus operator, was a stage carriage operator. He was issued a stage carriage permit on the route, namely, the New Bus Stand of Baldev (Mathura) on the route. The bus was plying on the route from the New Bus stand to the New Bus Depot. The bus operators were directed to stop the bus at the bus stand. The bus operator was directed to stop it at the bus stands. The bus owners filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order passed by the District Magistrate. The High Court held that the bus operators were entitled to ply their buses at the bus-stand. The High court held that the District Magistrate had no jurisdiction to pass an order fixing the area in question as a bus stand. It was further held that the power to compel persons in charge of motor buses to stop the buses at the Bus stand was a matter which relating to motor traffic and that the power of fixing a bus stand was a power to compel the persons in charge thereof to stop the running of the buses at a bus stand and that the District Magis trate had no jurisdiction over the area and therefore, the order passed under section 68(2)(r) of the Act was not open to challenge. The High Cour t was of the view that the District Forum had no jurisdiction. The High Cou rt held that the order passed in the writ petition was not a nullity. The HighCourt held that the decision of the District Forum was not a decision in the eye of law. The High Courts of Punjab and Haryana and Haryana and Chandigarh Administration, respectively, were of the opinion that the District Judge had no jurisdiction in the matter. The High T Court held that in the instant case no order was passed by the Regional Transport Authority, Mathura, and the power to fix a bus stand under section 76 of the Act had not been exercised by the Regional transport Authority. The High F ^ Court held that in view of section 68(1) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939, the power to issue a notification fixing a bus stands was a power of the Regional Transport authority to issue a notified order fixing a bus-stand for the purpose of determining the area in which the bus stands was plying. The High. Court held that there was no power to issue the notification fixing a notified bus stand. In the instant case the High Court held, that the power under section 76(2) of the act was a power not vested in the Regional Transport Author ity and that the order was not a quasi judicial order. The High, Court held that section 68(l) of the said Act was not applicable to the case. The High' Court held that it was not open for the Regional Transport authoriy to pass an ex parte order fixing the notified bus stand for the purpose. The High 'Court held that section 76(l) was not applicable in the case. In the result, the High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1.1 The power to fix the area in respect of a bus stand is a power to be exercised by the State Transport Authority. The power to issue notification fixing a particular area is a power of delegated legislation. [557 C] 1.2 The power to make a notification fixing the area is a quasi judicial power. The power of the State Transport authority to fix a particular area cannot be exercised by it. The power is a power vested in the State Transport Author it has to act in accordance with the provisions of the Act. [558 D] 1.3 The power to frame a notification fixing an area in respect to a bus stand cannot be exercised in the absence of any power to do so. [559 F] 1.4 The power to impose a tax is a power not delegated to the State Transport Authorities.

The appellants were convicted by the trial Magistrate under section 7 of the and the Act for the offence of export of paddy within the meaning of the said section. The appellants were prosecuted for an offence under section 7 read with section 7 of that Act. The trial Magistrate acquitted the appellants of the charge under section 7 and the appellants were convicted of an attempt to commit an offence under the said section and sentenced to pay a fine of Rs. 500. The appellants filed an appeal before the Sessions Judge, Delhi, and the High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellants then filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before this Court for a writ of certiorari quashing the order of the High Court. The High Court quashed the order of acquittal and directed the appellants to pay a sum of Rs. 1,000. The appellants challenged the order of this Court in this Court. The appellants contended that the High Court was not justified in quashing the order passed by the trial court and that the High court was not justified under Article 226 in quashing the proceedings. The High court held that the appellants were guilty of an attempt on the part of the appellants to commit an attempt to export the paddy within the definition of the said Section. The High, Court held that the prosecution was not maintainable under Article 226. The appellants, therefore, filed a petition for a writ in the nature of certiorari quashing that order. The High. Court held that there was no attempt on the side of the appellants by the appellants to committing an attempt to committing an offence under Section 7 read with Section 7 of the Act. The High' Court held that in the absence of any attempt on the appellants to commission of an attempt, the appellants were not guilty of an offence under [section 7] read with section7 of the Act and the High court quashed the order. The appellants have filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts were not justified in exercising their jurisdiction under Article 226 and the High Courts were justified in quashing that order in the circumstances of the case. [775 H] 2. The High-Court was not justified on the facts found by it to exercise its jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution. [776 H] 3. The High Curt was not justified when it quashed the order passed in the proceedings under section 7. [778 H] 4. The HighCourt was not right in quashing the proceeding. [779 H] 4(i) The High Court was justified in quashing a proceeding under section 7, read with section 8 of the Act, and the order of forfeiture passed by the Court was not liable to be quashed on that ground. [780 H] (ii) The High- Court was not right when it quashed a proceeding under Article 226 on the ground that the appellants had an intention to commit an act under section 7 or section 7 readwith section 7 of Act. [782 H] (iii) The High C Court was not wrong in quashing the orders of the trial Magistrate. [785 H] (iv) The High court was wrong in quashing a proceedings under section7 read with section8 of the Act on the ground of an attempt at committing an offence. [786 H] (v) The High Courts had no jurisdiction to quash the proceedings under Article 226, and that the appellants could not be convicted under section 7 for an attempt to do an act under the said Section or section 7 for which the appellants were accused. [787 H] (vi) The High.Court was not wrong when it quashed proceedings under Article 227. [790 H] (vii) The High,Court was not correct in quashing the criminal proceedings under section 406, I.P.C. and the order passed under section 7 was liable to be set aside. [791 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1427 of 1975.

The Managing Agency Agreement was executed on April 1, 1957, and the Managing Agency Agreement provided that the remuneration of the Managing Agency would be paid by the Company to the Managing Agent on the terms and conditions mentioned in the agreement. The Managing Agency Agreement contained a clause that the Managing Agency shall be paid by way of remuneration to the Managing Agency on the terms of the agreement. On the expiry of the agreement the Managing Agency was to receive the entire remuneration of the Company. The Managing Agent was to receive a commission of Rs. 1,000 per month for the entire year of the Managing agency. The Managing Agents were to receive a sum of Rs. 2,000 per annum for the entire period of the Managing Agent's service. The Managing agency was to receive remuneration for the entire term of the Managing Agents service. The remuneration was to be paid by instalments. The Managing Agencies were to receive the remuneration for the period of the managing agency service. The managing agency was to be in the same terms and conditions as the Managing Agency. The Managing agent was to receive his remuneration in the same manner as the Managing Agent. The Managing agents were to receive remuneration in the following terms: "The remuneration of the managing Agency shall be payable by the Company on the terms on which the remuneration was paid by the company to the Managing Agents." The Managing Agency was entitled to receive remuneration from the Company on terms and conditions of the Managing Agencies. The Managing Company was to receive, in the same way, remuneration for the whole year of the managing Agent. The remuneration of the employees was to be fixed by the Managing Agency and the remuneration was to become payable by the company on the terms as to remuneration. The Managing Partner was to receive only the remuneration of his own and not of the year of assignment.
