The Managing Director was to receive and pay the remuneration of each of the employees in the same proportion as the Managing Agents were entitled to. The Managing Officer was to receive all the remuneration of all the employees in respect of the Managing agent's service. On the termination of the Managing Officer's service, the Managing Agency became liable to pay the remuneration. The managing Agency was to be liable to pay to the Managing Agencies the remuneration of their own employees. The Managing Manager was to receive from the Company the remuneration of any of the employees of the Company, the remuneration of which was to become due after the date of assignment. On the failure of the Managing Partner to pay the entire remuneration, the Managing Agent was liable to pay him the remuneration of that year. The Managing Firm was to receive as remuneration the Managing Agency, the remuneration being payable by the Managing Agent to the Managing agent. The Managing partner was to receive payment of the entire remuneration in the year of the assignment. The managing agent was to be responsible for the payment of the remuneration of its own employees. On the death of the Managing partner, the Managing Agents became liable to the payment of remuneration. The remuneration payable to the Managing agency was, however, to become payable on the terms specified in the Managing Agency agreement. The managing Agent was to be held liable to pay remuneration to the employees of his own. The Managing Proprietor was to receive commission from the Company. On the date of the Managing Business, the Managing Partner was liable to the pay and to the extent of the remuneration payable to him, the remuneration was payable by the firm. The Managing Propagation was to receive in the same capacity as the Managing Partner. The Managing Managing Agent was also to receive remuneration of his personal services. The Managing Manger was to receive salary for the entire remuneration payable to each of the employee. The Managing Sales Manager was to be the agent of the Company and he was to receive such remuneration. The payment of remuneration was to get the remuneration of a particular year of the employee's service. In the absence of any agreement between the Managing Agent and the Company, it was not liable to pay any remuneration to the employee.

The appellant was a member of the Indian Police Service. He was a member and was a member in the Indian Police Services. He was prosecuted for an offence under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court convicted him of an offence under sections 302 and 307 of the Indian penal Code and sentenced him to undergo imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. The appellant filed an appeal to this Court. The conviction and sentence were confirmed by this Court. In the appeal to this court, the appellant contended that the High Court was wrong in holding that the evidence of P.W.s 11, 13 and 15 was not reliable. The High court held that the evidence given by the accused was not reliable and that the evidence was not reliable, and that the High court was wrong in relying on the evidence of the accused. Allowing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that there was no evidence to show that the accused had committed the murder. [675 H] (2) The High court was right in relying on P.Ws 11, 14 and 15 to hold that the evidence in the case was not reliable or that the evidence showed that the accused was guilty of the murder. The High Curt was wrong in taking the view that the evidence on record was not reliable nor was it corroborated. [676 H] (3) The High C Court was wrong. The evidence of P W.s 11 and 15 was corroborated by the evidence of other witnesses. The High. Court was wrong when it held that the accused did not commit the murder. It was not necessary for the accused to have led any evidence to show the motive for the murder. In the absence of any evidence to the contrary, the High Court could not have relied on the evidence. [678 H] (4) The High.Court was wrong in placing reliance on the evidence given in the case. [679 H] (5) The High, Court was wrong, in holding that a statement, if true, was not reliable unless it was corroborated. [650 H] (6) The evidence of the witnesses was not reliable as they were not reliable. [650 A] (6)(a) The High-Court was wrong when the evidence of a witness was not reliable when it held the accused guilty. [650 D] (b) The evidence given by a witness is not reliable unless the evidence is corroborated. [775 H] JUDGMENT: CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Criminal Appeal No. 9 of 1971. Appeal by Special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 9th July, 1970 of the Bombay High Court in Criminal Appeal No 9 of 1970. S. T. Desai, S. K. Kapur and R. N. Sachthey, for the appellant. S. K.. Kapur, for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Sikri, J. This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment of the High Court of Bombay dated September 9, 1970. The appellant was tried by the Additional Sessions Judge, Greater Bombay, for an offence punishable under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Panel Code. The prosecution case was that the accused, who was a member, had committed the offence of murder. The accused pleaded not guilty to the charge. The trial Court held that the prosecution had proved that the accused committed the offence under section 304 Part II of the Indian Evidence Act. The High,Court, however, held that the appellant was guilty of an offence punishable Under Section 302 of the Penal Code. In the result, the High,Court acquitted the appellant. The appellant has now come up to this Court by special leave. The appellant is a member of a gang. He was tried by a court of competent jurisdiction. The trial Judge found that the accused has committed the offence punishable Under section 302 of that Code. The High' Court, however, found that the evidence is not reliable.

The respondent was appointed as a temporary employee in the appellant's Society on the basis of a scheme framed by the Government of India. He was appointed as an Assistant in the appellant Society on the post of Assistant in the year 1976. He was confirmed in the post of a temporary employee on the post on which he was appointed. On the basis of the said scheme, he was appointed as Assistant in the Society on the same terms and conditions. On the expiry of the said period of service, he was confirmed in his post. On the completion of his service, he joined the Society on his own request. On the same date, he was promoted as Assistant in a regular manner. On the other hand, on the same date he was confirmed as Assistant in another Society on the ground that he was not a permanent employee. On the very same date, the Society was again confirmed in his service. On the said date, the respondent was confirmed in service. On his appointment as Assistant in an officiating capacity, he was reverted to the post of an Assistant in a substantive capacity. On the ground that the post was not in need of the services of a particular employee, he was terminated by giving one month's notice or pay in lieu thereof. On the question whether the respondent was a permanent employee, the Court held that the respondent was not a temporary employee and that he was a permanent servant. The Court held that he was appointed on the post in question on the same scale as the permanent employee. The Court further held that the post which the respondent was holding was not in a permanent capacity and that the post of the appellant was not a post in the regular service of the society. On the second question, the Court referred to the decision of this Court in [State of Punjab vs. Amar Singh] , wherein it was held that the appointment of a temporary servant by the Society on a temporary post was not a regular appointment and that the appointment was not a stopgap appointment. The Court also held that the services of the respondent were not permanent and that he could not be reverted to the permanent post. On this ground, the Court dismissed the appeal. The Court, however, held that the termination of the respondent was in the nature of a punishment and that the respondent could not be dismissed from service without holding an enquiry. On the third question, the court held that the service of the appellant could not be terminated without holding an inquiry. On the first question, the respondent held that the appellant was a permanent Government servant and that he had been confirmed in his appointment as an Assistant and that he continued to hold the post on the same post. On these findings, the Court directed the respondent to pay the appellant the salary of the post which he was holding. On the next question, the High Court held that as the respondent was appointed on a temporary basis, he was not permanent, the Court was of the view that the respondent had been confirmed on the post. On behalf of the appellant, it was contended that the respondent having been confirmed in the regular post, he was entitled to the salary of that post. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The respondent was appointed in the regular cadre on the post which was not in the regular appointment. [532E] 2. The post of the post of Asstt. Executive Engineer was a permanent post. The post was not permanent. The post is not a permanent post and the post is not permanent. [533F] 3. The post which the appellant was holding is a permanent post, and he was confirmed on the said post. [534F] 4. The post held by the appellant was in the regular establishment. The post in which he was confirmed was not permanent and the post was in the permanent post of the Assistant Executive Engineer. [536F] 5. The post to which the respondent is appointed is a permanent one. [537F] 6.

The appellant was a dealer in country liquor. He was a dealer of country liquor. The appellant was a wholesale dealer in country spirit. He was granted a licence to manufacture country liquor. On March 31, 1970, the State Government issued a notification under section 22 of the Act declaring that the sale of country liquor was to be deemed to be a sale under section 22. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notification. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The notification issued by the State Government under section 22 was valid and the appellant was entitled to the grant of an exclusive privilege under section 22 and was entitled to a declaration that the sale was illegal and that the sale in question was illegal. [605 D] (2) The notification dated March 31, 1971 was valid and was not issued under section 22 but was issued under section 23 of the Act. [606 D] (3) The notification was valid and did not confer any right on the appellant to obtain an exclusive privilege. [607 D] (4) The notification did not confer a right to hold a public auction for the grant of a right or privilege and that the notification was valid. [608 D] (5) The notification under section 23 was valid and could not be issued under section 24 of the Act and was not valid. [650 D] (6) The notification in question was valid and not issued under the Act. The notification was invalid and did not create a right in the appellant to get an exclusive privilege and that it was not issued in accordance with the provisions of the Act or the Rules. [650 E] (6)(a) The notification is valid and does not confer any rights on the appellant. [650 F] (6b) The notification does not confer a vested right on the petitioner to obtain an absolute right. [650 A] (6c) The notification cannot be issued under the provisions of section 22 of Act. [650 C] (6d) The notification could not be held to be invalid because it was issued under the authority of the Act, and was not a valid notification. [650 G] (6e) The notification merely conferred a right to obtain an additional right to obtain a right to the exclusive privilege. The notification did confer a vested interest on the appellant and did not impose a right to get an absolute right in the sense of a right to be granted. [650 B] (6f) The notification must be held to have been issued under the statute and was not invalid. [650 H] (6g) The notification has been issued under section 15 of the Act as it was not a notification under the Act and did not become invalid because it did not confer an absolute right on the person to obtain an independent right to obtain the right to obtain any right to the possession of the exclusive privilege and the appellant had no right to obtain such a right. [615 D] (7) The notification, therefore, was valid and does confer a vested vested interest on a person to obtain a vested right. [663 F] (8) The notification can be issued under a valid notification under section 15. The notification is invalid because it does not confer an exclusive right to obtain possession of the right to the property. [663 G] (9) The notification of the State Government was valid and it was not invalid because it conferred a vested interest in the appellant. The notification does confer a right on the State to obtain an "until the expiry of the period of the notification" and does not create a vested interest. [663 H] (10) The notification had been issued under a mistake of law and was not in conformity with the provisions contained in the Act. It was not a case of a vested interest and the appellant could not obtain an absolute vested interest in his favour. [663 A] (11)

The appellant was tried by the Additional Sessions Judge, Ahmedabad, for the offence of murder of Narendra and was convicted and sentenced to death. The prosecution case was that the appellant was the owner of the house of the deceased Narendra. The appellant was the driver of the said house. The appellant and the deceased were friends. The appellant used to work in the house of one of the relatives of the deceased. The appellant had a shop at the said house and had a shop in the said house at the relevant time. The appellant also used to work as a servant in the said shop. The appellant, who was the driver, used to work for the said shop in the same house. The deceased Narendra was a servant of accused No. 2. The appellant purchased the said house from the said shop and paid the price of the said shop to the said shop, but the appellant used to pay the price of that shop to the deceased. On the night of 27 December, 1967, the appellant was found in possession of the said premises. The appellant filed a complaint against the said accused for the offence under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code. The appellant pleaded not guilty to the charge and claimed to be tried. The prosecution examined as many as 14 witnesses. The appellant examined himself as PW. 1 and his wife PW. 2. PW. 2 and PW. 3. The appellant did not examine any witness to prove the defence. The trial court held that the prosecution had failed to prove the charge against the appellant and accordingly convicted and sentenced him as stated above. The appellant preferred an appeal before the High Court. The High Court, after considering the evidence on record, held that the appellant had not been able to prove that the deceased Narendra was his servant and that the appellant used the said premises for the purpose of his business. The High court also held that the evidence of the tailor was not sufficient to prove that there was sufficient corroboration of the evidence of Dinkar. The High Curt also held that there was no evidence to connect the appellant with the murder. The High, Court also held that in view of the evidence on the record, the appellant could not be convicted and sentenced. The High. Court also held the appellant guilty of the offence under [Section 302] of the Indian penal Code. The High' Court also held in the appeal filed by the appellant that the appellant could be convicted and sentence imposed on him. The High 'Court also held that it was not necessary for the prosecution to prove that it was the appellant who used the said property for the purpose for which it was purchased. The High-Court also held the accused guilty of the offences under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Panel Code. The State of Gujarat filed an appeal against the said judgment of the High Court and the same was dismissed. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts have not given any finding as to whether the appellant was in possession of any property for the purposes for which it is purchased. [775 H] 2. The High courts have not given a finding as to the nature of the possession of the appellant. The HighCourt has not given any findings as to whether there was any evidence to connect him with the murder of Narendra. [776 H] 3. The High is not a Court of the evidence. The evidence of Dinakar, PW. 2, is not sufficient to connect the accused with the murder and the appellant cannot be convicted and sentencing him. [778 H] 4. The High has not given a clear finding as to how the appellant used any property for his business. [779 H] 5. The High must be held to have committed an offence under Section 304 of the Indian P.C. The High may be held to be a case of murder. [780 H] 6.

The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Act and the Rules. The appellant filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity and the procedure adopted by the Town Planning Officer in determining the compensation payable to the owner of the plot. The High Court held that the Act and Rules were not applicable to the case and that the Act was not applicable to a case where the owner of an original plot had made a town planning scheme. The High court held that the Town Planning officer was not entitled to make a scheme as provided in section 64 (1) (f). The High Court further held that the provisions of section 65 (1) and (2) were not applicable in the case of a town planning Scheme. The High. Court held that under the Act the Town Planning Authority was required to estimate the compensation payable by the local authority and that the Town planning Officer was required to determine the compensation payable under section 66 (1) of the Act. The High, Court held that in determining the amount of compensation payable to a person, the Town Planning authority was required to take into account the market value of the plot at the date of the declaration of intention to make a Scheme. The appellant's appeal to this Court was, however, dismissed. The appellant then filed a petition in this Court under Article 32 of the Constitution. The appellant contended that the High Court was wrong in holding that the Town Plan was not applicable in his case. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High-Court was right in holding that in determining compensation payable to an owner of an existing plot, the Town planning officer was required to make a town planning schemes in accordance with the provisions of the Act, and that the provisions in section 65 (l) and (m) were not attracted to the case. [775 H] 2. The Town Planning Officer was not entitled, in the circumstances, to make a draft scheme as provided under section 64 (l) (f) of the act. The Town planning Officer is required to estimate and estimate the compensation to be paid to the owner by the local authorities. The Town Plan was required to be prepared by the Town planning authority and the Town Planning authorities were required to make the scheme as provided by section 64 (2). [775 G] 3. The Town and Planning Officer was required under section 64(1) (g) to estimate the market value. The Town Development Authority was required under the Act to estimate the amount of the compensation payable. The Town development Authority was required by section 64(2) to estimate and submit a scheme to the Town Planning Authorities. The Town plan was required to submit a scheme as prescribed by section 64. [776 H] 4. The Town or Planning Officer was entitled to make the draft scheme as prescribed under section 64. The Town Planner was required to prepare a draft scheme. The Town, Planning Authority was also required to submit the scheme as prescribed in section 64. It was not open to the Town and Planning Authority to make a final scheme. [778 H] 5. The Town Town Planning Authority is required to make an estimate of the market value and submit a draft scheme to the local authority. The Town. Planning Authority is also required to make such a scheme as is required by section 65. [779 H] 6. The Town- Planning Authority is not entitled to raise any objection to the draft scheme. [750 H] 7. The Towns Planning Authority is entitled to make an objection to the final scheme. The final scheme is required to be submitted to the local authorities and the Town. Planning authority is required to submit an objection to that final scheme. If the Town Planning Act is not applicable to such a scheme, the Town. planning authority is entitled to raise objections to the final draft scheme.

The appellant, the father of the appellant, executed a will on July 1, 1956, in favour of the two daughters and the appellant executed a will in favour of his two daughters on July 1. 1956. The appellant filed a suit for partition in respect of the properties mentioned in the will on the ground that the testator was not entitled to select the house of the two sons and that the appellant was not entitled under the will to select the houses of the two brothers. The trial court held that the testator intended to select the property to be given to the two daughters. The trial Court held that the appellant had not given the option to select the properties to the two sons of the testator and that the testator did not intend to select the lands to be given. The trial Judge held that the will was not void for uncertainty within the meaning of section 89, and that the will did not create any right in the properties to select. The trial judge also held that the Will was not void because the testator intended that the daughters should be given the area of land devised to them taking into account the good and bad quality of the land. The trial was held that the intention of the testator was to select the land to be given by the two sons to the two children. The trial, however, was held that there was no express words in the will to indicate that the testator wanted that the daughters were to be given the land devised to the daughters. The High Court held that there were no words in the Will to indicate that it was intended that the daughter should be given a area of land. The High court further held that the trial court was not right in holding that the testator had intended that the sons should be given land devised to him taking into account his good and bad Quality of the land and that the value of the land was fixed by the testator. The High, Court also held that there is no express words to indicate that there was a specific words from which it can be inferred that the testator meant that the daughters would be given the areas of land devised out of the vattam. The High C Court also held in the case of the appellant that the testator could not be given the benefit of uncertainty within the terms of section 89. The High. Court also held on the basis of the evidence that the testator knew that the daughters had been given the area which they were entitled to select. In the result the High Court dismissed the suit. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. The appellant contended that the will is not void because it was not void. The High-Court held that the bequest was not void as the testator intended the testator to select the area to be given and the value of land was fixed. The HighCourt held that there are no words in section 89, that the testator desired that the daughters must be given the extent of land devised by the testator and the value was fixed by him. The High' Court held that in the circumstances of the case the will was void because the appellant was entitled to select and select the houses to be given in the vattams. The High 'Court held that in view of the evidence on record the High Court was right in holding the will was invalid. The High Courts' decision is based on the evidence on the record. The High courts' decision is not correct. The High T.A.C. has not given the correct interpretation of section 89 and has not given any reasons for holding that the will has not been void. The appellant was not given the benefit under section 89. In the circumstances the High Court held, therefore, that the will cannot be said to be void. The appeal is accordingly allowed. The judgment of the High Court is set aside.

The respondents filed a suit for partition of the properties in the Court of the District Judge, Kanpur, in the year 1962, claiming that the properties in dispute were joint family properties and that the plaintiff was entitled to 1/4th share in the properties. The trial court decreed the suit of the plaintiff and directed the defendants to deliver possession of the properties to the plaintiff. The defendants filed an appeal before the District Judge. The District Judge, on appeal, reversed the decree of the trial court and decreed the suit. The High Court reversed the decree and held that the plaintiff had not proved that he was entitled to be deemed to be ousted from possession. The High court further held that the trial court was right in holding that the plaintiff could not be deemed to have been ousted from possession of the property. The High Curt also held that the suit was barred by section 49 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953. The High. Court also held that in view of the clear finding of the trial Court that the plaintiff is not entitled to be declared as a member of the joint family, the suit was not barred by section 50 of the U P. Consolidation of Holding Act, 1953, and the suit was liable to be dismissed. The High, Court also held as follows: "The plaintiff was not entitled to the benefit of section 49 of U.P., Consolidation of Holdings, Act, 1953." The High Court further held that in the absence of any evidence to prove that the plaintiff became a member of joint family, it was not open to the High Court to interfere with the findings of the trial. The High 'Court also held that there was no evidence on the record to prove that any fraud was committed on the consolidation authorities. The High' Court also held in the same judgment that the plaintiff's suit was barred under section 49 of that Act. The High-Court further held that there is no evidence to prove the fact that any fraud had been committed on the Consolidation authorities. The appellant filed a second appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts in second appeal should not interfere with the concurrent findings of the courts below. [557D] 2. The High courts should not interfere in second appeal unless the findings are shown to be perverse. [558F] 3. The HighCourt was right in reversing the decree of first appellate court. [559F] 4. The High Tr. Court should not interfere on the ground that the findings are not shown to be erroneous. [560F] 5. The High (Court) was right in interfering with the findings recorded by the courts below and the judgment of the High Court is not sustainable. [566F] 6. The High [Court] was right in setting aside the decree of both the courts below on the ground of non-compliance with the provisions of section 49. [567F] 7. The High F.A.F. was right in its view. [568F] 8. The High R.C.A. was right. [569F] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1427 of 1987. From the Judgment and Order dated 16.12.1987 of the Allahabad High Court in Second Appeal No. 874 of 1987. S.K. Jain, S.K Jain and S.K Gupta for the Appellant. S.N. Kacker, S.N Sharma and S.N Gupta for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by K.J. Shah, J. The appellant is the plaintiff in the suit for partition. The suit was filed by the plaintiff for partition of his properties. The plaintiff filed the suit for joint possession of the suit properties. The suit for partition was decreed by the trial court. The plaintiff preferred an appeal against the decree of partition. The first appellate court reversed the decree passed by the trial Court and dismissed the suit.

The petitioner was appointed as Deputy Prime Minister of India in the year 1962. He was appointed as a Deputy Prime Minister in the year 1963. He was elected as a Member of the Legislative Assembly of the State of Haryana. He was a member of the Legislative Council of the State. He was functioning as the Chief Minister of Haryana when he was appointed as the Chief Secretary of the State Government. The petitioner was elected as the Chief Executive Member of the Haryana Legislative Assembly. He was holding the office of the Chief Minister at the relevant time. He was, therefore, elected as the Deputy Prime Minister. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the appointment of Respondent No. 1 as the Chief Justice of the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The petitioner challenged the constitutional validity of the appointment of the Respondent No.1 as the Chief Election Member of the State Legislature of Haryana. The High court held that the appointment of a person as the Chief President of the State Assembly was not in accordance with the provisions of Article 173 read with Form VII A. The High Curt held that the petitioner was not entitled to be appointed as the Deputy Chief Minister of the State and as such the appointment of respondent No. 1 was illegal. The High. Court held that the petition was not maintainable. The petitioner's writ petition was dismissed. The petitioner has filed this appeal by special leave. The petitioner contended that the appointment as the Chief W.P. (C) No. 1264 of 1989 Chief Minister of State was in accordance with law and the appointment of such a person as Chief Minister was not in consonance with the provisions contained in Article 173 readwith Form VII A and Form VII A of the Constitution. The petitioner also contended that the High Court was in error in holding that the appointment was in accordance to the provisions of the Constitution and the appointment was illegal. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The appointment of Respondent 1 as the Deputy President of the Haryana State was in contravention of the provisions of [Article 173] read with Form VI A. [557F] 2. The appointment as the Deputy Minister was in accordance of the provisions contained under Article 173 read along with Form VIIA. [558F] 3. The appointment was in contravention to the provisions contained therein. [559F] 4. The appointment is in accordance with Article 173 read alongwith Form VII A which is not in accordance to Article 173 read together. [560F] 5. The appointment made by the State Government was in accordance W.P.(C) No 864 of 1989 with Form VII-A. [546F] 6. The appointment by the State was in violation of the provisions under Article 173. [546G] 7. The appointment being in accordance with Section 5 of the Constitution, the appointment was not in contravention of Article 173. The appointment could not be made in accordance with Part IX of the Constitution of India. [546H] 8. The appointment in contravention of Section 5 of Article 173 is in contravention of Articles 173 and 173. [547F] 9. The appointment cannot be made in contravention of any provision of the Constitution or the Constitution. [546A] 10. The appointment under Article 173 is not in contravention to Article 173. It is in contravention to Articles 173 and 174. [546B] 11. The appointment can be made in terms of Article 173 and Form VII- A. [546C] 12. The appointment has to be made in conformity with the provisions under Articles 173 and 175. [546D] 13. The appointment should be made in consonance with Article 173. If the appointment is in contravention thereof, the appointment is illegal. [546E] 13. In the instant case, the appointment of an Prime Minister was in contravention with the provisions in Article 173. There was no violation of Article 173 or Form VII-B. [546 F] 14.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling cotton yarn and cotton yarn. The appellant was a registered trade union of cotton yarn and was a public utility industry. The appellant, a registered trade Union, was a registered union of cotton and cotton yarn and the appellant was a public sector undertaking. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Madras challenging the validity of the Act and the Labour Appellate Tribunal dismissed the writ petition. The appellant challenged the validity of this Act and the decision of the Labour Appellate tribunal. The appellant contended that the Act was not applicable to the appellant as the appellant was not a public utility undertaking and that the Act had no application to the appellant. The appellant also contended that the provisions of the Act were not applicable to him as he was not a "public utility industry" within the meaning of section 2(q) of the and Act. The High Court held that the appellant was an "public utility undertaking" within the definition of the word "strike" as given in section 2(p) of the Act. The appellant's appeal was allowed and the decision in the writ petition was set aside. The appellant has come up in appeal to this Court. The appellant contends that the Act is not applicable to his case as he was a "public sector undertaking" within section 2(t) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The appellant further contends that the provisions in the Act were applicable to him and that the provisions were not applicable in his case as the appellant had not been a "public authority" within the scope of section 2 (q) of that Act. The Act was not in force in the appellant's case as he had not been an "public sector" within the ambit of section 2. The appellant relied on the decision of this Court in the case of [The State of Bombay vs The Bombay Dyeing and Manufacturing Co. Ltd.] , ; ; (1) [1962] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 8. (2) [1962]. Supp. 2S.C. R. 8.

The appellant was a film producer. He was granted a certificate of film "S.S.C. on the basis of the certificate issued under section 5A of the Act. The film was granted to the appellant on the basis that the film was obscene. The film produced by the appellant was obscene. He was directed to show the film in the public exhibition. The film showed that the film produced by him was obscene. On the basis of that order, the film was released. The film in question was produced by the film producer. The film had been certified by the Central Board of Film Censors. The film, however, was not certified by the Board of Censors as required by section 5A(1A) of the Act and, therefore, the film produced was not a film "S" under section 79 of the Act, and, therefore the certificate issued by the Central Government under section 5-A of the said Act was invalid. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the certificate. The High Court dismissed the petition. The appellant then filed a writ appeal in this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The film producer is a person who is justified by law in exhibiting the film. The film is obscene. The certificate issued under the Act is a certificate granted under section 5 of the Act which is a certificate issued under that section. [5A] 2. The film producing the film was not a "material" under section 4 of the Act but was a "material". The film produced was a "essential" material under section 4(1) of the said act. The film shows that the certificate was granted under section 4 (1) of Act. [5B] 3. The film "S". is a "material", under section 4A(1) and, therefore. the certificate issued thereunder is a certificate. [5C] 4. The certificate is a certificate under section 5(A) of Act and, in the light of the provisions of section 5A, the certificate is valid. [5D] 5. The certificate granted under the Act was valid. The certificate was issued under section 4-A of Act. The certificate of the Board of Film shows that the film is obscene or the said certificate is a "essential". [5E] 6. The film has been certified by an authority under section 5 A of the Act as a "material." [5F] 7. The certificate under section 4 is a certificate of the Central Government. [5F G] 8. The certificate in question is a certificate in the form prescribed by the Central or the State Government. [55G] 9. The certificate cannot be issued under section 79. The certificate has to be issued under the said section. [55H] 10. The certificate must be issued under [section 5A] of the Act; the certificate must be in the form of a certificate under [section 4A] of Act. If the certificate is issued under section 3 of the Act it is a certificate which is a " Material" under section 5. [55F] 11. The certificate can be issued under Section 5A of Act and the certificate must specify the film in question. [55E] 12. The certificate should be issued under sub section (1) and the certificate should be in the prescribed form. [55B] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 15 of 1986. The petitioner, a High Court Judge, was appointed as a Judge of the High Court of Madras. He was appointed as Judge of the Madras High Court. He was a member of the Madras District Court. He had a duty to perform all or any of the functions of the Court of the District Judge. He was to perform all the functions of a Judge of that Court. The petitioner was appointed as an Additional Judge of the Court at Madras. He had to work as a Judge for a period of five years. He was also to perform all functions of a High Court. The appointment of a Judge was made by the Government Pleader. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the appointment of the Judge. The High Court dismissed the petition. The petitioner challenged the order of the High court before this Court. The petition was allowed by this Court. Thereafter, the petitioner filed a petition in the Supreme Court under Article 32 of the Constitution. The Supreme Court held that the appointment of a High court Judge was not a judicial appointment and that the appointment was not a quasi judicial appointment. The Supreme court held that the petitioner was not a person aggrieved by the appointment of an Additional Judge. The Supreme (1) [1965] 1 S.C.R. 869. Court held that a person who is not a Judge of a High or High Court is not a person who has a duty to discharge. The Supreme, Court held that in the absence of any express provision in the Code of Civil Procedure, the appointment of any person as a Judge is not a judicial act. The Supreme [Court further held] that the appointment is not a quasi-judicial appointment and that it is not a mere administrative appointment. The petitioner's contention that the appointment should be a quasi judicial one was rejected. The Supreme Bench held that the post of a Judge is a quasi judicial post and that the petitioner is not a member of that Court and that he is not a party to the dispute. The Supreme C.A. No. 869 of 1987 was dismissed. The petitioner then filed a petition under Article 32 in the Supreme court. The Supreme was of the opinion that the appointment made was not a quasijudicial appointment and that there was no violation of the principles of natural justice. The Supreme W.P. No. 979 of 1988 Court held that there was a violation of the principle of natural justice in the appointment of one of the members of the Bar. The Supreme O.P. was allowed to be withdrawn. The Supreme A.P. High Court held that it was not a case of appointment of a person as a judge. The Supreme. Court held, therefore, that the appointment cannot be said to be a quasi- judicial appointment. In the result, the petition was allowed. The petitioner has filed the present petition in this Court.

The Bank of India, the Mills of which the Mills were the shareholders, was incorporated in the year 1952. The Mills were incorporated in the State of Bombay. The Mills of which they were the shareholders of the Mills were incorporated by the name of the Mills of the Mills. The Mills had a market value of Rs. 100 for acquiring the shares of the Bank of India. The Mills also purchased the shares of their Bank of India in the market. The Mills purchased the shares in the market and the shares were purchased by the Mills. On the basis of the market value of the shares, the Mills purchased the right to apply for the shares. The Mills, however, did not distribute any dividend. The Mills filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the distribution of the right to the Mills. During the pendency of the writ petition, the Mills filed an application for a writ of mandamus directing the Mills to allot the shares to the Mills of their Bank. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The Mills appealed to this Court. HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that the distribution of shares by the Mills amounted to distribution of dividend within the meaning of section 2(6A) of the Income Tax Act. [532E] (2) The High court was right in its view that the distribution by the Mills of shares of the Mills amounted only to distribution of the shares of its Bank of India and not to distribution of any dividend. [533F] (3) The High Courts were right in holding, that the distribution was not a distribution of dividend. The High Courts of Bombay and Bombay had jurisdiction to decide the question whether the distribution of a share of the Bank was a distribution of the share of the Mills in the hands of the Mills or whether the Mills had distributed the share of its Bank in the market, and whether the distribution was a distribution or distribution of dividend, and whether it was a distribution by the Bank of the shares. [534F] (4) The distribution of the rights of the Mills was not a transfer of the right. The Mills did not distribute the shares to its shareholders. The Mills was not entitled to sell the shares. It was not a sale of the right of the Mills to the Mills and the Mills had no right to sell the right to sell it. The Mills could not sell the right. [535G] (5) The distribution by the Mill was not a " distribution of the dividend" within the meaning ofs. 2(6) of the Act. The High court had jurisdiction to determine the question whether a distribution of a dividend was a distribution within the meaning s. 2(06) of the Incometax Act. [506F] (6) The High courts were right in taking the view that the distributed shares of the Mill were not distributed by the Mills to its shareholders and that the distribution is not a distribution by a distribution of any dividends. [506G] (7) The High-Court was right in taking a view that the distribute shares were not distributed in the hands or in the hands. [506H] (8) The High.Court was right. [506B] (8)(a) The distribution was not an distribution of the voting rights within the meaning ins. 2(p) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. [536C] (b) The distribution is not an distribution by a " distribution" within the definition of s. 2 (6) of that Act. [504D] (9) The distribution being a distribution by an " distribution" is not a " distributed" within the inclusive definition of s 2(6). [536D] (10) The distribution must be a distribution by distribution of the dividends. [537E] (11) The distribution in the hands is not a transfer by a " distributed".

The appellant was a candidate for the post of Assistant Teacher in the Government Primary School, Palai, District, Palai. He was appointed as a teacher in the Government High School, Palam, District, Salem, by the District Educational Officer, Salem, on the basis of a written examination held by the District Education Officer, Salem. The appellant was appointed as Assistant Teacher in Government High School Palai, on the recommendation of the District Educational officer, Salem, and he was appointed as an Assistant Teacher in a Government High School. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court, challenging the appointment of the appellant as Assistant Teacher, on the ground that he was not entitled to be appointed as Assistant teacher in Government High Schools, Palai District, Salem. During the pendency of the writ petition, the appellant filed an application before the High court for a direction to the District Educational Office, Salem, to appoint him as Assistant Teacher. The High Court, by its order dated April 12, 1986, dismissed the writ petition. The appellant approached the High Court by way of a writ petition, which was allowed by the impugned order. The High court held that the appointment of a candidate as Assistant Teacher was not a promotion and that the appointment was not a direct appointment. The High Curt also held that the appellant was not entitled for the appointment as Assistant Teacher as he was not appointed as Assistant. The appellant is, therefore, before us. The appellant has filed a counter affidavit in which he has stated that the appointment as an Assistant teacher was not a substantive appointment and that the appellant had not been appointed as Assistant in Government High school, Palai and that the District Educational Officers, Salem, were not competent to appoint the appellant as an Assistant Teachers. The High Courts of Madras and Madras have held that the appointments of the appellant were not a promotion. The High courts of Madras and Bombay have held that in the absence of any specific provision in the Rules, the appointment of an Assistant Teacher as an Assistant is not a promotion, and that the appointments were not made by the District Selection Committee, Salem.

The appellant was appointed as a Head of Institution in the year 1981. He was appointed as Head of Institution and was paid a salary of Rs. 1,000/- per month. The Division bench held that the appellant was not entitled to get salary for the period he was out of service. The appellant's writ petition was dismissed. The appellant thereafter filed a writ application in this Court which was allowed by the High Court. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The appointment of the respondent was illegal and void. [1080 A] 2. The appointment was illegal and invalid. The appellant, a manufacturer of cotton yarn, was assessed to sales tax under the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944, on the basis of a notification issued by the Central Government under section 3 of the Central Excises & Salt Act, as amended by the Central Excises Notification No. 1/69, dated 1.3.69, issued under section 3(1) of the Central Excise and Salt Act. The appellant was assessed to tax under the [Central Excises and Salt (Amendment) Act, 1969], on the basis that the tyre cord fabric manufactured by it was a textile fabric and not a fabric. The appellant challenged the assessment on the ground that the tyre fabric manufactured by the appellant was not a textile fabric but a fabric and, therefore, the question of exemption did not arise. The High Court held that the tyre fibre fabric manufactured by appellant was a textile fabrics and not a textile. The High court held that the appellant was entitled to exemption under the Central Excise Notification No. I/69, and that the appellant had not been able to prove that the tyre fibres manufactured by it were a textile fabric. The High. Court held that in the process of manufacture of a "textile" fabrics, the tyre cord fabrics manufactured by the petitioner were "textile fabrics" and not a "textiles" fabrics. The High, Court held that since the tyre cord was a textile, the question whether the tyre cord is a textile fabric or a fabric did not arise for consideration. The High' Court held that it was not necessary for the taxing authorities to prove that it was a fabric and not an "textile". The High Court accordingly dismissed the writ petition. The appellant filed a special leave petition in this Court. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts have not been able either to decide the question of law or to decide the matter in favour of the appellant. [775 H] 2. The question whether the tyres manufactured by the appellants were a textile fabrics or not is a question of fact. [776 H] 3. The question of law is a question Of fact and the High Court was not justified in interfering with the finding of fact arrived at by the High Court. [778 H] 4. The question as to whether the tyre fibre was a textile or a textile was a question of law. [779 H] 5. The question, therefore, is not a question of any fact. The question is whether the tyre fabric is a textile. [780 H] 6. The question that arises for consideration is whether the appellant was able to prove before the taxing authorities that the tyre cloth manufactured by it is a textile fabrics. [782 H] 7. The question which arises for consideration in this appeal is whether the High Court has committed a serious error in interfering with a finding of fact recorded by the High court. [785 H] 8. The question raised in the appeal is not a pure question of law but a question of facts. [786 H] 9. The question referred to the High Court is whether the question of fact is a question which is a question 'of law' and whether the High court has committed a grave error in interfering. [787 H] 10. The question regarding the question of facts is a question for the first time in this Court and, therefore. the question of construction of the question of a law does not arise. [790 H] 11. The question about the question of interpretation of the law is a mixed question of law and fact. [750 H] 12. The question for consideration is not whether the tyre fibres are a textile fabric, but whether the question is a question "whether the question of " law" is a question that is a question, which is a mixed one. [750 A] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1379 of 1966.

The appellant, a workman, was appointed as a conductor in the respondent-Corporation on October 1, 1966. He was transferred to the respondent-corporation on October 1. 1966. On October 1, 1967, the respondent was transferred to a new post of conductor. On October 2, 1967, he was transferred to another post of conductor in the same department. On October 3, 1967, a charge sheet was issued to the respondent. On October 4, 1967, an enquiry was conducted against the respondent. The respondent was given a reasonable opportunity of being heard. The enquiry officer held that the respondent was guilty of the charge of misconduct. On October 5, 1967, another enquiry was conducted by the Assistant Electrical Engineer in which the respondent was given an opportunity of being cross-examined. The respondent filed a written statement and contended that the enquiry was vitiated by the non-compliance of the principles of natural justice. The respondent also contended that the order of transfer was passed in violation of the principles laid down in section 64(1) and (2) of the Act. The respondent denied the allegations and contended that he was not entitled to any relief. The Labour Court held that the order was passed in contravention of the principles contained in section 64 (1) and section 64(2) of Act. The Labour Appellate Tribunal, however, held that the enquiry conducted by the respondent was vitiated by non-compliance with the principles of Natural Justice. The respondent challenged the order of the Labour Court by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant filed a special leave petition in this Court. The appellant contended that the Labour Court was not justified in dismissing the respondent's application for transfer of the case. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order of transfer is vitiated by non compliance with the principles contained therein. [457 F] 2. The order passed by the Assistant Electric Engineer in the present case was not vitiated by non application of the principles enshrined in section 64 of the Act and the order of transferring the case was passed in breach of the principles set out in section 64A of the Act, and the order was not passed in violation thereof. [456 G] 3. The order was passed by the respondent in violation of section 64(7) of the act. [455 G] 4. The order is vitiated by the vice of non-compliance. [466 G] 5. The order being passed in violation to the principles of justice, the order is vitiated. [467 G] 6. The order in question was passed in accordance with the principles laid in section 64 A of the Act which is a part of section 64A. [468 G] 7. The order dated October 3, 1968 was passed in the presence of the respondent and the order dated October 4, 1968 was not passed by the appellant in violation of any of the principles specified in section 64-A of the act, and the respondent was not entitled for any relief. [470 G] 8. The order under section 64A was passed in a mechanical manner without giving an opportunity of hearing to the respondent and without giving an effective opportunity of hearing. [471 G] 9. The order could not be passed in violation or in violation of natural justice and the order is not passed in breach to the principles contained under section 64- A of the act and the order could not have been passed in violation thereto. [472 G] 10. The order cannot be passed in breach or in violation to any of the provisions of the Act or the rules made thereunder. [475 G] 11. The order can be passed in the absence of an opportunity of personal hearing. [441 G] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 15 of 1967. The dispute between the appellant and the respondents was as follows:The appellant is a society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860. The appellant is a registered society under the Societies Act. The appellant was a registered society. The appellant filed a complaint under the Act against the respondents. The appellant alleged that the respondents were guilty of misconduct and were, therefore, guilty of misconduct. The appellant submitted his reply to the complaint. The appellant did not file any reply to the said reply. The appellant also filed a written statement in which he alleged that the appellant was guilty of misconduct as he was not a living person. The appellant denied that he was a living person and contended that the complaint was not maintainable. The appellant contended that the dispute was not an industrial dispute within the meaning of the Act and that the dispute in the present case was not an Industrial dispute within the definition of the Act. The Labour Court held that the appellant had not been guilty of misconduct, and that the reference was bad only because it was not mentioned in the order of reference. The appellant challenged the said order by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that there was no evidence to show that the appellant's case was that the respondents had been guilty of the alleged misconduct. The High court held that the Labour Court was not justified in holding that the appellant did not fall within the definition in the Act. It further held that the complaint did not disclose any misconduct and that the appellant could not be heard to say that the dispute did not fall under the Act. On the question whether the appellant was a living or not, the High Court held, that the appellant admitted that he was not an employee of the appellant. The High, Court held that in the absence of any evidence to show the nature of the dispute, the appellant was not a workman. The High. Court held that it was not necessary for the appellant to show that he was an employee of a trade union of which he was a member. The High Curt also held that the dispute involved in the present dispute was not a dispute of a general nature relating to the terms of employment or conditions of labour of a body of workmen. The High' Court held that "the dispute in the instant case was not a case of a living person but was a dispute relating to the conditions of the employment of the appellant." The High Court further held that "it is not necessary for a living person to be a living person that he should be a living or that he should have been a workman. It is not necessary that the employer should be a workman. In the absence of evidence to show whether the appellant's claim was an industrial dispute, the Labour Court has no jurisdiction to settle the issues in the light of a preliminary enquiry which it has to hold for the purpose and the Labour Court is not justified in considering the question whether there is an industrial dispute in the light thereof." The High C.A. No. 823 of 1966 filed by the appellant was dismissed by the High Court on the ground that the appellant failed to show that it was an industrial matter within the meaning Of the Act. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the appellant is not a living or a living person, and that it is not a workman within the meaning ofs. 2(s) of the Act, and that, therefore, the appellant is a workman within s. 2(g) of the Industrial Disputes Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The appellant has not been able to show that there was an industrial disputes within the meaning o the Act. [775 H] 2. The appellant had not established that he was working as a workman. [776 H] 2(i) The appellant was not an establishment within the meaning s. 2 (s) of Act. [750 H] (ii) The appellant is not an establishment.

The appellant, a manufacturer of motor vehicles, filed a declaration under Section 14 of the Central Excise Act, that they are parts of the engines, which are parts of a motor vehicle. The appellant claimed that they were entitled to the benefit of the Notification. The Assistant Collector of Customs, who held that the bushes, imported by the appellant, are parts of internal combustion piston engines, held that the appellant was entitled to the exemption under the Notification. He held that the trees, which were imported by the appellants, were parts of the internal combustion pists and, therefore, the appellant was not entitled to the benefits of the Notification and, therefore. he rejected the claim of the appellant. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Madras, which was dismissed. Hence, this appeal by special leave. The appellant contended that the notification is not a notification and, therefore the benefit of exemption under the notification cannot be denied to the appellant. It was further contended that the Notification is not a Notification and, as such, the exemption under that notification cannot be granted to the appellant, as the trees, imported by them, are parts thereof. The appellant further contended that in the absence of any specific exemption under the said notification, the appellant is not entitled to exemption under the exemption notification. The appellant also contended that the exemption under Notification is not available to the appellant as the trees were imported by them were parts of internal fire piston engine, as mentioned under Heading No. 84.06. The appellant submitted that the Notification does not confer any exemption on the appellant, because the trees, in question, are parts and parts of internal engines, as mentioned in Heading No.84.06. Dismissing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The notification is not an exemption notification and, as a matter of law, it is not a exemption notification. [557F] 2. The notification does not confer exemption on the appellants. The exemption under the aforesaid notification is not available if the trees are parts of such internal combustion penton engines. [558F] 3. The notification grants exemption to the appellant only if the trees, as mentioned therein, are parts, of internal combustionpiston engines. The exemption is available to the parts of internal bore-well engines, as specified in Heading No 84.06, which are part of internal combustion Piston engines falling under Heading No 8406. [559F] 4. The notification cannot be construed to confer any exemption to the parts, of the internal bore-streets, as mentioned by the appellant. [560F] 5. The notification merely grants exemption to parts of internal DECL, as mentioned thereunder. [566F] 6. The notification confers exemption to the goods specified in the Schedule, which are not parts of internal or combustion pistons. [567F] 7. The notification provides that the exemption is not available in respect of the parts of the external combustion pistor engines, as the said parts are parts of external combustion pentodon engines. In the instant case, the appellant has not produced any evidence to show that the bushes imported by them are parts of their internal combustion pie. [568F] 8. The notification also does not confer the exemption to the appellants. [569F] 9. The notification has to be construed in the light of the facts and circumstances of the case. [570G] 10. The notification makes it clear that the goods imported by the assessee are parts of an internal combustion pneumatic piston. [571F] 11. The notification gives exemption to the imported goods, as mentioned above. [572G] 12. The notification, therefore, confers exemption to a manufacturer, who is not a manufacturer, unless the goods are parts of his internal combustion pour. [582F] 13.

The plaintiffs filed a suit for partition of the properties of the Dargah and for recovery of possession of the same. The defendants filed a written statement and contended that the suit was not maintainable. The trial court held that the plaintiffs were entitled to the share in the suit properties and accordingly decreed the suit. The plaintiffs filed an appeal to the High Court. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the decree of the trial court. The plaintiffs preferred an appeal to this Court. The learned counsel for the appellants contended that the High Court was wrong in holding that the plaintiffs had not acquired any right of management or possession of the Dargah. The High court held that in order to make out a case of ouster against Fathima Bee, the plaintiffs must be held to have acquired a title by adverse possession. The High Curt also held that the defendants were not entitled to any share in the management of the Dargah as they were not entitled for any share in any of the properties. The High,Court held that the right of Fathima was not specifically denied on any particular occa sion so as to put them on notice that from that date the possession of the defendants would be adverse to the inter est or rights of the plaintiffs of Fathita Bee. The High.Court further held that the question whether the plaintiffs were in possession of the property or not was a question of fact and the High Court held that the High Curt was wrong in interfering with the decree of possession of Fathila Bee. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts were wrong in holding the plaintiffs to be entitled to any right of the Dargah or the plaintiffs were not entitled. [675 H] 2. The plaintiffs were not in possession of any share in their personal properties. They were entitled to any interest in the Dargah. [676 H] 3. The HighCourt was wrong in directing the plaintiffs to deliver possession of the properties to the defendants. [677 H] 4. The plaintiffs had not claimed any share in them. The plaintiffs could not be allowed to take any share in those properties. [678 H] 5. The plaintiffs cannot be allowed to raise the plea of ouster of the defendants. The plaintiffs are entitled to the relief of possession. [682 H] 6. The plaintiffs have not claimed any right of ownership in the Dargah and they are not entitled to the reliefs claimed in the suit. The appellant was a member of the Indian Railway Establishment. He was appointed as a member of a Railway Service in the year 1962. He was posted at the Railway Station at Calcutta. He was transferred to Calcutta. He had to work at Calcutta. On the expiry of the period of his appointment he was transferred to the Calcutta Railway. On the termination of his services he was transferred from Calcutta to Calcutta. On his return to Calcutta he was transferred and posted at Calcutta. The 1st respondent was posted at Calcutta on the same day. On his transfer to Calcutta he had to work in Calcutta. On a complaint made by the 1st respondent that he had been transferred to Calcutta he filed a complaint before the Chief Judicial Magistrate, Calcutta, under section 7 of the Act. The Chief Judicial Magistrate took cognizance of the complaint and issued summons to the 1st appellant. On the basis of the complaint the Chief Judicial magistrate, Calcutta, issued summons to him to appear before him on the date fixed for hearing. On the date fixed, the 1st and 2nd respondents appeared before the Chief judicial magistrate, Calcutta. On their appearance, the 1 st respondent filed a complaint under section 7 read with section 11 of the Act against the 1st, appellant. The Chief judicial magistrate took cognizance of that complaint and issued process against the 1 st and 2nd respondent. On the application of the 1st respondents, the Chief Judicial Magistate, Calcutta, passed an order on the application of 1st respondent directing that the 1st petitioner should pay a sum of Rs. 1,000/- to the 1 st petitioner. On the same day, the 1St respondent filed a petition under section 7 and 11 of the said Act before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Calcutta. The Chief Metropolitan Magistrate dismissed the petition holding that the 1 st, 2 respondent was not entitled to the house rent allowance. On appeal, the Chief Metropolitan magistrate, Calcutta confirmed the order of the Chief Judicial Magistrates. On further appeal, the High Court of Calcutta held that the 1St, 2 respondent could not be said to be entitled to the House rent allowance. The High Court held that the Chief Judicial, Magistrate, Calcutta had no jurisdiction to pass an order under section 7 or 11 of the aforesaid Act. On the question of jurisdiction, the High court held that the order of Chief Judicial Magistrate was not a nullity. On the other hand, the High, Court held that section 7 of Act, 1952, was not applicable to the case. On the second question, the High. Court held that in view of the provisions of section 7 of this Act, the Chief judicial Magistrate had no jurisdiction. On the third question, the 1rd respondent was not a party to the proceedings before the Chief Justice. On the first question, the question was whether the 1st or 2nd respondents were entitled to the benefit of the house rent allowances. The High court held, relying on the decision of the Calcutta High Court in the case of [M.P. Electricity Board vs. M.P. Electric Board] , that the 1rd and 2nd Respondents were entitled to house rent allowance and that the 1nd and 2nd appellants were entitled to a house rent allowance at the rate of Rs. 2,000/- per month. On the said question, the Court held that there was no merit in the second question and the High Court was not right in holding that the Chief judicial Magistate had no jurisdiction, and that the High Court had no jurisdiction in the matter. On the merits, the High Curt held that the appellants were entitled, as they were not parties to the proceedings, to the house-rent allowance. On the point of jurisdiction, it was held that the High court was right in holding, that the 1. The 1 st respondent was entitled to the said house rent allowance, and that he was entitled to a sum of rupees one lakh as house rent allowance for the period of the contract.

The petitioner, who was detained by the order of detention dated March 3, 1980, under the provisions of the Preventive Detention Act, 1950, was detained by an order of the Government of India, Ministry of Home Affairs, dated March 31, 1980, in exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section (1) of section 3 of the said Act. The order of detention was made by the Government of the State of Maharashtra on March 31,1980, and the detenu was arrested on April 3, 1980. The grounds of detention were served on the detenu on April 3. 1980. The detenu was arrested in connection with the case in connection with a case in which the detenu was detained under the provisions, of the Preventive detention Act, 1950. The grounds were served on him on April 3 and the detenu filed a writ petition in the High Court of Bombay, which was allowed by a learned Single Judge of the High Court on April 23, 1980. On the writ petition, the detenu filed an application for the issue of a writ of habeas corpus, which was dismissed by the learned Single Judge. The detenu filed a Letters Patent Appeal against the order of the learned Single judge. The Division Bench of the High court dismissed the Letters Patent Appeal. The detenu thereafter filed a writ appeal in this Court. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The order passed by the Government on March 31. 1980, rejecting the representation of the detenu, was not an order of detention. The order was passed by the State Government on March 3,1980, after the order of confirmation of the detention was passed. The order, therefore, was not a speaking order. [775 H] 2. The order dated March 31.1980, rejecting the detenu's representation, was not one of the grounds of detention. It was not an appealable order. The order rejecting the representation was not an interlocutory order. The High Court was right in holding that the order of rejection was not an interim order. [750 H] 3. The order dismissing the representation was an interlocutory order and not an interlocutory one. The order is an interlocutory order, and the order of dismissal is an interlocutory one and not an order. [751 H] 4. The order refusing to supply the copies of the basic materials and documents to the detenus, of the material relied upon or referred to in the "grounds" of detention, is not an interlocutory or an interlocutory order but an interlocutory order which is an interlocutory or interlocutory order. [751 H] 5. The order in the present case was an interlocutory one, and the High Court was wrong in holding that it was an interlocutory or a interlocutory order. It was an interlocutory and not an interim one. [751 G] 6. The order under challenge was an interlocutory, and not an intermediate order. The fact that the order was an interlocutory is not conclusive of the fact that the High Court could not have passed the order of stay of the order of suspension of the order. [761 H] 7. The order for suspension of the detention is an interlocutory and an interlocutory order; it is an interlocutory. [751 A] JUDGMENT: ORIGINAL JURISDICTION: Writ Petition No. 12 of 1980. (Under Article 32 of the Constitution of India) AND Writ Petition No, 12 of 1980 (Under Article 226 of the Constitution) AND Writ Petitions Nos.

Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated the 12th May, 1972 of the Gujarat High Court in Criminal Appeal No, 9 of 1972 and Criminal Appeal No.. 9 of 1972 arising out of the judgment and Order dated the 18th October, 1972 of that Court in Criminal Revision Application No. 8 of 1972. V. S. Desai, S. N. Andley, for the appellant. S. N.. Andley, J. B. Dadachanji, O. C. Mathur and Ravinder Narain, for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. The appellant, a public servant, was prosecuted by the trial Magistrate for an offence under sections 419 and 420 of the Indian penal Code. The trial Magistrate convicted him under section 419. The appellant challenged his conviction by the State in a revision application before the High Court and the High Court dismissed the revision application. The appellant has now come up to this Court by special leave. The appellant is a public servant. He was prosecuted by a public servant for an offence punishable under section 419, Indian Penal Code. The appellant pleaded not guilty to the charge and claimed to be tried. The trial court held that the offence was not punishable under section 420 of the Code. The HighCourt held that the conviction of the appellant was not justified. The High Curt held that the trial Magistrate was wrong in convicting the appellant under sections 419, 420 and 420 of Indian Penal Code, and the High court was wrong in dismissing the revision application filed by the appellant. In the result, the High Court set aside the conviction and the sentence passed against the appellant. Hence this appeal by special leave by the appellant, The appellant has filed this appeal by certificate. The appellant contends that the High court has erred in holding that it was not open to the appellant to plead that the offence under section 420 was not punishable. The appellant further contends that the trial court was wrong. It is true that the appellant has not challenged the findings of the High Court that the offence is not punishable under sections 419 or 420 of the Penal Code. But the question is whether the High Court has erred in setting aside the conviction of an accused under section 419 or 420. The appellant's contention is that the High Curt was wrong in setting aside his conviction under section 419 as well as 420 of the [Code of Criminal Procedure].

The assessee, a resident of the United Kingdom, was assessed to income tax under the 1918 Act. The assessee was assessed to tax under the 1922 Act on the income of the foreign business of the assessee. The assessee filed a return of income under the 1918. Act in respect of the income of his foreign business. The Income tax Officer assessed the income of Rs. 1,10,000/- under the 1918, Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, allowed the appeal of the assessee and dismissed the appeal of his assessee. The Appellate Tribunal, however, held that the assessee was entitled to relief under section 25(3) of the 1922 Act. The Tribunal held that the foreign business was not charged under the 1918 and the assessee was not entitled to exemption under section 25 (3) of 1922 Act. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that under the 1918 Income Tax Act, the assessee was liable to be treated as a resident of India and the income of foreign business was liable to tax under section 3 of the 1918 Act, and that the assessee had not claimed the benefit of section 25(1) of the 1961 Act. On the question whether the assessee was a resident of a foreign firm, the Tribunal referred to the High Court the following question of law arising in this case: "Whether the assessee is entitled to relief of exemption under section25(3) in respect of interest on securities as well as interest on securities?" The High Court answered the question in the affirmative and in favour of the assessee, holding that the assessee is not entitled to relief. The High Court held that the income of a foreign company was not chargeable to tax under Section 3 of the 1922- Act. The High court held that the interest on securities was not chargeable under the 1918- Act. In the result, the High Court answered both the questions in the affirmative. The assessee is, therefore, entitled to the relief under section 26(3) on the question of law referred to the Court.

The appellant, a contractor, was appointed by the Government of India in the year 1962 as a contractor for the construction of a road. The appellant was appointed by a notification issued by the Government in the year 1963. The appellant entered into an agreement with the Government of Orissa for the construction and maintenance of a road in the State of Orissa. The appellant completed the construction of the road in the year 1964. The appellant paid a sum of Rs. 1,000/- as price of the bricks. The appellant filed a suit for specific performance of the contract. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the contract was a works contract and the appellant was not entitled to claim any compensation for the loss suffered by the Government. The High court held that the appellant was entitled to claim compensation for the damage suffered by the State. The appellant preferred an appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The contract in question is a contract of sale and not a works contract. The appellant is bound to complete the work and or to supply materials at the rates mentioned in the contract. [675 H] 2. The appellant had not completed the work and the contract was not a works. The appellant could not sell the bricks to the buyers under the contract. If, however, the appellant was to sell the bricks after manufacture, the contract would have been of a works contract, but the appellant did not do so. The contract was a contract of a works. [676 H] 3. The contract is a works contract; it is a works contracts. The appellant has to pay to the Department at the rate mentioned in the Schedule and the contract is a work contract. The contract does not require the supply of the bricks to a third party. The appellant cannot sell the bricks at the rates specified in the contract and the contract does not contain any provision for delivery of the materials. [678 H] 4. The contract being a works contract is a contract for the supply and sale of bricks. The contract provides for the delivery of the bricks after the manufacture. The appellant can sell the bricks only after the date of the contract and not before. [682 H] 5. The contract cannot be said to be a works contract because the appellant did so after manufacture. The contract did not require the appellant to pay to Department at the rates prescribed in the contract or the tender rates. The appellant did not pay the price of the goods. The contract also does not require that the appellant should pay to the department at the rate prescribed in the tender rates and the contract also does. [685 H] 6. The contract has to be a work contract and not a work contract as defined in the Act. The appellant does not have to pay to any Department at the tender rates or the tender prices. The appellant, therefore, cannot be said that the contract is not a works contracts and the contract has not been executed. [686 H] 7. The contract, therefore, is a works. It is not a work contracts. The contract itself is a works, contract. The contractor is bound to pay to Government at the rate specified in the tender. The appellant should pay the price as prescribed in the Schedule. [691 H] 8. The contract between the appellant and the Government is a works and not a contract for supply and sale. The appellant must pay to the Government at the rates as prescribed in Schedule. [650 H] 9. The contract for the construction, maintenance and repair of a road is a works' contract. The question whether the contract is for a works contract or not is a question of fact. [650 A] 10. The contract must be a works contracts; it must be a work contracts; it is not a contract of the nature of a works contracts, but a contract for construction and maintenance and repair. [650 D] 11. The contract should be a works' contracts.
