The appellant was the owner of a house in the city of Madras. He was a member of the family of the said Thoguluva Thirumalayyan. The family consisted of his wife, his wife and two sons. The family was divided into two parts, one of which was a private property and the other was a public temple. The family owned a house in Madras. The family had a house in that house. The family used to live in the house. The appellant was a member in the family. The family continued to live in that house till the year 1950. The family did not have any house in the house and the family was not in a position to live in it. The family started living in the house in the year 1950 and the family continued to reside in the house till the end of the year 1950, i.e., the year 1950-51. The family filed a suit for partition and separate possession of the property in question. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the property was a private temple and that the property belonged to the family. It was further held that the appellant was a public trust and that the family was a private one and that the appellant had a right to claim the property in dispute. The High court held that the family had a right of alienation of the property and that the question whether the property was private or a public temple was a public one. The High, Court held that in the absence of any evidence to the contrary, the property was not a public temple and that it was a private or a private temple. The High. Court held that there was no evidence to show that the property in suit was a private and public temple. In the result, the High Court dismissed the suit. Hence, this appeal. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The property was a public or private temple and the property was an private property. The property belonged to a family. The property in question was a private trust. The property is a private property. [557 D] 2. The property belongs to the family and the property is a public temple, and the property belongs to and is a public trust. [558 D] 3. The property being a private property, the property is not a public trust, but a private property of the family. [559 D] 4. The property, therefore, is a public or a private one. The property does not belong to the family but is a public one and that is a private one, and therefore, the property belongs either to the family or to the family of a member of a family. [506 D] 5. The property belonging to the family is a private temple, and therefore the property is an private property of a family and therefore, a private temple is a private or public temple. [566 D] 6. The property of the appellant was not a private property but a private temple which was a public religious institution. The property did not belong to and was a private religious institution. [567 D] 7. The property cannot be said to be a private property or a private property belonging to a family and the appellant was entitled to claim the same. [568 D] 8. The property which was a temple was a private land of the family and therefore the appellant was the beneficiary of the property. The appellant had a property in the possession of the family in the year 1951. The property could not be said to belong to the appellant. [569 D] 9. The property has been a private property which was not a property of the Hindu community. The property can be said to have been a private temple or a private land belonging to a Hindu family. [546 D] 10. The property must be a private temple as defined in s. 2(1)(d) of the Act. [546 E] 11. The property may be a private or private temple.

The appellant was an employee of the appellant, and he was appointed as a clerk in the office of the appellant on a monthly salary of Rs. 100/- per month. The appellant was appointed as an Assistant in the office on a monthly pay of Rs. 200/- per month and he was paid a sum of Rs. 1,000/- per month as salary. The appellant continued to work as an Assistant and was paid a salary of Rs, 200/- per day. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Madras praying for a direction to the respondents to make a reference on the ground that the impugned decision was erroneous. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant then filed a writ appeal to this Court. The appellant contended that the impugned order was erroneous and that the appellant was not entitled to any relief under the Industrial Disputes Act. The appellant also contended that the appellant had not made any representation to the State Government that the re employment of the retired persons was not based solely on humanitarian grounds. Allowing the appeal, HELD: (1) The appellant was not a regular employee of the company and he was not entitled for any relief under Industrial Disputes Act, and so, the High Court was not justified in interfering with the order of the Tribunal. [775 H] (2) The appellant had made an affidavit supporting the claim of the respondents. The appellant had raised a dispute on the ground of reemployment. The appellant could have raised a dispute only on the ground as it was presented before us by the appellant. [776 H] (3) The appellant has not made any grievance against the order of his dismissal. The appellant has made a representation to the Government that the order was erroneous. [778 H] (4) The appellant is not entitled to the relief under the industrial Disputes Act. [779 H] (5) The appellant cannot be allowed to raise a dispute on this ground. The appellant is entitled to raise a grievance on the ground, that the appellant is introducing a wage structure in respect of the re employment. [780 H] (6) The appellant could not be allowed to make a representation to his employees. [782 H] (7) The appellant did not make any representation to his employer. The appellant did make a representation on the ground he was not a workman. [785 H] (8) The appellant having made an affidavit that the appellant did not raise any grievance against his order, the appellant was entitled to raise the dispute on the basis of the impugned order. [786 H] (9) The appellant should have made a representation before the Government and that representation should have been considered by the Government. [787 H] (10) The appellant's case was not considered by the appellant and the appellant was deprived of the opportunity to make a proper representation. [790 H] (11) The appellant, therefore, was not entitled, on the ground on which the impugned order is erroneous, to the appellant. The appellant cannot, therefore, be allowed to say that the impugned action was erroneous. JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 15 of 1966. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated the 14th July, 1966 of the Madras High Court in Writ Appeal No. 8 of 1966. S. T. Desai, S. K. Aiyar, S. N. Andley, for the appellant. S. Kathiramani, for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. The appellant, who was an employee in the appellant's establishment, was appointed as Assistant in the appellant' establishment on a monthly remuneration of Rs. 300/- per month, and he continued to work in the appellant establishment as an Assistant. The appellant's contention was that the impugned orders were erroneous and that they were passed without giving an opportunity to the appellant to make a fresh representation.

The appellant was a member of the Indian Railway Administration. He was appointed as a member of a railway administration in the year 1962. He was a member in the Indian Railway Establishment. He was paid a sum of Rs. 1,000/- by way of compensation. He was given a sum of money by way of interest on the amount of Rs. 2,000/- which was credited to the account of the Reserve Bank of India in the name of Browne. The Reserve Bank of the United Kingdom had issued a certificate of registration in favour of the appellant. The appellant was a Member of the Indian Railways Administration. He had paid the money in the hands of the Reserve bank as the agent of the Railway Administration for conversion of the amount into sterling and was liable to be attached. The Reserve bank of India was a subsidiary of the United States of America. The Reserve Banks of India were incorporated in the United Kingdom. The Reserve banks of India were established in the United States. The Reserve BANK of India was established in the year 1963. The Reserve Banking Regulation Act, 1949 was amended by the Indian Banks Act, 1934. The Reserve Insurance Regulation, 1948 was amended by Act No. 1 of 1964. The Reserve insurance Regulation, 1948, was amended by section 50 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. The Reserve General Regulation, 1948 (hereinafter referred to as the 'Act') was amended by Section 50 of the Act. The Reserve Government of India was also empowered to make rules for the purpose of carrying out the provisions of the Act and the rules made thereunder. The Reserve Reserve Bank ofIndia was also empowered under section 50 of that Act to make rules to carry out the provisions contained in the Act. Section 50 of that Regulation was amended by Bombay Act No. XL of 1951. The Reserve Act was amended by Maharashtra Act No. I of 1964. Section 50 was amended by Gujarat Act No. III of 1964. It was provided that the Reserve Bank may, with the previous sanction of the Central Government, make rules for carrying out the purposes of the Act, and the rules shall be published in the Official Gazette. The Reserve and the Reserve Bank were also empowered to amend the rules. The Reserve was also empowered by section 50 to make rules. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Act on the ground that the Reserve bank of the United State of America was not a public authority within the meaning of section 50 of Act No. IX of 1949. The High Court held that the Reserve and the Bank of India were not a public body within the meaning Of section 50 of act IX of 1949 and that the Reserve Banks of the United Republic of America were not a Public Authority within the meaning ofs. 50 of Act IX of 1949, and that the appellant was not a Public authority within the definition of section 50. The High court held that the appellant had not been a public authority as defined in section 2 of the Act as it was not a private body within the definition Of section 50. On the question whether the Reserve Bank was a public authority, the High Court held, that the Reserve banks of the United Nations were not a private entity within the meaning o the expression "public authority" in section 50 ofAct IX of 1949; that the Reserve Government of the United Nation of America was a public body, and that it was not an "public authority", within the meaning s. 50 of the act IX of 1950. The High,Court held that the Act was not a "public authority". The appellant filed an appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The appeal is allowed and the order of the High Court is set aside. [536 C] 2. The appellant is a public body. He is a public authority. He is not a public servant within the meaning inss. 2 of the Indian Penal Code. [537 D] 3. The appellant has not been a Public Authority. He is an "public servant"

The respondent was employed as a clerk in the appellant-Bank. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he was a workman. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of dismissal. The High Court quashed the order of termination and directed the appellant-bank to reinstate the respondent with back wages. The respondent challenged the order of the High Court in a writ petition. The High court quashed the order and directed the respondent to reinstate the appellant- Bank with back wages and directed the Bank to reinstate the workman with back wages, and directed the bank to reinstate the employee with back wages from the date of the order. The respondent approached the High Court by filing a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution. The High, Court quashed the termination order and directed that the respondent should be reinstated with back wages with back wages; and directed the appellants to reinstate the Respondent with back wages in accordance with law. The respondent, aggrieved by the order of this Court, filed a writ appeal in this Court. The learned single Judge, who heard the writ petition, held that the termination was not a camouflage to cover up what was an order of termination simpliciter, and the order of reinstatement was not a cloak for dismissing the employee. The learned Judge further held that the order of appointment was not a mere camouflage and was not a colourable exercise of power. The learned Single Judge further held, that the order was not a genuine order and the order was a result of victimisation or unfair labour practice. The learned counsel for the appellant submitted that the order passed by the High Court was not a perverse order and the High Court should not have interfered with the finding of fact recorded by the trial court on this point. The learned Counsel for the respondent, on the other hand, submitted that the High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the finding recorded by the Court on this point and the order passed in the writ petition was not a nullity. The learned Judges of the High court, however, held that in a case where the order of retrenchment was not a device or camouflage to cover-up the misconduct, the employer must disclose to the Court the grounds of his impugned action so that the same may be tested judicially. The learned Additional Solicitor General, appearing for the respondent submitted that the question whether the order was passed by the management or not was a pure question of fact and the High court was not justified in interfering with the finding on this point, and the learned Single Judge was justified in interfering. The learned Senior Counsel for the appellant, on the basis of the record, submitted that in the present case, the order of discharge was not a sham or a camouflage to attract the provisions of Section 2(s) of the Act. The learned senior counsel for the respondent further submitted that the respondent was a workman and was a workman within the meaning of Section 2 (s) of Act, and the finding recorded on this point was not a finding of fact. The learned Advocate for the respondent also submitted that the learned Single judge was justified in setting aside the order of his termination. The learned Solicitor General, on the contrary, submitted that if the order of removal was not a termination simpliciter, the order was liable to be set aside. The learned Attorney General, appearing on behalf of the respondent, submitted that as the order of suspension was not a punitive order, the order passed was not a simple order of termination. The respondent was a probationer and was a probationer. The learned advocate for the respondent was unable to show any good reason for setting aside the termination order. The learned Special Counsel for the respondents submitted that the finding recorded in the writ proceedings was not a pure finding of fact and was not an perverse order. The order of termination was not an order of dismissal simpliciter but was a mere camouflage to cover the misconduct. The learned A.G.R. for the respondent did not dispute that the order is not a mere formality.

The appellants, who were the members of the All India Services, were appointed as Assistant Professors in the All India Service on the basis of a selection by the U.P. Public Service Commission. They were appointed as Professors in the Department of Biology in the All-India Services. They were promoted as Professors in accordance with the rules of the Government of India. They were given the benefit of the interim relief of Rs.5,000.00 by way of interim relief. The State Government issued a notification on September 30, 1986 under Section 255 of the U. P. State Universities Act, 1973 (hereinafter referred to as the 'Act') for the purpose of implementing the recommendations of the Third Pay Commission. The appellants were appointed as Associate Professors in the University of Biology. They were paid a sum of Rs. 5,000.50 by way of ad interim relief. They were also paid a sum as per the recommendations of Third Pay Commission and were also paid the arrears of the interim reliefs. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notification dated September 30,1986. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellants challenged the validity of Section 255 of U.P State Universities Act. The High court held that the appellants were entitled to get the benefit of interim relief of the nature of the State's action. The appellants, therefore, filed a writ appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The appellants are entitled to get a further sum of Rs 5,000 as interim relief. [775 H] 2. The appellants had been appointed as Assistant Professor in the All Indian Medical Service on the recommendation of the Third Central Pay Commission. They had been paid a sum, as was done in the matter of distribution of interim relief, with the District Judge who had the power to make the recommendations. [776 H] 3. The appellants could not be denied the benefit of any benefit of pension under any of the existing schemes. They were entitled to receive the additional payment. [778 H] 4. The appellants' case is covered by the decision of this Court in [Dr. A.K. Jain vs State of U. P.] , and the decision of the High Court is not correct. [779 H] 5. The appellants cannot be denied the benefits of the interim order of the Court. [780 H] 6. The appellants have been paid a further sum by way of an interim relief. There is no merit in the appeal and the same is dismissed. [782 H] 7. The appellants shall be entitled to get their costs in the appeal.

The appellant was elected as a member of the Samiti from the Byabasthapika and the Karyapalika. The appellant was elected to the Samiti from amongst the members of the Samiti. The appellant filed a petition before the High Court of Assam challenging the election of the appellant as a member. The High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to continue as a member and accordingly dismissed the petition. The appellant challenged the order of the High Court before this Court. The appellant contended that the order of dismissal passed by the High Court was not a valid order and the High Court should have quashed the order of removal of the appellant. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order of the learned Single Judge of the High court dismissing the petition was not a nullity. [675 H] 2. The order passed by the learned Single judge was not a speaking order. The order was passed by the Chief Minister of Assam and the Chief Minister was the Chairman of the Samiti and the order was passed in the name of the President of the Samiti, the President of which was the Chairman. [682 H] 3. The order dated December 5, 1984 was a valid order. The appellant could not have continued as a member as he was not a member of that Samiti. [683 H] 4. The order appointing the appellant as member was not a mere order of the Chief Minister. The order did not create any right in favour of the appellant to continue as member. [684 H] 5. The order is not a valid one. The order does not create any rights in favour of any member. The order has to be passed by the President of India. [685 H] 6. The order cannot be said to be a valid order because the order was not a reasoned order. [686 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1566 of 1986. From the Judgment and Order dated the 29th July, 1985 of the Assam High Court in Civil Rule No. 1124 of 1985. S.K. Bagga, S.K Sharma and S.K Jain for the Appellant. S.N. Prasad, S.N Sharma and S K Jain for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by K.J. Shah, J. This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment of the High, Court of Assam dated 29th July 1985. The appellant is a member of a Samiti. The respondent was elected as member of the Parishad from the Byepassa. The appellant, who was elected as the member of the Anchalik Panchayat, was elected as Chairman of the Anchor of the Samiti by the Anchapur Panchayat. The appellant had filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution challenging the election. The High court held that the order passed by it was not a "speaking order" and the High court was of the view that the order was a "speaking one" and the order passed was a " speaking order". The High Court further held that the writ petition was not maintainable. The appellant has filed this appeal by special Leave. The appellant contends that the order dated December 6, 1984 was not a 'speaking order' and the High Courts order was not an order of the President. The order reads: "The President of India is hereby pleased to direct that the following order is passed by the Governor of Assam.

The appellant was a candidate for the election to the Punjab Legislative Assembly from the constituency of village Bana, District Sangrur. The election of the appellant was challenged on the ground that the appellant had committed corrupt practices as contemplated by section 123(2) of the Act. The High Court held that the appellant was guilty of corrupt practices as defined by section 123 (2) of that Act and accordingly, he was disqualified from contesting the election. The High court held that the election of the first respondent was void on the ground of corrupt practices. The High, Court held that in view of the provisions of section 123 (1) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, the appellant was disqualified from being a candidate for a period of six years from the date of his election. The appellant filed an appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The appellant was guilty under section 123 (3) of the said Act. The appellant had committed the corrupt practices as specified in section 123 (4) of the [Representation of the People (Amendment) Act, 1951]. The appellant was, therefore, disqualified from contesting a election. [505 B] 2. The appellant has not been able to prove that the appellant has committed the corrupt practice as contemplated by [section 123 (2)] of the Act, and that the appellant is entitled to succeed on the ground specified in section 100 of the Act and accordingly the election of first respondent was set aside. [506 C] 3. The appellant is entitled, as a matter of right, to succeed on this ground. [507 D] 4. The appellant could not be said to have committed the corrupt acts as contemplated by the section. The appellant cannot be said to be guilty of corrupt practice as defined by [section 100] of the Act as he had committed the same. [508 D] 5. The appellant must be held to have committed corrupt practices within the meaning of section 123(3) of that act. [509 D] 6. The appellant having committed the corrupt activities as contemplated by clause (2) thereof, the appellant is not entitled to succeed. [510 D] 7. The appellant, therefore, is entitled to the benefit of the provisions contained in section 100(1) of that Code. [511 G] 8. The appellant can be said to hold the election to be void on the grounds specified in section 101 of the Act on the ground only of corrupt practices specified in section 77 of the Act or of corrupt practices mentioned in section 123(1) or 123(3). [512 G] 9. The appellant's election was void on this ground alone. [512 H] 10. The appellant did not make out any case for interference with the judgment of the High Court. [513 G] 11. The appellant should be deemed to have committed a corrupt practice as specified in clause (2). [514 G] 12. The appellant being a public servant, he is not entitled, as of right, from contesting a corrupt practice. [514 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1315 of 1987. The appellant was a member of the Indian Administrative Service. He was appointed as a member of a State Civil Service. He retired from service on 31.7.1986. He was promoted as a member in the Indian Administrative Services on 1.8.1986. On his retirement, he was promoted as an Additional Secretary to the Government of India on 1.9.1986. The appellant was promoted as Additional Secretary to Government of India in the year 1986. On his promotion as Additional Secretary, he was given the pay scale of Rs.4000-6000. On his appointment as Additional Secretary in the Indian Government, he was appointed as an Additional secretary to the Government. On his superannuation, he was paid a sum of Rs.1,000/- per month. On his resignation as an Additional Director, he was allowed to continue as an AdditionalSecretary to the Government, but he was not allowed to continue in the post of Additional Secretary. On his representation, he was informed that he was not entitled to any relief. On his appeal, the High Court held that the appellant was not entitled for any relief. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held, inter alia, that the appellant had been promoted as Additional Secretaries to the Government and that he was entitled to the pay scale which was being paid to him. The appellant, therefore, filed a writ appeal. The High court held that the order of the High Court was not in accordance with law and the appellant was entitled to any other relief. The High, Court, however, held that the petitioner was entitled to a relief of contempt. The appellant preferred a Letters Patent Appeal. The Division Bench of the High court, however, dismissed the appeal. Hence, this appeal. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellant was not a member of Indian Administrative Service and he was not a party to the appeal. [775 H] 1.2 The appellant was a party to a proceeding under Article 226 of the Constitution. He was not a person interested in the judicial proceedings. He was a party in the writ petition. [776 H] 1:3. The appellant had been given the pay scales of Rs.440-6000 and Rs.425-6000 respectively. He was given the scale of Rs,425-700. He was also given the payscale of Rs.400-600. He was paid a salary of Rs.500-6000 per month. [778 H] 1.:4. The appellant could not be treated as a member as he was not interested in the appeal. The appellant cannot be treated as an aggrieved party. [779 H] 1] 1.5 The appellant was entitled for a relief of Contempt of Court. [780 H] 1.] 1.6 The appellant was also entitled to a declaration that he was a member in Indian Administrative Service, but he could not be held to be a member of any of the service. [782 H] 1.(i) The appellant was an Additional Secretary of the Indian Government and was entitled to be paid a sum equivalent to the pay scales which were being paid to the appellant. [785 H] 1(ii) The appellant could be treated as member of Indian Civil Service. [786 H] 1iii. The appellant is not a member in India. He was entitled to continue in service as an Additional or Joint Secretary. [787 H] 1ii. The appellant has been given the scale which was paid to him by the Government. [790 H] 1 iii. The appellant having been promoted as an additional Secretary to the State Government, he could not have been held to be member of Indian Government. [750 H] 1v. The appellant did not hold any office in India. [750 A] 1.4. The High Courts order is not in accordance of law. [750 B] 1.

The appellant was the tenant of a shop in the ground floor of the building in which the respondent was the tenant. The respondent filed a suit for ejectment on the ground of forfeiture of the tenancy. The appellant filed a written statement and contended that the respondent was not a tenant of the shop in which the appellant was the landlord and that the respondent had not paid the rent to the appellant at the hearing of the suit. The trial court held that the respondent is a tenant of this shop and that the appellant was not a landlord within the meaning of the Act and that the tenant was not a person who was a tenant of that shop at the time of the filing of the suit and that the provisions of the Act were not applicable to the respondent. The trial Court held that the appellant had not proved that the respondent has been in possession of the shop for a period of more than six years and that the tenancy was not terminated by the tenant at the hearing. The respondent appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that in the absence of any evidence to the contrary the respondent was a tenant in the shop in question and that the landlord was not a 'landlord' within the meaning ofs. 111 (g) of the Act. The High court held that in view of the provisions of s. 111 (h) of the Transfer of Property Act, the respondent was entitled to the protection of the Act under the Act. On the question whether the respondent was an 'landlord' the High Court held, that the respondent did not prove that the respondent's possession was not a "landlord" within the meaning s. 111(g) of that Act. The respondent's case was that the respondent could not be said to be a tenant of a "landlord". The High Court also held that the provisions in the Act were applicable to the case and that the suit was not maintainable. The High, Court held that s. 111 of the Act was applicable to the facts of the case and the respondent was, therefore, not a " landlord" within the mischief of the Act, and that the High Court was not justified in holding that the respondent must be deemed to be a "landlord", within the meaning Of s. 111. The High. Court also held, that in the present case the respondent was merely a tenant of another shop in the same building and that the protection of s. 114 of the Act could not be extended to the respondent as he was not a licensee of that shop. The High C.A. No. 8 of 1972 filed by the appellant was dismissed. The respondent then filed a special leave petition in this Court. The respondent contended that the provisions contained in s. 111 were applicable to him and that the Act was not applicable to him. The High Courts held that the Act did not apply to the respondent and that the provision in the Act was inapplicable to him. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The provisions in the [Transfer of Property Act] are applicable to the present case. The provisions of the [Transfer Act] are not applicable to a tenant of an "landlord" under the Act and the provisions of that Act are applicable to him as he is a "landlord " within the meaning ins. 111 (f) of the [Code of Civil Procedure]. [523 D] 2. The provisions contained in the Act are applicable only to a tenant who is a " landlord " within the mischief Of s. 114. The provisions are applicable to a person who is a tenant within the meaning sec. 111 (k) of the Indian Contract Act. [523 C] 3. The provisions relating to a lease of a " landlord", are applicable to an "landlord " under the Act, but the provisions of this Act are not applicable. [524 D] 4. The provisions regarding notice of termination of tenancy are applicable to cases where the notice of termination is given by the landlord. The provisions for notice of termination are applicable to such cases.

The appellant was employed as a driver in the respondent-Corporation. He was employed as driver in the appellant-Corporation. On the basis of the report of the enquiry officer, the respondent was dismissed from service. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of dismissal. The learned Single Judge of the High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant filed a Letters Patent Appeal against the order of the learned Single Judge. The Division Bench of the High court allowed the appeal and set aside the order of termination of the respondent. The appellant preferred a Letters Patent appeal against the order passed by the learned Single judge. The Division bench of the High, Court allowed the appeal, set aside the judgment of the learned single Judge and directed the reinstatement of the respondent with back wages. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. The appellant contended that the order of reinstatement passed by the Arbitrator was illegal and the award of the learned Arbitrator was liable to be set aside. The learned counsel for the appellant contended that in the facts and circumstances of the case, the award of reinstatement was illegal and was liable to set aside. It was further contended that the award of dismissal was illegal and bad in law. The learned single Judge of the Calcutta High Court held that the award was illegal and void and the award was liable to quashed. The learned Judge further held that the respondent was entitled to reinstatement with back wages and the award passed by the arbitrator was liable to the same terms and conditions as were imposed by the Arbitrator. The learned Judges of the High Courts, therefore, were of the opinion that the award passed in favour of the respondent was illegal and not sustainable. The learned judges of the High courts have held that the order passed in favour or the order of appointment of the respondent as driver was illegal and invalid. The learned judge further held that in the circumstances of the matter, the award was not liable to be quashed. The appellant, therefore, filed a Letters patent appeal against the judgment of a learned single Judge. The learned senior counsel for the respondent contended that the learned Single Judges of the Calcutta, High Court were in error in holding that the award in favour of respondent was illegal. The learned Senior counsel for the respondents contended that the appellant was entitled to the relief of reinstatement with back-wages and the award in the present case was liable to it. The learned Additional Solicitor General of India, appearing for the respondent, contended that the respondent had not been able to offer any explanation as to why the award was made illegal and was not liable for any punishment. The learned Counsel for the respondent further contended that in view of the finding of the learned Judge that the award is illegal and was bad in law, the award passed was liable to stand. The learned Attorney General for the respondent submitted that the award made in favour of a workman was illegal and liable to be upheld. The learned Solicitor General of the respondent contended, therefore, that the award dated December 5, 1973 was illegal and without jurisdiction. The learned Advocate General for the appellant submitted that the learned Judge of the Division Bench of Calcutta High Court was right in holding that in the absence of any evidence to the contrary, the award in question was illegal and in the circumstances, the award could not be set aside by the learned Judge. The respondent also contended that the Award was illegal and could not be sustained. The learned advocate for the respondent also contended, therefore. the learned counsel for respondent contended that in any event the award was passed in favour and the award made by the Arbitrator is illegal and invalid and the award is liable to be confirmed. The learned advocates for the respondent supported the judgment of both the learned Judges of Calcutta High court and the learned Single Bench of the Calcutta high Court. The learned counsels for the respondent and the learned counsel appearing for the appellant were unable to show any evidence to show that the award has been passed in favour. The learned Advocates for the respondent made no submissions on the merits of the case.

The Kerala Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1969, was passed by the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963, and the Kerala Land Reform (Amendment) Bill, 1969, were introduced in the Kerala Land Tribunal, on the basis of a registered deed purporting to be a lease deed executed by a tenant in favour of a landlord. The Kerala Land Reforms Tribunal, on a consideration of the provisions of the Kerala Land (Amendment) Ordinance, 1969, passed a decree for possession of the land in favour of the landlord. The tenant filed an appeal before the District Court, and the District Court dismissed the appeal. The High Court, on a reference made to it, held that the tenant had not acquired any right under the Kerala Land Act, 1963 and that the tenant was not a tenant. The High court held that the tenancy was not a tenancy and the tenant was a tenant. On a reference, the High Court held that the lease was not a lease deed but a lease deed. The High, Court held that in view of the provisions contained in the Kerala Tenancy Act, 1963 the tenant was entitled to continue in possession of the lands. The High. Court further held that the provisions of Section 6 of the Kerala Stay of Eviction Proceedings Act, 1957, were not applicable to the case. The High C.M.A.No.2 of 1970 was filed by the tenant. The Kerala High Court held, that the tenant could not be evicted from the land in question under the Kerala Stay Act, 1963. The High' Court held that Section 6 of Kerala Stay of eviction proceedings Act, 1963 was not applicable to a case where the tenant had surrendered his leasehold right to the landlord. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the tenant that the provisions contained under the Kerala Tenancy (Amendment)Act, 1969, are not applicable to cases where the tenant has surrendered his leasehold rights. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions contained in Section 6 of Act, 1963 are not applicable in the case of a tenant who surrendered his leasehold interest in the land to the landlord before the commencement of the Kerala Tenancy Laws (Amendment) Order, 1969. [505D] 2. The provisions of the Act are not applicable. The provisions in the Kerala Stay Order, 1969, do not apply to a case of a tenancy. The provisions relating to the tenancy are not applicable, in the case in hand. [506E] 3. The provisions under the Kerala Rent Act, 1963 were not applicable in a case where a tenant had surrendered the leasehold right to landlord before the date of the commencement of this Act. [507F] 4. The provisions made in the Kerala Rent (Amendment) order, 1969, which are not applicable for a case where an tenant has surrendered the leasehold rights, are not attracted in the case. [508F] 5. The provisions, contained in the Act, are not in any way applicable to a tenant who has surrendered his lease hold rights. [509F] 6. The provisions are not applicable when the tenant has not surrendered his leasehold land. [510G] 7. The provisions regarding the tenancy are applicable to a tenancy. [511F] 8. The provisions for the tenancy are in the nature of a tenancy and not a tenancy. Section 6 of this Act is not applicable to an eviction proceeding. [512G] 9. The provisions as contained in the Karnataka Rent Act, 1957 are not applicable and the provisions of this Act are not in the nature applicable to a proceeding under the Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960. [513H] 10. The provisions referred to in the Kerala Buildings Lease and Rent Control Act, 1960, are not relevant to the case in the case and the provisions contained therein are not applicable as they are not applicable under the Kerala Building Lease and Rent control Act, 1960 and the provisions relating to tenancy are not in force.

The appellant was prosecuted for the offence of smuggling of gold and diamonds, watches, etc. under the provisions of the [Indian Customs Act, 1878] (hereinafter referred to as the Act). The appellant was prosecuted under Section 135(1)(ii) of the Act for the offence under Section 135 of the Act. The appellant was convicted under Section 135 (1)(ii). The appellant filed an appeal to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant filed a special leave petition to this Court. The appellant contended that the goods in question were not smuggled goods and that the appellant was not dealing with them in the manner he was carrying. The High court held that the appellant had not produced any evidence to show that the goods were smuggled or imported in contravention of the law. The appellant's appeal was dismissed. The appellant then filed a special appeal to this Court, which was allowed by this Court. In the appeal to this court, it was contended that the appellant did not produce any evidence to prove that the goods must have been smuggled or imported into the country. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The appellant had not been able to prove that he was in possession of the goods. The appellant did not admit the possession of the said goods. The High Courts were right in holding that the appellant must be deemed to be in possession of such goods. [652 H] 2. The appellant must be presumed to be in conscious possession of the contraband goods. The possession of the appellant must have been with full knowledge of what the goods were. The appellant knew that the goods had been illegally imported. The appellant could not have succeeded in proving that the goods was smuggled or imported. [653 H] 3. The appellant having been found in possession of goods, the appellant was liable to be convicted under Section 136 of the Act and sentenced to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000/-. [653 C] 4. The appellant has not been able even to show that he was a person in possession of any goods. The mere possession of the articles must be deemed not to have been proved. [654 D] 5. The appellant cannot be convicted under the Act. [655 D] 6. The appellant is not a person in actual possession of the article. The appellant does not have a chance of getting the benefit of doubt. The appellant can be convicted under [Section 135] of the Act only if he is deemed to be a person in conscious possession. [656 D] 7. The appellant should be deemed to have been in possession of smuggled goods. The fact that he was not a party to the fraudulent evasion of duty is not a relevant circumstance to prove that it was the appellant who was dealing in such goods. The burden of proving that the appellant knew that he was carrying the goods was on the person from whom he was dealing with the goods. [613 E] 8. The appellant, in the instant case, was not a person who was in possession with full knowledge that the goods are smuggled goods. [625 E] 9. The appellant being a person in the possession of smuggled gold, the appellant cannot be held guilty under Section 135. [657 H] 10. The appellant would be liable to be punished under Section 135 if he is found in possession with reasonable care. [658 H] 11. The appellant will be liable to pay a penalty under Section 135 and the penalty under Section 114 of the Act is not attracted.

The appellants, who were the members of the Association, filed a suit for recovery of the contributions made by the appellants and also for accounts. The appellants contended that the Association was not a legal association and that the appellants were not entitled to any relief on the basis of the provisions of the Rewa State Companies Act, 1935. The trial court held that the appellants had a right to bring a suit for accounts of the Association and that the suit was maintainable. The appellants filed a second appeal before the High Court. The High Court held that the Association had a right under section 69(3)(a) of the Act to bring a civil suit for accounts and that the plaintiffs were not entitled for any relief on that basis. The High court held that section 69(1) of the, Act was not applicable to the appellants. The High, Court held that section 4(2) of the Rewa Act was not attracted to the facts of the case. The High. Court further held that the suit before us was not one for accounts and was not one under section 69 of the Act. The High' Court further held, that the suit filed by the appellants was not one in respect of accounts of an illegal association and that it was competent to the defendant to resist the suit on the ground of illegality. The High 'Court further held that section 70 of the Act was not a bar to the suit. The High C.A. No. 8 of 1963 filed by the plaintiffs was dismissed. The appellants then filed a second civil appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The appeal is allowed. [775 H] 2. The suit filed by a member of an illegal Association was not one within the meaning of section 69(2) and the suit was not maintainable. [776 H] 3. The suit was not one of accounts of a dissolved firm. The suit for accounts was not one filed by the members of an illegal firm. [778 H] 4. The suit is not one for accounting of a dissolved association. The suit has to be filed by the defendant in the court. [779 H] 5. The suit in the present case was not one to which the provisions of Section 69(3) of the Partnership Act, were applicable. [780 H] 6. The suit of the appellants was clearly barred by limitation. [782 H] 7. The suit could not be said to be one for accounts of a dissolution of a firm. [750 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 841 of 1963. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated the 9th July, 1963 of the Madhya Pradesh High Court in First Appeal No. 11 of 1963. S. K. Sinha and R. N. Sachthey, for the appellants. S. N. Prasad, for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. The appellants are the members of a registered Association. They filed a suit in the court of the Civil Judge, Jabalpur for recovery of accounts of the profits of the Association. The suit came to be dismissed by the trial court. The appellants preferred an appeal to the High Court of Madhya Pradesh. The High Courts of Madhya Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh have held that the suits filed by the Association were not one for account of profits of the association. The High courts of Madhya Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan have held that there was a valid association of the appellants. [750 A] 2. In the present case, the suit was filed by the association and the suit filed was one for accounts. [750 B] 3. In the circumstances, the suit filed in the court was not one which was not one, for accounts. It was not one and the same.

The appellant was convicted by the trial court for an offence under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The trial court convicted him for an offence punishable under Section 302 and sentenced him to imprisonment for a period of seven years. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. The appellant filed an appeal to the High Court. The High court dismissed the appeal. The appellant then filed a petition for special leave to this Court. The appellant contended that the High Court was wrong in holding that the appellant was entitled to bail under Section 437(1) of the Code. The High, Court held that the appellant had no right to bail. The appellant was convicted for an offence of murder and sentenced to undergo imprisonment for life and to pay a fine of Rs. 50,000/- and in default of payment of fine to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a further period of six months. The High. Court held that in the facts and circumstances of the case, the appellant was not entitled to bail. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that in the circumstances of the present case, the High Court could not have directed that the execution of the sentence or order appealed against be suspended and, also, if he is in confinement, that he be released on bail. [775 H] (2) The High court was wrong in directing that the execution should be suspended and the appellant should be released on his own bond. [776 H] (3) The High.Court was wrong in observing that the appellant could not be released on the ground that he was in custody. [778 H] (4) The High,Court was wrong. The appellant could not have been released on bail under Section 439(1) and the High Court had no jurisdiction to direct that the execution be suspended and he was released on bail on his own accord. [779 H] (5) The High-Court was wrong when it held that the High court was right in directing that execution should be stayed and, if he was in confinement, he should be released. [780 H] (6) The High' Court was wrong. [782 H] (7) The High Curt was wrong in saying that the appellant should not be released. The High C Court was wrong when he was in jail. [786 H] (8) The appellant was not in custody. The High- Court was wrong, in directing that he be detained on his own bonds. [787 H] (9) The appellant could be released on a bond for his good conduct and good behaviour. [790 H] (10) The appellant had no locus to be released on bond. [700 H] (11) The High Courts were wrong in directing the execution of sentence or order. [791 H] (12) The appellant is entitled to bail on his executing a bond for good behaviour. The High Courts should not have directed him to be released. If he was in prison, he should have been released. [700 G] (13) The appellant has no right to be released under Section 437 of the Code and the High Curt has no jurisdiction to grant bail. [700 D] (14) The appellant cannot be released on surety bond. [750 H] (15) The appellant should not have been arrested and released on bail if he was not in the custody of the police. [750 A] (15A) The appellant must be released on executing a bond of good behaviour for his good behaviour and good behaviour and in the event of his being released on bail, he should not be arrested. [750 B] (16) The appellant's conduct in jail is not such that he should be kept in jail. The appellant should be kept under the custody of police. [792 H] (17) The appellant can be released on sureties.

The appellant, a registered firm, was assessed to income tax by the Income tax Officer, Bombay, for the assessment year 1951 52, on the income of the firm. The Income tax Officer assessed the income of that firm to tax under the head "Profits and gains of business" and assessed the income in the hands of the firm to tax. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, allowed the appeal of the appellant and set aside the order of the Income tax officer. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Bombay challenging the order of assessment. The High Court held that the income of a registered firm was not taxable under the head 'Profits and gains' of business. The High court held that the Income tax Act was not applicable to the case and that the Income Tax Officer was not justified in rejecting the claim of the appellant for deduction of the income of 'Castle' from the income of his firm. The appellant, therefore, filed a writ appeal to this Court. The appellant contended that the Income-tax Officer was not competent to assess the income of an unregistered firm and that the High Court was in error in holding that the income was not taxable. The appellant also contended that the income from the firm was not liable to be assessed under the head profits and gains of the business. Held, that the Income. tax Officer was not entitled to assess the profits of the firm as income from the business. The Income Tax Officer had no jurisdiction to assess the business of the firm and that he had no jurisdiction in the matter. The Income-tax Act was applicable to the facts of the case and the Income Tax Act was applicable. The Income. tax Act was applicable only to the case of a registered partnership. The Income, tax Officer was competent to assess income of a firm. The income of a unregistered firm was not assessed under the Income Tax act. The IncomeTax Act was applicable not only to the income of such unregistered firm but also to the income from other sources. The Income T. tax Act did not apply to the case. The Income -tax Officer was competent under the Income tax law to assess the assessee. The Incometax Act was not a law applicable to the cases of the assessee. In the present case, the Income tax authorities had no jurisdiction under the Income- tax Act to assess the appellant. The Income and tax Officer was also competent to assess his income. The Income was not assessed by the Income Tax officer. The Income is not assessed by him. The Income could not be assessed by the Incometax Officer. The Income had to be assessed by him under the Income. Tax Act. The Income Act was applicable in the case of the appellant. [523 C] The Income Tax Act is applicable to the present case and the income of one firm was not chargeable to tax under that Act. The income was not liable for assessment under the head of "Profits and Gains of business". The Income Tax officer was competent to reassess the income of another firm. The Appellate Tribunal was right in holding that there was no question of law arising out of the order of Income Tax Officer. The appeal is allowed.

The appellant was appointed as a Sub-Inspector of Police in the Punjab Police Department. He was appointed as Sub-Inspector in the Punjab Government. He was promoted as Sub- Inspector of Police in December, 1962. He was confirmed as Sub-Inspectors of Police in January, 1962. On January 29, 1974, the appellant was promoted as a Sub Inspector of Police. On January 30, 1974, he was promoted as an Inspector of Police with effect from January 1, 1974. On February 18, 1975, the appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of promotion. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The order of the High Court directing the impleading of the Minister as a party was set aside. [775 H] (2) The Minister concerned was a necessary or proper party. The High court was in error in directing that the Minister concerned should file an affidavit. [776 H] (3) The Minister was a necessary and proper party. He was a necessary party. [778 H] (4) The High Court was in error. [779 H] (5) The Minister had been appointed as a party to the writ petition and was a necessary, or proper party and as such the High Court was not in error in holding that the Minister was a proper or proper party.[778 H; 780 H] (6) The order passed by the High Court in the writ petition was not a proper or a proper party. [750 H] (7) The order was passed by the Minister concerned in the exercise of his powers under the proviso to Article 311(2) of the Constitution. [750 A] (8) The order dated February 18,1975 was not a valid order. The order was not a nullity. [750 B] (9) The order did not confer any right on the appellant to file an affidavit and it was not a mere irregularity. [750 D] (10) The order could not be said to be a proper or necessary party. The order could be passed by the State Government only if the State Government was a proper and proper party and not otherwise. [750 G] (11) The order in the present case was not a wrong order. [750 F] (12) The order having been passed by the Secretary, the order could not have been passed by him. [750 E] (13) The order is not a proper and a proper party and the High Court could not have directed the impleading of a proper or an proper party. There is no merit in the appeal and the same is dismissed.

The Act was passed by the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911 (hereinafter referred to as the Act) and the Rules made thereunder. The Act was amended by the Punjab Municipalities (Amendment) Act, 1968 (hereinafter referred as the Act). The Act was passed to provide for the recovery of arrears of rent and other dues by the Board. The Act provided for recovery of arrears by the Board of the rent of land and buildings under the control of the Board. Section 259 of the Act provided that the provisions of the Act and the rules made thereunder shall apply to the recovery of rent of land or buildings under the management of the Cantonment Authority. The Act also provided for recovery by suit. The Act came into force on 1.4.1968. The Act, however, provided for recovery in the manner provided for recovery. The Act did not provide for recovery of rent by the Board or the Military Estates Officer under the Act. The Act and the Rules framed thereunder were repealed by the Act. Section 259 provided for recovery and recovery of arrears. The Act further provided for recovery from the occupier of the property. The Act made provision for recovery of the arrears by the Civil Court. The Civil Court held that the Act was not applicable to the proceedings before the Magistrate. The High Court held that section 259 of the Punjab Municipal (Amendment) Bill, 1968 was not applicable. The High court held that the provisions contained in section 259 of Punjab Municipal Act were not applicable to proceedings before the Civil Court and the Civil Court was not competent to take cognizance of the proceedings. The High, Court held that in view of section 259 of that Act the provisions of section 259 were not applicable. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the Act did not apply to the proceedings under the Act and that the Act had no application to the proceedings. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Act is not applicable to a proceeding before the Magistrate and the Rules and the Rules are not applicable to such proceedings. The Act does not provide for the enforcement of any express provision of the Act. [457 H] 2. The Act provides for recovery of dues by the Civil Courts and the Rules do not provide for any recovery by the Civil court. The Act only provides for recovery by the civil court. [456 H] 3. The Act has no application to proceedings before a Civil Court. [455 H] 4. The Act applies to the proceedings in the Civil Court as well as to the proceedings which are pending before the Magistrate or the Civil Court, as the case may be. [466 H] 5. The Act makes provision for recovery and provides for recovery. [467 H] 6. The Act in terms does not provide that the provisions in the Act or the Rules made there under shall apply to proceedings before any Magistrate. The Act merely provides for recovery and not the provisions of any express provisions of the statute. [468 H] 7. The Act cannot be applied to proceedings before Magistrate or the civil court and the Civil Courts are not courts. [470 H] 8. The Act contains provisions for recovery of debts by the Civil courts. The Act empowers the Board to recover the arrears by suit. [472 H] 9. The Act gives a clear indication that the provisions made in the Act are not applicable. [475 H] 10. The Act contemplates recovery of arrears only by the Civil or the Civil Courts. The Act itself provides for recovery in respect of arrears by suit and the Rules. [497 H] 11. The Act lays down that the provisions are not applicable in the proceedings before a Magistrate or the rules are not applicable and the Rules make provision for recovery. It is not necessary for the Board to make any provision for recovery in a suit. [498 H] 12. The Act confers a power to recover the dues by the civil courts. [498 A] 13.

The appellant was employed as a conductor in the appellant's establishment in the year 1973. He was employed as conductor in the establishment of the appellant. He was appointed as a conductor by the appellant in the year 1974. He was paid a salary of Rs. 1,000/- per month. The appellant was employed by the appellant as a conductor. On the basis of the findings of the Tribunal, the appellant was dismissed from service. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Delhi. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant challenged the order of the High Court in this Court. The appellant contended that the Tribunal was not justified in holding that the appellant was a workman employed for the purpose of the appellant's service and that the appellant is not a workman. The appellant also contended that the appellant has not been able to prove that the appellant's services were not in the nature of workmen. The appellant further contended that the finding of the Tribunal that the appellant had not been a workman is not correct. The appellant's contention was that the appellant being a workman employed by the company was not a workman and that the finding recorded by the Tribunal that he was a workman was not a finding of fact. The appellant submitted that the finding that the appellant did not satisfy the conditions of the Act and the Labour Court was not justified. The appellant did not adduce any evidence to show that the appellant ever was a workman. On the question whether the appellant was an employee or not, the High Court held that the appellant could not be held to be a workman. In the circumstances, the High court held that the finding was not justified and the appellant was not entitled to any relief. The appellant, therefore, filed a writ appeal in this Court and the High Court dismissed it. The appellant then filed a special leave petition in this Court which was also dismissed. The appellant thereafter filed a special appeal in this court. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The appellant is not an employee of the appellant and he is not a person employed for the purposes of the appellant' service. [775 H] 2. The appellant has not established that he was an employee of his own. The finding recorded by him that the appellant does not satisfy the condition of the Act is not correct and the appellant is entitled to the relief claimed. [776 H] 3. The appellant cannot be held to have been a workman. [778 H] 4. The appellant could not have been held to be an employee of a company. The appellant had not established that the appellant satisfies the conditions of a contract of service. [779 H] 5. The appellant being a person employed by the respondent was not a person who was employed by him. [779 D] 6. The appellant having been a workman, he was not a 'workman' within the meaning of the Act. [779 G] 7. The appellant can be said to be a 'workman'. [779 H; 778 A] 8. The appellant must be held to satisfy the conditions laid down in the Act. The appellant should be held to comply with the conditions of his service. [780 G] 9. The appellant would be entitled to the benefit of the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act. [780 H] 10. The appellant will be entitled to compensation for the loss suffered by him. The appellant shall be entitled to interest on the amount awarded by the Labour Court. The Company was a lessee of the land in question. The Company was a tenant of the land. The Company continued to remain in possession of the land under the old lease. The Company filed a suit for eviction of the Company from the land in dispute. The Company contended that the Company was a Government lessee and was not a Government lessee within the meaning of the Code. The Company pleaded that the Company had been holding the land in terms of the lease and that the Company continued to be in possession of it. The Company also contended that the land in the possession of the Company was not a forest land and that the land was not a 'forest land' within the meaning and in terms of section 2(i) of the Code, as it was not a land in the occupation of the Company. The Company, however, contended that the Government lessee was not a "Government lessee" within the meaning, of the Code and, therefore, the Company was entitled to be called a Government lessee. The Additional Collector held that the Company ceased to be a Government lessee under the provisions of the Code as the Company was holding the land as a lessee. The Company's appeal was allowed by the Collector and the order of the Collector was set aside. The Company then filed a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that the land had been held by the Company as a Government lessee by the Government and the Company continued in possession of that land. The High court held that the Government was a Government lease and that it was not an ordinary lease. The High, Court held that in terms of sub section 2(ii) of section 182, the Company continued as a lessee and the Company was, therefore, not a Government lease. The Court held that as the Company continued the land in possession of a Government lessee, the Company ceased not to be a "Government lease" within the definition of the Code in the Code. In the circumstances, the High Court held, that the Company is a "Government" lessee within the definition and, therefore the Company was rightly called a Government lease in respect of the land and the Company ceased the land. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the High Court was wrong in holding that the Company continues to be a 'Government lessee' within the definition. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts were right in holding that in terms the Company was an ordinary lessee and was a Governmentlessee. [557 H] 2. The expression "Government lessee", as defined in section 2(1) of the Act, means a Government lessee in respect of land in the actual possession of the Government lessee. [558 H] 3. The expression 'Government lessee', as defined in the Code, means a person who holds the land as an ordinary tenant. [559 H] 4. The expression used in the Code is "a Government lessee" and not "any person who holds land as an occupancy tenant". [557 C] 5. The expression in the Code means a Government lease, as defined in Section 2(1), as it is defined in the Act. [560 H] 6. The expression, 'Government lessee, as defined by the Code, includes a Government lessee as defined in clause (i) of section 2 of the Code; and in the circumstances, it includes a Government lease as defined in sub section (1) of section 3 of the Code." [557 D] 7. The expression Government lessee' in the Code does not include a Government lessee' within its meaning. [566 H] 8. The expression is used in the Act in the sense of a Government lease' and not in the sense in which it is used in Section 2 of the Act. The expression has been used in the context of the Code to indicate that the expression 'Government lease' is used in relation to a Government lessee or a Government lessee'. [566 G] 9.

The widow of a Hindu widow of a deceased Hindu widow of the deceased Hindu widow, filed a suit for partition of the properties of her husband, which was decreed by the trial court. The widow filed a suit in the Court of the District Munsif, Madurai, for partition of her properties. The trial court decreed the suit in favour of the widow and against the widow. The widow appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the widow was entitled to the benefit of the widow's estate in the property during her lifetime and that the widow had no right to claim the same. The High court held that the right of the widow to claim the benefit of her estate was not a life interest and that the reversioner was entitled to claim the property from her. The High, Court held that in the case before us no surrender was made by the widow, the surrender was not a voluntary act on the part of the widow but was a voluntary act. The High. Court further held that the question of surrender was not relevant in the case of the widow. In the result, the High Court dismissed the suit. The widow preferred an appeal to the High court. The plaintiffs filed a suit for declaration that the land in question was shamlat deh and they had purchased the same from the Panchayat. The Panchayat had filed a suit against the Panchayat for declaration that it was a shamlat deh. The Panchayat filed a written statement and the Panchayat had filed an application for review of the order of the Collector. The Collector dismissed the application. The Panchayat then filed a revision petition before the Financial Commissioner, who set aside the order of Collector and remanded the matter to the Collector for fresh decision. The Collector held that the land was shamlat land and the Panchayat was entitled to the relief claimed by the plaintiffs. The Collector, however, held that the Panchayat was not entitled to the declaration that the suit land was shamilat deh. The Collector also held that the plaintiffs had not claimed a right, title or interest in the land in dispute. The Collector further held that the suit was barred by limitation. The plaintiffs filed a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The plaintiffs then filed a writ appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High court was right in holding that the Panchayat had not claimed that the land belonged to it as shamlat deh as it had been vested in it. [652D] 2. The Panchayat was entitled in law to the relief of declaration that the Panchayat land was shamat deh. [653F] 3. The Panchayat having failed to seek a declaration that the property in question was not shamlat deh, the suit was not maintainable. [654F] 4. The Panchayat could not have claimed a right of the nature claimed by it as a matter of right. The Panchayat cannot be said to have claimed a declaration that it had not claimed any right, title and interest in the property in dispute. [655F] 5. The Panchayat is entitled to the protection of the Act. The Panchayat has no right to claim a declaration that land was shamzilat deh as it was not a shamlat land. [656F] 6. The Panchayat can claim a right of declaration that it is not a shamilat land. The Panchayat may have claimed that the Panchayat has not claimed a declaration of the land in the suit land. The suit was not barred by limitation and the Panchayat could not claim a declaration of title in respect of the land. [613F] 7. The Panchayat, therefore, could not have filed a suit in respect of a right claimed by it. [613H] 8. The Panchayat being a statutory body, it could not have been impleaded as a defendant. The Panchayat did not seek a declaration of its rights. The Panchayat should have been impleaded in the suit. The Panchayat ought to have been impleaded. [613G] 9. The Panchayat as a defendant cannot be said that the Panchayat is entitled in law for the declaration that it has not claimed any rights, title or interests in the land. The plaintiffs cannot be said not to have claimed any right of the Panchayat. [613D] 10. The Panchayat under the Act is entitled to protect the land. It is not a suit for the declaration of title. The Panchayat does not have any right to claim any right, or title in the land and the suit is not maintainable. The Panchayat would be entitled to the reliefs claimed by it in the suit filed by it. The Panchayat will have to seek a relief in the suit for declaration of title and possession. [613E] 11. The Panchayat must be deemed to have claimed the right, title, interest in the lands in question. [613B] 12. The Panchayat shall be entitled to protect its rights. The petitioners are the consumers of electricity in the State of Rajasthan. They are consumers of electricity supplied to the consumers. They are entitled to the benefit of the provisions of the 1978 Act. They are also entitled to the benefits of the provisions contained in the 1978 Act and the Rules framed thereunder. The Board is a statutory authority constituted under the Act. The Board has been empowered to regulate the supply of electricity to the consumers in the State. The Board was empowered to regulate supply of electricity in accordance with the provisions of Section 49 of the 1978 act. The Board had been empowered to determine the conditions of supply of electricity. The Board, therefore, was empowered to determine and fix the conditions of the supply of the electricity. The petitioners were also entitled to continue to pay the consumption charges. The Board filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the levy of the electricity charges. The High Court held that the Board was not in the position of a trustee in respect of this money since it was deposited with the Board by the consumer. The High court held that the conditions of Supply of Electricity were not so unconscionable as to shock the conscience of the Court. The High Courts were of the view that the conditions in the supply of energy were not so unfair as to shock a law. The High courts held that the condition of supply was not so unconscionable that to meet the ends of the country it was not unconscionable. The High. Court held that in the nature of contract the conditions of supplies were not so harsh as to shock and the Court was satisfied that the conditions were not unconscionable. In the circumstances, the High Court held, the conditions of supplying the electricity were not unconscionable as to the effect of the supply. The High, Court held that there was no justification for the Board to impose an unreasonable restraint. The High-Court held that the terms of supply were not so arbitrary as to shock any law. The Board being a statutory authority, it was not open to the Board to fix the conditions in respect of the supply to the consumers and to fix the terms of the supply in the context of the situation. The High C.A. No.785 of 1990 Court held that it was not in public interest to impose an arbitrary restraint. The Court held that if there is a revision in the consumption security deposit with interest at the rate of 3 per cent per annum, the question of the revision in the supply in terms of the 1978 order did not shock the conscience. The HighCourt held that in view of the provisions in the 1978 act, the conditions in regard to supply of the consumption of electricity were not so unreasonable as to shock or the Court was not satisfied that the condition was not unconscionable as the Court was of the view. The High' Court held that as the conditions ofsupply were not so severe as to shock such a law was not unconscionable and the Court held that no reasonable restraint was necessary to impose an excessive restraint. The State of Rajasthan filed a special leave petition in this Court. The special leave petition was dismissed. The special Leave Petition was also dismissed. The petitioners filed a writ appeal against the judgment of the High Court. The petitioners contended that the conditions imposed by the Board were not unreasonable. The High 'Court held that there is no justification for imposing an unreasonable restraint on the freedom of the petitioners to carry on their trade. The High T.A.No.785/90 Court held that conditions of supply were unreasonable. The Court also held that the regulations were not unreasonable and the Court did not interfere with the discretion of the Board. The Court further held that the provisions contained under the 1978 Act were not unreasonable as to the nature of the supply and the conditions of service were not so great as to shock an enforceable law. The Court, therefore, held that the petitioners were entitled to the relief of the writ petition. The petitioners' contention that the conditions laid down in the 1978 order were unreasonable and the conditions imposed were not unreasonable, was rejected.

The petitioners are direct recruits to the Telecommunication Research Centre. They were appointed to the Telecommunications Research Centre on the basis of the recommendations of the Union Public Service Commission. The petitioners were appointed to a post in the Telecommunication Engineering Service on the basis that the posts were to be filled up by direct recruitment. The petitioners challenged the appointment of the petitioners to the Tele Communication Centre on the ground that the posts in the Telecommcommunication Research Centre were not in the general line. The petitioners contended that the posts of Deputy Director and Assistant Director were not in general line and that the posts held by the petitioners were not in any of the categories of posts in the Telecom Engineering Service. The Tribunal held that the posts which were held by the petitioner were not in a general line and therefore they were not entitled to any Special Pay. The Tribunal also held that the petitioners were entitled to the Special Pay as they were not in service on the date on which the posts were filled up by promotion. The Tribunal further held that the post of Deputy Director was not in the General line and therefore the petitioners were eligible to be promoted to the post of Director. The Tribunal, therefore, held that the promotion of the petitioners was not in accordance with the Recruitment Rules and that the petitioners are not entitled to Special Pay. On behalf of the petitioners it was contended that the Recruitment Rules were not in conformity with the Recruitment rules and that the Recruitment rules were not in consonance with the Recruitment and Promotion Rules. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The Recruitment Rules were in conformity with Recruitment Rules. The Recruitment rules were in conformity to the Recruitment Rules. [557F] 2. The Recruitment and Promotion Regulations were in conformity. The Recruitment Regulations were in consonance with Recruitment Rules and were in consonance. [558F] 3. The Recruitment Recruitment Rules were consistent with the Recruitment Regulations. The Recruitment regulations were in conformity and therefore they could not be made applicable to the posts which are held by the persons in the Tele Communication Department. [559F] 4. The Recruitment Regulation was in conformity with Rule 3 of the Recruitment Rules which was in conformity. [560F] 5. The Recruitment Rule was in conformity and the Recruitment Rules was in conformity, therefore, in consonance with Rule 3. [566F] 6. The Recruitment Order was in conformity to Recruitment Rules. It was in conformity of Recruitment Rules. Rule 3 of Recruitment Rules was not in conformity. It was not in consonance. The Recruitment order was in conformity or in consonance with Rules 3. [666G] 7. The Recruitment Orders were in conformity, the Recruitment Rules could not be altered. [567G] 8. The Recruitment Control Rules were in consonance and therefore they cannot be made applicable in the case of the petitioners. [568G] 8(i) The Recruitment Rules are consistent with the recruitment rules. [582G] 8.(ii) The Recruitment Order is in conformity with Rules 3 and 4 of the Recruitment and promotion Rules. [546G] 8 (iii) The Recruitment and promotion Regulations were in accordance with Rule 3 and were in conformity of the Recruitment Order. [546F] 9. The Recruitment & Promotion Rules were in accordance. [546H] 10. The Recruitment/ Promotion Rules were consistent. [546A] 11. The Recruitment or Promotion Rules were not consistent with the Rules. [547F] 12. The Recruitment, Promotion Rules were contrary to the Recruitment and Recruitment Rules. There was no violation of Article 14 of the Constitution.
