The appellant was employed as a clerk in the office of the respondent, a company, in the year 1962. The respondent was employed as an Assistant in the office at the relevant time. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he was guilty of misconduct, and was, therefore, dismissed from service. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of dismissal. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant filed a writ appeal to this Court. The appellant contended that the Labour Court was not justified in directing the reinstatement of the respondent in service. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Labour Court was justified in directing reinstatement of the appellant. [775 H] 2. The Labour court was not justified under the provisions of the Act in directing reinstatement. The Labour Appellate Tribunal was not justified to direct reinstatement of the employee in service. [776 H] 3. The Labour Courts are not expected to interfere with the award of the Labour Court unless the Labour Court is satisfied that the order of the Labour court is perverse or illegal. [778 H] 4. The Labour Commissioner is not a court and he is not bound to follow the procedure prescribed by the Act. The Labour Officer is not a Court. He is not a Tribunal. [779 H] 5. The Labour and Industrial Court was not right in directing reinstatement in service. The Labour & Industrial Court was justified under the Act in ordering reinstatement of the workman. [780 H] 6. The Labour is not a tribunal. The Labour or Industrial Court is not a forum. The Labour Act is a self-contained Code. The Labour, Court is not bound by the provisions of that Code. [782 H] 7. The Labour Judge was not justified. [785 H] 8. The Labour was not justified by the provisions contained in the Act. [786 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 14 of 1976. The appellant is a company which is a company registered under the Indian Companies Act. The respondent is a company incorporated under the Indian law. Court was not wrong in directing reinstatement with the appellant. The Labour' Court was not correct in directing reinstatement to the petitioner. The appellants filed a suit for eviction of the appellants from the suit premises on the ground of non-payment of rent. The appellants filed a written statement and contended that the suit was not maintainable in the facts and circumstances of the case as the respondents had not filed any application under section 12 of the Act for an extension of the period of the lease. The trial court held that the appellants were entitled to continue in possession of the suit premises as a tenant. The appellants preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellants then filed a second appeal before this Court. The question was whether the appellants were tenants within the meaning of section 12 of Act. The High court held that section 12 of that Act was not applicable to the present case as the appellants had not filed an application under section 13 of the Act. The question whether a landlord after the expiry of the period prescribed by section 12 of this Act had filed an application for an extension was not decided by the High Court in the second appeal. The High Curt held that section 11 of the Act was not attracted to the present proceedings. The High. Court held that section 13 of Act was not relevant for the purpose of determining the question whether a person was a tenant within the meaning ofs. 12 of Act and as such the application for extension of the term of the lease was not maintainable. The High, Court held that the question whether section 12 of act was applicable to the case was not decided in the facts of the case. The High' Court held that in the facts the appellants were not tenants within the purview of section 12 and as such they were not entitled to execute the decree in accordance with law. The High 'Court further held that the provisions of section 12 were not applicable to a case where the matter was covered by section 12. The High-Court further held, that the question was not decided on the basis of the first appellate court in the second court. The High Courts, therefore, held that section 14 of the Act did not apply to the present cases. The HighCourt further held in the second case that section 12 was not applicable in the facts as the matter was not covered by section 11 of Act. In the second case, the question was whether section 12 was applicable to a suit and the second appeal was dismissed. The High -Court held that section 15 of the Act provided that the provisions contained in the Act were applicable to the facts of that case. The question in the second suit was whether section 11 of act was attracted to the case. In the first suit the appellants were claiming to be tenants within the ambit of section 12. In the third suit the appellants claimed that they were tenants within section 12 of. Act. The appellants also claimed that section 12 should be read as a whole and not as a whole. The High courts held that section 16 of the Act applied to the present matter and the appellants were also entitled to execute a decree in accordance therewith. The High T.A. No. 1 of 1966 was filed by the appellants in the second Court. The appellants contended that section 12 is not applicable to cases where the matter is covered by section 14 of Act. It was also contended that section 15 was not applicable as the appellants were in possession of a building within the meaning s. 12 of the act. The High (Court held that the questions involved in the second appeals were not decided on merits. The High F.A.O. was dismissed. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that section 14 was not applicable. The question of law was not decided. The question as to whether section 12 is applicable to the cases before the High Court or not was not decided, and the High Court was not right in holding that section 12 did not apply. The question is whether section 12 applies to a case when the matter is not covered by the first appellate Court in the first suit.

The appellant was the Secretary of the appellant Society. The respondent was the Secretary in the appellant Society and was elected as the Secretary of a Society. The appellant was elected as Secretary of the Society. The Society was registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860. The Society had been registered under the provisions of the Societies Registration and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1860, and the Society was registered in the year 1960. The Society filed a suit for eviction of the Secretary of Society from the Society. During the pendency of the suit, the Society filed an application under section 15 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoration of the suit. The trial court dismissed the application. The appellant filed an appeal before the High Court. The High Court held that the appellant was not a party to the compromise petition filed by the Society and the High Court was wrong in dismissing the appellant's application. The High court held that the compromise petition was not maintainable. The High Curt also held that the trial court had jurisdiction to cancel the order permitting the withdrawal of the suit under section 15 of the Code. The High. Court also held that Hari Narain Swami was not the Secretary of appellant Society and, therefore, the order was not maintainable and the High court was also wrong in dismissing his appeal. The High, Court also held, that the appellant had not filed an application for withdrawal of the appeal under section 15(1) of the Code and the High Curt was wrong in holding that the appellant could not be permitted to withdraw the suit. In the result, the High Court dismissed the appeal. Hence, this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts in exercise of inherent power under section 15 (1) of Code of Civil procedure are vested with the power to cancel the compromise petition. The High courts have inherent power to cancel an order permitting the compromise. [775 H] 2. The High-Court has inherent power to pass an order for withdrawal of suit. The power of the court is not to be exercised in the interest of justice. [776 H] 3. The HighCourt has inherent powers to cancel the consent order. The High' Court has inherent power under Section 15(1). [776 B] 4. The High 'Court has inherent jurisdiction to cancel an application filed under section 15. [778 C] 5. The High -Court has inherent inherent power to set aside an order. [779 G] 6. The High Tr. Court has inherent powers. The High Cou rt has inherent power. [780 G] 7. The High cour t has inherent power, and the High Cou il Court has inherent jurisdiction. [781 G] 8. The High Fr Court has inherent inherent powers. [782 G] 9. The High COurt has inherent power in the interest o f justice. [750 G] 10. The High Court has inherent powers, and the power of the Court is not to act as inherent power. The High Commis sion has inherent power and the Court has inherent authority to pass an ex pane order. [750 H] 11. The High S Court has inherent Power to cancel an ex p ead order. [751 H] 12. The High LC Court has inherent Powers.

The appellant was a member of the Indian Civil Service and was posted as a member of that service. He was appointed to the Indian Civil Services on April 1, 1946, and was confirmed in that service on April 1. 1946. He was confirmed in the Indian Civil services on April 1,. 1946, and he was confirmed in his appointment on April 1., 1946, and thereafter, he was confirmed on April 1; 1946, and, on April 1 he was confirmed as a member in the Indian Police Service on April 1 and April 1, 1947, and was also confirmed in the State of Jammu and Kashmir on April 1 'A' and April 1 'B' respectively. The appellant was confirmed in a post in the Indian Administrative Service on April 2, 1947, but he was confirmed later on on April 1 3, 1947, on April 2. 1947, and he continued in that service till April 1, 1948, and thereafter he was confirmed. On April 1, 1949, he was appointed to officiate as a member to the Indian Police Services on April 2 and April 1. On April 2, 1949, the appellant was confirmed as an officer in the Indian police Service on April 3, 1949, and he joined the Indian Police service on April 4, 1949, but he continued in the Indian Judicial Service on April 5, 1949, till April 1. 1949, and thereafter on April 1 1, 1949. On April 4, 1950, the appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Jammu and K Kashmir praying for a writ of mandamus directing the State of J&K and the appellant to declare that he was confirmed and confirmed in the post of a member in that service. The High Court dismissed the writ petition on the ground that the appellant was not entitled to the relief claimed by him. The appellant filed a special leave petition in this Court which was dismissed on April 1 9, 1961. The appellant then filed a writ of certiorari in the High court of Jammu andKashmir, and the High Court dismissed his writ petition. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. The appellant is a member of Indian Civil Service. He was a member to a service on April 2 of the Indian Police. He was also confirmed as a Member in the Indian Criminal Service on April 4. 1949, but was confirmed in April 1, 1950, and was appointed to a post in that service by the Indian Police, Service on April 6, 1949, on April 4,. 1949, and was subsequently confirmed in the same service on April 5. 1949. The appellant challenged the validity of the order of the High Court by means of a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution. The High court dismissed the writ petitions. The appellant, therefore, filed a writ appeal in this Court. The appellant contended that the order of confirmation of the appellant was illegal and void and that the order was not a nullity. HELD: (1) The appellant was not a member of a service on the date of the order, and he could not be confirmed in the service of the State of the Union of India. [675 B] (2) The appellant could not be regarded as a member on the date when the order of his confirmation was made. The order of confirmation was not a valid order. The order was not an order of confirmation. [676 D] (3) The order of the Government of the Union Territory of Jammu and kashmir was not a law passed by the Parliament. [678 D] (4) The appellant had no right to the post of member in the State Civil Service. [679 D] (5) The order was passed by the President of India and was not a judicial order. The appellant could be confirmed in his post. [682 D] (6) The order passed by the Government of Jammu andkashmir was a nullity.

The appellant, a member of the Indian Police Service, was convicted by the Court of Session, on a charge of murder, under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, and sentenced to death. The appellant was convicted by a Court of Session for murder and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The appellant filed an appeal to the High Court, which was dismissed. The appellant then filed a petition under Article 32 of the Constitution for a writ of habeas corpus, which was allowed by the High Court by its judgment dated April 14, 1981. The appellant challenged the correctness of the judgment of the High Court in a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the appellant was guilty of murder and sentenced him to imprisonment for a term of life. The High court held that the sentence of death was not justified. The appellant, who was convicted by Court of Session under section 302, was sentenced to imprisonment of life. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was not justified in confirming the death sentence passed under section 302. The appellant contended that the High court was not justified, in confirming the sentence of imprisonment for life, and that the High Courts were justified in confirming that sentence. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts were not justified in interfering with the death sentence. [775 H] 2. The High courts were justified in interfering in the death sentence and the judicial discretion vested in the Court regarding its imposition on an accused is well merited. [776 H] 3. The High Curt was justified in confirming death sentence. The High. Court was justified in upholding the death sentence of the appellant. [778 H] 4. The High-Court was justified in interfering, in the death penalty. [779 H] 5. The High, Court was justified, in upholding the sentence of life imprisonment. [780 H] 6. The High' Court was justified. [791 H] 6 The High Court was justified on the facts and circumstances of the case, and the sentence of the two appellants was not justified.[791 H,792 A] 7. The High 'Court was justified on a consideration of the facts and the circumstances of the present case. [792 A B] JUDGMENT: CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Criminal Appeal No. 8 of 1981. This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment of a Division Bench of the Allahabad Court dismissing the appeal filed by the appellant against the judgment and order of the High court dismissing the appeal of the appellant against his conviction under section 302 and the sentence imposed on him by the Court below. The High appeal was allowed by this Court by its order dated April 14. 1981. The High 2 Court dismissed the appeal of appellant against his sentence. The appellant has filed this appeal by special Leave. The appellant's counsel has filed a petition for special leave to appeal against his conviction and sentence. The appeal is directed against his conviction. The appellant challenges his conviction under [section 304] and the sentence passed on him by Court below. It is not necessary to refer to the facts of the case.

The appellant was a member of the Indian Police Service. He was appointed as a member of a Police Service on January 1, 1950. He was promoted as a member from the Indian Police Services on January 1. 1950. He had been promoted as a result of the disciplinary proceedings initiated against him. He was, however, not given a special leave to appeal against the findings of the departmental authorities. The appellant was, however not given a further opportunity to meet a new case. The appellant, however, did not avail of that opportunity. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the disciplinary authority. The High Court dismissed the petition. The appellant then filed a writ appeal to this Court. The appellant contended that the order of dismissal was illegal and void. The appellant urged that the order was illegal and that the order passed by the disciplinary authority was illegal. The appellant also contended that the disciplinary authority had not given a second opportunity to the appellant to meet a fresh case. The High court held that the order dated April 30, 1971, was illegal and the order was liable to be set aside. The appellant's writ petition was dismissed. The appellant thereafter filed a writ application in the High court for a writ of mandamus directing the disciplinary authority to give a second opportunity of hearing to the appellant. The High, Court dismissed the writ petition. The High. Court held that the appellant was guilty of misconduct and accordingly dismissed the writ application. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The order of the High Court is illegal and void and the appellant is entitled to a writ of certiorari. [775 H] 2. The order passed by a disciplinary authority is illegal and invalid. The order is illegal and the appellant has no right to appeal against it. [776 H] 3. The order was passed in violation of the principles of natural justice. The appellant had been given a second chance to meet a case. The order dated April 29, 1971 was illegal and invalid and the appellant was entitled to a second opportunity. [778 H] 4. The order in question was illegal and bad. The appellant could not be heard to say that the order is illegal. [779 H] 5. The order cannot be sustained. The order has been passed in violation or in violation of principles of natural Justice. [780 H] 6. The order does not suffer from any infirmity. [782 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 15 of 1971. Appeal by Special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 14th July, 1971 of the High court of Delhi in Civil Writ Petition No. 12 of 1971. S. N. Andley, for the appellant. S. K. Bagga, for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by RAY, J. This appeal by special Leave is directed against the judgment of the High, Court of Delhi dated April 14, 1971. The appellant is a member of Indian Police Service and is aggrieved by the order of his dismissal. The appellant challenged the order of termination of his services by the Delhi Police. The appellant raised a preliminary objection that the order in question is illegal and bad in law. The appellant submitted that the order terminating his services was illegal and was, therefore, liable to be quashed. The appellant further submitted that the appellant had been promoted to the post of a member of Delhi Police and, therefore, the order of removal was illegal and liable to be declared as illegal. The High-Court, however, held that the respondent was guilty of the misconduct and accordingly, directed the disciplinary authority, to give a fresh opportunity to the petitioner to meet a further case. The respondent filed a writ-petition in the High-Court challenging the order dated May 14, 1971, and the writ petition was allowed by the High Court.

The appellant, a dealer in the goods, filed a return of sales of goods in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The Sales Tax Officer, who assessed the sales tax payable by the appellant, assessed the sales-tax payable by the dealer. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the assessment. The High Court held that the sales tax paid by the dealer was not a tax on the sale of goods. The High court held that the Sales Tax Act, which came into force on the date of the sale, was not applicable to the facts of the case. The High. Court held that in the case of sales tax paid on the sales of goods, the purchase by the State Trading Corporation from the merchant was the last purchase in the State and, therefore, the purchase was not a sale of goods and the purchase by it was not a case of sale of goods within the State. The High, Court held that there was no sale of goods in respect of which the sales tax was payable by the assessee. The High' Court held that as the sales tax had not been paid by the appellant and the sales tax assessed by the Sales Tax Officer was not a "tax on sale of goods", the purchase by him was not a sales tax. The High 'Court held that the purchase by a dealer from the merchant, was not a purchase tax and, therefore. the purchase by that dealer was not "tax on the sale or purchase of goods". The High Court further held that the sale by the appellant was not a 'tax on sale' within the State of the Andhra Pradesh. In the result, the High Court held, that the sales by the appellant were not a sale within the State and the purchase was a "tax" on the sale. The appellant is now before us. The appellant has filed a special leave petition in this Court against the judgment of the High Court. The appellant contended that the sales in question were not a " tax on the sales" within the State, and, therefore the purchase by them was not a transaction of sale within the meaning of the Sales Tax. The appellant also contended that the Sales tax payable by him was a tax on sale of the goods within the meaning ofs. 2(f) of the Sales-tax Act and, therefore he was not a dealer. The High-Court held that there is no sale of the appellant within the State in the case. In the case of the sales by a dealer in goods, the purchases by the State Government from the merchant were the last purchase, and, in the case, the purchase of the goods was not a transfer of the goods, but a sale of the same goods. The appellant was not an "tax on sales" within s. 2(i) of the Act. The High C.A.T. dismissed the writ petition. The appellant then filed a special appeal in this Court. The special leave petition was dismissed. The appellant thereafter filed a special special leave petition against the judgment and order of the High C. A.T. The appellant obtained special leave from this Court.

The appellant was employed as a workman in the appellant's establishment for a period of 12 calendar months preceding the date of his retrenchment. He was appointed as a workman under the appellant's employer on a temporary basis for a period not exceeding one year. He was retrenched from service on account of the failure of the appellant to comply with the provisions of section 25B(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The appellant was served with a notice of termination of his service on the ground that he was in continuous service for a period exceeding one year and that he was not in continuous service within the meaning of section 25-B(2)(a) and he was, therefore, not entitled to be reinstated in service. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice of termination. The High Court held that the appellant was in continuous employment for a period beyond one year and, therefore, he was not entitled to reinstatement in service. It was further held that the termination of the appellant was illegal and inoperative and a declaration was made that he was entitled to be in continuous service with all consequential benefits. The appellant's appeal was dismissed. The appellant then filed a writ appeal in this Court. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The termination of the services of the appellant is illegal and inoperative. [775 H] 2. The termination is illegal and void. The termination was illegal and void and a declaration that the workman concerned continued to be in service with all consequences. [776 H] 3. The termination in the present case was illegal and a declaration is made that the workman was in continuous services for a period extending one year and six months. [778 H] 4. The termination, therefore, was illegal and invalid. [779 H] 5. The termination being illegal and inoperative, a declaration is necessary. [780 H] 6. The termination does not amount to retrenchment within the meaning ofs. 25B(1) of the Act. The termination therefore, is illegal and invalid and a declaration has to be made that the appellant is entitled to be paid in terms of the provisions of sub section (2) of section 25F. [782 H] 7. The termination order is illegal and is not a declaration of the termination. [785 H] 8. The termination cannot be declared illegal and inoperative merely because the appellant was not in service for a long period. [786 H] 9. The termination can be declared illegal only if it is illegal and in the circumstances, a declaration can be made that he is in continuous service. [787 H] 10. The termination must be in the nature of a declaration of termination of service. [750 H] 11. The termination will be illegal and inoperative only if it does not amount either to a declaration of a termination of service for a specified period or is in the nature thereof. [750 A] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1379 of 1989. From the Judgment and Order dated the 14th July, 1989 of the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad in Civil Misc. S K Srivastava and S S Srivastava for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by K. JAYACHALIAH, J.

The appellant was appointed as a temporary employee in the office of the Deputy Commissioner of Police, District, Amritsar. He was dismissed from service on March 17, 1955. The appellant was dismissed from the service on March 18, 1955. On March 17, 1956, the appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of dismissal. The High Court dismissed the petition on March 17. The appellant filed a petition in this Court under Article 32 of the Constitution. The appellant contended that the order of termination of his service was not a punishment and that the order was not a dismissal or removal from service. The appellant also contended that the termination of his services was not a penalty and that the termination was not a removal or dismissal but was a dismissal. HELD: (i) The order of termination was not an order of dismissal but was an order of termination simpliciter. The order of dismissal was not an award or order of dismissal and was not a termination simpliciter. [652 F] (ii) The order terminating the services of the appellant was not an "order of dismissal" but was an "order" of dismissal. [653 G] (iii) The order was not an 'order of dismissal but an order of discharge simpliciter. [650 D] (iv) The order passed by the Settlement Officer was not an administrative order but an order discharging a probationer. The order was an order discharging the appellant from service. [650 A] (v) The order dated March 17, 1954, was an order terminating the appellant's services for unsatisfactory work and conduct. The order dated April 17, 1955, was an " order of termination simplicitor. The order terminating his services was an order simpliciter. [663 F] (vi) The order in question was an order "an order" of termination simpliciter, and therefore, there was no stigma affecting the future career of the appellant. [654 D] (vii) The order did not amount to an order of punishment. The order did amount to an "order " of dismissal. It was not an ex parte order. [655 G] (viii) The order under appeal was not an Award or order of termination but an order discharge simpliciter. The appellant could not be said to be a probationer. [656 H] (ix) The order dismissing the appellant was an order or discharge simpliciter. It was an order simplicitor. An order of termination could be passed. [657 H] (x) The order is an order of removal simpliciter. The termination of the appellant's service was not an act of dismissal but only an order of suspension. [658 H] (xi) The order, therefore, was an ex parte one. [659 H] (xii) The order does not amount to a termination simpliciter, but an order terminating an appointment simpliciter. [600 H] (xiii) The order could not be passed by an order discharging an employee from service. It was a termination simpliciter and not an order simpliciter, and that the appellant was a probationer. It was only an order simpliciter and not a termination simplicitor. [660 H] (xiv) The order having been passed by the order of discharge, the order was an ex-parte order. [600 A] (xv) The order being an order of penalty, the order of the termination was an order which was an order discharge simplicitor. [600 B] (xvi) The order for termination of the services of a probationer was an order not an order discharging him from service. An order discharging a temporary employee from service is an order discharging simpliciter. [613 C] (xvii) The order appointing the appellant was merely an order of appointment simpliciter. The appointment was an order and not an " order" of dismissal simpliciter. [625 D] (xviii) The order itself was an order.

The appellant, a candidate for the post of Professor in the college, was appointed as a Professor in the College on November 15, 1968. He was appointed to the post of a Professor in a college on November 15. The appellant was appointed to a post of Professor on November 15 and was appointed to that post on November 15 on November 15 after the selection made by the Commission. The appellant, who was appointed to an additional post in the college on November 16, 1968, was appointed to another post in the College. The appellant challenged the appointment of the appellant by a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the appointment of respondent No. 1. The appellant filed a writ petition before this Court. The appellant contended that the appointment of Respondent No. 1 was invalid for that reason. The High court held that the appointment was invalid for the reason that the Selection Committee was not consulted in the manner required by section 133 of the Constitution. The High, Court held that the Selection committee was not consulted and that the Selection was not vitiated for that reason and that the High Court was in error in holding that the Selection Board was not consulted. The appellant's writ petition was dismissed. The appellant then filed a writ appeal in this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The appointment of Respondent 1 was valid for the reason of his appointment. [775 H] 2. The appointment was valid for a period of one year and was, therefore, valid. [776 H] 3. The appointment is valid for a further period of one month. [778 H] 4. The appointment being valid for a long period, the appointment was valid. [750 H] 4(i) The appointment was invalid because the Selection Committee had not met in the manner prescribed by section 133(b) of the Constitution and the Selection Committee did not have the power to approve or disapprove the committee. [750 A] (ii) The appointment of the respondent was valid for one year and the Selection was valid for that reason, [750 A B] (iii) The appointment is invalid for the reasons mentioned in the writ petition. [750 B] (iv) The appointment being invalid for the other reason, the appointment is invalid. [750 D] (v) The appointment cannot be invalid for the simple reason that the selection was not made by the Selection Committee. [750 G] (vi) The appointment could not be invalid for that reasons. [750 F] (vii) The appointment having been made in the prescribed manner, the appointment cannot be said to be invalid for any other reason. [750 C] (viii) The appointment made was valid for two years and was, accordingly, invalid. [785 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1566 of 1967. Appeal by Special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 14th July, 1967 of the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad in Civil Misc. Writ Petition No. 1135 of 1967. S. K. Sinha and P. C. Agarwala, for the appellant. S. N. Prasad, for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. The appellant is a candidate for appointment to the post in the Government College. He was selected for appointment to a post in the said College on November 16. The appellant applied for the post in question. The Selection Committee was appointed by the Government on November 15 to the post. The Selection committee was appointed to consider the appellant's case. The Selection was not made on the basis of the recommendation of the Selection Committee and the Selection committee did not have any power to approve the appointment. The appellant has challenged the appointment on the ground that the Selection is not made by a Selection Committee. The appellant also challenged the validity of the appointment of his selection. The High. Court held that there was no infirmity in the appointment of a candidate.

The petitioner was elected to the Legislative Assembly of the United Kingdom on the basis of a resolution passed by the House of Commons of the United States of America on the ground that the House of the Legislature of the United State had the power to make a law for the removal of the petitioner from the House of Lords. The petitioner was elected as a member of the House of Parliament of the United Republic of America on January 26, 1950. The petitioner challenged the election of the petitioner on the ground of violation of the fundamental right under article 19(1) of the Constitution. The High Court held that the petitioner was entitled to succeed. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the election of his election. The High court held that the provisions of article 19(2) were not made subject to the provisions of the Constitution and that the petitioner had not been shown to have done so. The High, Court held that article 19(3) was not made subject, and that the provisions were not made in accordance with the provisions of that article. The petitioner then filed a writ appeal to this Court. The petitioner contended that the provisions in article 19(4) were not applicable to the petitioner as he was not a member of a House of the legislature of the United countries of America. The petitioner also contended that the petitioner could not be said to have done anything in contravention of the provisions of [article 19(1)(a).] Held, that the petitioner is not a member or a member of any House of the United Nations and, therefore, the provisions of section 3(1)(b) of the Act were not made applicable to him. The petitioner could not, therefore, be said to be a member of an House of the Parliament of the U.S.A. of the United Nation of America.

The appellant was appointed as a Reader in the Government College on April 9, 1966. He was appointed as Reader in the College on April 10, 1966. On April 10, 1967, he was confirmed as a Reader. On April 11, 1967, the Government issued a circular in the matter of appointment of the Respondents as Readers. The Respondents were appointed as Readers on April 10. 1967. On April 12, 1967, they were confirmed as Readers. On April 13, 1967, a notification was issued by the Government inviting applications for appointment as Readers in the College. The Respondents, who were appointed as Professors, were appointed as Lecturers on April 10,. 1967. On May 14, 1967, an advertisement was issued by a Public Service Commission inviting applications for the post of Readers. The Appellant was selected and appointed as Readers. He was confirmed as such on April 13, 1968. On April 14, 1968, the Respondents were appointed to the post of Reader. On May 15, 1968, a notification in the matter was issued by which the Respondents were confirmed as Professors. On May 16, 1968, an advertisement in the matter had been published in the newspaper. The Respondents had also applied for the post. The Appellant, who was appointed as Readers, was appointed as Lecturers. On May 17, 1968, he was appointed as an Assistant Professor. On May 18, 1968, another advertisement was issued in the matter. On May 19, 1968, Respondent No. 1 was appointed as Assistant Professor. The Appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. On appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The High court was right in holding that the Respondents were eligible to be referred to the Public Service Commission for the post as Readers. [775 H] 2. The appointment of the Appellants as Readers was made by the Public Service commission on April 10 and not on April 10 as contended by the Respondents. The appointment was made on April 10 in the Public Service. The appointment made was on April 10 but not on April 11. The appointment is made on April 11, 1968. The appointment as Readers was on April 11 and not on May 14. The appointment by the Public service Commission was made on May 14, 1968. [776 H] 3. The appointment on April 10 was made on the basis of the recommendation of the Public Service Commissions. The appointment order was issued on April 13. 1968. On May 20, 1968, no appointment order was passed. On May 21, 1968, there was no appointment order. On May 22, 1968, it was made on behalf of the Respondents. [778 H] 4. The appointment to the post was made on June 14, 1968 and not on the date of taking over. The appointment could not be made on April 13 and the appointment was made in the Public service. [779 H] 5. The appointment in the Public Services Commission was made by a Public service Commission. The appointment, therefore, was made on a post on April 11 but not on the post of a Reader. [780 H] 6. The appointment being made on April 12, 1968, was made by an order of the Government. The appointment letter was issued on May 14 and not on June 14. The appointments were made on April 14. 1968. [750 H] 7. The appointment cannot be made on the date on which the Public Service Comforts Commission was constituted. The appointment can be made on a Post in the Public services Commission. [750 A] 8. The appointment must be made on June 13, 1968 and the appointment is made in the public service. [750 G] 9. The appointment has to be made on May 22, 1967. The appointment should be made on that date. [750 B] 10.

The appellants were appointed as drivers in the State Transport Authority, Madras, on the basis of a scheme published by the Corporation under section 68F(1) of the Act. The scheme was published in the Gazette on the basis that the scheme was published by the State Transport Authorities under section 68C of the Act and the scheme was approved by the State Government. The scheme provided that the scheme would be published in the official gazette. The scheme also provided that the State Transport authority would be entitled to grant temporary permits to any one else if the Corporation applied for all the permits. The scheme further provided that the remaining vacancies and the remaining vacancies would be filled up by the Corporation. The scheme then provided that the Corporation would be entitled, subject to the provisions of section 68F, to the exclusion of others. The scheme, however, provided that the existing operators would be entitled for the remaining 4 vacancies and the Corporation would have to make all the necessary arrangements for the grant of temporary permits. The Corporation issued a notification in the official Gazette on the same day inviting applications for the remaining 5 vacancies and the scheme provided that all the temporary permits would be granted to any one. The scheme stated that the scheme should be published in all the cases and the Corporation was to be entitled to apply for all the temporary permit. The scheme indicated that the existing operator would be entitled only to the remaining 4 posts and the remaining 5 posts would be filled by the Corporation in the remaining 5 vacant posts. The scheme stipulated that the remaining 5 post would be filled in by the Corporation and the remaining 4 post would be made available to the Corporation. On the basis of the scheme, the Corporation issued a notice in the official newspapers inviting applications for all the remaining 5 temporary permits. On the same day, the Corporation published a notification in respect of the remaining 5 vacancy and the Corporation issued another notification in the Gazette dated the same day. The scheme specified that the remaining 4 vacant posts would be made out of the remaining 4 temporary permits. It was further stated that the Corporation was also to apply for temporary permits only if the Corporation was willing to operate vehicles to the maximum number of the existing operators. The scheme contained a provision that the remaining 3 vacancies and the balance 5 posts would not be filled up. The Corporation filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the scheme. The High Court held that the scheme did not provide for any additional posts and that the scheme provided for the remaining 3 vacant posts and the Corporation could not have granted temporary permits to the existing operators for the remaining five vacancies. The High court held that the Corporation could have granted temporary permit to any one of the existing operator who was willing to be granted temporary permits. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The scheme did not contain any provision for the grant or renewal of temporary permits to a particular individual. The scheme only provided that the balance 5 vacancies and other additional posts would be kept vacant. The scheme contemplated that the remaining four vacancies and the rest of the remaining vacancies were to be filled up in the remaining five vacant posts. [505 G] 2. The scheme provides that the remaining three vacancies and the additional posts would not exceed the number of the remaining posts. The Corporation could not be permitted to have the additional posts and the balance of the remaining additional posts would exceed the number specified in the scheme. [506 G] 3. The scheme does not provide for the additional posts. The additional posts and additional posts are to be filled in the remaining additional vacancies. [507 G] 4. The scheme is not a mere scheme or a scheme or a part of it. The scheme itself provides that the balance of additional posts and other additional additional posts would include the additional posts, additional posts and extra additional posts. [506 G] 5.

The appellant was a minor. He executed a will dated January 11, 1934, in favour of his maternal grandfather. The appellant was a widow. The respondent was a minor at the time of the execution of the will. The appellant filed a suit for partition in the Court of the District Judge, Delhi, on the ground that the property in suit was ancestral property and that the respondent was a Hindu. The trial court held that the property was ancestral property. The respondent filed an appeal to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant then filed a second appeal to this Court. The appellant contended that the High Court was in error in holding that the property inherited by a Hindu from a maternal grandfather was ancestral property, and that the High court was in error. HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that there was no evidence to show that the property which was inherited by the respondent from a maternal grand father was ancestral property or that the respondent had no right to challenge the alienation of the property. [775 H] (2) The High court was right in not following the earlier Full Bench decision in the case of Narotam Chand 's case (1). [775 G] (3) The High Courts were in error in not following that decision. [776 H] (4) The High Curt was in error when it held that the respondent could not claim that the property acquired by him from a maternal grandmother was ancestral property in the hands of a grandson. [778 H] (5) The High, Court was in wrong in not following this decision. [750 H] (6) The High. Court was in a wrong in not applying the earlier Full bench decision to the facts of the case. [750 A] (7) The High-Court was in error, in not following a previous Full Bench decision. [751 A] (8) The High' Court was in fact in error in thinking that the earlier Full Court decision was erroneous. [751 B] (9) The High 'Court was in a correct error in not applying that decision. The High C Court was in an error in not considering the earlier Full-Bench decision. [751 H] (10) The High T.C.C. was in error as it was in error by the first Full Bench decision and the High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the decision of the first Full-Benches. [751 D] (11) The High F.C.I. was in a position to say that the earlier decision was erroneous and that the earlier decisions were erroneous. [753 H] (12) The High A Court was in the wrong in not considering that the earlier judgment was erroneous. The High F,C.I., was in error and the High Curt had no jurisdiction. [751 G] (13) The High R.C. C. was in the error of law. [751 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 14 of 1966. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated the 8th July, 1966 of the Delhi High Court in Civil Writ No. 10 of 1965. S. K. Sinha, for the appellant. S. N. Prasad, for the respondent. The appellant was a member of the Indian Police Service. He was convicted by the trial court and sentenced to death. The appellant was convicted by a court of law under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The appellant filed an appeal to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant then filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court for a writ of certiorari quashing the order of the trial court. The High court held that the offence under section 307 read with section 149 of the Indian penal Code was not established and that the conviction of the appellant was not illegal. The High, Court held that the appellant was guilty of the offence under sections 302 read with Section 34 of the I.P.C. and sentenced him to imprisonment for a term of one year. The High. Court held that in view of the provisions of section 34 of Indian Penal Code, the appellant was liable to be convicted under section 307 of the Indian I.P.'C. and was liable to suffer imprisonment for life and to a fine. The appellant preferred an appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The offence under section 302 of the Indian Code was not proved. The offence was not proved against the appellant. [557F] 2. The offence of murder was not established by the prosecution. The offence did not fall within the purview of section 34. The offence fell within the purview thereof. [558F] 3. The offence punishable under section 307 was not established. The offence could be proved only by the evidence of the witnesses. [559F] 4. The offence committed by the appellant was clearly not established. [560F] 5. The offence in question was not established against the appellant and the conviction of him was not illegal and was liable for dismissal. [566F] 6. The offence is not established by evidence. The offence falls within the purview ofs. 34 of the Act. The offence must be proved by the evidence. [567F] 7. The offence would be proved only if the evidence is such that it is so established. [546F] 8. The offence can be proved only in law. The offence has been established by the evidence and the conviction is not illegal. [546G] 9. The offence cannot be proved by evidence. [546B] 10. The offence does not fall within section 34 of IPC. The offence comes within the purview s. 34 of Indian penal Code. [546C] 11. The offence being not established by any evidence, the conviction of an accused under section 307 is not illegal and is liable to be set aside. [546D] 12. The offence for which the appellant was convicted was not established beyond reasonable doubt. [546E] JUDGMENT: CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Criminal Appeal No. 11 of 1977. The appellant was a minor. He was a minor at the time of the death of his father. He was the son of the appellant. He was born on the 1st January, 1946.
