The appellant, a member of the family of the respondent, was the owner of a house in the city of Madras. He executed a power of attorney in favour of the respondent in respect of the house in question. The respondent executed a power-of attorney in favour and in the name of the appellant in respect of all the matters in which he was to act for him. The respondent was the owner and in possession of the house. The appellant executed a power in favour of his father, the respondent. The appellant was the owner in respect of certain properties. The respondent filed a suit for partition and separate possession of the properties. The trial court decreed the suit. The respondent appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the power of attorney executed by the respondent in favour of a co-sharer in the house in which he had a share was not a valid power of attorney and that the power was not a document of power of attorney. The High court further held that the document in question was not a deed of power of Attorney and that the document was not a registered document. The High. Court further held that in the absence of any power of attorney, the power of Attorney was not a legal document. The respondent, therefore, filed a suit in the court of the Subordinate Judge, Madras for a declaration that the power in question was a valid power. The High, Court held that in view of the terms of the power of the attorney, the document in respect of which the power of power of the Attorney was executed was a deed of Power of Attorney and not a deed in respect of any property. The High C.A. No. 12 of 1986 filed by the appellant was dismissed. The appellant filed a second appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The power of attorney is a document of Power of attorney. It is a document executed by the executant in favour of one of the co-sharers. The power is not a document executed in respect of a property. The power was not an instrument of power of power. [557 C] 2. The power to execute a power of Attorney is a document in respect to a property. It is not a deed executed by the donor in favour of another person. [558 D] 3. The power conferred on the attorney is a power of power and not a power of an attorney. The power cannot be split up into separate instruments. [559 F] 4. The power in respect of property cannot be split into separate instruments and that the instrument in question cannot be split in individual acts. [560 D] 5. The power given to the attorney is not a power to execute the document. The power has to be exercised in the name and in the names of the executant. [566 D] 6. The power can be split up in individual acts and the power is not an instrument executed by the donee in favour of any other person. [546 D] 7. The power under the power of a power of the power is a power to be exercised by the donor. [546 F] 8. The power could be split up. [546 G] 8. In the absence of power of an agent, the power is an instrument of Power of power. The power may be a power of a Power of Attorney. [546 H] 9. The power must be exercised in a name and in a name. [546 B] 10. The power should be exercised in respect of properties. [546 C] 11. The power does not include the power to execute an instrument of powers of power. It is an instrument executed in respect to property. [546 E] 12. The power vested in the attorney is an instrument in respect of immovable property. [547 G] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1266 of 1986. From the Judgment and Order dated the 9th May, 1986 of the Madras High Court in C.M.

The assessee, a firm, was assessed to tax on the income of the firm. The firm was assessed to income tax on the total income of the assessee. The firm filed a return of its income for the assessment year 1962-63. The Income tax Officer, on the basis of the information contained in the return, assessed the assessee to tax on its income. The assessee filed a return for the assessment years 1962-63 and 1963-64. The Income Tax Officer, on receipt of the information, assessed the firm to tax on income. The Income-tax Officer, on a reference made to him under section 66(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, assessed the income of Rs. 1,10,000/- and Rs. 1 lakh as depreciation. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Tribunal, on a further reference, held that the depreciation was allowable under the provisions of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922 and that the assessee was entitled to the benefit of the depreciation under the Indian Income Tax Act. The Tribunal, on further reference, referred the following question to the High Court: "Whether, on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the depreciation allowable under the Indian Incometax law is allowable under the Income tax Act." The High Court answered the question in the affirmative and against the assessee. Hence this appeal by special leave. The question is whether the High Court was right in law in holding that the depreciation allowable to the assessee under the Indian law is allowable in computing the written down value of the assets. The assessee, in the assessment year, claimed depreciation under the provisions contained in the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922. The Income. tax Officer rejected the claim of the assessee and held that the assessee had not claimed depreciation under section 10(5) of the Income tax. The assessee then filed a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that the provisions of section 10(2) (b) of the Act were not applicable to the assessee. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the High Court had erred in law in not considering the effect of the provisions of sections 10(2), 10(3) and 10(5), and that the High court was wrong in holding that it was not open to the Income tax Officer to consider the effect of section 10 (5) (b). Dismissing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The High court was right in holding that section 10(3)(b) of The Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1962, was not applicable to an assessee who had claimed depreciation under Section 10(5). [775 H] 2. The words "or any law relating to tax on profits of business" in the proviso to section 10(4) of the Amendment Act, 1962 must be construed in the light of the words "any law relating to income tax and super tax on profits" in the Explanation to section 10 (4) (b), and the words "or law relating to" in the explanation to section 10 of the Amendment act, 1962. [775 G] 3. The words 'or any law' in the Explanation must be construed as "any law" in the sense in which it is in the Act. [776 H] 4. The words used in the Explanation are "any law", in the context of the Explanation. [778 H] 5. The words in the explanation are not intended to be used in the sense of "any law " in the sense that it is not applicable to a case where the provisions of a statute relating to tax are not applicable. [780 H] 6. The words of the Explanation are not intended by the Legislature. The words are not intended for the purpose of the Explanation and the words used are not intended. [782 H] 7. The words employed in the Explanation should be construed in their natural and ordinary sense.

The appellant was a contractor for the supply of certain materials and for the construction of the building. The appellant was a registered contractor for the construction work of the building and the contractor was required to execute the work. The appellant had executed the work and the contractor had executed the same. The appellant completed the work and submitted the bills for the work. After completion of the work, the appellant was required to pay the bills. The appellant filed a suit for specific performance of the contract. The trial court decreed the suit. The appellant preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. The appellant contended that the High Court was wrong in holding that the appellant was not qualified to tender for the contract. It was further contended that the appellant had not complied with the requirements of para I of the N.I.T. and that the appellant could not be said to have been qualified to tender the contract. Dismissing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The High court was wrong in observing that the appellant did not comply with the requirements in para I of N.I,T. and the appellant was therefore not qualified to be appointed as a contractor. [775 H] 2. The appellant could not have been permitted to tender for a contract. The appellant did not have the requisite qualification to be appointed. [776 H] 3. The appellant having not complied with para I of para I, the High Court should not have dismissed the suit. [778 H] 4. The appellant is entitled to the relief claimed in the suit. He was not qualified for the contract and the High Court rightly dismissed the suit filed by the appellant. [779 H] 5. The appellant cannot be said to be qualified to tender a tender for the work and he was not qualified. [780 H] 6. The appellant should have been qualified for the work as he did not comply. [782 H] 7. The appellant must be deemed to have been duly qualified to tender. [785 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 15 of 1972. Appeal by Special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 9th May, 1972 of the High Court of Delhi in Civil Writ Petition No. 11 of 1972. S. N. Prasad, for the appellant. S. K. Sinha, for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. The appellant, M.C.C. has filed this Appeal against the judgment and order of the High court of Delhi dated September 9, 1972 in Civil Writ No. 11/72. The appellant challenges the judgment and decree of the High. Court of Delhi dated October 9, 1972 dismissing the suit filed against him. The appellant's case is that the appellant has not complied with paras I and II of the N,I.T., and has not complied the requirements of paras I and III of the N.,I.T, and has not been able to show that the appellant is qualified to tender his tender. The appellant also challenges the finding of the High' Court that the appellant failed to comply with para I and II. The appellant further contends that the High court was right in holding that para I of Part I of the said N.I.,T. and not para I of that N.I.-T. and, therefore, the appellant is not qualified to bid for the contract in question. The appellant contends that the appellant should have complied with para II of Part I and should have been disqualified to tender the tender. The High. Court has held that the appellant cannot be held to have been disqualified for the contract as he was not eligible to tender for contract. The High' Court has held in the judgment under appeal that the appellant must be held to be qualified for the tender. It is not necessary to go into the question whether the appellant was qualified to tender in the contract.

The appellant was an employee of the appellant, who was an employee in the appellant's factory. He was appointed as a Manager in the appellant' factory. He had been appointed as a manager in the appellant factory. He continued to be an employee of that factory. He retired from service on attaining the age of superannuation on 31.12.1965. He was, however, not paid his salary for the period of his suspension. He was served with a charge-sheet on the same date. He was also served with a notice of demand for the amount of Rs. 1,000/- and Rs. 1 lakh on the same day. The appellant filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 2,000/- on the ground that the order of confirmation passed by the Additional Custodian in the appellant was not in accordance with the provisions of section 58 of the Act. The trial court decreed the suit and directed the appellant to pay the amount of the amount of money. The appellant preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant then filed a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed. The appellant thereafter filed a writ appeal in this Court. The appellant contended that the order passed by the Custodian General was not in conformity with the provisions contained in section 58 of Act XXXI of 1950 and that the order was not in consonance with the provisions. The High court held that the order under appeal was not in the nature of a quasi judicial order and that the Custodian General had himself passed the order under section 58 of that Act. The High, Court held that the Custodian had not been given an opportunity to show cause against the order of the Custodian General and that the appellant was entitled to a hearing. The appellant was, therefore, not entitled to any relief. The appellant, therefore, filed a writ application in the High court. The High. Court held that section 58 of act XXXI of 1950 was not applicable to the appellant. The appellant's writ petition was dismissed. Hence the present appeal.

The Act was passed by the Central Government in exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section (1) of section 32 of the Act. The Act was passed to provide for the payment of bonus to employees in certain circumstances. The Act provided for payment of bonus in certain circumstances and provided for payment to employees in such circumstances. The Industrial Tribunal held that the bonus payable to employees in the two categories of employees was not a customary or contractual bonus and so, the bonus payable under the Act was not a bonus. The Tribunal held that in the case of bonus the payment of the bonus was not a condition of service and so, it was not a payment of bonus. The High Court held that the Bonus Act was not applicable to the case of the respondent. The High court held that the Act was a complete Code and was not exhaustive of the subject. The High, Court held that in view of the provisions of the Act and the Bonus Act, the bonus was a customary or contract bonus and so the bonus payable by the employer to his workmen was not a " customary or contractual payment" within the meaning of the Bonus Act. The High. Court held that as the Bonus Act did not provide for payment of any bonus, it was a "contract bonus" and so, there was no question of the bonus payable in the case. The High' Court held that it was not open to the workmen to claim bonus under the Act only and not under the Act. In the result, the High Court held, that the bonus was payable by the employers to their workmen and so, they were entitled to bonus under the provisions of section 32(1) of the Act, and so, in the case before it, the bonus paid by the employer was not a ' customary or contractual' bonus. The appellant is now before us. The question whether the bonus payable is a customary or a contractual payment is a question of fact and so, we have to decide the question whether the Bonus Act is applicable to the respondent. Section 32(1)(b) of the Industrial Disputes Act provides that the provisions of this Act shall not apply to any industrial dispute which is pending before any authority under the Act and so, if the Bonus Act does not provide for any payment of bonus, it is not open to a workman to claim bonus by way of industrial adjudication for the year 1965. The question is whether the Bonus is a "contract" within the definition of the term " customary or contract" within the Act. Section 32 of the Industrial Tribunal Act provides that if the Tribunal is of the opinion that the bonus is not payable by the contractor to his workmen, it may, by order, direct that the same shall be paid to the workmen in such manner as may be prescribed. The Tribunal is also required to go into the question whether bonus is payable by the appellant to its workmen in the case referred to it. The Tribunal has to go into that question and decide the same. The Tribunal will decide the question of bonus only in the case where the bonus is payable under the provisions contained in the Act. If the Tribunal is satisfied that the bonus has been paid by the appellant, it can direct the same to be paid to its workmen. The question of bonus is not a "contract". The question of payment of bonus under the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act is not a question of law. The question as to the bonus payable for the year is not a matter of law. It is not open for a workman to ask for bonus under the statute. The question, therefore, is not a pure question of law and so, no question of bonus arises in the case and so, therefore, the question of the Bonus payable by the respondent does not arise. The appeal is accordingly dismissed.

The petitioners were appointed to the Superior Judicial Service of the State of Punjab by direct recruitment on December 31, 1976. They were appointed to that Service by promotion and by direct recruitment. They were confirmed in the Service on December 31. 1976. They filed a writ petition in the High Court of Punjab and Haryana challenging the validity of the seniority list. The High Court dismissed the petition. The petitioners filed a writ appeal to this Court. The High court held that the seniority list was valid and that the seniority of the petitioners was to be determined by the length of continuous service on a post in the Service. The High, Court held that the petitioners were appointed by promotion and direct recruits and direct recruits were appointed to a post in a service on or after December 31,1976. The High. Court held that, on the basis of the respective dates of confirmation, the seniority of all officers appointed to the Service was determined with reference to the dates of confirmation. The High' Court held that as the petitioners were promoted to the Superior judicial Service, they were confirmed in that Service on December 30, 1976. The High 'Court held that the inter se seniority of the members of the Superior Judicial Services was to be fixed with reference to their dates of confirmation and not with reference to any date of confirmation. In the result, the High Court held that there was no infirmity in the seniority list and that the petitioners are entitled to be confirmed in the Superior Judicial service of the State. The petitioners have filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts of Punjab andHaryana and Haryana have taken a contrary view. [557F] 2. The High-Court was not justified in holding that the seniority was to be decided by the length, of continuous service of the petitioners. [558F] 3. The High C Court was right in holding that as the seniority list had been prepared on the basis that the petitioners had been appointed to the service on or before December 31, 1977, the seniority list would be the basis of seniority. [559F] 4. The HighCourt was not right in holding otherwise. [560F] 5. The seniority list was not valid and that is the position in law. [566F] 6. The High T Court was right. [567F] 6(a) The seniority list is valid and the seniority list is to be drawn by the High Court. [568F] 6.(b) The seniority of the petitioner was to be regulated by the rules of the service. [570F] 6 (c) The seniority was to determine the seniority of officers appointed to a service on the basis on the basis, of the respective date of confirmation, without applying the rule of rotation and not with regard to any date in which the seniority was determined. [571F] 7. The seniority of a person appointed to a Service on the basis or the date of confirmation is to be determined with reference, to the date of his confirmation. [572F] 8. The seniority is to be fixed on the basis with reference to a date in which a person is appointed to a particular service. [546F] 9. The seniority in the Service is to be decided on the basis as laid down in the rules of service. [547F] 10. The seniority cannot be determined by a mere method of appointment. [546G] 11. The seniority was not to be determined on the basis either of the date of appointment or the date on which the person was appointed to a cadre. [546H] 12. The seniority has to be determined in accordance with the rules of recruitment. [546A] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1320 of 1989. From the Judgment and Order dated the 14th July, 1989 of the Punjab and Haryana High Court in Civil Writ Petition No. 1203 of 1976. S.K.

The State of Andhra Pradesh, by an order dated November 30, 1975, issued by the Government of Andhra Pradesh in exercise of the powers under proviso to paragraph 3(1) of the Order, issued under proviso to sub paragraph (1) of paragraph 3 of the Order in G.O.Ms. No. But, as stated earlier, the State Government issued orders in G. O.Ms.No. But, the power to organise class or classes of posts in the civil services of and class or classes under the State into a further local cadre within a zone. The power given to the State Government under the Order was to create a division and maintain separate seniority of Junior Assistants and Senior Assistants for the purpose of recruitment, appointment, discharge, seniority or promotion etc., as the case may be. The power to organise classes of posts was given to the President and the President alone was given power under proviso to paragraphs 3(1), 3(1). The power given under the Order to organise class and classes of posts of civil service of and class was not to be exercised by the State Government in respect of any class or classes or classes of civil posts under the State. The power was given to create class or classes within a zone and to pass an order in that regard requiring the State Government to create a separate cadre in relation to any class or class of civil posts. The power conferred on the State Government was not to create any class or category of posts in any department. The power under the Order, as stated, was to create separate seniority of junior Assistants and Senior Assistant and Senior Assistants. The power of the State Government, therefore, was not to organise class of posts in relation to a class or classes thereof. The power, given to the Government under the order, was not a power to organise any class or categories of posts. The State Government was also not competent to create class of posts for the purpose. The power vested in the State Government by the Order was not to confer any power on the State to create class and classes or classes thereof, as the case might be. The State was competent to create a class or class or classes for the purpose, as the cases may be. In the circumstances, the power given to it under the Order could not be exercised by it. The power in the present case was not to hold a general cadre or to create class, classes or classes within the zone. The State could not create class or class within a zone, as the power was given under the order. The power could not be conferred on the Government under paragraph 3(2) of the order.

The appellant, who was the mortgagee in possession of the land in question, filed a suit for redemption of the mortgage. The appellant filed a written statement and contended that the mortgagor had no right to redeem the mortgage. It was contended that the mortgagee had no right of redemption in the land in dispute and that the mortgagor was not entitled to redeem the mortgaged property. The trial court held that the mortgagor in possession had no right in the land and that the mortgage was not binding on the mortgagee. The trial Court held that the mortgagee was not entitled for redemption of mortgage. The trial Judge held that the appellant was not entitled in law to redeem the property in dispute and accordingly decreed the suit. The appellant preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that in view of the provisions of section 65 of the Transfer of Property Act, the mortgagor was entitled to redeem his property. The High court further held that the mortgage in question was not binding against the mortgagee. On the question whether the mortgagor had any right of redemption, the High Court held, that the mortgagor could not redeem the mortgage if he so desired but the mortgagor was bound to redeem the same. The High C.A. filed by the appellant was allowed and the decree passed by the trial court was set aside. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. The appellant contended that the mortgage executed by the mortgagee in favour of the defendants was not binding upon the plaintiff. The High. Court held that as the mortgagor had not exercised his right of redemption as the mortgagee had not exercised the right of redemption the mortgagor was liable to be ejected. The High, Court held that there was no question of the mortgagor being entitled to redeem. The High' Court held that it was not open to the appellant to redeem the land in the usual course of management by the mortgagor. The High 'Court further held that in the absence of any allegation in the plaintiff's plaint that the mortgagor's right of redemption was a dealing with the mortgaged property in the usual way, the mortgage was binding on the plaintiff. In the result, the High C. A. filed by special leave was dismissed. The appellant then filed a second appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts in the country have concurrent jurisdiction to decide the question whether a mortgagor has no right of redeeming the property in question. [557F] 2. The High-Court has no jurisdiction to decide a question of law in the absence Of a finding that the mortgagor has no power of redemption. [558F] 3. The HighCourt has no power to decide a matter which the mortgagor has not exercised his rights of redemption. The High courts have concurrent jurisdiction. [559F] 4. The High T. A. was not competent to decide the issue of a mortgage. The High F.A. was not right in holding that the mortgagor did not exercise his right of redeemation. [560G] 5. The High Cou-f has concurrent jurisdiction to determine the question whether an mortgagor has no such right of redemption. It is not open to a mortgagor to redeem the mortgagor when he so desired. [566G] 6. The High R.C. was not entitled, in law, to redeem the mortgagee. [567G] 7. The High L.A. has concurrent jurisdiction. The High O.P. was not maintainable. [568G] 8. The High P.C. is not competent to determine the issue of the mortgage in the absenceof any finding that the mortgagee has no such power of redemption as is given to the mortgagor. [569G] 9. The High COurt has concurrent jurisdiction in the matter of redemption. In the instant case, the mortgagor had exercised his right under the mortgage in his favour. The High Co-operative Court has concurrent jurisdiction and the High Court has rightly held that the High Court had no jurisdiction to determine that issue.

The respondent entered into an agreement with the appellant for the construction of a building on the land and building of the appellant. The appellant entered into an arbitration agreement with the respondent. The respondent filed a suit for specific performance of an agreement to sell the property. The appellant filed a suit in the court of the Subordinate Judge, Ernakulam, for specific performance. The appellant contended that the respondent was not entitled to the benefit of the arbitration clause in the contract and that the arbitration clause was not attracted to the arbitration agreement. The Subordinate Judge held that the arbitration agreement was not a valid arbitration agreement and that the respondent had not performed his part of the contract. The appellant preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that the respondent could not be said to have committed breach of the contract and accordingly dismissed the appeal. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. The appellant contends that the arbitration clauses in the contract were not binding on the respondent and that the arbitrator was not competent to decide the dispute. The appellant further contends that the arbitrator had no jurisdiction to decide the disputes and that the award was not liable to be set aside. The appellant also contends that the respondent having failed to perform his part of contract, the arbitration clause could not be invoked. The appellant relies on the decision of this Court in [S.P. Sampath Kumar vs The State of Tamil Nadu & Ors.] , wherein it was held that the arbitrator is not competent to entertain the dispute and that the court has no jurisdiction to entertain the claim. The appellant, therefore, contends that the High Court was wrong in holding that the arbitration was not a proper arbitration agreement and the arbitration clause had not been performed. The appellant submits that the High court was wrong in coming to the conclusion that the arbitration is not a proper one. The appellant argues that the arbitration Clause was not a nullity and the High Court should not have entertained the petition. The appellant relied on the decision in [Silver Jubilee vs The State Bank of India & Ors.] ; ; ; (i) that the arbitration proceedings were not a valid and legal arbitration agreement and therefore the arbitration clause did not apply to the arbitration. The appellant therefore contends that the award is not liable to set aside the award. The appellant points out that the respondent has not performed his obligation under the contract and therefore the award is liable to be quashed. The respondent contends that the appellant has not performed the obligation under the agreement and that it is not open to the respondent to plead that the arbitration has not been performed by the respondent. In the alternative, it is contended that the award being a nullity, the appellant is not entitled to any relief. The respondent has filed a counter affidavit in which it is stated that the arbitration proceeding was not a judicial proceeding before the arbitration and that the appellant had not performed the obligations under the contract. It is further stated that the respondent is not entitled for the benefit of arbitration under the arbitration clause. The appellant states that the respondent cannot be said to be guilty of breach of contract. The respondent relies on the decisions of this Court and the High court. The appellant is not a party to the arbitration proceedings. The respondent is not a necessary party to the proceedings. The appellant denies that the respondent acted in breach of the agreement. The respondent also contends that in the absence of a valid arbitration clause, the arbitration is a proper one and the arbitration is an independent and separate legal arbitration. The respondent further contends that in view of the arbitration agreement, the arbitration agreement is not a valid one. The respondent denies that the arbitration in the present case is a valid arbitration. The arbitration agreement is a valid one and the respondent has no right to enforce the arbitration agreement and it is not a nullity. The appellant's contention is that the arbitration being a proper one, the arbitration proceedings are not maintainable. The respondent argues that the appellant is entitled to the relief sought for.

The State of Uttar Pradesh acquired the estate of a deceased proprietor of a village under the provisions of the [U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950] (U.P.) (hereinafter referred to as the 'Act') and the State of Uttar Pradeshik was declared as a 'protected tenant' under the Act. The State of Uttar pradesh acquired the estate under the Act and the State Government issued a notification under section 3 of the Act declaring that the estate of the proprietor was an estate. The State Government issued an order under section 3(1) of the Act on the basis of the provisions of section 4(d) of the said Act. The estate of the deceased proprietor was declared as an 'protected tenant'. The State of U.P. issued a notification on the basis that the estate was an estate, and the State was entitled to retain possession of the estate. The estate was declared as such by the State Government. The State filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notification. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The State preferred an appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The notification issued under section 3 (1) of Act was valid and the State had no jurisdiction to proceed against the estate of an intermediary. [616 G] 2. The notification under section 4(1) was issued on the basis, that the estate is an estate. It was not a case of the State Government acquiring the estate as an ' protected tenant' under section 4 (d) of Act. [617 G] 3. The notification was valid and was not a valid one. [618 G] 4. The notification dated the basis of section 4 (1) was valid and did not affect the rights of the petitioners. [619 H] 5. The notification is valid and does not affect the petitioners' rights. [620 H] 6. The notification in question was valid and does affect the petitioners. The notification did not affect any of the petitioners' right. [621 H] 7. The notification does not affect any right of the petitioners in the land. The notification merely provides for the transference to the State of the estate of which the proprietor has been declared as an "protected tenant". [621 G] 8. The notification cannot be said to be a valid one and does not operate as res judicata. [622 H] 9. The notification has to be in terms of section 4 of the Act and it is not a valid notification. [623 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 13 of 1971. Appeal by Special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 9th July, 1971 of the Allahabad High Court in Civil Misc. The High court dismissed the writ application. The appellant filed a writ appeal against the judgment of the High Court. The appellant contended that the notification issued under s. 3(1), is invalid. The notification, therefore, is valid and the High Court was in error in holding that the notification is invalid. [624 B] JUDGMENT: Civil Appeal Nos. 13 of 1972, 13 of 1972 and 14 of 1972. Appeals by special leave from the judgment and order dated the 9 th July, 1971, of the Allahabad, High Court in Misc. Writ Petition Nos. 816 and 816 of 1967. S. P. Sinha, for the appellants.

The respondents, who were allocated to the I.P.S. and Central Services Group 'A' on the basis of the previous examination, were allocated to a service on the basis that they were allocated to that service on the ground that they had been allocated to the Central Services Group "A" and "B" services. The respondents were allocated to one service on the same date. The respondents, however, did not join the service on the date of the first examination. They were allocated to another service on the result of the previous CSE examination. The respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the second proviso to Rule 4 of the CSE Rules. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the second proviso. The respondents challenged the order of the High Court in this Court. The High court held that the second proviso was not applicable to the case of the respondents. The High C Court held that the proviso to Rule 2 of the C.S.E. (Main) Rules, was not applicable in the case of a candidate who was allocated to the service on a date earlier than the date of first examination. The High. Court held that Rule 4 of C.S.(E) Rules was not applicable and the respondents were not entitled to appear in the subsequent examination. The appellants filed a writ appeal against the judgment of the High court. The High, Court held that there was no bar to the second proviso in the case. The High' Court held that in the case where the respondents were allocated the service on an earlier examination, the second proviso would not be applicable. The High 'Court held that the respondents were entitled to appear for the examination on the date when the first examination was held. The High-Court held that Rule 17 of the CSR was not applicable. The appellants, therefore, filed a writ application in the High court challenging the second Proviso to Rule 4. The High: Court held that it was not applicable as the respondents were required to be given the benefit of their success subject to the provisions of Rule 17 of C. S.E. 5 (ii) was not applicable, and that the respondents could not be allowed to sit at the next Civil Service Examination. The High,. Court held that as the respondents had been allocated the service to the Central Service Group 'A', they were entitled to sit for the main examination. The appeal filed by the appellants was allowed by the High Court. The appellants then filed a writ Petition in the High' Court. The respondents contended that the second Proviso was not applicable because the second proviso did not apply to the case. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The second proviso to rule 4 of the rules was not applicable when the respondents were allotted to the service. The proviso to Rule 3 of the rules did not apply in the case in which the respondents were to be allocated to the Service on the basis on the basis thereof. [775 H] 2. The proviso is not applicable to a candidate who is allocated to the State Services Group 'B' or 'B' services. The proviso does not apply to a candidate belonging to the State Service Group 'B'. [775 G] 3. The proviso cannot be read in the context of the second proviso and it cannot be read to mean that the second provision does not apply. [776 H] 4. The proviso was not attracted when the respondents had not been allocated to Central Services Group B. [778 H] 4(i) The proviso to rule 3 of the Rules was not attracted because the respondents were in the service of the Central Services, Group 'A'. [778 A] (ii) The proviso is applicable to a person who is allocated the service by the Central Services.

The appellant was detained under Section 3(1) of the Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act, 1974. The appellant was arrested on 25th November, 1986 and was produced before the Board on 25th December, 1986. The Board, after considering the materials placed before it, passed the order of detention on 25th January, 1987. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Madras challenging the order of the Board. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant then filed a writ appeal to this Court. The appellant contended that the order of his detention was vitiated because of the non-compliance of the provisions of the Act and the order of preventive detention. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order of detention was vitiated by non-compliance with the provisions of Article 14 of the Constitution. [775 H] 2. The order was passed by the Board after considering the material placed before it and after giving an opportunity to the detenu to make a representation. [776 H] 3. The order passed by the Government was not vitiated because of non-compliance. [778 H] 4. The order is vitiated because of noncompliance with the provisions. [779 H] 5. The order cannot be sustained because of non compliance with the provisions as contained in Article 14 of Constitution. [750 H] 6. The order must be sustained because it was passed by a competent authority or the Government. The order should be passed by the Advisory Board. [750 A] 7. The order in question was passed by an officer of the Government of India who was not a party to the proceedings before the Advisory Board and the order was not passed by the State Government. [750 B] 8. The order could not be sustained because the appellant was not given an opportunity to make a proper representation. [750 D] 9. The order under Article 14 is not vitiated because it was not passed on the material placed by the appellant before it. [750 G] 10. The order can be sustained because, in the circumstances, the order is not justified. [750 E] 11. The order does not suffer from any infirmity.
