The appellants, the owners of the two mills, and the mills, filed a writ petition in the High Court of Madras challenging the validity of the orders of requisition and the notices of acquisition. The High Court held that the delivery orders were valid and binding on the mills and that the delivery order was valid and binding. The High court held that the order of requisition was valid and that the order was valid. The High. Court held that as the delivery orders had been served on the mills as owners of the goods, the delivery order could not be said to have been validly served on the mill. The High, Court held that in the absence of any service of the notice on the mills, the delivery orders could not be held to be valid and binding and that the High Court was in error in holding that the delivery was valid and the delivery order had not been served on them. The High' Court held that there was no service of the notices of the acquisition and the delivery orders did not become invalid. The High C Court held that since the delivery orders in the case of orders of requisition were valid and the orders of requisitioning were valid, the delivery was invalid and that the orders of the High Court were valid. The appeal of the Union of India to this Court was directed against the judgment of the High. Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The delivery orders were validly served on both the mills and the mills. The delivery orders had not been made in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The delivery order was not valid and binding as between the mills and their mills. [775 H] (2) The delivery order had been served by the mills as owner of the goods. The delivery was valid. [776 H] (3) The delivery was not valid. The delivery of the goods was valid and it was not open to the mills to take delivery of the same goods. [778 H] (4) The delivery of goods was not valid because the delivery orders made by the mills were valid and they were not properly served in the case. The delivery Orders were valid and there was no delivery order. [779 H] (5) The delivery Orders had been served in the manner prescribed in the Act. [780 H] (6) The delivery Order was valid and there is no infirmity in the order of the High court. [782 H] (7) The delivery is valid and binding only on the mills. [750 H] (8) The delivery in the case was not valid as between the Mills and the mills as the owners of mills were addresses and the mills were not served on the Mills as owners of goods. [750 A] (9) The delivery had been made in the manner provided in the Act and the delivery was not invalid. [750 B] (10) The delivery could not be deemed to have been made in pursuance of the provisions of s. 18 of the Act and that the provisions of ss. 18 and 19 of the Act were not applicable to the case. [750 C] (11) The delivery to the mills was valid and they could not be treated as valid. [750 D] (12) The delivery by the mills was not valid but only a delivery order was made in accordance therewith. [750 E] (13) The delivery has been made in terms of the provisions contained in s. 18 and the delivery is valid. [751 G] (14) The delivery under the agreement was not valid when the delivery was made. [750 G] (15) The delivery and the delivery were not valid because they were not valid. [75 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1165 of 1966. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated April 20, 1966 of the Madras High Court in Writ Petition No. 1166 of 1966. S. T. Desai, S. K. Sastri and R. H.

The assessee is a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The assessee is a registered company. The assessee was assessed to income tax under the head "Profits and gains of business or profession" for the assessment year 1963 64. The assessee filed a return of his income for the assessment years 1963 65 and 66. The Income Tax Officer assessed the assessee under Section 23A of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, who allowed the appeal, held that the assessee was a provision and not a reserve. The Appellate Tribunal, however, held that in view of the provisions of Section 23A, the assessee was not a provision and was not a reserve and, therefore, the assessee could not be treated as a reserve. On appeal by the assessee, the Tribunal held that the provisions of the Income tax Act, 1961 were not applicable to the assessee. The Tribunal held that in the circumstances of the case the provision made by the assessee in its Books for meeting the anticipated liability of tax (under Section 23A) was a provision. The Tribunal further held that the provision made in the books of the assessee was an integral part of the assessee's business and, therefore the assessee was entitled to the benefit of the provisions contained in Section 23A. The Tribunal, therefore, held that since the provision made under Section 23 A was a provision, the assessee is not a provision. On the question whether the provision made for meeting the deferred liability of tax was a provision or a reserve, the Tribunal referred to the High Court the question whether in view of Section 23 A, the assessee had a provision and the reserve was a provision in the books. The High Court answered the question in the affirmative and in favour of the assessee. Hence this appeal by the Revenue. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The provision made in Section 23 A is a provision and is a provision. It is a provision which is a provision, and is a reserve. [675 H] 2. The provision in question is a provision made in a statute. The provision is a provision in respect of a provision. [676 H] 3. The provision contained in Section 22(1) is a provision for a reserve and is a section. The provision makes a provision for the reserve and is not a reserve but is a provision to be made for meeting a deferred liability of the tax (under the provisions of Sections 23A and 23A). [675 G] 4. The provision for meeting the liability of tax is a provision of a reserve and not a provision for meeting a liability. [682 H] 5. The provision of a provision is a reserve and the provision is a section and not a section. [683 H] 6. The provision as a reserve is a provision only and not a part of the reserve. [650 A] 7. The provision under Section 23(A) is a reserve, and is not an integral part thereof. [685 H] 8. The provision does not make a provision for any reserve. The provision, therefore, is a provision as a provision. If the provision is not a part or a reserve the provision is an integral part or a provision. Therefore, the provision is only a provision for payment of a reserve. It is not a section but a provision for repayment of a reserve, which is a reserve or a provision for interest. [686 H] 9. The provision must be a provision for carrying forward of the liability of the income tax liability. [650 H] 10. The provision that is made for meeting any deferred liability of a tax (under this section) is a section or a provision in a statute and is a proviso. [650 D] 11. The provision has to be read in the context of the provision. [650 E] 12. The provision cannot be construed as a provision for paying a reserve. A provision is a proviso and is a subterfuge.

The petitioners were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the Indian Railways. They were appointed as temporary Assistant Engineers on the basis of the results of competitive examinations held by the Indian Railways Board. They were confirmed in the Indian Railway Service of Engineers Class I on the basis that they were recruited by selection by the Union Public Service Commission. They were also confirmed in the post of Assistant Engineers on their basis. They were promoted to the post of Executive Engineers on the ground that they were appointed by selection by a Union Public Service commission. The petitioners were appointed to the post by selection by Union Public Service Commissions. They were, however, not appointed to the posts by selection by an Union Public ServiceCommission. They were not appointed to any post by selection. They were absorbed into the Indian Railway Services of Engineers Class 1 on the basis, of the results, of the competitive examinations held in the years 1955 and 1955. They were given the benefit of the service rendered by them in the Indian railways. They were further promoted to the posts of Executive Engineers by selection by way of selection by the UPSC. They were again confirmed in the posts of Assistant Engineers by the Union of India. The petitioners filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the impugned order of the Union Public Services Commission. The High Court held that the petitioners were appointed by the Union Government in the Indian railway Service of Engineers, Class I on their own terms and conditions and they were not entitled to the benefit of promotion to the post. The High court held that the impugned order was not in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution and was, therefore, invalid. The High, Court held that in view of the history of the case, the impugned order could not be sustained. The High. Court held that there was no infirmity in the impugned order. The High' Court held that it was not open to the petitioners to challenge the validity of this order. The petitioners have filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The impugned order of appointment of the petitioners was not in conformity with the provisions contained in the Constitution. [775 H] 2. The impugned orders were passed by the Union, the Union Public service Commission and the Union Public services Commission. The impugned Government order was not a mere executive order. The impugned action was not in consonance with the provisions in the Constitution and the impugned order is not in accordance. [776 H] 3. The impugned notification was not in compliance with the provisions as contained in the appointment orders. The impugned circular was not in contravention of the provisions of Article 14 of the Constitution. The impugned letter was not in violation of the provisions contained therein. [778 H] 4. The impugned decision was not in the teeth of the provisions as embodied in the Constitution, and was not in breach of the provisions. [779 H] 5. The impugned judgment is not sustainable in law. [780 H] 6. The impugned executive order was not passed in accordance with law. [750 H] 7. The impugned government order was not issued in accordance with Article 14 of Constitution. [750 A] JUDGMENT: ORIGINAL JURISDICTION: Writ Petition Nos. 823 and 824 of 1978. (Under Article 32 of the Constitution of India). S.K. Bagga, S.K Srivastava, S.N. Bagga and S.K Gupta, for the petitioners. S.K Sharma, for the respondents. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by K.J. Shah, J. The petitioners in these writ petitions are employees of the Indian Railways, who were appointed by way of direct recruitment to the Indian Railways Service of Engineers and Class I on temporary basis. They are working as Assistant Engineers on temporary basis in the Indian Rly. Service of Engineers. The petitioners are working as Assistants in the Indian Civil Service of Engineers in the Northern Railway.

The West Bengal Special Courts Act, was passed by the State Legislature in exercise of the powers conferred by article 14 of the Constitution. The West Bengal Special Court Act was passed by a State Legislature in the exercise of its powers under article 14 of that Constitution. The State Legislature passed the West Bengal Special courts Act, which was passed by an appropriate legislature in the exercise or purported exercise of its power under article 14. The West Punjab Act was passed to provide for the trial of offences and classes of offences and for the trial by the Special Court constituted under the West Bengal Act. The State Government was empowered to direct any class of offences or classes of cases to be tried by the Special Courts constituted under the Act. The West Calcutta High Court by a notification issued by the State of West Bengal under section 11 of the West Bengal General Courts Act, transferred the West Bengal case to the State Government and the notification was issued by the Government of West Bengal in that behalf. The West Ben. Bengal Act was passed in exercise of its legislative power under article 13 of the Constitution and the notification issued by it was published in the Official Gazette. The West BENGAL Ordinance was passed by Parliament in exercise of powers conferred by section 11 of that Act. The Bengal Special Courts Ordinance was passed in the exercise and purported exercise of the power under article 12 of the Constitution, and the notification which was issued under that Act was published in that behalf in the Official gazette. The West Kolkata Special Courts Act was passed with the sanction of the State Government. The West West Bengal Act was made by the State Government under section 11(1) of the West Ben. Act. The notification issued by that State was published in a newspaper in the "Official Gazette" and the notification published in the " Official Gazette" was published in "Official Gazette". The West Bengal Act, as it was passed by it, was passed in pursuance of the power conferred by article 12 of that Constitution and the State Government was also empowered to make a law for the State Government in the exercise, of the power, conferred by article 13 of that Constitution, for the State of Calcutta. The WestBengal Special Courts Ordinance, was passed on the basis of the power vested in the State Government by section 11(2) of the Bengal Act. It was published in Gazette of India, Extraordinary, dated the 24th March, 1951. The West B. Bengal Act, which came into force on the 24th April, 1951, was passed with effect from the 24th May, 1951. Section 11 of the Bengal Special Courts Bill, 1951, provided that the State Government may, by notification in the Official Gazzet, direct that the provisions of the said Act shall, as from the date of the notification, be in force in the State of the West B. The West-Bengal Special Courts Act is not applicable to the West Bengal State. The West - Bengal Act was enacted by the State legislature in exercise of power conferred by section 3 of the West- Bengal Act. Section 3 of the Act provides that the State Legislature may make laws for the State Legislature for the State. The State legislature has power to make laws for that State. The power to make a laws is conferred by section 4 of the West - Bengal Special Courts (Amendment) Act, 1951. It is not disputed that the West Bengal Legislature passed the Act in exercise of that power. The West-- Bengal Special Courts Acts were passed by the States Legislature in exercise or purported to exercise the power under section 11. The West -- Bengal Act was not passed by the appropriate legislature in exercise or purporting to exercise the powers under article 12. The West.- Bengal Act was also not passed by Parliament. The West-' Bengal Act was, therefore, not passed by it. The West, Bengal Act was promulgated by the State. Under section 11 of this Act, the State Legislature has power to pass laws for the whole or any part of the territory of the State.

The appellants were convicted by the Sessions Judge for the offence under section 396 I.P.C. and sentenced to death. The prosecution case was that the appellants were found in possession of a large number of articles and were found in the house of the deceased. The appellants were found guilty of the offence under sections 396 I. P.C. The prosecution examined P.Ws. 1, 7 and 8 and also produced P.Ws 1, 7, 8 and 9. The appellants denied the prosecution case and claimed that they were in possession of the articles. The learned Sessions Judge disbelieved the evidence of P.Ws 2, 7 and 9 and held that the appellants had not been found in possession. The learned Judges of the High Court held that the evidence of the P.Ws 3, 4 and 5 was not reliable and that the evidence was not reliable. The learned Judge held that the prosecution had proved the case against the appellants beyond all reasonable doubt and that the conviction of the appellants was not warranted. The learned Additional Sessions Judge acquitted the appellants of the charge under section 396 of the I.P.'C. The learned counsel for the appellants submitted that the evidence given by P.Ws 4, 5 and 6 was not reliable because they were injured witnesses and that the learned Judges of both the High Court and the Sessions Judge were not justified in rejecting the evidence of these witnesses. The learned Counsel for the appellants further submitted that the learned Sessions Judge was not justified in relying upon the evidence of a witness who was not present at the time of the occurrence and that the appellants should have been acquitted. The learned Addl. Sessions Judge rejected the evidence of this witness and held that it was not safe to place reliance on the evidence of such witness. The learned trial Judge held that it is not safe to rely on the evidence given in the case of the prosecution. The learned Single Judge of the High court also rejected the evidence given on behalf of the appellants. The learned Advocate for the appellants contended that the evidence on record was not reliable as the learned Sessions judge was not justified on the evidence and that the High Court was not justified. The learned Senior Counsel for the respondents submitted that the prosecution has proved the case beyond all reasonable doubts and that the prosecution case was not reliable since the appellants were not found in possession thereof. The learned senior counsel for the respondents contended that the learned Judge of the Sessions Judge was justified in rejecting their evidence. The learned Government Advocate, on the other hand, supported the judgment of the learned Sessions Court and contended that the prosecution was not able to prove the case against them. The learned Chief Judicial Magistrate was justified in holding that the evidence in the case was not credible. The learned Magistrate was justified on the basis of the evidence given before him. The learned Judicial Magistrate was not justified when he held that the learned Magistrate was not right in rejecting the prosecution evidence. The evidence of P W. 1 was not reliable when he was examined as a witness. The evidence given by the P.W. 1 was also not reliable. In the circumstances, the learned Sessions Judges were justified in rejecting his evidence. The High Court was also justified in rejecting that evidence. The appellants' counsel submitted that the High court was not justified by the evidence of any of the witnesses who were present at the relevant time. The learned Solicitor General submitted that the appellants could not be convicted for the offence of murder under section 396 and section 396 I,P.C., and that the case was clearly established against the appellants.

The appellant was appointed as a probationer in the respondent company on the basis of a written examination held by the management for the purpose of recruitment of workmen in the respondent-company. The respondent company was appointed as an Assistant Manager in the respondent's company on the recommendation of the Labour Court. The respondent was appointed as Assistant Manager in a temporary capacity in the respondent' company on the recommendations of the Labour Commissioner. The respondent challenged the appointment of the respondent by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court quashed the order of the Labour court and directed the appellant to reinstate the respondent in service with back wages. The appellant filed a writ petition before this Court. The appellant contended that the respondent was not a workman within the meaning of s. 2(oo) of the Act and that the order of dismissal was bad and illegal. The appellant also contended that the order terminating the services of the respondent was bad and void. Held, that the order was bad and the order of termination was bad and was liable to be set aside. The order of termination of the respondent's service was bad and bad and was therefore, liable to be quashed. The respondent had not been appointed as an employee of the respondent company and the order terminating his services was bad and liable to be struck down. The order terminating the service of the respondent in the present case was bad and therefore, the order of his termination was bad. The respondent could not be said to be a workman within s. 2 (oo) of Act. The order was bad because the respondent was appointed on the recommendation by the Labour Commissioner and the order was passed by the Labour Court in a proceeding under s. 25F of the Act. The High court was in error in holding that the order passed by the respondent was illegal and void. The order passed by a competent authority was bad and not a valid order. The order dated December 10, 1966 was bad and invalid. The order in the present appeal was passed by a learned Single Judge of the High Court in a writ petition filed by the respondent. The order under appeal was not a nullity and was liable for dismissal. The order dismissing the respondent was also bad. The order having been passed by the competent authority, the order was not bad and was, therefore, liable for dismissal under s. 2 of the Act as it was passed without jurisdiction.

The appellant is a dealer in goods carrying goods in the State of West Bengal. The appellant is a registered dealer under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. The appellant purchased the goods from the State Trading Corporation of India Ltd., Calcutta, and sold them to the State Trading Corpn. The Sales Tax Officer, West Bengal, who assessed the appellant to sales tax under the Bengal Act, issued a notice under s. 34 of the Bengal Finance Act, 1941, to the appellant, calling upon him to show cause why the sales tax should not be levied on the appellant. The appellant filed a reply to the notice. The Sales tax Officer, West Calcutta, by his order dated April 17, 1961, assessed the appellant as a dealer. The appellant challenged the assessment order by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant then filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution in the High court. The High court held that the sales tax was not a tax on the sale of goods and that the sales were not liable to be taxed under the Bengal Taxation (Sales Tax Act, 1941). The High Court held that the Sales Tax Officer was a dealer within the meaning of s. 2(c) of the Bengal Act and that the appellant was a dealer liable to assessment under the Bengal General Sales Tax Act, 1948. The appellant, therefore, filed a writ appeal to this Court. The appellant contended that the sales in question were not liable for assessment under the Act. The High. Court held that s. 2 (c) of Bengal Act, 1948, was a dealer for the purpose of the Bengal Taxation Act, 1948 and that the Sales tax was not leviable on the appellant as he was a dealer. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The sales tax was a tax on sale of goods. The sales were not taxable under the Bengal Sales Tax Act. The sales in question did not constitute a sale. The sales did not constitute sales. The sales are not liable to assessment. The sales could not be taxed under s. 2 of the Bengal General Sale Tax Act, 1949. [775 H] 2. The sales of the appellant were not liable as a dealer for a period the sale was not liable to tax under the Act and the Sales Tax Act was not a dealer. [776 H] 3. The sales by the appellant were liable to be assessed under the Bengal Tax Act. [778 H] 4. The sales had not been assessed under the Act, and the Sales tax had not been levied on the sales. The Sales-tax Officer was not a "dealer" within the meaning ofs. 2(f) of the Act. [750 H] 5. The sales, therefore, were not liable under the Act as they were not liable. [750 A] 6. The sales being not liable to the assessment, the sales were liable to assessment and the Sales-tax was not leviable. [750 B] 7. The sales which were not liable, were not taxable. The sales must be deemed to constitute a sale within the meaning s. 2. The Sales. tax was not levied on the sale. The Sales were not liable on the sale but were liable to tax. [750 G] 8. The sales cannot be taxed under any of the provisions of the Bengal Sales-tax Act. The Sales Act was a taxing statute. The Sales of the appellant was not liable as an assessee under the Act because the sales were exempt from tax under the Bihar Sales Tax Act and the sales were taxable under the Act only. [750 C] 9. The sales made by the appellant are not liable for tax under the [ Bengal Finance ( Sales Tax) Act]. The Sales Tax Act is a law relating to the tax on the sales of goods. [750 D] 10. The sales to the appellant were exempt from the tax under the provisions of Bengal Act.

The appellant, a Director of the Company, was a Director of a Company, and was a Director in a firm of which the appellant was a Director. The Company was incorporated in the year 1955 and the appellant was the Director of the said Company. The Company had a share capital of Rs. 1,50,000 and the appellant had a share of Rs. 2,50,00,000. The appellant was a director of the Company. The appellant had a stock account in the name of the Company in the name and style of Bhagwati Trading Company. The accounts of the Company were audited by the Chartered Accountants of the appellant. The appellant filed a return of his income on the basis of the said accounts. The Income Tax Officer, on the basis that the appellant was in charge of the business of the Company and that the appellant had not paid any money to the Union Agencies, held that the appellant did not include the securities in the said letter. The Income tax Officer, however, held that he had no knowledge of the source of the money he had received from the Insurance Company and that he had not given any instructions regarding the activities of the Union Agencies. The appellant, therefore, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Income Tax Officer. The High Court held that the Income Tax officer had no knowledge about the source of money he had to give instructions to the Delhi Office of the Bharat Union Agencies to meet the losses. The High court held that the assessee was not entitled to the benefit of the exemption under section 4(1)(a) of the Act. The appellant then filed a writ appeal to this Court. The appellant contended that the Income tax Officer had no knowledge that the securities were sold or pledged by the Insurance Company to the Union agencies and that the Income-tax Officer had no information about the source or the source of such money he had not disclosed. HELD: The appellant was not entitled, as he was not a Director of any Company, to the extent of Rs. 3,50, 000. The Income-tax officer had no information regarding the source of any money he had given to the Delhi office of the Bharat union Agencies. The Income.tax Officer had not given the information regarding the sources of money he was not entitled. [557 C] The appellant was entitled to the exemption under the Act. [558 D] The appellant had no knowledge regarding the source or source of money that was he receiving for the Union Agencies to the extent he had received the money from the Insurance Companies. The Income,tax Officer had knowledge of the sources of the money the appellant had to give instruction regarding the source. The Incometax Officer had jurisdiction to direct the Income- tax Officer to direct the appellant to give instructions regarding the source and source of money. [559 D] The Income- tax officer had no authority to direct the assessee to give instructions for the source of his money he had no information. [560 D] The fact that the appellant could not have given instructions regarding the sources and source of the amount he had given, was not a relevant fact. The Income -tax Officer had the information regarding sources and source. The appellant could not be held to have given instructions for the sources and sources of money. The IncomeTax Officer had no authority under the Act to direct the income tax officer to direct the petitioner to give instructions on the source. [566 D] The High Court was wrong in holding that the IncomeTax Officer was not entitled under the Act, to direct the Commissioner to direct the respondent to give instructions in the matter of the source and sources of the amount which was he had given. [567 D] The respondent was not entitled in law to the exemption claimed under section 4 of the Act and the Income-Tax Officer had jurisdiction under the Act and he had no authority. [568 D] The appeal was, therefore, without merit and should be dismissed.

The appellants were appointed to the posts of Assistant Secretaries in the Secretariat of the State of Gujarat. They were appointed to officiate in the posts of Secretaries in the State of Bombay. The appellants were appointed as Assistant Secretaries in a substantive capacity in the Secretariat. The posts of Assistant Secretary in the Secretariat were filled by promotion from amongst the Assistant Secretaries in accordance with the rules of the State Government. The appellants, who were working as Assistant Secretaries, were absorbed in the Secretariat with effect from November 1, 1956. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court of Gujarat challenging the order of the State Govt. dated November 1, 1955. The High Court held that the appellants were entitled to be absorbed in the posts in the Secretariat and that the State Government was competent to transfer the appellants to the Secretariat. It was further held that the State of Saurashtra was competent to make a final order of absorption of the appellants in the Secretariat, and that the appellants could not challenge the authority of the Government of Gujarat to absorb the appellants in any post in the Secretariat or to fix their pay and seniority among the officers in the Secretariat in the State. The appellants challenged the order of their transfer before the High Court. The High court held that the order of transfer was not a final order and that the order was not open to the officers of the Secretariat to challenge the authority or the power of the Government to transfer the appellant to the Secretariat and the order of appointment was not a provisional order. The appellants contended that the order dated November 1. 1955 was not a permanent order and that it was not open for the officers of Secretariat to challenge it. The High. Court held that in view of the provisions of the proviso to section 115(7) proviso, the State Government could not have transferred the appellants to any other department of the State. In the result, the High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellants then filed a writ appeal in this Court. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The order of the High Court was not a speaking order. The order was not a quasi-judicial order. The High Courts of Gujarat and Gujarat had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order of transfers. [557 G] 2. The order dated November, 1, 1955 was not an order of transfer. The order passed by the State Government on November 1, 1957 was not a mere order of transfer but was an order of a provisional arrangement. [558 G] 3. The order in question was not a temporary order. The State Government was not competent to transfer any officer from the Secretariat to the Secretariat or the State Government had no jurisdiction. [559 G] 4. The order transferring the appellants to a post in the secretarians of the State was not a regular order. The transfer of the appellants to an office of the Secretariat was not a transfer in the administrative exigencies. [560 G] 5. The order could not be challenged by the appellants in a writ petition. [566 G] 6. The order did not create any right in favour of the appellants. The order is not a final one. The order does not create any vested right in favour the appellants. [567 G] 7. The order cannot be challenged by any other person. The order can be challenged only by the State of the Central Government. [568 G] 8. The order being a quasi- judicial order, the State of Rajasthan was competent to pass the order of transferring the appellants. It was not open either to the State Government or to the Central Government to transfer any of the appellants from the Secretariat. [570 G] 9. The order, therefore, was not a nullity. [571 G] 10. The order must be held to be a nullity. The order should be treated as a nullity. It was a nullity. There was no question of the State's power to transfer the petitioners to any other post. [572 G] 11.

The appellant, a registered dealer, was assessed to tax under the Central Act, by the Sales Tax Officer, on the purchase of goods, on the ground that the tax was levied at the rate of six naye paise in a rupee. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Andhra Pradesh challenging the levy of tax on the ground of discrimination. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant then filed a writ appeal to this Court. The appellant contended that the tax levied by the State was not at the same rate and therefore the tax was not at one stage and was not at all levied at the same time. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The tax was levied by the Central Act and the rules thereunder. The tax is levied at the rates specified in the Schedule. [775 H] 2. The tax levied by a State is a tax at the same rates and therefore the State is not liable to pay the tax. [776 H] 3. The tax imposed by the State is a duty of excise and not a tax at all. [778 H] 4. The tax cannot be said to be higher in the case of imported goods. [779 H] 5. The tax can be levied at one stage. [780 H] 6. The tax could be levied at the highest rate and that stage is not at all stated in the Act or the rules thereunder and therefore the levy of a tax at one stage cannot be said that the tax is higher in the matter of levy of tax. [750 H] 7. The tax has to be levied at a different rate and it is not at the rate at which it is levied. [750 A] 8. The tax must be at the same or higher rate. [750 B] 9. The tax may be levied at different rates. [750 C] 9. In the case of goods imported into the State and similar goods imported in the State, the stage of tax is the sale of such goods by the last dealer liable to pay tax. [751 H] 10. The tax on the first purchase in the case in which the goods are manufactured or produced in the State is prohibited by the said clause. [751 G] 11. The tax under the Act is a duty at the same stage and is not at any stage at all. The tax does not exceed the maximum rate. [751 A] 12. The tax in the case at the same point is not at one time and therefore the rate of tax is not at a higher rate. The tax, therefore, is not at more than the maximum rate but is at the same amount. [751 B] 13. The tax which is levied by the Government is a duty on the goods manufactured or produced within the State and the tax is not higher in the nature of tax. The tax being higher in the form of tax, the tax is at the higher rate. In the absence of any such restriction, the tax cannot be levied at more than one stage. The tax will be levied at two different stages. [751 C] 14. The tax shall be levied at such rates as are specified in the Schedules. [751 D] 15. The tax so levied is a duty not at the time of the levy of the tax. The rate of tax fixed by the State Government is not at least higher than the rate fixed by the Central Government. [751 E] 16. The tax leviable by the State under the Act cannot be levied by the authorities concerned. [751 F] 16. In the instant case, the tax was at the same level and the tax was also at the same scale. [751G] 17. The tax at the rate fixed under the Act was not at any time at the same higher rate. It is not at that rate. The rate fixed by a State Government is higher than the one fixed by the Government. [751 H] 18.

The appellant, who was the owner of the mortgaged property, was the owner in respect of the mortgaged properties. The mortgaged property was mortgaged by the mortgagor to the mortgagee. The mortgagor had mortgaged the mortgaged property to the mortgagee on the basis of a mortgage deed executed by the mortgagor. The mortgagor was in possession of the mortgaged land and was in possession thereof. The mortgagee executed a mortgage deed in favour of the mortgagee on March 31, 1957. The mortgagee was in possession and enjoyment of the mortgaged lands. The mortgagee filed a suit for redemption of the mortgage. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the mortgage debt and the security were not liable to be sold. The High Court held that the mortgage was not a mortgage and the mortgage was a mortgage. The High court held that the mortgagee was entitled to get the benefit of the Act, as he was not an agriculturist. The High C Court held that by the operation of the provisions of the Act the mortgage debt was a mortgage and not a mortgage. In the present case, the mortgage was executed by the mortgagee in favour of his vendor on March 31. 1957. The High, Court held that in the absence of any clear directions to the mortgagee to release the interest of defendant No. 2 the purchase money was not an agricultural debt and the entire mortgage debt was not liable to the mortgage. In this view, the High Court held, that the mortgage in question was not a loan and the mortgage could not be sold. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was wrong in holding that the mortgagee had not been able to get the benefits of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The mortgage was a loan and not a loan. The mortgage in question is a mortgage. [557D] 2. The mortgage debt and security are not a loan but a loan. [558F] 3. The mortgage is a mortgage and is a mortgage by conditional sale. The mortgage deed is a mortgage, and the mortgage is a loan. It is a mortgage only. The mortgage does not create any interest in the mortgaged property. [559F] 4. The mortgage being a loan, the mortgage is not a mortgage but a loan and is a loan and therefore the mortgage is an agricultural debt. [560F] 5. The mortgage, therefore, is a loan, and not a debt. [546F] 6. The mortgage cannot be sold. [566F] 7. The mortgage amount and the security are not agricultural debt. The mortgage has been created by the mortgagor in favour of a purchaser. The mortgage money and the security have been split up, and in our opinion, the High court was right in holding that it is not a loan, but a loan, as defined in the Act. [546G] 8. The mortgage bond is a loan but not a loan; it is a loan; and the mortgage does not become a loan. Therefore, the mortgage does, not create any right in the mortgaged properties, and the mortgagee cannot sell the mortgaged property by sale. [546H] 9. The mortgage by the mortgagor is a loan only. The mortgagee is entitled to get his interest in the mortgage property. [546A] 10. The mortgage also does not create a mortgage. It is only a loan. If the mortgage is for a loan, it is a mortgage; but the mortgage is only a mortgage. Therefore, a loan is a loan which is a loan because the mortgage is created by the mortgagee. [546B] 11. The mortgage-deed is a loan document. The mortgage document is a loan deed. The mortgage provides that the mortgage is one of loan. [546C] 12. The mortgage under the mortgage deed is not a debt and the mortgage cannot be executed. [546D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 15 of 1971.

The appellants were tenants of the premises in question. They were tenants of a premises in the city of Bombay. They were inducted into the premises by the appellants in the year 1949. They were the tenants of the said premises. The appellants filed a suit in the City Civil Court for eviction of the tenants on the ground that the premises were not a tenant within the meaning of the Act. The appellants contended that the suit was not maintainable in the City civil court. The City Civil Court held that the suit filed by the appellants was not maintainable. The appellants then filed a suit for eviction of tenants and for recovery of possession. The City civil court dismissed the suit. The appellants preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that in view of the provisions of the Act and the Act, the suit filed in the City Court was not maintainable and dismissed the appeal. The appellants thereafter filed a second appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High court was right in holding that the suit in the city civil court was not maintainable because the appellants were the tenants. [675 H] 2. The provisions of the [U.P. Urban Buildings (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1947] and the Act are not applicable to the suit filed before the City Civil court. The provisions in the Act and Rules are applicable to the suits filed before the city civil courts. [682 H] 3. The provisions contained in the Act are applicable to suits filed before a court. The Act does not apply to the suit in a City Civil Court. The provisions relating to the filing of any suit relating to the suit to which any of the provisions applies are applicable to a suit filed in a City civil court and not to the suit which is filed in the city court. [685 H] 4. The provisions regarding the filing of a suit relating to a suit to which the provisions of Part 11 of the Act apply are applicable to all suits filed before any court. The suit in the Civil Court is not maintainable. [686 H] 5. The provisions made in the Act do not apply to suits filed in the Civil Courts. The provisions are applicable to cases where the suit is filed in a city civil court. [650 H] 6. The provisions for filing a suit relating thereto are applicable to proceedings relating to the eviction of tenants. The provisions under the Act are in addition to the provisions of any other law. [650 A] 7. The provisions as to the filing and disposal of suits relating to the recovery of possession of premises in the City court are applicable to such suits. [650 D] 8. The provisions referred to in the Act make it clear that the provisions of that Act are applicable only to suits filed by the tenants. The Act is not applicable to suits in the City courts. The provisions, therefore, are applicable to those suits. [691 H] 9. The provisions with regard to the filing or disposal of suits in the city courts are applicable to suit filed in any other court. The suits in the Civil courts are not maintainable. There is no provision in the Act which makes the provisions relating to suits relating to eviction of tenants applicable to suits to which any other law applies. [650 C] 10. The provisions to the contrary are applicable to other suits. The provisions that apply to suits in a City court are in addition. The provisions mentioned in the Act have to be read in the context of the Act, and the Rules made thereunder. [650 G] 11. The provisions which apply to suits relating thereto are in addition and not in derogation of the provisions contained in any other law for the time being in force. [650 F] 12. The provisions applicable to suits relatingto eviction of tenants are in addition, and not in addition to, the provisions of other law. The provisions governing the suits relating to recovery of possession are in addition in the nature of the provisions relating thereto.

The appellant was a director of a company which was incorporated in the year 1948. He was appointed as a director of the company on the basis of a resolution passed by the board of directors of the company. He was elected as a director in the year 1960. He was removed from the office by the company on a report made by the Registrar of the High Court. The appellant filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court for a writ quashing the order of the Registrar of Companies, Madras, dated March 31, 1962, and for a writ of mandamus directing the respondents to appoint him as the managing director of the appellant. The High Court held that the appellant was not a director of any company and that he was not the nominated representative of the shareholders. The High court held that the appointment of the appellant as the managing Director was not a promotion and was not an assignment of his office. The High. Court held that in the absence of a nomination by the company, the appointment of a person as the managing agent of the company was not an appointment by the company. The High, Court held that as the appellant was a Director of a company, he was not a member of the company and the appointment of his successor was not an act of appointment. The High' Court held that since the appellant was appointed as the managing partner of the appellant, he was a member of his own office and therefore, he was entitled to be appointed as the Managing Director of the appellant and that the appointment was not an incident of the appointment. The appellant was, therefore, not a director. The High 'Court held that the order of appointment of the managing director was not an order of appointment by the appellant and the High Court was not right in holding that the appointment did not amount to an assignment of the office. The appellant, therefore, was not a shareholder of the company, and the High court was right in holding, that the appointment as the managing trustee was not an assignable appointment.

The appellants are the partners of the firm M/s. Adeshwar Glass Mart. They are partners of the said firm. The respondent-landlord filed a suit for eviction against the appellants on the ground of subletting. The appellants filed a written statement and contended that the respondent was not a tenant of the said shop. The respondent contended that the appellants were not tenants of the said premises and that the respondent had not sublet the said shop to M/s Adeshwar Glass M.s. and that the appellants had not sublet any other shop to M.S. Adeshwar glass Mart. The Trial Court held that the appellants have not proved that the respondent has sublet the said premises to M/S Adeshwar GlassM.s. The respondent filed an appeal before the High Court. The High Court held that in the absence of any evidence to show that the appellants or M/s, Adeshwar Glass Mandal were carrying on business in the said premises, the respondent was entitled to be declared as a partner of the said partnership firm. The High court further held that the respondent could not be said to have sublet the said business to M/ s. Adeshwar Gas Mart. The High Curt also held that the partnership firm was carrying on business at the said premises for some time during which the appellants firm had ceased to carry on the business. The High. Court also held that in view of the provisions of the said Rent Act, the respondent could be said to be a tenant of M/s S. Adeshwar G.s. or Adeshwar Glass Mazdoor. The High, Court also held, that the respondent did not prove that the appellants' had sublet the said shops to M/ S. Adhiraj Glass Mandal. The High' Court also held in the said judgment that the respondent failed to prove that the respondent is a tenant of that shop. The High 'Court also held that there was no evidence to show how rent was received by the appellants from M/s s. Adhiraj Gas Mart. In the result, the High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellants have filed this appeal by special leave. The only question that arises for consideration in this appeal is whether the appellants are tenants of the shop in question. The respondent has not proved that he had sublet the shop to M-S. Adhiraj G.s., or Adeshwar Gas Mazdoor. The respondent had not proved that M/s has sublet the shop. The appellants had not proved the subletting. The respondent was not the tenant of the shop. In the absence of evidence to show the subletting, the respondent cannot be said to hold that the appellants are a tenant of another shop. The question whether the respondent has subletting the said shop is a question of fact. The Andhra Pradesh Act was passed by the Andhra Pradesh Legislature on the basis of the recommendations of the Andhra Pradesh State Legislature. The Andhra Pradesh Legislature passed the Andhra Pradesh Act on the basis that the ceiling area of a Hindu undivided family was to be determined on the basis on the basis, of the income derived from the family. The Andhra State Legislature passed the Madras Act on the same lines as the Andhra Pradesh Land Revenue Act, 1964. The Andhra Legislature passed the Tamil Nadu Act on the lines of the Andhra State Legislature. Section 2(n) of the Andhra Act provided that the ceiling on holding of land in excess of the ceiling area would be applicable to the land held by a Hindu undivided Hindu family. The Act provided for the ceiling on the holding of land. The Andhra Act provided for a ceiling on holding. The Andhra area was to be divided into two categories, namely, (i) land held by an individual, (ii) land held in excess of ceiling area. The Andhra Area was to be treated as an urban agglomeration. The Andhra was to be converted into urban agglomeration into urban agglomerations. The Andhra High Court held that the land held in the hands of a Hindu Undivided family was not liable to be clubbed with the land held under the Andhra Act. The Andhra Court held that in view of the provisions of the Andhra Area Act, the land held as a joint family was liable to be treated to be an urban agglomeration. The Andhra Civil Court held that since the land held was not liable for partition, the land in question was liable to tax. The Andhra, High Court held, that the Andhra Pradesh (Amendment) Act, 1972 was not valid. The Andhra. High Court held: "The Andhra Pradesh Legislature was competent to enact the Andhra Pradesh Amendment Act. The Madras Act was not valid as it was not valid because the land held on partition was not liable as part of the joint family unit. The Andhra is not a urban agglomerate. The Andhra has been held to be a separate unit. The Madras Legislature was competent under the Andhra Pradesh General Clauses Act to enact the Tamil Nadu Amendment Act. Under the Andhra Pradesh Amending Act, 1972, the Andhra Pradesh amendment was valid. The Madras High Court held in the case of Andhra Pradesh (supra) that the Andhra Act was valid. In view of the fact that the Andhra was not a separate unit, the Andhra was competent to levy tax on the land held. The Andhra legislature was competent to impose tax on the lands held by a joint family. The Madras Court held that as the land held is not liable to tax, the land was liable to pay tax. The Madras Courts held that the Andhra is not an urban agglomerated land. The Madras, High Court in the case referred to above held that the Madras Legislature was incompetent to enact the Madras Act. The Karnataka Legislature was competent in view of section 4 of the Andhra. Act. The Mysore Legislature was competent for the purpose of imposing tax on land in excess thereof. The Andhra in the case was held to be not a separate case of urban agglomerating land. The Karnataka Act was not invalid because the Andhra was a separate unit and was not liable under the Andhra. [501 G] The Andhra was not competent to levy the tax on land held by the joint family. [502 G] The Madras High court held that the Karnataka Legislature was incompetent under the Andhra State Act to enact a law imposing tax on lands in excess of its ceiling area. [503 G] The Karnataka Legislature had no competence to enact the Karnataka Act. [504 G] The Mysore Legislature had no power to enact the Mysore Act. [511 G] The Hyderabad Act was not competent under the Madras Act and the Andhra was incompetent. [505 G] The Madhya Pradesh Legislature was incompetent. The Andhra had no competence.

The Company was a registered trade union of workmen in the year 1953. The Company was a limited company, and it was a registered union of workmen. The Company had a limited company in which the workmen were employed. The Company, therefore, was not justified in refusing to give leave to the Company. The Company filed a petition under Art. 226 of the Constitution before the High Court of Calcutta, praying for a writ of certiorari quashing the order of dismissal and for a direction to the Company to give permission to the Company for giving leave to the workmen. The High Court held that the Company was not justified, in refusing to grant leave to the company for the reasons that the Company had not been given an opportunity of meeting the charges against the workmen. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that the Company did not have the right to give leave under the Standing Orders of the Company. [775 H] (2) The Standing Orders of a company are not binding on the Company and the Company is not justified in declining to give leave. The Standing Orders are not binding upon the Company. It is only the Company which has the right to refuse to give leave and it is for the Company to decide whether the charges have been proved or not. [776 H] (3) The Standing Order of the Company is a statutory one and the Company has a right to give permission for giving leave. [778 H] (4) The Standing orders of the Company are not binding. The Standing Order is not binding on a Company. The Standing orders are not binding to the Company and it is only the company which has the power to give leave for giving leave and it cannot be said that the Standing Orders are binding on the company. [779 H] (5) The Standing order of the Company does not confer any right on the Company to terminate the services of the workmen. [780 H] (6) The Standing Standing Orders are statutory in character and they are not binding in the sense that they are binding on a company. [750 H] (7) The Standing Instructions of the Company do not confer any rights on the Company. They are not binding as to the rights of the Company and they are binding upon the company. The Standing Instructions are not binding because they are not enforceable against the Company. In the absence of such a provision, the Standing Orders cannot be said to be binding on the workmen. In the instant case, the Standing Order of a company is not binding upon a Company. [750 A] (8) The Standing instructions of the Company cannot be said of the Company as they are binding. [750 B] (9) The Standing Instruction of the Company, therefore cannot be said not to be binding upon the workmen. It is not open to the Company, in the absence of a provision to the contrary, to refuse to grant leave for giving the Company permission to the company. In the circumstances, the Standing Instructions of a company cannot be said merely to be binding. [785 H] (10) The Standing Notes of the Company were not binding on it. [750 G] (11) The Standing Note of the Company was binding on the employees. [750 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1124 of 1966. Appeal by Special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 9th July, 1966 of the Calcutta High Court in Misc. Petition No. 11 of 1966. S. K. Sinha, for the appellant. S. N. Prasad, for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. The appellant, a registered trade Union, was a registered Trade Union of workmen. It was registered as a trade union of its workmen. The appellant was a registered Union of workmen in which the appellant was a member. The appellant filed a petition before the High court of Calcutta under Art. 227 of the Constitution.

The appellant was appointed as a lecturer in Botany in the University of Rajasthan on a temporary basis on a temporary appointment on a temporary post. The appellant was appointed to a post in the University on a temporary or officiating basis on a permanent basis on a fixed salary of Rs. 500 per month. The appointment was made on a temporary and officiating basis on the basis of a temporary appointment. The appointment of the appellant was made on temporary and officiating capacity on a temporary arrangement on a temporary scale. The appointment made on a permanent post was confirmed on a permanent appointment on a permanent or temporary basis on the same terms and conditions of service. The appointment on a regular basis was made on an ad hoc basis on a monthly salary of Rs, 500 per month and was confirmed on the same date on a permanent and temporary basis on an ad-hoc basis on a regular scale of pay. The appointment in the University was made on the basis that the appointment was temporary and was made on probation for a period of one year on a permanent scale of pay of Rs. 250 per month. On the expiry of the period of probation the appointment was confirmed on an adhoc basis on the terms and conditions mentioned in the appointment order. The appointment order was issued on the basis thereof by the University. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the appointment on the ground that the appointment of the respondent was not in accordance with the provisions of the Act and the Rules. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant preferred a Letters Patent Appeal against the judgment of the High Court. The Division Bench of the High court held that the appointment made by the University was not in conformity with the provisions contained in the Act and was not in consonance with the provisions. The Division bench also held that the appointments made by the Selection Committee were in conformity with Section 6 of the Act. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1.1 The appointment of a lecturer in a college is not in accordance either with the provisions or the provisions of Section 6 of Act. The appointment is made on a regular post. [605 C] 1.2 The appointment of an employee is not in conformity either with the provision of the Act or the Rules. [606 D] 1.3 The appointment of any teacher is not in consonance either with the Act or Rules. The appointment by the Selection committee is not in contravention of the provisions of any statute or the Rules but is in conformity with provisions of the statute. [607 D] 1:3. The appointment being made on a sanctioned post, the appointment is not in violation of the provisions. [608 D] 1.:4. The appointment cannot be made on a post sanctioned by the statute. The appointment can be made on the sanctioned post only on a regular appointment. [609 D] 1.(i) The appointment of every teacher is not a regular appointment and the appointment is made in accordance with Section 6. [610 D] 1(ii) The appointment is not made on a substantive or temporary basis. [611 D] 1a. The appointment does not in any manner interfere with the right of the appointee to hold the post. [613 E] 1.4 The appointment of teachers is not in the prescribed manner. [613 F] 1.5. The appointment itself is not in compliance with the provisions and the provisions of law. [613 G] 1.6. The appointment has to be made on an sanctioned post. [625 G] 1:4. The appointments made by selection committee are not in accordance. [612 G] 1.(iii) The appointment made by selection Committee is not in terms of the Act, and is not in conflict with the provisions thereof. [614 G] 1(iv) The appointment was not made on an ex post sanctioned by law. [615 G] 1.:5.

The provisions of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as amended by the Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1984, were amended by the [Land Acquisition (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1985], and the Land Acquisition Officer was appointed under section 11 of the Act. [780 H] 1,5. The provision in the Land acquisition Acts were not in conformity with the provisions contained in the Land Act. [782 H] 1 [782 A] 1:6. The provisions made in the Land Acquistion Act were not inconsistent with the provisions in those Acts. [750 H] 1 D] 1:7. The provisions regarding the acquisition of the land designated for any public purpose under [section 7] of the said enactments were not applicable when the provisions of those Acts were not made applicable to the said acquisition proceedings. [750 A] 1.8. The provisions under sections 4 and 5 of the said enactment were not applicable because the provisions of Section 4 and 11 were not in consonance with the provisions made in those Acts and the provisions in regard to the acquisition thereof were not in consistent with the provisions under the said enactments. [750 B] 1:8. The provision contained in sections4 and 11(4) of the Bombay Land Acquisition Act were not made in accordance with section 4 and11(2) were not applicable at all. [750 C] 1:9. The dispute between the parties was whether the territory of the State of Kutch merged with the Dominion of India and the dispute was referred to the Tribunal for adjudication. The Tribunal held that the territory of Kutch was a part of the territory of India and that the dispute was not a dispute between the Government of India and a State Government. The Tribunal, however, held that the dispute between the State Government and the State Government was not a matter of dispute between the two States and that the State Government had no power to make any law in respect of the territory in question. The Tribunal accordingly held that the State of Gujarat had no power under the Indian Constitution to make any laws in respect of territory in question and that the claim of the claimants that the territory was not a part of India was not a question of dispute between them and the State of Saurashtra. The Tribunal also held that the claim made by the claimants that in the event of the dispute being referred to the tribunal, the State of Bombay had no power, was not a claim in respect of any territory in the territory of Gujarat and that the award was not a law made by the State of the State. The Tribunal further held that the award did not purport to, nor did it operate as giving rise to, an obligation to cede any part of the State and that the finding of the Tribunal that the dispute in question was not a " dispute " was not a finding of fact. The Tribunal then held that the Government of the State had no power or jurisdiction to make any such law in respect to territory in question; and that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to make the law in respect the territory of that State. The High Court held that the Tribunal was not competent to make any order under the Indian law and that the order of the Tribunal was a nullity. The High court held that the order passed by the Tribunal was an order of the State Government in exercise of the power under the [Indian Constitution Act]. The High Court also held that in the absence of any evidence to show that the territory in dispute was originally governed by the Maharao of Kutch, the claim made in the claim made on the basis of the award of the International Tribunal was not a suit in respect of that territory. The High, Court also held, that the claim was not a plaint in respect of a territory in the State of which the Maharao had sovereign rights. The High. Court also held in the case of the State that the claim that the dispute raised by the claimants was not a subject matter of dispute in respect of which the State had power to make law in respect thereof was not a case of dispute between a Government of the States and the State. In the result, the High Court held, that in the case in hand, the dispute was a dispute between a State Government and a State and that it was not a civil dispute. The High' Court also held on the basis that the dispute involved in the case was not a private dispute between the Central Government and the Government of State of Gujarat and the State had not made any law in that behalf. The High C.A. No. 823 of 1966 filed by the State Government of Gujarat was dismissed. The State of Gujarat filed an appeal against the judgment of the High Court. The High-Court held that the question whether the dispute was an industrial dispute or not was a question of fact and the High Court was not competent. The HighCourt further held that in view of the provisions of the Indian Constitution, the dispute raised in the case did not fall within the purview of the Indian law. The High Courts' decision was affirmed by the Supreme Court. The State Government of the appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Gujarat. The High 'Court held that in any event the dispute in the case involved in the dispute was one which was not a public dispute. The appeal was accordingly dismissed. The appellant filed a special leave petition in this Court.

The appellants are the owners of a motor vehicle bearing registration No. TL-7/412. They were carrying passengers in a bus bearing registration No, TL-6/412 and were also carrying passengers in the said bus. The appellants were carrying passengers on a public service vehicle. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court of Bombay challenging the levy of tax on the said vehicles. The High Court held that the transport provided to the employees by the appellants was a public service vehicles and the transport provided by the appellants would be a public service Vehicle. The High court held that the said vehicles were not public service vehicles within the meaning of the provisions of the Bombay Motor Vehicles (Taxation of Passengers) Act, 1958. The High. Court held that it was not open to the appellants to contend that the transport was not a public service car within the meaning and that the said vehicle was not a private service vehicle. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the transport of the appellants was not a service vehicle within the meaning. The High, Court held that in view of the Preamble of the Act, the tax was leviable only on passengers carried by a private company and no other member of the public was a public servant. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The definition of 'public service vehicle' in the Act is wide enough to include a motor vehicle. The definition is wide enough. The definition in the Act does not include a motor car. [510 G] 2. The definition given in the Act includes a motor vehicle within the ambit of the provisions contained in the Act. The definition does not include the transport provided in the Act and the transport is not a public services vehicle. [511 G] 3. The definition under the Act is wider than the definition under the provisions of section 2(7) of the Act. [512 G] 4. The definition contained in section 2(1) of the Bombay Act is wide and includes a motor car within the ambit thereof. [513 G] 5. The definition being wide enough to cover a motor vehicle, the question of the said definition being wide does not arise. [514 G] 6. The definition as given in the statute is wide enough and includes a vehicle which is not a private vehicle within the purview of the provisions. [515 G] 7. The definition clause in the Act makes it clear that the transport is a public service motor vehicle. [546 G] 8. The definition makes it clear beyond doubt that the transport vehicle provided to the employee by the appellants is a public services car within the purview thereof. [546 H] 9. The definition also includes a motor vehicles within the ambit and the definition of the provisions in the Act also makes it clear as a fact that the transport provides to the employees of the appellants. [546 D] 10. The definition clearly excludes the transport provided for the employees by a private service car. [546 F] 11. The definition excludes a motor vehicle which is a publicservice vehicle within the definition of section 2 (7) of Act. [546 E] 12. The definition has to be read in the context of the definition of ' public service vehicle' and not in the context in which it is used. [546 A] 13. The definition includes a motor cab within the ambit, and the definition is wide and include a motor cab. [546 B] 14. The definition shows that the definition is wider than that under the provisions contained therein. [546 C] 14. In the instant case, the transport provided is a public vehicle within the scope of the provisions under the Act. It is not a service car within its ambit. [546F] 15. The definition provides for the definition of a 'public service car' and not a 'public servant vehicle' within the ambit. [547 G] 16.
