The appellant, a partnership firm, was a partnership firm. The partnership was registered on September 2, 1957. The partnership deed provided that the lease was to be for a period of one year from the date of the execution of the lease deed. The lease was to expire on September 2. 1957. The lease deed provided that in case of breach of the terms of the lease, the lessee would be liable to pay a penalty of Rs. 1,000 per month. The lease period was to expire at the end of the period of the lease. The lease expired on September 2 1957. The appellant filed a suit for specific performance of the contract on the ground that the contract was not concluded by an oral agreement. The trial court held that the contract dated September 2, 1958 was concluded by an agreement between the parties and that the contract to assign the mining lease was concluded by a written agreement between the appellant and the respondent. The trial Court held that the lease deed was concluded by oral agreement between the respondent and the appellant and that the respondent was entitled to get a decree for specific performance. The High Court held that there was no concluded contract between the parties. The High court held that there is no concluded contract and the contract was concluded by the oral agreement between both the parties. In the result, the High Court dismissed the suit. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. The main question for consideration is whether the High Court was right in holding that the contract in question was concluded by agreement between the respondents. The appellant contended that the contract did not come to an end by an oral contract and that the appellant was entitled to the relief of specific performance. It was further contended that the High Court erred in holding that there was concluded contract between both the appellant and respondent. The High Curt held that the appellant had not terminated the contract by giving notice to the respondent. In the alternative, it was contended that the appellant could not be said to have terminated the contract on account of the breach of the contract. The High. Court held that in the circumstances of the case, the contract was completed by an oral application of an oral agreement between parties. The appellant was entitled, therefore, to the relief claimed by him. The High, Court held that it was not open to the appellant to seek a decree for the specific performance of a contract. The appellant's suit was dismissed. The appellant then filed a second appeal. The High' Court held that as the contract was held to be concluded by an implied agreement between the two parties, the contract could not be specifically performed. The High 'Court held that the agreement was concluded by mutual agreement between the plaintiff and the respondent and that the agreement did not come into existence by an oral oral agreement between them. The High-Court held that there could be no concluded contract. The respondent filed a second suit for specific Performance. The High T.A. No. 1 of 1958 was dismissed. In the appeal to this Court, it was submitted that the High Curt was right in dismissing the suit. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts order was correct. The HighCourt was right in rejecting the appellant's suit. [529 G] 2. The appellant had not pleaded that the contract between the appellant was concluded by any oral agreement between him and the respondent, and that the terms of that agreement were not binding on him. The appellant could not seek to enforce the contract by seeking a decree for a specific performance. [530 G] 3. The High R.A. is not competent to the appellant. The contract was concluded on the oral agreement. [531 G] 4. The appellant cannot seek to enforce a contract by seeking to enforce the terms of a contract by the respondent. [532 G] 5. The appellant is entitled to the decree for specific Performance of the contract and the respondent is entitled to recover the amount of the contract from the appellant. [533 G] 6.

The appellants were the owners of a tea estate in the State of Bihar. They were assessed to the price of sugarcane at the rate of Rs. 2,000 per quintal. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court of Patna praying for a writ of mandamus directing the State of Patna to pay to the appellants the price of the sugarcane purchased by them. The High Court held that the appellants were guilty of an offence under section 3 of the Act and accordingly quashed the proceedings. The appellants challenged the correctness of the decision of the High Court in a writ petition. The High court held that the provisions of the Act were not attracted to the facts of the case and the appellants were not guilty of an offences under section 3(1) of the Act. The High, Court held that in view of section 11 of the Act the prosecution of the appellants was not maintainable. The appellants then filed a writ application in the High court for quashing the proceedings. It was contended that the provisions contained in section 11 of Act were not applicable to the facts and circumstances of the case. The High. Court held that section 11 of this Act was not applicable to a case where the prosecution was not maintainable and as such the prosecution was maintainable. The High' Court held that there was no contravention of section 3 of Act and the prosecution was bad. The appellants, therefore, filed a writ appeal in this Court. HELD: The provisions of section 11 were not applicable in the facts of this case. The provisions of the section were not applicable. The provisions contained in sections 3 and 4 of the Act are not applicable to cases where the prosecution is not maintainable. [775 H] The provisions of sections 3 and 5 of the Act have to be read in the context of the provisions of section 3 and 4. The provisions in section 3 of this Act are not attracted to a case of an offence punishable under section 3. The provisions are not applicable in a case where an offence is punishable with three years ' imprisonment and as such it is a cognizable offence. [776 H] The provision contained in section 3(2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, is not applicable to an offence punishable with three months' imprisonment and as the provisions of sections 4 and 5 of this Act were not made applicable to a particular case, the provisions of this Act would be applicable to the case. [778 H] The question whether the provisions contained therein are applicable to a situation where the prosecution of an offence is not maintainable is a question of fact. [779 H] The decision of the Patna High Court in the case of the State of Punjab vs. The State of Bihar, [1962] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 8, relied on. The provisions relating to the control of the price of a tea factory in the State were not applicable as the provisions contained under section 11 of that Act were not in the contemplation of section 11. [780 H] The fact that the provisions were not applicable would not make the provisions of [section 11] inapplicable to a case when the prosecution is in respect of an offence. [750 H] The offence under section 11 was not punishable with three- years' imprisonment and the provisions of s. 11 were not attracted. [750 A] The provisions contained under sections 3 and 6 of the Act would be attracted to a situation when the prosecution was in respect of a case where prosecution was not filed. [750 B] The provisions relating thereto are not applicable. [750 C] The provisions in the Act are applicable to cases of an offence which is punishable with imprisonment and as a result of which an offence is committed in respect of the food and food articles. [750 D] The provisions are applicable to the cases of an accused where the prosecution in respect of any food article is not maintainable and the provisions contained thereunder are not applicable as they are not applicable and the provisions relating to prosecution are not applicable thereto.

The appellants are engaged in the manufacture of sugar. They were assessed to sales tax under the provisions of the said Act. The appellants purchased sugar from the State Government for the first five years from the date of the said order. The State Government issued a notification dated 12th January, 1977 under which the exemption granted to the appellants was withdrawn. The said notification was challenged by the appellants by filing a writ petition in the High Court of Karnataka. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the notification dated 12.1.1977. The appellants filed a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed. The appellants then filed a writ appeal before this Court. The said appeal was allowed by a Division Bench of the High Court by a judgment dated 12th May, 1987. The Division Bench held that the doctrine of Promissory Estoppel was not applicable to the facts of the case. The Division bench held that the said doctrine was not good law and the exemption granted under the said order was not available to the appellants. The said decision was challenged by special leave by the appellants. Dismissing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The doctrine of Prom promissory estoppel is not applicable to a case where the source of power under which it was issued was not stated in an order but only a power under which the said power was issued. [775 H] 2.1 The doctrine of promissory estoppel is applicable to the fact of the case and the doctrine of promissory Estoppel is not applicable in the facts of this case. [776 H] 2:2. The doctrine is not applicable when the source of the power under which such power was issued is not stated in the order but can be found on the examination of the relevant Act. [778 H] 2] 2.2 The doctrine ofpromissory Estoppel is applicable to a situation where the source is not stated or can be found by the person who has issued the said order and not merely a power under the said Order. [779 H] 2 2.3 The doctrine of ' Promissory Estopple' is applicable to cases where the source was not stated or the law was not stated.

The appellants were convicted under Section 302 read with Section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced to undergo imprisonment for life. The appellants were convicted for the offence under Section 302 I.P.,C. and were sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for life and to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000/- each. The appellants filed an appeal before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellants then filed a petition under Article 136 of the Constitution before this Court for special leave to appeal against the judgment of the High Court and the same was dismissed. The appellants thereafter filed a petition for special leave before this Court. The appellants contended that the High Court was in error in holding that the appellants were guilty under Section 302 and sentenced to imprisonment for life, and that the High court was in error. The High court held that the appellants had formed an unlawful assembly and had committed the murder of Madda Lakshamandas and that the appellants could not be convicted under Section 148 I.P,C. The High. Court held that the prosecution had failed to establish the commission of an offence under Section 149 I.P,.C. and the appellants were, therefore, entitled to the benefit of doubt. The High, Court held that there was no evidence to show that the appellants formed an unlawful unlawful assembly and were guilty under Sections 148 and 302 I. P.C. The appellants, therefore, were acquitted. The appellants preferred an appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The appellants could not have been convicted under Section 149, I.P..C. and they could not be sentenced to imprisonment. [775 H] 2. The High Courts were in error in convicting the appellants under Section 302, I. P.,C. The conviction of the appellants under Sections 148, 302 read with 149 I. P,C. and sentence of imprisonment for life was, therefore, not sustainable. [776 H] 3. The High Curt was in error when it held that the conviction of the accused under Section 302 was not sustainable. The HighCourt was in error, in holding that there was evidence to show the commission of the offence under Sections 148 or 302 read with section 34 I. P,.C. The evidence on record shows that the appellants did not commit the offence under [Section 302] read with Section 149 I, I.p.C. [778 H] 4. The High-Court was in agreement with the finding of the trial court that the appellants committed the offence under section 302 read with [section 34] I.P.'C. and that the conviction under Section 302/34 I.P./C. was not sustainable in law. [779 H] 5. The High' Court was in agreement. [780 H] 6. The High 'Court was in wrong in holding that it was not in error. [782 H] 7. The High T.A.C. was in error as it was in error by the trial court. [785 H] JUDGMENT: CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Criminal Appeal No. 8 of 1986. From the Judgment and Order dated the 12th May, 1985 of the High court of Judicature at Allahabad in Criminal Appeal No 8 of 1985. S.K. Sinha, for the appellants. S.N. Prasad, for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by K.J. Shah, J. The appellants are the members of the unlawful assembly and have been convicted by the trial Court under Section 302 IPC and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for a period of five years and to pay fine of Rs 1,000/-, in default of payment of fine, to undergo rigorous rigorous imprisonment for one year. The appellants have been convicted for the offences under Sections 148/149 and 302 read with Sections 149 I.p./34 I. P.'C.

The assessee, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, for the assessment year 1957-58. The assessee claimed that the capital asset purchased by him was not a capital asset and that the value of the capital asset was not disclosed by the assessee. The Income Tax Officer, on the basis of the evidence produced before him, held that the value declared by the assessee was not a genuine and correct one and that the assessee was entitled to the benefit of the exemption under s. 10(2) of the Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, allowed the appeal of the assessee and held that the capital assets purchased by the assessee were not a capital assets and that the amount of the consideration received by the assessee as a result of the transfer was not a gift liable to tax under the provisions of the Gift Tax Act, 1958. The Appellate Tribunal, however, held that in the absence of any evidence to the contrary, the assessee was liable to pay the tax under the Gift Tax law. The Tribunal, however held that the assessee had not disclosed the true value of the consideration in respect of the transfer and that the consideration was not a mere device or device to evade tax. The Tribunal held that the amount received by the appellant was a gift liable for tax under the Act. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that in view of the fact that the assessee did not disclose the true value, the difference between the market value and the full value of the amount received in respect of transfer was not an amount which was not a part of the consideration declared by the appellant. The Tribunal accordingly held that the sum of Rs. 1,00,000/- was a gift within the meaning of s. 10 of the Act and that the difference between market value and full value of consideration was not an allowable deduction under s.10(2) and that the Tribunal was right in holding that the amount was not a receipt liable to tax. The High Court, however, dismissed the appeal of Revenue and allowed the appeal. The Revenue is in appeal against the order of the High Court. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The High court was right in its view that the amount paid by the assessee in respect of a capital asset was a gift and not a mere means of collection of the consideration. [557D] 2. The amount received by way of gift was a mere device and device to evade the tax. The amount of the gift was not a cash receipt but a mere device to evade payment of tax. [558F] 3. The amount was not an asset purchased by the appellant but was a mere means or device to avoid tax. [506F] 4. The amount paid by way of consideration for the transfer was a mere measure of collection of consideration and the burden of proving that the amount had not been truly received by the Revenue was on the Revenue. [559F] 5. The amount which was received by the respondent was a mere mode of collection of a consideration. The amount actually received by the Respondent was a mere method of collection of tax. The respondent was not entitled to the relief under s. 11 of the Act on the ground that the amount is not a mere method or device to escape tax. [504F] 6. The amount is not an asset or a valuable asset. The amount has to be a mere device. [566F] 7. The amount must be a mere means and device to avoid the tax. [500G] 8. The amount in the hands of the assessee is not a receipt of the assessee. [567G] 8(i) The amount received is a mere device for evading tax. [525H] (ii) The amount is a mere means to avoid tax and the burden is on the Revenue to prove that the amount has not been truly paid.

The appellant was convicted by the trial court for an offence under Section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955. The appellant was convicted for an offence punishable under Section 7 and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two months. The appellant filed an appeal before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant then filed a petition for special leave to appeal to this Court. The appellant contended that the provisions of the Act were not complied with by the appellant and that the provisions were not complied. The High court held that the provisions contained in the Act were complied with by P.M.P. The High Curt held that the appellant was guilty of an offence under the Act and sentenced him to undergo rigorous rigorous imprisonment for one month. The appellant, therefore, filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution for a writ of certiorari quashing the order of the High Court and for a writ in the nature of mandamus directing the respondents to comply with the provisions of Section 10(7) of the Act. The High, Court held that the provision contained in the statute was not complied with and the provisions of Act were not mandatory. The appellant thereupon filed a petition in this Court under Article 32 of the Constitution. The appellant also contended that the High Court was in error in holding that the provisions in the Act did not apply to the case. The appellant further contended that the Act was not complied in this case. The High. Court held that it was not necessary to comply with Section 10(8) of the said Act. The appellant accordingly filed a petition before this Court under Art. 32 of the constitution. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The provisions contained in Section 10(6) of the Indian Electricity Act, 1910, are mandatory in character and the provisions are not mandatory in character. [775 H] 2. The provisions of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885, are mandatory and the provisions contained therein are not mandatory. [776 H] 3. The provisions in the Indian Electricity (Amendment) Act, 1956, are mandatory. The provisions are mandatory in nature. The provisions have to be complied with by a person who is not a citizen of India. [778 H] 4. The provisions relating to the use of the word "food" are mandatory in the sense that the provisions are mandatory. [750 H] 5. The provisions made in the Act are mandatory in respect of the use of any word for human consumption. [750 A] 6. The provisions regarding the use of "food", "food". [750 A-B] 7. The provisions for the use of a word for human use are mandatory in a sense that the provision is mandatory in character, and the provisions relating to use of the said word for human usage are not mandatory, but are mandatory in terms. [750 B] 8. The provisions as contained in the Indian Telegraph (Amendment) Bill, 1956, do not apply to a case where the provisions contained are mandatory in law. [750 D] 9. The provisions referred to in the Act have to be strictly complied with. [750 E] 10. The provisions, as contained in Section 7 of Act are mandatory. Section 7 of that Act provides that the provisions relating thereto are mandatory in its application. [750 G] 11. The provisions under the Act are not mandatory and the provision contained therein is not mandatory. Section 10(9) of the Code is mandatory in nature and the provisions in question are not mandatory but are mandatory. It is not necessary to do so. [750 F] 12. The provisions mentioned in the Act do not apply in the case of a case where there is no provision for the use or use of the words "food, " or "food " or "good" in the Act. [750 C] 13. The provisions which are mandatory in themselves are mandatory in their application.

The appellant was a member of the Bihar State Judicial Service. He was appointed as a District Judge in the year 1962. He was promoted as District Judge in 1962. He had been promoted as District Judges in the year 1963. He was confirmed as District Judge on the basis of the recommendation of the High Court. He was, however, promoted as District and Sessions Judge in the years 1962 and 1963. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of his reversion. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant filed a writ appeal in this Court. The appellant contended that the order of reversion was not passed in the interest of justice and that the High Court was not justified in issuing a writ to the appellant. HELD: (i) The order of reversion passed by the High Court in the interest o f justice was not at all sustainable. [775 H] (ii) The order passed by the State Government was not a speaking order and the High Court had no jurisdiction to issue a writ to a subordinate court. [776 H] (iii) The order was passed in the interests of justice and the High court was not justified to issue a Writ to the appellant for the reasons stated. [778 H] (iv) The order dated December 14, 1963 was passed in exercise of the powers conferred by Article 226 of the Constitution. The order was not a judgment in rem. The order of the High court dated December 14 1963 was not a mere order of dismissal. [779 H] (v) The order in the present case was passed in a judicial capacity and was not a judicial order. [780 H] (vi) The order is not a judgment within the meaning of Article 226 of The Constitution. [782 H] (vii) The order could not be passed in the absence of any order of the higher authority. [785 H] (viii) The order having been passed in the exercise of the power conferred by Article 227 of the Constitution, the High Court could not issue a writ in the nature of certiorari to quash the order. [750 H] (ix) The order under Article 226 of Constitution is not a mere administrative order. The order is passed in the administrative capacity. [750 A] (x) The order cannot be passed in a routine manner. [750 B] (xi) The order can be passed in an administrative capacity. The order can only be passed in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution and the High Courts have no jurisdiction to entertain a writ petition. [750 D] (xii) The order has to be passed in exercise o the powers conferred under Article 226. [750 G] (xiii) The order does not contain any order of any authority. [750 F] (xiii] (xiv) The order must be passed in terms of the provisions of Article 226. The order must contain a direction in the order. The High Courts have jurisdiction to issue the writ to the High Court to issue a mandamus. [750 E] (xv) The order being a mere order in the exercise o the power conferred under Article 227 of The Constitution, the order cannot be issued in the absence o any order of a superior court. [750 C] (xvi) The order, therefore, cannot be passed by the court in the absence thereof. [750D] (xvii) The order should be passed in conformity with the provisions contained in Article 226. If the order is passed by the higher authority, the High Courts are not justified in issue a writ. [750F] (xviii) The order may be passed in any other manner. [786 H] (xix) The order would be passed in consonance with the provisions in Article 226 of [Article 227] of the Constitution; (xx) The order shall be passed in such a manner as may be prescribed.

The appellant, a minor, filed a suit for partition and separate possession of the properties in suit. The trial court decreed the suit in favour of the appellant and directed the appellant to pay a sum of Rs. 1,000/- to the respondent. The respondent filed an appeal to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant filed a second appeal to this Court. The appellant contended that the High Court was in error in holding that the decree passed by the trial court was not a decree of affirmance and the decree passed in the suit was not a nullity. Held, that the High court was in error of law in holding that in the absence of a concession in that behalf, the decree passed was not a judgment of affirmance. The High court was not in error in thinking that the decree was a nullity. The High Courts decision was not a decision of affirmance but a judgment of the trial court. The High courts decision was not an order of affirmance or the judgment of the appellate court. The appellant was entitled to go to the Privy Council in appeal. The High. Court was in appeal against the judgment of a Single Judge of the High Court in second appeal. The respondent was not entitled to go before the Privy Council. The High, Court was in fact in error in saying that the decree in the suit passed by the High Court did not bind the appellant. The High-Court was in error. The appellant could not be allowed to raise the plea of estoppel by way of appeal. The judgment of the High court is not a judgment in the discretion of the Court under section 35 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The High Curt was in error by holding that the judgment of this Court in the case of [S. K. Das v. The State of West Bengal] , was not a final judgment. The High T.A.C. was in error, in holding that it was not a case of affirmance, but a case of a decree of confirmation. The appellant had not challenged the judgment of an appellate court. In the absence of any concession in that regard, the High Court could not have allowed the appeal.

The respondent, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1956, was incorporated in the year 1956, and was registered as a limited company under the Indian companies Act, 1956. The respondent was a company incorporated in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The company was incorporated under the Companies Act, 1913, and was incorporated in Uttar Pradesh. On the basis of the memorandum of association of the company, the State Government issued a notification under section 25 of the Act, declaring its intention to establish a new industrial undertaking. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court of Allahabad, challenging the validity of the notification issued by the State Government under section 25, Provincial Small Cause Courts Act, and the High Court quashed the notification issued under section 25. The High Court held that the notification issued in the year 1973 was not a valid notification and, therefore, the notification issued on the basis of that notification was not a nullity. The High court held that the respondent was not a "consumer" within the meaning of section 25, and, therefore the notification issued was not a legal one. The respondent, therefore, filed a writ appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts in exercise of their revisional powers under section 25 are not courts of law. The High courts have no jurisdiction to make an order under section 25 or section 115, Code of Civil Procedure. [557F] 2. The High-Court has no jurisdiction to entertain a revision petition under section 115, code of Civil Procedure, against a notification issued under the Act. [558F] 3. The High, Court has no jurisdiction under section 25 to entertain a petition under section 25 and the High Courts have no jurisdiction. [559F] 4. The High. Court has no power to make an interim order of the District Judge under section 25 without a reference to the High Court. [560F] 5. The High Curt was not competent to entertain a writ petition under Article 227 of the Constitution. [566F] 6. The High' Court has no inherent jurisdiction to make any order under section25, Provincial Small Causes Courts Act. [546F] 7. The High 'Court has no inherent power to make any interim order of a District Court under section 25 in a case where the High Court is of the opinion that a revision petition is not maintainable. [546G] 8. The High [Court] has no jurisdiction. The High T.A.C. has no jurisdiction, and the appeal and the connected special leave petitions must be dismissed. [546H] 9. The High (Court) has no jurisdiction in the matter. [546B] 10. The High A Court has no such jurisdiction. [546C] 11. The High F.A.F. has no power of revision under section 115 of the Code of Civil procedure. [546D] 12. The High] Court has no authority to make an interlocutory order of the High Court under section25. [546E] 13. The High "Court" has no inherent powers of revision under sections 25, Provincial Civil Courts Act. The High B Court has no revisional power under section 115. [546A] 14. The High L.A. Court has jurisdiction to make the order under section 10, Provincial Small causes Courts Act. It is not competent to make an application under section 25 for revision under section 25 against an order passed under section 25 by a District Court. [546 F] 15. The High R.C.A.T. has no authority under section 25 nor is it competent to make any interlocutory order of a High Court under the Code of Criminal Procedure. [546 G] 16. The High O.P.C. is not a court of law. [546 B] 16.

The respondents filed a writ petition before the High Court of Rajasthan challenging the notification issued by the State Government under section 52 (1) of the Act on the ground that the notification issued under section 52(1) of that Act was not in accordance with the provisions of the Act and that the notification was not in conformity with the provisions contained in section 52 (2) of the said Act. The High Court held that the notification under section 52 was not in consonance with the provisions in section 52(2) of that act and that the entire cause of action culminating in the acquisition of the land was not a mere pretence and he was satisfied on the material on record that the land was needed bona fide and their real object was just to get the land released from acquisition on one ground or the other. The High court held that the respondents were not entitled to the relief prayed for by them in the writ petition. The High, Court held that there was no material on record to show that the land in question was not needed by the respondents bona fide and that the respondents had not raised any objection as to the power of the State Government to acquire the land under section 52 of the Act. The respondents filed a special leave petition in this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The notification under section 51(1) was not in the prescribed form and was not in compliance with the provisions. [505 G] 2. The notification issued under s. 52(1), is not in conformity of the provisions of section 52(3) of the act. The notification is not in accordance therewith. [506 G] 3. The notification was not published in the prescribed manner. The notification did not specify the land required for the purpose of the scheme. The notification does not in any way indicate that the land is needed bona fide. [507 G] 4. The notification in question was in conformity with section 52(4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. [508 G] 5. The notification dated February 8, 1984 was not in terms of the provisions contained therein. The notification, therefore, was not in violation of the provisions. The notification cannot be said to be in conformity with provisions of section 51(2) or section 52(5) of the Indian Act. [509 G] 6. The notification could not be issued under section 51 of the Act as it was not in contravention of the provisions in the Act. [506 G] 7. The notification should be in conformity therewith. [506 H] JUDGMENT: ORIGINAL JURISDICTION: Writ Petition Nos. 823 and 823 of 1984. (Under Article 32 of the Constitution of India) AND Writ Petition Nos, 823 and 923 of 1984 (Under Article 226 of the Constitution) AND Writ Petitions Nos. 824 and 923 and 924 of 1984 (under Article 32 of Constitution) AND Civil Appeal Nos. 825 and 923 to 923 of 1985 (Under Article 136 of the Constitution). AND Civil Appeal No. 923 of 1986 (Under Article 132 of the Constitution), Civil Appeal No, 923 of 1987 (Under Article 133 of the Constitution); and Civil Appeal No.. 923 of 86 (Under Article 134 of the Constitution, and Civil Appeal Nos.. 923 and 933 of 1986 (under Article 136 of Constitution) and Civil Appeal no. 923/86 (Under Article 135 of the Constitution and Civil Appeal nos. 923 and923 of 1986) and Civil Appeals Nos. 923, 923 and 930 of 1986 ( Under Article 136 of The Constitution). AND Writ Petition No. 823 of 1985. (Under article 32 of the constitution) AND Writ petition No. 924 of 1985 (under Article 226 of The Constitution) AND writ petition No. 824 of 1985.

The appellant was the tenant of a building in the city of Madras. He was a tenant of a house in the city. He was in occupation of a building on the date of the application for the grant of a licence to run a business in the city and was paying rent to the landlord. The appellant was a tenant in the city in which the building was situated. He was served with a notice of demand for arrears of rent and damages for use and occupation of the building. The appellant filed a suit for eviction on the ground of arrears of rent. The trial court decreed the suit. The appellant preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the decree of the trial court. The appellant's appeal was allowed by the High Court and the decree of eviction was set aside. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. The appellant contended that the building in question was not a building in which the appellant was in occupation and was not liable to be evicted on the ground that the building was not completed on the date when the revision petition was heard by the High court. The High court held that the building had become vacant on the date the revision petition had been heard by the court and, therefore, there was no question of giving the benefit of s.39 of the Act to the appellant. The High, Court held that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of the new Rent Act. The appellant, therefore, filed this appeal. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The appellant is entitled to the protection of s. 39 of the new Act. [775 H] 2. The appellant would be entitled to the benefits of s.40 of the new rent Act. [750 H] 3. The appellant could not be denied the benefit of S.39 of Act. The High. Court was right in holding that the appellant would be entitle to the benefit under s.39 to the benefit conferred by s.39. [750 A] 4. The appellant had not been able to show that the building which was in possession of the appellant was not completed before the revision petition could be heard by the III Additional District Judge. [750 B] 5. The appellant cannot be denied the benefits of the new legislation on the ground the arrears of rent as directed by the High. Court. [750 D] 6. The appellant must be held to be entitled to benefit of s..39 of the new. Act. [751 H] 7. The appellant should be given the benefit of section 39 of the old Act. [751 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 14 of 1972. Appeal by Special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 14th May, 1972 of the Madras High Court in C.M.P. No. 11 of 1972. S.T. Desai, S.K. Bagga and S.K Jain for the Appellant. S.K Sharma, for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by K. JAYACHANDRA REDDY, J. This appeal by special Leave is directed against the judgment and order of the High Court of Madras dated April 14, 1972 in C.R.P. Nos. 14 of 1971 and 15 of 1971. The appellant-tenant is the tenant of the building in dispute. The appellant instituted a suit for ejectment on the ground, inter alia, that the building is not a building within the meaning of the new-Act. The appellant also filed a suit in the year 1971 for eviction on that ground. The appellant pleaded that the building has become vacant on account of the construction of the building on the relevant date and, therefore the building was required to be vacated on the ground specified in the second proviso to s.39(1) of the new, Act. The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was incorporated in the year 1948. The appellant was a company incorporated in the State of Bihar. The appellant, a Government company incorporated under a statute, was incorporated under the [Indian Companies Act, 1956]. The appellant was incorporated in 1948. The company was incorporated in 1950. The appellant filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 1,10,000/- on the basis of an agreement dated February 6, 1948, and claimed that the agreement dated February 5, 1948, was an instrument of arbitration and that the agreement was an instrument relating to the execution of the agreement. The trial court held that the agreement in question was an instrument in the nature of an instrument of exchange and that the appellant was entitled to recover the amount of Rs. 2,10,500/- from the respondent. The High Court, however, reversed the decree of the trial court and dismissed the suit. The appellant has come up in appeal to this Court. The appellant contended that the agreement, dated February 6., 1948, was a document of exchange and not a deed of exchange and, therefore, the agreement was not an instrument of settlement. The appellant also contended that the document was an instrument which was not an agreement of exchange and therefore the agreement was a document relating to the performance of the agreement and that the document in question was not an instruments of exchange. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The agreement dated February, 6, 1948 was an instrument for exchange and not an instrument relating thereto. The document in question, therefore, was an agreement of arbitration. [532 H] 2. The agreement was an agreement for arbitration and not a document relating thereto. [533 H] 3. The agreement in question is an instrument of Exchange and not a registered document. The document is an instrument relating not to the execution or registration of the document. The agreement is an instrument in writing and is an instrument which is an instrument for the execution of a document. [534 H] 4. The document was an agreement to exchange and not the document relating thereto and therefore the document was not an Instruments of exchange. [535 H] 5. The document, therefore, is an instrument containing an instrument of transfer of property and not a contract relating to the receipt of the amount of the consideration. [536 H] 6. The document does not create any title or interest in the property. The document cannot be treated as an instrument of mortgage. [537 H] 7. The document being an instrument of trust, the document is an agreement of trust. [538 H] 8. The document may be an instrument relating only to the execution and registration of the deed. [539 H] 9. The document must be an instrument of a mortgage. [500 H] 10. The document has to be an instrument in respect of the execution and execution of the document and not a lease. [540 H] 11. The document can be executed only by a registered instrument. [541 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 13 of 1966. Appeal No. 422 of 1988 imprisonment for a further period of one month. The appellant was convicted and sentenced to pay a sum of Rs. 1000/- and to undergo rigorous sentence of one year. The appellant filed an appeal in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal and confirmed the conviction and sentence. The appellant challenged the order of the High Court in this Court. The appellant contended that the High Court was not justified in quashing the First Information Report as against Kailash Nath and the order of conviction passed by the trial Court was illegal. The High court held that the First Information report was not a valid one and the High Court quashed the First Information. The appellant, therefore, filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts were not justified in interfering with the conviction of the appellant under Sections 5(1) (d) and 5(1). [775 H] 2. The High courts were justified in quashing and setting aside the First Information Reports. [775 G] 3. The High Curt was justified in quashing a First Information Report on the ground that the same was not a fit case for quashing the First information report. [776 H] 4. The High [Court] was not justified under Article 226 and 227 of the Constitution in quashing the first information report. The High (Court) was justified in setting aside the first information Report. [778 G] 5. The High-Court was justified in exercising its jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution. [779 H] 6. The High 'Court was justified under Article 227 and 227 of Constitution. [750 H] 7. The High' Court was justified in interfering in the exercise of its jurisdiction under [Article 226] and 227 of The Constitution. [751 H] 8. The High "Court was justified on the ground, if any, that may have been raised by the appellant for quashing of the First Information, the High Court should have decided the petition on merits. [751 G] 9. The High. Court was justified under [Article 227] and 227. [751 A] 10. The High, Court was justified on a ground, which was not justified. [751 B] 11. The High F.C.I. was justified in holding that the First information Report was not a "fresh one" and the High Curt erred in quashing the said First Information Report. [751 D] 12. The High T.A.C. was justified under the provisions of Section 5(2) of the said Act. [751 E] 13. The High A Court was justified. [751 G] 14. The High B Court was justified when it held that the High C.A.T. was justified on an erroneous view of law. [751 F] 14. In the instant case, the High C Court was justified, in quashing the proceedings of the First information, the High court should have decided whether the First Information Officer was justified in not quashing the First F.C..I.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was a shareholder of a public limited company, which was a subsidiary company of a company, which had a fixed rate of dividend. The company was incorporated in the year of account of the company in the year ending on 31st March, 1955. The company had a fixed capital of Rs. 1,500 per cent of the total voting power was held by the shareholders of the company. The appellant was a shareholder in the company. On the basis of the capital of the company, the appellant was entitled to a fixed rate at Rs. 1.500 per cent. The appellant, therefore, filed a petition under section 23A of the Act for a declaration that the provisions of section 23A were not applicable to the appellant. The High Court held that the provisions contained in section 23A(1) were not applicable in the case of the appellant. It held that the appellant was not a company in which the public were substantially interested and that the company was one in which the company was substantially interested. The High court further held that the Explanation to sub section (1) of section 23 A was not applicable to a company in whose case the public are substantially interested. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Explanation was not applicable in this case as the appellant was a company in the same position as the company in which it was substantially interested and therefore in assessing whether the company was a company within the meaning of section 23(A) or not, the question whether the company in question was a company or not was a question which was a question of fact to be determined in each case. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Explanation to sub sections (1) and (2) of section 24A is not applicable to an assessee in whose case a fixed rate or dividend has been issued unconditionally to, or is acquired unconditionally by or beneficially held by the public. The Explanation is not applicable in a case where shares not entitled to a fix rate of dividend have been allotted unconditionally to, and are acquired unconditionally by the public as would render the company one in which it is substantially interested. [775 H] 2. The Explanation does not apply to a company where the public are not substantially interested. It is a question of law to be determined by the or dinary shareholders, and not by shareholders. [776 H] 3. The Explanation in section 24A(1)(a) is not applicable when the public are interested in such a case. The Explanation applies to a company which is substantially interested in such an assessee. [778 H] 4. The Explanation makes it clear that the company in whose favour the public are substantial interested is a company in whom the public are well-known. The Explanation merely makes it clear to the public that the company is substantially interested and not to the public. [779 H] 5. The Explanation cannot be applied to a company, where the public have not been substantially interested in the company, and the company is a substantial interested in such company. The Explanation must be read in the context in which it has been enacted. [780 H] 6. The Explanation has to be read in a manner which would render the Company a company in a position in which thepublic are substantially interested and the company has a fixed rate. [782 H] 7. The Explanation, therefore, makes it clear, is not applicable where the public is substantially interested, and the Explanation applies to an assessee. The Explanation only applies to a Company in which the Public are substantially interested, but not to a company. [785 H] 8. The Explanation gives the Explanation only to a company to which the public are large in number and does not apply in a case of a company in question. [786 H] 9.

The Mills were carrying on business in the manufacture of cotton, cotton, cotton and cotton fabrics. The Mills were carrying out the business of manufacturing cotton, cotton fabrics, cotton fabrics and cotton fabrics and were carrying on the business of selling cotton, cotton cotton, cotton fabric, cotton fabrics. On the basis of the information given by the Mills, the Mills were arrested and released on bail. On the same day, the Mills filed a complaint before the Magistrate, who, after hearing the parties, acquitted the Mills. On appeal, the High Court of Bombay, reversed the order of acquittal and convicted the Mills under s. 13(1)(d) of the Act and sentenced them to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000. The Mills appealed to this Court. HELD: (1) The Mills were not liable to pay any fine under s.13(1)(a) of the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1947. [775 H] (2) The Mills had not paid the amount of Rs. 2,000 to the Mills. The Mills had paid the amount to the Mills in the same truck as the 13 bales. The Mills was not liable to make any payment for the 13 bales, but only for the remaining amount of Rs, 2,000. [776 H] (3) The Mills was liable to pay the amount of the loss incurred by the Mills in respect of the 13 bales and the amount of compensation payable to the Mills was not a part of the compensation payable to them. [778 H] (4) The Mills could not be said to have paid the amount for the 13 tons of cotton, and therefore, the Mills was liable for the loss incurred. [780 H] (5) The Mills did not pay the amount for 13 bales. It was not a case of a mere technical breach of the law. The Mills could be said to be guilty of a breach of the Law. [782 H] (6) The Mills having not paid the amounts for the 13 cotton, the Mills could not have been convicted under s. 135 of the Act. [786 H] (7) The Mills are not liable to be punished for the breach of the provisions of the Act, [786 B] (8) The Mills have not paid the money for the 13, bales. The amount of compensation paid to the Mills is not a part and parcel of the compensation. [787 H] (8)(a) The Mills cannot be said to hold the goods in the possession of the Mills for a long time. [785 H] (b) The Mills must be held to have paid for the 13. bales. The Mill was not liable for the losses incurred by the mills in respect of 13 bales. [791 H] (c) The Mills, therefore, cannot be said that the Mills were liable to pay compensation to the Mills for the 13- bales. [750 H] (d) The Mills being an industrial undertaking, the Mills cannot be held to be liable to pay damages to the Mills under the provisions of s. 13 of the Act.[787 H,787 H;787 H-787 H.787 H.] (e) The Mills should be held to pay the amounts for 13 bales and not for 13 bales, and therefore the Mills was entitled to recover the amount of loss incurred by it in respect of these 13 bales. If the Mills were not entitled to recover any amount for 13, bales, the Mills would be liable to make good the amount of such amount. [788 H] (f) The Mills is not liable to refund the amount of any amount for the 14 bales. [800 H] (g) The Mills has not paid the entire amount of the 13, and therefore it is not liable for any loss.

The appellant was a Head Master of a college. He was appointed as a Head Master in the college. He had been paid a salary of Rs. 500 per month. He was paid a salary at the rate of Rs. 100 per month. The appellant was a teacher in a Government College. He was a teacher of a college in the State of Kerala. He was also paid a salary in the same scale. The appellant had been working as a Head master in the college for a period of six months. He was, therefore, not a public servant. The High Court held that the appellant was not a public officer and that the appellant could not be said to be a public servant within the meaning of section 5 (1) (d) of the Corruption Act. The High court held that the abuse of position as a public servant was a necessary ingredient of the offence. The High. Court held that in the case of the appellant the abuse of his position as a teacher was of the essence of the offence and the appellant was entitled to the protection of section 5(1) (c) of the Act. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court. The High, Court held that there was no question of the appellant being a public servant and that the abuse was not of an offence under section 5 (2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The appellant is a public servant as defined in section 5 (3) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act. The offence under section 3(1) of the said Act is a public offence. The offence is a public wrong and the public servant is not a public wrong. [775 H] 2. The abuse of position is a necessary ingredient in the offence. [776 H] 3. The abuse is a necessary element of the offence, and the appellant is not a Public servant. [778 H] 4. The offence of criminal misconduct under section 5(2) of Prevention of Corruption act is a serious offence. The appellant has been guilty of the offence under section 4(1)(d) of Prevention and Corruption Act. [779 H] 5. The offence punishable under section 5 of the Prevention and Corruption act is not a serious offence and the offence is a continuing one. [780 H] 6. The offence committed by the appellant is a serious one and the appellant has been rightly convicted. [782 H] 7. The offence was committed by the public servant in the discharge of his duty. [785 H] JUDGMENT: CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Criminal Appeal No. 9 of 1977. No. 8 of 1977. S. T. Desai, S. T.. Desai and S. S. Khanduja, for the appellant. S. K. Bagga, for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by K.N. SASIDHARAN, J. This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment of the High Court of Kerala in Criminal Appeal Nos. 9 of 1976 and 10 of 1977. The appellant, who was a Head master of a college, was appointed as Head Master of the college on a salary of a sum of Rs. 200 per month. The petitioners were appointed as casual labourers in the Railway Department. They were appointed as temporary status casual labourers on completion of the period of service. They were given temporary status. They were granted temporary status. The petitioners were appointed on probation for a period of one year. They were confirmed in the post of Junior Telecom Assistant on completion of one year of service. The petitioners filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of their appointment. The High Court quashed the order of appointment and directed that the petitioners should be treated as temporary status employees. The High court held that the petitioners were entitled to all the rights and privileges admissible to temporary railway servants as laid down in Chapter XXIII of the Indian Railway Establishment Manual. The High Courts held that the provisions of Chapter XXIII of Indian Railway Establishment manual were applicable to casual labourers and, therefore, that retiral benefit was not available to the petitioners. The High courts held that the services of the petitioners were temporary and were not entitled to pension. The High, Court held that the writ petitions were not maintainable. The petitioners challenged the correctness of the decision of the High Court. The High. Court held that since the petitioners were appointed in the regular cadre, they were entitled to the same pay as was 1) admissible to others either in the project or in the open line. The High Curt also held that the regularisation of the petitioners was not in accordance with the directions of this Court, and that the petitioners could not be treated as regular employees. The petitioners' writ petitions were allowed. The High' Court held that as the petitioners were not appointed as casual labour, they were not entitled for the same pay. The petitioners have filed these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals, the Court, HELD: 1.1 The petitioners were entitled for the benefits of the provisions of the Railway Establishment Manual and the Railway Administration was not in a position to absorb them in regular posts. [775 H] 1.2 The petitioners were not entitled, as they were not selected through regular selection Boards for absorption in regular posts, but were appointed as regular employees on completion of a period of 10 years of service. [776 H] 1:3. The petitioners could not claim parity with regular employees. They were entitled to be treated as regularised in regular posts and they were entitled for all the benefits. [778 H] 1.:4. The petitioners had been appointed as casual labourer on completion of 10 years service. They could not be denied the same pay and allowances as was 1.1. The High-Court held that the provision of the Railway Administration Manual was applicable to the petitioners and they were not appointed on probation. [779 H] 1] 1.5 The petitioners were also not entitled to the benefits of regularisation. The petitioners should be given the same pay which was 1.5. The petitioners must be treated as appointed as regular workmen. [780 H] 1.] 1.6. The petitioners cannot be treated as casual labour. They were not appointed by the Railway Administration. They were only appointed as casual workmen on completion of 9 years of service and they were regularised in regular service. [750 H] 1.(i) The petitioners were only appointed on probation and they were confirmed in regular posts on completion of 18 years of service, but they were not regularised in regular post. [750 A] 1.7. The petitioners are entitled to the benefit of the provisions contained in Chapter XXIII-A of the Indian Railways Establishment Manual. [750 B] 1.8. The petitioners did not get the benefit of regularisation. They were regularised in the regular posts. The petitioners, therefore, cannot be treated to be regularised in regular vacancies. [750 D] 1.9. The petitioners can not claim parity of pay with regular employees as was 1,5. The HighCourt held that as they were appointed as daily wagers on completion of 12 years of service they were not eligible for regularisation.

The Government of India, by a notification dated January 21, 1956, issued under section 12 of the Act, issued a notification closing out all contracts of the nature referred to in section 11 of the Act. The relevant provisions of the Act were as follows: "11. (1) The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, direct that any power exercisable by it under this Act shall, in relation to any class or classes of transactions or transactions, be exercised by the Central Government. (2) The Central government may, by order published in the Official gazette, direct that the power exercisable by the Central government under this section shall, in respect of any class or class of transactions or transaction or transactions or transactions or transaction, be exercised in relation to such class or classes or transactions or cases or transactions or such transactions or transactions. (3) The Central Govt. may, by an order published in a newspaper, direct that all or any of the powers exercisable by it in relation to the matters specified in section 11 shall, in so far as they are not inconsistent with the provisions of this Act, be exercised, in relation, to such class of transactions and transactions or transactions and in such manner as may be prescribed by the rules made under the Act. (4) The Central Govern-ment may, by a like order, direct that such power exercisable by itself shall, in the relation to any classes or classes of transaction or transactions, or transactions or the transactions or transactions shall be exercised in respect of such class or class or transactions or those transactions or transactions as may be specified in the order. (5) The Central, Government may, either on a request in writing made by it in this behalf from a recognised association or if in its opinion it is expedient to do so, make a bye-law with retrospective effect. (6) The Central and the State Governments shall, as soon as may be, make a report to the Central Government in the prescribed manner. (7) The Central Governments shall, within a period of six months from the date of the receipt of the report, make a reference to the Central Advisory Board in accordance with the provisions contained in section 12 of this Act. (8) The Central Advisory Board shall, after considering the report of the Central Advisory board and after giving the parties an opportunity of being heard, make a fresh report to the Government. (9) The Central Board shall, as far as may be within a period to be specified in such report, make an order under section 12, in relation thereto, and in such form as may be determined by the Central Advisory Committee. (10) The Central advisory board shall, after taking into consideration the report of such Central Advisory Committee and after giving a reasonable opportunity of being given to the parties concerned, make a final report to the President on the question whether the Central Government is expedient in the circumstances of the case. (11) The Central or the State Governments may, either in the opinion of the President or the Government of the State Governments, make a special reference to the President or to the Government of a State, as the case may be, in the matter. (12) The Central Administrative Tribunal shall, as early as may be after the receipt of a reference from the Central Government under section 12 or section 13, as the cases may be, pass orders thereon. (13) The Central administrative Tribunal shall, after the receipt by the Central Board, make a further report to the president or the Government, as the ease may be, on the question as to whether the Central government is expedient in any circumstances, and make a report thereon to the President.

The Income tax Officer, who assessed the assessee, assessed the income of the assessee to tax under section 12 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, on the ground that the assessee had not paid the tax due on the income of his previous year. The Income tax Officer assessed the assessee to income tax under section 10 of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922. The assessee filed an appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee was entitled to the benefit of the provisions of section 12 of that Act and the assessee was not entitled to the relief of the deduction of the amount of tax paid by him on the income from the capital gains. The Appellate Tribunal held that the amount of income tax paid by the assessee was capital gain and not revenue receipt. The High Court held that the receipt of the amount by the assessee from the capital gain was not income liable to tax. The High court held that the payment of the amount was not a revenue receipt and the assessee could not be treated as a revenue receipt. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the receipt was not a capital receipt and the receipt was capital gain. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts of Calcutta and Calcutta have taken the view that the receipt by the assessee of the amount received by him from the capital asset was not a receipt of revenue receipt. [775 H] 2. The expression "income" is defined in section 2(6A) of the Indian income tax Act, and the expression "income " is defined in the Explanation to section 2(5A) of that Act. [776 H] 3. The expression 'income " is used in section 2 (6A) in the Explanation. The expression used in section 12 of this Act is "income " and " income " is defined by section 2(7) of the Income tax Act. [764 H] 4. The expression income " is not income " is used not in section 12 but in section 12. [778 H] 5. The expression revenue receipt is used in the Explanation and the expression 'income ' is used in Section 2(6) of the Act. [774 H] 6. The expression capital gain' is used in [section 12] of the Indian Act. [773 H] 7. The expression business' is used not only in section 12, but also in section 12 and in section 12A. [773 G] 8. The expression in section 12 is used in a restricted sense and it is not used in section 13 of the Indian Companies Act. [777 H] 9. The expression is used in sections 12 and 12A of the Indian Trusts Act. [779 H] 10. The expression has been used in section 10 of that Act to indicate that the receipt from the capital is not a revenue expenditure. [785 H] 11. The expression employed in section 12 means that the receipt is not a receipt in the hands of the assessee. [786 H] 12. The expression, 'income ' means income " and " ' income " means income " or " ' income ". [786 G] 13. The expression must be used in section 11 of the Indian Indian Income tax, 1922, and the Explanation to [section 2(6)] of the Indian Finance Act, 1922 must be construed in the context of the Explanation to the section. [787 H] 14. The expression was used in section 8 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, and the explanation to section 2 (5) of the said Act was not used in the explanation to the section and the Explanation was not used for the purpose of the said section. [773 C] 15. The expression actually used in section 9 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, must be construed as referring to the expression 'business' in section 12(1) of the I.T.

The appellant was a member of the Forest Force of the State of Gujarat. He was prosecuted for the offence under section 3 of the Bombay Forest Act, 1963. The appellant was convicted and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of one year and to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000/- and in default to undergo rigorous rigorous imprisonment for one year. The appellant filed an appeal before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant then filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the High Court and the order of this Court. The appellant contended that the word 'forest produce' in the definition of the word 'land' in section 2 (f) (i) of the Act was not a forest produce and, therefore, the word 'gam' in the Act was a forest produce. The High court held that the word "gam" in the definition was not a 'forest produce'. The High Court held that the term 'gam', in the definition, was not a term of art and therefore, the meaning of the word "forest produce" in the Act could not be extended to the facts of the case. The High, Court held that it was not a case of forest produce and the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the definition of 'forest produce. The appellant, therefore, filed a writ appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The term 'forest produce', in the context in which it is used in the definition is not a term which is defined in the Act. The term is not defined in the statute. The term forest produce is defined in section 2(f) of the Bombay Act to mean any forest produce which is a forest produce within the meaning of section 2 (g) (i). [775 H] 2. The term "forest produce " in the definition means any forest produce. [775 G] 3. The word 'forest' in the context of the definition is a term which means 'forest produce '. [776 H] 4. The word "forest" in the context means any forest land. [778 H] 5. The word forest produce' in section 3(1) of the Forest Act, as amended by the Bombay Forest (Amendment) Act, 1960, means any forest, produce, not being forest produce, within the meaning or the term in the Act, and includes any forest produce, but does not include any forest produce; but does not exclude any forest produce from the definition of forest produce. Section 2(f)(i) of Act, as it stood prior to the amendment by the Bombay Act, 1960 and the definition of "forest produce", in section 2, clearly indicate that the term "forest" is not a word which is defined either in the Act or in the Act and, therefore. the appellant was entitled to the benefits of the definition. [785 H] 6. The word Forest' in the meaning of 'forest' is not defined either in section 2 or in the definition in section 2. The word used in the Act is not a 'Forest produce'. [785 A] 7. The word, 'forest produce" is not defined under the Act. [786 B] 8. The word has been used in the context and the meaning of "forest" has to be understood in the context. [787 G] 9. The word is not defined anywhere in the Act but is used in a statute. [788 G] 10. The word found in the definition includes forest produce. It is not defined by the Act. It is a term used in the sense of 'forest'. [787 A] 11. The word in the definition has to be construed in the context as it is used either in the definition or in the context, as the meaning of such term in the definition.

The appellant was married to one of the accused. The deceased was a minor. The accused was a young man of about 18 years. The deceased had a daughter. The accused had a daughter and a daughter. On the date of the incident the deceased was in a position to speak. The accused, however, did not take any steps to make any statement before the police. The accused filed a petition before the Sessions Judge for permission to examine the witnesses. The Sessions Judge allowed the application and directed the accused to produce the witnesses. On appeal the High Court set aside the order of acquittal and directed the Sessions Judge to record the evidence of the witnesses. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the Sessions Judge was not justified in holding that the evidence of a witness was not "in accord with the opinion expressed in books on Medical Jurisprudence by authors like Modi and Lyon. The learned Judges of the High Court were of the opinion that the evidence in the present case was not " in accord with the opinions expressed in books of law by authors like M.O. and M.O." The High Court held that the evidence was "in accord" with the opinion of the authors. The High Court observed that the evidence showed that the accused was in a fit state of mind to make a statement before the Police. The High court further held that the Sessions Court was not justified under the circumstances of the case in holding that there was no sufficient ground for holding that the accused is guilty. The High, Court also held that the medical evidence showed that there was a fracture of the left side of the head and the doctor was not in a position therefore to make a report. The High. Court also held in the appeal that the evidence given by the doctor was "in accordance with the opinion" expressed in books. The High' Court also held on the evidence that the doctor was in a better position to make a definite opinion. The High 'Court also held that there was "in the circumstances of this case" that the evidence shows that the accused were in a fit condition to make a dying declaration. The High Curt also held that in the circumstances of that case the evidence showed "in accord " with the opinion in books on medical Jurisprudence by authors. The learned Judge of the High court was of the opinion, that the evidence as to the guilt or innocence of the accused was not " In the circumstances of these cases the High Court was not right in holding that evidence was " in accord" with "in accord". The High Court also held, therefore, that the Sessions judge was not justified. The High-Court also held on a consideration of the evidence that there was nothing in the evidence to show that the accused had taken any steps to made a statement before a police. The HighCourt also held, relying on the evidence of Dr. S. P. Singh, that the medical opinion was "in consonance with the opinion given in books on the Medical Jurisprudence by the authors". The High court also held that it was not open to the Sessions Judge, in the circumstances, to hold that the evidence established that the accused did not take steps to make a declaration before the police and that the evidence is "in accord", with "in accordance" with "the opinion expressed in book on Medical Jurisprudence. The High Courts were also of the opinion on the evidence given in the case that the evidence, as to the commission of the offence, was "in conformity" with " the opinion expressed by the authors" and the High Court held on the basis of the evidence given before it that the evidence proved that the accused "had taken any steps" to make a voluntary statement before a Police. The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1962 as a company registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The appellant company was established in the year 1963 and was incorporated in 1963. The appellant was incorporated in 1964. The appellant's company was incorporated on January 6, 1964. The company was incorporated under the Indian Company Act, 1913, and was registered under the [Indian Companies Act, 1956]. The appellant company is a company incorporated under the [Companies Act, 1956] and is engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling of pharmaceutical products. The appellant is a company registered with the Registrar of Companies, West Bengal, and is engaged mainly in the business, of manufacturing and supplying pharmaceutical products. On January 6, 1963, the appellant company issued a notice to the appellant company to show cause why the award should not be made absolute and the award was confirmed by the Tribunal. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Calcutta, challenging the validity of the award. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant challenged the correctness of the decision of the High Court. The appellant contended that the award was not binding on the appellant company and the award is not binding on it. The appellant also contended that the Tribunal was not justified in holding that the union 's consist of the workmen of the appellant company 's factory at Jamshedpur and the workmen of its other establishments. The High court held that the union was a registered union and the union was not a registered union. The High. Court held that the appellant company was a registered Union and was not a 'State' within the meaning of Article 12 of the Constitution. The appellant, therefore, filed a writ application in the High court. The High, Court held that there was no valid agreement between the appellant company as representing the workmen concerned in the appellant company. The High' Court held that as the appellant company had not filed any appeal against the award, the award was binding on it and the Tribunal was justified in holding the award to be binding on it, the appellant. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The award is not a binding contract between the appellant and the union. The award was not a binding agreement between the parties. [675 H] 2. The award does not bind the appellant company nor does it bind the appellant. [676 H] 3. The award cannot be sustained. The award must be held to be binding. [678 H] 4. The award being a binding contract, the appellant cannot be allowed to challenge the validity of it. [679 H] 4(i) The award is a binding contract. The appellant cannot challenge the validity or the validity of its award. [682 H] (ii) The award was a binding contract and the award cannot be challenged on the ground that it is not binding. [650 H] (iii) The award cannot, therefore, be sustained. [691 H] (iv) The award does, therefore, suffer from the vice of non-application of mind. [692 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1320 of 1967. Appeal by Special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 14th July, 1967 of the Calcutta High Court in Misc. The assessee was a firm of Hakam Mal Tani Mal and R. B. Hakam Mal. The assessee was a partner in the firm of Hakham Mal. The firm of Hakim Mal was dissolved on March 31, 1943. The assessee filed a return of income for the assessment year 1943-44, in respect of the income of the firm of J. Mal Tani. The Income tax Officer, on the basis of the material evidence, held that the assessee was carrying on business at the commencement of the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act 7 of 1939, and that the assessee commenced business at Abdullapur in the year 1943. The Income Tax Officer, on appeal, held that it was not a case of a change in the constitution of the firm from April 1, 1943 to March 31, 1939. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, on a reference, held that in the absence of any evidence in that behalf, the assessee was not entitled to the benefit of section 25(4) of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922, and that it was open to the Income tax Officer to hold that the assessee had started business at the time of the dissolution of the firm. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that the income, profits and gains of the firm were not liable to be included in the income of that firm. On the question whether the assessee was entitled to the benefits of section 25 (4) of Indian Income tax Act, 1922. Held, that the assessee is not entitled to any benefit under section 25 (1) of the Income tax Act. The assessee is not a dealer in the business of the assessee. The assessee has a right to the benefit under section 10(2) of the Act. The income, profits or gains of the business are not liable to tax. The assessee cannot claim the benefit of the provisions of section 25 of the Indian Act. The Income-tax Officer was not entitled, on the facts of the case, to hold that it was a case of change in the Constitution of the firm and that the firm was not carrying on business in the name of the firm at the time the dissolution of that firm from April, 1943. In the absence of other evidence, it was not open to the assessee to hold that he commenced business at the date of the dissolution from April 1 , 1943. The High Court was in error in holding that the assessee started business at Abdulla in the name and style of J.M. Mal Toni Mal.

The High court held that the appellant's election was not proved to be a candidate for election. The High. Court held that there was no evidence to show that respondent Prakash Vir Shastri had committed any corrupt practice in relation to the personal character and conduct of the appellant, and that the publication of the respondent's election expenses in the newspaper was not proved as to the truth of the contents therein. The High, Court held that in the absence of any evidence to show the truth of contents therein, the publication of respondent Prakash Vir, the appellant was not entitled to any relief. The High' Court held that no evidence was produced to show that the respondent Prakash Vir was a candidate at the election. The appellant's election petition was accordingly dismissed. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. The appellant contended that the High Court was wrong in holding that the respondent is a candidate for a candidate and that the High court was wrong in dismissing the petition. The appellant also contended that the respondent has been convicted under sections 7 and 8 of the Representation Act, 1951. The High Curt held that the publication in the newspaper of the respondent was not proved. The High 'Court held that the newspaper publication in the case was not proved and that the newspaper published in the case did not contain the name of the appellant as having been assaulted or chased. The High-Court held that in view of the evidence of the respondent Prakash, the publication in question was not proved, and that, therefore, the publication was not proved in relation to his personal character and the publication of his election was not established. The HighCourt further held that the evidence of respondent Prakash was not sufficient to prove that respondent Prakash was a candidate. The High,.Court further held, that the publication was proved as to his truth. The High: Court held that it was not proved that respondent Prakash had committed any offence. The High T.A. No. 1 of 1967 was dismissed. The respondent has filed this petition under Article 136 of the Constitution. The appellant contends that the High Curt was wrong in law in holding that there was a publication of respondent Parkash Vir Shastri in the newspaper. The High Courts of Punjab and Haryana and the High Courts of Madhya Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh have held that the printing of the respondent is not proved. In the present case, the High Court held, that in view the evidence of, the respondent Prakash was convicted under section 8 of The Representation of the Act, the High C Court held that publication of respondent's election was proved. The appellant further contended that the publication made by the respondent was proved as a result of the evidence adduced by the respondent Prakash. The High F.A.f. The appellant, therefore, contends that the publication is not proved as required by section 8 of Act No. 1/67. The High Cou. Court held, therefore, that the respondent cannot be convicted under section 11 of the Act and that the evidence adduced in support of the case of the respondent, was not sufficient. The High Count, however, held that the published publication in the newspapers of the respondent and his election was proved as required under section 8.
