The appellant, who was the auction purchaser, filed a suit for possession of the property in execution of a decree for possession. The appellant filed a petition for setting aside the sale on the ground that the sale was not absolute and the sale was confirmed on the ground of fraud. The appellant contended that the sale in favour of the respondent was not a nullity and that the sale could not be set aside on the ground on which the sale was set aside. The learned Single Judge of the High Court held that the sale of the property was not a sale in execution of the decree and that the application for setting aside sale was not maintainable. The learned Judge held that the application was not maintainable and that the order of the learned District Judge was not a final order. The learned single Judge of the Calcutta High Court held, that the sale by the auction purchaser was not a valid sale and that the appellant was not entitled to set aside the sale. The learned Judges of the High court held that the order passed by the learned District judge was a nullity and the sale could be set aside only on the ground mentioned in the said order. The appellant preferred an appeal to the Division Bench of the High. Court. The Division Bench of that Court held that in the circumstances of the case, the sale was absolute and the decree was confirmed on that ground. The learned Counsel for the appellant contended that in the facts and circumstances of the present case, the application for set aside the order of sale was not a proper one and that the learned District Court was not justified in setting aside the order passed on the ground stated in the said application. The learned counsel for the respondent decree holder contended that the application filed by the appellant for setting aside an order setting aside the sales was not maintainable as the sale was a nullity. The learned Senior Counsel for the respondentdecree holder contended that in view of the provisions of Article 134 of the Limitation Act, the application filed for setting aside a sale on the grounds mentioned in the second application for setting setting aside the said sale was not barred by limitation. The learned senior counsel for the appellant submitted that the application under Order XXI Rule 95 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not maintainable because the application for execution was not maintainable on the ground as mentioned in the first application for setting the order setting aside of the sale. In the circumstances, the learned counsel for respondent decree holder submitted that the order setting the order of setting aside the earlier order of the High Curt was a nullity, and that the High Court was not right in setting aside that order. The question whether the application for condonation of delay was maintainable or not was a question of fact. The learned Additional District Judge, however, held that the appellant had not filed the application for condoning the delay in the first appeal and that the appeal was not maintainable in view of Article 134(1) of the Limitation act. The learned Addl. District Judge held that in view the provisions of Section 114 of the Code, the application was maintainable. The High Court held: "The question whether the sale was made in favour of respondent decree was a question which was not a question of law. The question was whether the application was a proper one. The application was not a petition for condonation of the delay in filing the application for the setting aside of sale. The application for setting it aside was not maintainable." The learned Addl District Judge further held that the High Courl was right in holding that the application in the first instance was not maintainable, and that it was not a fit case for setting aside that sale. The High CourL also held that the question whether the order setting it aside the sale was an order of setting the order in the second appeal was a question for the first time. The learned Advocate for the respondent Decree holder contended that since the application for bringing the order setting setting aside sale in the second appeals was not maintainable before the High Court, the application under Section 114 of Code of Civil procedure was maintainable.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the [Indian Companies Act, 1956], was closed down on April 8, 1980. The appellant company was closed down with effect from April 8, 1981. The appellant, a statutory body, was closed down by the Government of Maharashtra on April 8. 1981. The company filed a petition under Section 33-C(2) of the Act before the Industrial Court, Maharashtra, challenging the closure of the appellant company. The Industrial Court held that the closure was a result of a lock out and that the closure of a business was a result not only of the closure but was a device or pretence to terminate the services of the workmen. The Industrial court held that the lock out was a device to terminate the employment of the workmen and that the lockout was a device and pretence to terminate services of the appellant. The IndustrialCourt held that the strike was a device for terminating the services of workmen and that it was a device, device or pretence for terminating the employment of workmen. The industrial court held that it was not a device or device to terminate services and that the strike in question was a device device or device for terminating services of the employees. The Industrial Courts held that the appellant had contravened the provisions of Section 33- C(2) and Section 33-D(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The Industrial Tribunal held that the illegal closure was a device of victimisation and the lockout had been closed down. The Industrial Appellate Tribunal held that it had no jurisdiction to go into the question whether the closure was an unfair labour practice. The Industrial Appeal was allowed and the order of the Industrial Court was set aside. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that it could not go into the questions whether the closure of an industrial establishment was a device. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Industrial Disputes Act is a beneficial legislation and the Industrial Disputes (Amendment) Act, 1984, does not apply to the industrial dispute. The Industrial Employment (Amendment) Ordinance, 1984, was promulgated on April 8 1980 and the Act was passed on April 8 when the Act was in force. The Industrial Dispute Act, 1947, was enacted to provide for the establishment of a new industrial establishment and to provide for its continuance in service. The Industrial disputes Act, 1947 was enacted to give effect to the objects of the Act. The Industrial dispute was a device devised for terminating the service of the workmen by the employer. The Industrial Tribunals Act, 1947 is a beneficial piece of legislation and the industrial dispute is a device or camouflage to terminate the service of a workman. [505 C] 2. The Industrial Arbitration Act, 1947 does not apply in the case of a device or disguise to terminate the existing employment of the workman. The Industrial Act, 1947 applies to the industrial disputes. The Industrial Law is a beneficial statute and the Industrial Law is beneficial legislation. [507 D] 3. The Industrial Conciliation Act, 1947 has no application to the industrial establishment. The Industrial law is a beneficial law and the Industrial Court has jurisdiction to go in the question whether it has jurisdiction to decide the question whether a strike is a device to terminating the services. [508 D] 4. The Industrial courts Act, 1947 makes no distinction between a device or a device to be employed for terminating the existing employment. The Industrial https://hcservices.ecourts.gov.in/hcservices/ Courts have jurisdiction to go on strike. [509 D] 5. The Industrial Forums Act, 1947 and the Industrial Dispute Act 1947 are beneficial legislation and they are beneficial legislation. The Industrial forums Act, 1947 are beneficial legislations and they are not intended to be used for the purpose of terminating the services and the provisions of the Industrial Dispute (Amendment) Bill, 1984 are not applicable to the industrial establishments. [510 E] 6.

The assessee company was a registered company carrying on business in shares, securities and immovable properties. The assessee company was incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The assessee was a registered society under the Societies Registration Act, 1860. The assessee had a registered office in the State of Bombay. The assessee's income was assessed to income tax in the hands of the assessee company. The Income Tax Officer, on an application made by the assessee company, referred the question of law to the High Court under section 66(1) of the Act. The High Court answered the question in favour of the assessee. The High court held that the assessee company was not a dealer in shares, security and immovable properties and that the assessee was a dealer in investments and properties. The High. Court held that the question of fact was not a question of fact. The High, Court held that in the circumstances of the case the question of the nature of business in shares and securities was a mixed question of fact and law. The High 'Court further held that the questions involved in this case were questions of fact and the High Court was of the opinion that the question was a mixed one and the question of facts was a mixed issue of fact and it was not open to the assessee company to be treated as a dealer in investment and properties. In the result the High Court answered both the questions in favour of assessee and against the assessee. Hence the present appeal by the assessee. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The question of law referred to the High court was not a mixed question and the High court could not be said to have jurisdiction to decide the question. [775 H] 2. The question as to whether the assessee company is a dealer in securities and immovable property or not is a mixed question. The question is not a mixed one. The question whether the assessee is a dealer or not is not a pure question of fact but a mixed question or a mixed question, and therefore, the question of a mixed question is a mixed one, and the question is a pure question. [750 H] 3. The question referred to the Court is not a question which is required to be decided by the High Court. The question, therefore, is a mixed issue and the High Courts are under an obligation to decide it. [750 A] 4. The question which the High Court is required to decide is whether the question of " law" in the circumstances is a mixed questions of fact or law. [750 B] 5. The question that the High Court has to decide is not a " mixed question of law" but a mixed one of fact and a mixed question has to be decided in the light of law. [776 H] 6. The question in the present case is not a mere mixed question of facts and law but a mixed issue. [750 D] 7. The question raised in the present appeal is not a ' mixed question of a fact' but a mixed mixed question of the facts and law. [751 H] 8. The question for consideration is whether the High Court should be asked to decide the said question. [751 G] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 15 of 1966. The appellant was a Judicial Officer in the State of Madras. He was appointed as a District Judge in the State Judicial Service on October 1, 1953, and was confirmed in that post by the High Court of Madras on January 28, 1954. On January 28, 1955, he was suspended from service by the High court of Madras, and was removed from service by an order of the High Court dated January 28, 1956, on the ground that he had been guilty of misconduct in the discharge of his official duties. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court, which was dismissed by the High. Court on January 28. 1957. The appellant then filed a writ appeal to this Court, which, by its judgment dated January 28. 1958, was delivered in the case of the appellant. The appellant contended that the order of suspension made by the High, Court was not one of dismissal or removal from service within article 311 of the Constitution, and that the order passed by the High' Court on January 29, 1954, was not one passed by the Governor of the Province, and that, therefore, the order of the Government of Madras, dated January 28., 1954, was bad. Held, that the order dated January 28,. 1954, was one of dismissal and not removal from service, and that it was not one for dismissal or removal within article 311, and that as the order of dismissal was passed by the Government of the Province in exercise of the powers conferred by article 311 of, the Constitution, it was not necessary to pass an order of dismissal or remove the appellant from service. The order of suspension was not one made by the Governor, and therefore, the Government of India was not bound to hold a fresh enquiry into the conduct of the appellant, and that therefore, the appellant was not entitled to have his case decided by the High 'Court. The order passed by a Government of India, dated January 29, 1957, was not a one-sided order, and therefore the order passed on January 28., 1955, was not an order of removal or removal within the meaning of article 311. The order dated January 29., 1954, passed by the State Government, dated January, 28, 1954, is not one passed under article 311, but is one passed by a competent authority, and therefore it was not a decision of the Government. The order, therefore, was not passed by the President, and therefore was not one under article 311.

The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, for the assessment year 1953-54. The Income tax Officer, on the basis of the information furnished by the Income tax Officer under section 24B of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 (hereinafter referred to as the Act), assessed the appellant to income tax. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Bombay, challenging the assessment order. The High Court held that the income received by the appellant was not his personal income and therefore he was not liable to be taxed as income of the deceased. The High court held that the appellant was liable to be assessed as the personal income of the legal representative of the deceased and therefore he could not be taxed as the personal property of the deceased, and that the appellant could not be assessed as his personal income. The High, Court held that in the assessment proceedings the appellant was assessed as the owner of the estate of the deceased person and therefore he is not liable to pay tax on the income received from the estate of a deceased person. The High. Court further held that the Income tax officer was not competent to assess the appellant as the personal owner of the deceased in the assessment proceeding. The High 'Court held that the provisions of the Act were not applicable to the assessment proceedings and the appellant was entitled to be assessed on the basis that the income was the personal income. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was wrong in holding that the appellant had not been assessed as the legal representative to the estate of his deceased person. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922 are applicable to the proceedings under the Act. The provisions in the Act are applicable to proceedings under the Indian Incometax (Amendment) Act, 1953, and the Act does not apply to the proceedings before the Income tax authorities. [775 H] 2. The provisions contained in the Act have to be read in the context of the Act and the Act. [776 H] 3. The provisions relating to assessment proceedings are applicable to all proceedings under the Income tax Act. The Act does not provide for any procedure to assess the income received or receivable by a legal representative of a deceased, and therefore the provisions of that Act are not applicable to proceedings before the authorities. [750 H] 4. The provisions made in the Act will not apply to proceedings under section 24A of the Act. Section 24A of that Act provides that the provisions contained in section 24A shall not apply to any proceedings under the said Act. [750 A] 5. The provisions regarding the assessment proceedings are not applicable in the case of the assessment proceedings. The provisions are applicable to assessments proceedings under the provisions of section 24A. [750 B] 6. The provisions for assessment proceedings are made applicable to proceedings for assessment proceedings under the Central Act. The Income Tax Officer is not competent to make assessment proceedings under section 23A of the Income Tax Act. [751 H] 7. The provisions under the Act are not attracted to the proceedings for assessment. [751 G] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 15 of 1967. Appeal by Special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 9th July, 1967 of the Bombay High Court in Writ Petition No. 11 of 1967. S. T. Desai, S. K. Kapur and R. N. Sachthey, for the appellant. S. S. Khanduja, for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. The appellant, a firm, was assessed as a Hindu undivided Family. The assessment proceedings were completed under section 24-A of the Indian income-tax Act, 1922. The appellant claimed that the income of the firm was not his income from the estate and therefore he should be assessed as a member of the Hindu undivided family. The Income-tax Officer rejected the claim.

The appellant was a maufidar of an Indian State. He was a moufidar of a village. He was an Indian State and was a member of the Indian State. The appellant was a member in the Indian State of the State. He had a right to recover rent or revenue from persons holding land in such village. The appellant had given no evidence to establish that the villages in question were assessed to land revenue. The High Court held that the appellant was a Moufidar and that he had a right of recovery of rent or revenue. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the High Court. The High court held that the petitioner was a mirafidar and therefore was not a person who by or under the provisions of the Constitution had a right in respect of rent or Revenue from persons holding lands in such village and that the appellant had a right under the Constitution to recover rent from persons holding the land in such villages. The High, Court held that in the case of a moufi village the appellant had given a no evidence to prove that the villages were assessed to the land revenue. In our opinion, the High Court was right in holding that the petitioner had a right, under the Constitution, to recover rent and revenue from persons who holding land in the village. The High. Court also held that the petition was not maintainable. The appellant, therefore, filed a writ appeal against the judgment of the High court. The appellant contended that the High Court had erred in holding that in the absence of any evidence to establish the fact that the appellant as a maufiidar had a right over the land in question it was not a maufaidar. The High Curt held that the case was covered by the definition of 'Mahal' in the Constitution and the High Court rightly held that the High court was right in taking the view that the petitioner could not be treated as a mouz. The High-Court also held that in view of the definition of the term 'Mahal', the petitioner was not a "person" within the meaning of the Constitution. The High' Court also held in the case under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution that the petitioner did not have a right to claim rent or revenue or to recover rent. The High 'Court also held in this respect that the petitioner having given no evidence in this respect the High Court could not be said to have erred in holding the petitioner to be a mauz. The appellant accordingly filed a writ application in the High court and prayed for a writ of mandamus directing the State of Madhya Pradesh to recover rent of the land in dispute from the petitioner. The High -Court allowed the writ petition and directed the State of M.P. to recover rent in accordance with the provisions of article 226 of the Constitution from the petitioner and directed the petitioner to pay the same within a period of six months from the date of the order. The appellant then filed a writ Appeal against the judgment and order of the learned Single Judge. The Division Bench of the High Curt allowed the appeal and held that the writ petition was not competent. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts of Madhya Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh have concurrent jurisdiction to decide the question of law raised by the appellant in this appeal. [532E] 2. The High courts of Madhya Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Orissa have concurrent jurisdiction. [533F] 3. The High (Court) was right in not interfering with the judgment of a learned Single Judge of the High. Court. [534F] 4. The appellant is a mauja of the village. He is a mouja of the State of the village and is a member of a village and is entitled to recover rent for the land in the villages. [536F] 5.

The respondent was appointed as a Judge of the High Court of Delhi. He was appointed as Judge of the Delhi High Court. He was transferred to Delhi High Court on the ground that he was posted at Delhi. He filed a writ petition before the Delhi High court challenging the order of transfer. The High Court quashed the order of the Tribunal and directed the Tribunal to consider the case of the respondent in the light of the observations made in the judgment. The respondent filed a writ appeal before this Court. The learned Single Judge of the Calcutta High Court dismissed the writ petition. The respondent challenged the order of learned Single Judge before the High Court. The Division Bench of the High court allowed the writ petition and quashed the order passed by the Tribunal. The respondent then filed a writ application before the High court. The learned single Judge allowed the writ application and quashed the transfer order. The respondent thereafter filed a writ Appeal before the Division Bench. The Division bench of the High, Court allowed the writ appeal and quashed the impugned order of the learned Single Judge. The Division Benches of the High Courts held that the transfer order was vitiated by malafides and was liable to be quashed. The DivisionBench of the High. Court held that the respondent was posted at the same place and he was posted in Delhi. The Division, therefore, allowed the writ. The respondent preferred a writ appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The order of the High Curt is vitiated by malafides. [775 H] 2. The order passed by learned Single Judge is not vitiated by malafides or is liable to be set aside. [776 H] 3. The order is vitiated by mala fides. [778 H] 4. The order was passed by the learned Single judge in exercise of his jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution. [779 H] 5. The order does not suffer from any infirmity. [780 H] 6. The order cannot be sustained in law. [782 H] 7. The order dated 27.7.1986 passed by the Central Administrative Tribunal, Delhi Bench, is not vitiated on any of the grounds. The appellants were tried for the murder of Jawahar and were convicted by the Trial Court for the murderous assault on Jawahar. The appellants were convicted for the murder and were sentenced to undergo life imprisonment. The appellants filed an appeal before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellants then filed a special leave petition in this Court. The appellants contended that the conviction of the appellants was not based on the evidence of the eye witnesses and the High Court was in error in holding that the appellants were guilty of the murder of the deceased Jawahar. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The conviction of the accused under Section 302, I.P.C. read with Section 34, I. P.C. is not sustainable. [775 H] 2. The High court was in error when it held that the appellants had not committed the murder of J.S.P. The conviction was not based solely on the evidence. The High Curt was in error. [776 H] 3. The conviction under Section 302 I.P., C. read with [Section 34], I.P,C. readwith Section 34, is not sustainable in law. [778 H] 4. The conviction is not based on any evidence. The conviction cannot be based solely on evidence. The evidence of the witnesses is not sufficient to prove the guilt of the appellants. [779 H] 5. The High Courts were in error in convicting the appellants under Section 302 read with Section 149, I.p.C. and sentencing them to undergo life sentence. [780 H] 6. The High courts were in error when they held that the conviction under Section 304 Part I, I.PC. read with Sections 34, I, P.C., read with Section 302, is not justified. [782 H] 7. The HighCourt was in error while holding that the conviction was not supported by the evidence.

The appellant Bank was incorporated in the year 1947 and it was incorporated in 1947. The appellant Bank was formed by the Government of India Act, 1935, and it was established by the Government. The appellant was incorporated in 1948 and it was registered as a society under the Societies Registration Act, 1860. The appellant had a branch at Madras and it was functioning as a branch at the relevant time. The appellant bank was incorporated in 1950 and it was formed in 1947. It was registered under the Societies Act. The appellant's branch was registered under that Act. The Bank was incorporated under the Societies' Act, 1860, and it is the appellant Bank which was established by it. The Bank is a statutory corporation established by a special Indian law. The appellant is a statutory Corporation established by a statute. The appellant has a branch at Bombay and it is a statutory body. The appellant, therefore, is a statutory authority established by a general Indian law. [532E] The appellant Bank is a society registered under the [Societies Registration Act, 1960] and it is an autonomous body. The Bank has been established by the appellant Bank under the [Cooperative Societies Act, 1912]. The appellant Bank has been incorporated under the [Companies Act, 1956] and it was a statutory corporation. The appellant cannot, therefore, be said to be a statutory corporation constituted by a special Act. [533F] The appellant was a statutory Corporation constituted by a statute and it was not a statutory corporation, but was a statutory body established by a statutory corporation and it was an autonomous body established by the statute. [534F] The Bank was established by a society registered by the name of the society under the [Indian Societies Act, 1860]. The appellant was registered under a special Indian Law. The appellant could not, therefore, have been a statutory corporation registered under the Co. Act. [511F] The question whether the appellant Bank was a statutory authority or not was not decided by the High Court. [511G] The appellant had no locus standi to file the appeal. [511H] The appellant is not a statutory Corporation. The appellant can only be held to be a body established by an Act of the Parliament of the United Kingdom or the State Legislature. [511B] The appellant cannot be said to have been a body established under the statute. The Bank cannot be said that the appellant Bank is an autonomous corporation. [511D] The appellant could have been a Statutory Corporation established by the Central Government. [511E] The Bank is an independent body established by statute. The Central Government is a statutory entity. [511C] The appellant has no locus standi in the matter. [511A] The appellant, however, cannot be said whether the appellant has a locus standi to challenge the validity of the Act. [ 511D] The Bank cannot, therefore be said to constitute a statutory corporation within the meaning of the Act and the appellant cannot be held to have been established by it by the appellant. [511 E] The appellant can be said to hold a statutory corporation only by a statute of the Parliament. [511 F] The appellant having been incorporated under a statute, it cannot be said, as a statutory corporation or a statutory corporation which is established by a Central Government, the appellant cannot, in the circumstances, be said that it is a body established for a public body. [511 G] The appellant's case is clearly distinguishable. [511 D] The appellant did not have a locus standi in his application for the enforcement of the Act, and the appellant could not have been a party to the proceedings. [511 H] The appellant does not have a statutory corporation under the [Sick Industrial Companies Act, 1948] and it cannot be held that the appellant has been established under the Act. The respondent cannot be said in the circumstances that the appellant is a body constituted by a Central or State Government.

The petitioner, a manufacturer of sugar, was a producer of sugar in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The petitioner was a producer in the State. He was a producer at the relevant time. He was also a producer in sugar in the other areas. He was, however, not a producer in any of the other areas of India. He was not a producer at all in the other parts of India. The petitioner's case was that the prices of sugar in India were fixed by the Government by the impugned notification. The Government of Uttar Pradesh issued a notification on July 30, 1958, under section 3 of the Act, fixing the prices of the sugar in the three regions. The petitioner challenged the validity of the said notification on the ground that the prices fixed by the impugned notifications were not reasonable and that the prices were not excessive. The High Court held that the prices in the three States were reasonable and that there was no discrimination after the control of the price of the sugar was controlled. The High court held that the price fixation was not arbitrary and that the price fixed by the State was not reasonable. The High, Court held that in the circumstances of the case the prices were reasonable and there was no justification for the fixation of the price. The High. Court further held that the petitioner was not a manufacturer at all in Punjab and the contention that there was discrimination was not found to be justified. The High' Court further held, that the price control was imposed on the factories in Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and North Bihar and that the Government of Uttar Bihar was of the view that the prices at which the three regions were controlled were sufficient to control the price of sugar in these three regions. In the result, the High Court dismissed the petition. The petitioner has filed this petition under Art. 32 of the Constitution. The petitioner contends that the impugned notification is arbitrary and that it is not in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The petitioner further contends that the prices fixation was not reasonable and there is no justification for such a discrimination. The petitioner is a producer in a sugar in the same area and the contention is that in the circumstance of the case it is not necessary to fix prices separately so far as factories in the other part of India are concerned. The petitioner also contends that the price of Sugar in India was not reasonable as the prices of these three regions were not adequate. The High 'Court held that the impugned notifications are not reasonable and they are not in accordance. The petitioner relies upon the decision of the High Court in the case of the petitioner's case. The petitioner challenges the validity of this decision on the ground, that the impugned orders are arbitrary and are not in consonance with the provisions contained in the Act. In the circumstances, the petitioner prays that the petition should be dismissed. The petitioner in support of his contention relies upon the decisions of the High Courts in support of the contention that the prices are reasonable. The petitioner points out that in the case before the High Court the prices were fixed by it in the same manner as the prices fixed in the other regions of India. In the case of other regions, the petitioner relies upon a decision of the Bombay High Court in which the prices fixed under the impugned notifications have been upheld. The petitioner submits that the impugned order is not in consonance of the provisions contained under the Act. It is further contended that the impugned rates are reasonable and there are no justification for imposing the prices of Sugar in the other region. The petitioner therefore prays that the petitions should be dismissed with costs.

The Company was incorporated in the year 1947, and it was incorporated in 1947, and the Company was incorporated on April 1, 1947, and was registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The Company was incorporated under the Indian Company Act, 1913, and was incorporated in 1956. The Company had a total income of Rs. 1,000 per annum from the year 1947 to 1956. The company was incorporated in 1958, and was also incorporated in 1956, and was formed in 1956. On April 1, 1957, the Company was registered under s. 7 of the Act. The Company filed a petition under s. 33A of the Act before the Tribunal, which was dismissed. The Company then filed a petition in the High Court of Calcutta under Art. 226 of the Constitution for a writ of certiorari quashing the order of the Tribunal and for a writ in the nature of mandamus directing the Company to pay the amount of Rs. 2,000 per month to the Company as a result of the increase in the cost of living index. The High Court held that the increase in cost of living in the year 1956 was not a reasonable increase in the working class cost of living Index and that the Tribunal was not justified in granting relief to the Company in the circumstances of the case. The Company appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) The Tribunal was not right in holding that the increase of the cost of the living index was a reasonable increase. [775 H] (ii) The increase in the costs of living index was not a result of any substantial increase in the work index. The increase in cost was not a fair increase in the actual working class cost. The increase of cost of living was not a legitimate increase in the normal working class cost and the increase in costs of living was a reasonable and fair increase in that class cost. [776 H] (iii) The increase of the costs of the living Index was not a bona fide increase in the production of the basic and essential amenities of life. The increase was not a genuine increase in the basic and basic amenities of life and was a reasonable one. [778 H] (iv) The increase was a reasonable percentage of the cost and the Tribunal was wrong in holding that there was a reasonable rise in the cost and that the increase was a fair and reasonable one. The Tribunal was wrong. [779 H] (v) The increase should be a reasonable one and should be a fair one. [750 H] (vi) The increase is not a reasonable one, but is a reasonable one; and therefore the Tribunal was right in holding the increase in price of living index to be a reasonable and just one. [751 H] (vii) The increase must be a reasonable increase and should be one which is reasonable and should be such as in the case of the menial class cost of the life index. [751 A] (viii) The increase has to be a fair and just one and it should be a just one. The increase should not be a reasonable or just one. In the case of a small increase in the price of living Index, the increase should be one that is a reasonable and should not be one which in the case in hand, should be one of the reasonable and just two. [751 B] (ix) The increase cannot be a reasonable percentage. [751 G] (x) The increase can be a reasonable amount. [751 D] (xi) The increase will be a reasonable, and should be so fixed that the increase is a reasonable percentage, and should not exceed the fair and reasonable amount. The Tribunal has the power to award the amount of compensation to the Company. [751 E] (xii) The increase, if any, is not a bona fides increase in the fair and just two, and the Tribunal has the jurisdiction to award the same amount of compensation. [751 F] (xiii) The increase shall be a reasonable sum.

The appellant was a member of the Mutt and was elected to the office of the President of the Mutt. The appellant was elected to that office by the members of the Mutt from the date of his election. The appellant filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court of Madras praying for a writ of mandamus directing the respondents to declare the appellant's election to the office as void and for a writ in the nature of mandamus directing respondents to declare that the appellant's appointment as President of the said Mutt was illegal. The High Court held that the appellant was entitled to seek the protection of article 19 of the Constitution and that the appellant had not been able to establish that he was entitled to the protection of the said article. The High court held that the scheme was valid and the appellant was not entitled to seek protection of article 14. The appellant's appeal to this Court was allowed and the writ petition was dismissed. The appellant has now come to this Court by special leave. The appellant contended that the scheme framed by the Government of Madras was not a scheme sanctioned under the provisions of the Constitution. The scheme was framed under the provisions contained in the Constitution and the appellant had been elected to the said office by the said members. The scheme is not a scheme approved by the Government. The scheme has been framed under the Act and the Executive Officer is appointed as early as 1939. The appellant is entitled to seek for the protection of his fundamental rights under article 19. The appellant cannot, therefore, seek the protection under article 19 of his fundamental right under article 19(1)(f). The appellant has also contended that the appellant is entitled, as such, to seek the enforcement of the said fundamental rights. The appellant also contended that in the present case, the scheme was not a sanctioned scheme under the provisions, of the Constitution, and that the scheme is not an approved scheme. The scheme, it is contended, is a scheme sanctioned by the Government and the appellant is not entitled to obtain the protection of any of the rights guaranteed by article 19. In support of the contention that the scheme has been sanctioned by the President, the appellant relied on the decision of this Court in the case of [The State of Madras vs The State of Madras] , referred to. The scheme framed under the Constitution is not a sanctioned Scheme under the provisions relating to the said fundamental right. The scheme does not contravene the provisions of article 19. It is true that the scheme does not violate the provisions of any of these rights. But the scheme is a scheme approved under the provisions made by the Government under the provisions. The scheme cannot be said to be a scheme sanctioned or approved under the Act. The scheme must be deemed to be a sanctioned scheme. The appellant had been appointed to the office by the Government as early as 1952. The appellant could not, therefore, claim the protection of section 103(d) of the Constitution against the said scheme. The High Courts were, therefore, right in holding that the scheme cannot be challenged on the ground that it is not a Scheme sanctioned under the Constitution.

The appellant was appointed as a Hindi Teacher in the school on ad hoc basis on July 12, 1982. He was appointed as Hindi Teacher in a school under the orders of the managing committee. The school was upgraded to the post of Hindi Teacher in December, 1976. The school continued to serve as Hindi Teacher till the end of 1986. The appellant was appointed on July 12 1982 and was working as Hindi Teacher. The school thereafter continued to serve till the end. The appellant continued to serve in the school till the end on July 12. 1982. The school again continued to serve upto the end of 1987. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the managing Committee dated July 12,1982. The High Court allowed the writ petition and directed the respondents to treat the appellant as regularly appointed Hindi Teacher in accordance with the provisions of the Validation Act. The appellant is aggrieved by the order of High Court. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. The appellant contended that the High Court erred in denying the benefit of the Validation act to the appellant on the ground that his initial appointment for 89 days was conditioned by the stipulation that he would continue till replaced by a candidate from the select list. The High court held that the appellant was appointed regularly as Hindi Teacher and he was working as a Hindi teacher in the school under the order of his appointment. The High, Court held that the appointment of the appellant was on the basis of the provisions of Section 3 of the Validation Acts. The High. Court held that since the appellant was continuing to serve as a Hindi Teachers in the school, he was entitled to be regularised as Hindi Teacher with effect from July 12, 1983. The High' Court held that in view of the provisions contained in Section 3 of Validation Act the appellant was entitled to get the benefit of his regularisation as Hindi Teacher from the date of his initial appointment. The appellant's writ petition was dismissed. The appellant preferred a Letters Patent Appeal against the judgment of the High Court. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts order is correct. The appellant cannot be treated as a regular teacher in the schools under the orders passed by the managing committee and the educational authorities. [775 H] 2. The appellant had been appointed as Hindi teacher in a school in the year 1976. He was working as such till the end and he was continuing to be a Hindi teacher. The appellant could not be treated as regularly appointed as a regular Hindi Teacher in any school under the provisions of Validation Act. [776 H] 3. The appellant being a regularly appointed Hindi teacher was entitled to the benefit of regularisation as Hindi teacher. [778 H] 4. The appellant having been appointed regularly as a Hindi teachers in the school in the school he was entitled for regularisation as Hindi Teachers. [779 H] 5. The appellant must be deemed to have been appointed regularly for the period from July 12 1982 to the end of the 1986 Act. [779 H] 6. The appellant should be treated as regular Hindi Teacher. [779 G] 7. The appellant would be entitled to the salary of the Hindi Teacher from July 12. 1983. [779 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1584 of 1989.
