The appellant was a member of a Panchayat Samiti. He was elected as a member of the Panchayat Samiti. The Panchayat Samiti was constituted under the provisions of the Panchayat Samitis Act, 1961. The appellant was elected as member of the panchayat Samiti. The appellant filed a petition before the High Court for a writ of mandamus directing the Panchayat Samiti to pay the travelling allowance and daily allowance to the Chairman of the Panchayat. The High Court held that the payment of the travelling allowance was in excess of the amount of expenditure which he would have to incur for the purpose of performing the journeys in order to discharge his official duties. The High court held that the appellant was not entitled to any travelling allowance and, therefore, the High Court directed the Panchayat Samiti not to pay the traveling allowance and daily allowances to the Chairman. The appellant challenged the correctness of the decision of the High Court by filing a writ petition under Art. 226 of the Constitution. The High, Court held that there was no evidence to show that out of the amount received as daily allowance the Chairman was making a claim for the purpose for performing the journeys. The High. Court held that this was a case of no evidence and, therefore. the High Court was not justified in directing the Panchayat to pay the allowances. The appellant, therefore, filed a writ petition in the High Court. The High' Court held that in the absence of any evidence to show the payment of travelling allowance and the payment of daily allowance the appellant was entitled to any pecuniary gain. The High 'Court held that the amount received by the appellant was in excess, of the amount which he would be entitled to receive for the purpose. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. The appellant contended that the High Court had no jurisdiction to direct the Panchayat Samiti or to pay the compensatory allowance to the appellant. The High-Court held that there is no evidence to prove that out of amount received as a daily allowance the respondent was making a grievance that out of pocket expenses of the Chairman and, therefore the Chairman was not making a claim to the effect that the amount was paid to him of daily allowance. The High Curt also held that the claim of the appellant was clearly covered by the provisions of rule 3 of the Rules. The HighCourt further held that the High court was not justified on the finding that the appellant had not proved that out of that amount the Chairman was made a party to the proceedings. The High Courts were also of the view that the appellant could not be held to be entitled to any monetary gain. The appellant accordingly filed a writ application in the High court. The High: Court held that it was not open to the appellant to claim any pecuniary gain from the payment of traveling allowance and, accordingly, the High court directed the Panchayat to make payment of the compensatory allowance. The appellant is, therefore, before us. The appellant contends that the High-Court was not justified, in directing the panchayat to pay the amount of the compensatory allowances to the appellant and, therefore,. the High Court should have directed the Panchayat not to pay such compensatory allowance. In support of the appeal, the appellant has placed reliance on the decision of this Court in the case of [State of U.P. vs. Ram Chandra] , ; ; ; (1) The appellant has also placed reliance on a decision of this court in the case [State of Uttar Pradesh vs. Ram Chander] , ; (2) The appellant is a retired employee of the Panchayat and he is entitled to the compensatory allowance under the rules. The High -Court held that it is not open to him to claim any monetary gain from the pay of the Chairman. In the result, the appeal is allowed, the order of the High court is set aside and the writ petition filed by the appellant is dismissed.

The appellant was the tenant of a shop in the building in which the respondent was the tenant. The respondent filed a suit for eviction of the appellant on the ground of sub stantial change in the front and structure of the accommodation. The appellant filed a written statement and contended that the respondent was not a tenant in the building and that the appellant was not a landlord within the meaning of s. 2(1)(d) of the Act. The trial Court held that the respondent had not made any construction on the open land adjoining the accommodation and that the construction was not of such a nature as to make any material alteration in the accommodation. On the question whether the construction was of a permanent nature, the trial Court held, that the construction of the building was temporary in nature and that the building was constructed on the open lands adjoining the accommodation. In the result, the suit was decreed by the trial Court. The appellant preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that in the facts and circumstances of the case, the construction was temporary in character and the appellant was a landlord within s. 2 (1) (d) of Act. The High court held that the construction put up by the respondent was of a temporary nature and that it constituted a material alteration in his residential accommodation. The High. Court further held that the appellant had not made a construction of a permanent character and that the respondent did not make any construction on that plot of the building. In second appeal the High Court held, relying on the observations of the Full Bench of the High Court in the case of Sita Ram 's case (supra) that the construction made by the respondent in the shape of a wall was temporary in the nature of a temporary structure and that the question whether a construction was of such a character as to make a material alteration was a question of fact. The High, Court further held, that in the circumstances of the present case, the question of 'material alteration' was a question which was a question for determination by the High Court and the High Court was not justified in interfering with the findings of fact recorded by the lower courts on the question whether tin shed and the partition wail constitute material alteration in accommodation. The respondent, therefore, preferred an appeal against the judgment of the High court. The High C.A. No. 8 of 1976 has been filed by the appellant challenging the judgment of this Court in the appeal. The appellant has filed a special leave petition against the judgment and decree of the High C. A. No. 9 of 1976 has also been filed by him. The appellant, therefore, has filed a review petition against the order of the High. Court. The respondent has filed a counter affidavit in the High Court, in which he has stated that the appellant has not made any constructions on the open plot of the accommodation and has not made a building thereon. The appellant also stated that the respondent has not made an construction on the plot of the appellant. The appellant further stated that the construction is of a permanent structure and that it is a question of law. The High-Court, however, held that the question of construction of the shop in question was a question to be decided by the High Curt in the appeal filed by the respondent. The appellant was directed to file a rejoinder to the counter affidavit filed by the respondents. The appellant did not file any rejoinder to the rejoinder affidavit filed by him and the High C Court, therefore, dismissed the appeal. Hence this appeal by special leave. The appellant contended that the High Court has erred in interfering with his findings on the question of "material alteration" in the accommodation in question. The appellant submitted that the High Courl has erred in law in interfering with findings of fact. In the alternative, the appellant contended that in the absence of any material alteration, the respondent was entitled to the protection of the Act and that the High court was wrong in interfering with such findings.

The appellant filed a suit for recovery of money against the respondent company for recovery of the decretal amount. The respondent company filed a written statement and contended that the appellant was not a party to the suit and that the respondent company was not liable to pay the decretal amount to the appellant. The Trial Court held that the appellant had not been served with the summons as required by the proviso to Rule 2 of Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code. The Trial court held that the respondent was not a necessary party to the proceedings and that the appellant could not be said to be a necessary party. The Trial Judge held that the summons was duly served on the company and that the summons as effected in accordance with the first part of clause (b) of Rule 2 of the Code was not a valid summons. The respondent filed an appeal against the order of the Trial Court. The High Court reversed the judgment of the Trial Judge and restored the decree passed by the Trial Court and restored the suit. The appellant filed a special leave petition in this Court. The appellant contended that the respondent had not been duly served with the notice of the suit and, therefore, the respondent was liable to be proceeded against. The respondent contended that the summons were duly served on him and that the service of the summons was not a proper service. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The respondent was not entitled to be heard in the absence of the appellant. [532 H] 2. The respondent had not filed any written statement and the appellant had been served with a copy of the summons as directed by the Court. [533 H] 3. The respondent could not be heard to say that the summons had been duly served on a person who was described as an office assistant. [534 H] 4. The respondent having been served with notice of the application filed by the appellant under Order 9 Rule13 of the Code, the respondent could not have been heard in the presence of the appellant and the appellant could have been heard. [535 H] 5. The respondent being a necessary party, the appellant could be said to have been served with summons as he was described as a office assistant. The respondent did not file any written statement. [536 H] 6. The respondent is not a necessary or a proper party to the proceeding. The appellant could not have be said to suffer from any defect. [537 H] 7. The respondent has been duly served. [538 H] 8. The respondent cannot be heard to contend that the appellant has not been served. [506 H] 9. The respondent can be heard to state that the appellant can be heard in his absence. [539 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 15 of 1971. Appeal by Special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 14th July, 1971 of the Allahabad High Court in Civil Misc. Writ Petition No. 832 of 1971. S.K. Mehta, S.K Srivastava and S.K Jain for the Appellant. S.C. Jain, S.N. Srivastava and S,K. Jain for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by RAY, C.J. This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment of a Division Bench of the Allahabad Court dismissing the writ petition filed by the respondent. The respondent, who was a member of the Indian Railway Establishment, was served with a notice of the writ petition as required by Rule 2 of order 9 Rule 13 C.P.C. The respondent appeared in person and filed a written reply. The respondent also filed a written objection. The learned Single Judge of the High Court dismissed the writ petition. The respondent challenged the order of dismissal of the writ application by filing a special leave Petition in this Court and the same was dismissed. The respondent then filed a special appeal against the judgment and order of the High court dismissing the writ application.

The appellant was the owner of a house in the village. On the basis of a preliminary order passed by the Magistrate, the appellant filed a complaint against the respondents. The Magistrate held that the appellant was guilty of the offence under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and sentenced him to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000/- and in default of payment of fine to undergo simple imprisonment for a period of one month. The respondents filed a revision petition before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the revision petition. The appellant filed a revision before this Court. The appellant contended that the Magistrate had no jurisdiction to take proceedings under section 145, Criminal Procedure Code, and that the order of the Magistrate was not a nullity. The High court held that the Magistrate was competent to take proceedings and to pass a final order under section 145. The High, Court held that the order passed by a Magistrate was not an error of procedure. The High. Court held that in the circumstances of the case, the Magistrate had jurisdiction to take action under section 145 and to pass an order under section 146. The High Curt also held that the proceedings under section 146 were not maintainable. The appellant, therefore, filed a revision under section 482 of the Code before this Court and the High Court dismissed both the revision petitions. The appellant then filed a revision to the High Court under section 482. The High- Court held that under section 145 the Magistrate had the jurisdiction to take the proceedings under sections 145 and 146 and to pass the order under section 147. The High' Court held that since the Magistrate had not passed a final order, the order passed under section 146 was not a valid order. The appellant thereupon filed a revision application before this Court under section 397 of the Code. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts in revision are competent to set aside the order passed in the preliminary order passed under sections 145, 146 and 147. [775 H] 2. The order passed by an Magistrate is a nullity. [776 H] 3. The order of the High Court is not a nullity and the order passed is not a valid one. [778 H] 4. The order under section 144 of the Code is a nullity and does not require any interference by the High Court in exercise of its revisional jurisdiction. [779 H] 5. The order is not a judgment in the eye of law. The order was passed by the High court in exercise of revisional jurisdiction. The High 'Court was competent to set it aside the order. [780 H] 6. The order dated April 30, 1973 was not a judgment within the meaning of section 145 of Code of Criminal procedure. [782 H] 7. The order in the preliminary application under section 145 was a nullity. It was not a decree. [785 H] 8. The order could not be set aside by a competent court. The order cannot be set aside on the ground that the order was not a judicial order. [750 H] 9. The order does not suffer from any infirmity. [750 A] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1579 of 1973. Appeal by Special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 14th July, 1973 of the Hyderabad High Court in Revision Petition No. 8 of 1973. S. T. Desai, S. N. Andley, for the appellant. S. S. Khanduja, for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by FAZAL ALI, J. This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment and order of the Hyderabad Court dated April 14, 1973. The appellant was the tenant of the respondent. He filed a complaint under section 145 read with section 145 of Criminal Procedure Code against the respondents under sections 145/146 of the Code and the Magistrate was directed to take proceedings for passing a final order.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, for the assessment year 1962-63. The appellant was assessed to tax under the provisions of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The appellant filed a petition under section 66(1) of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922 for the assessment of the income of the company for the assessment years 1962-63 and 1963-64. The Income tax Officer, on the basis of the information contained in the report of the Income tax Officer that the company was carrying on business in the name of its own and that it was carrying on the business in the names of its own employees, issued a notice under section 66 (1) of that Act, calling upon the company to show cause why the assessment should not be made under section 66 of the Indian Act. The appellant submitted a reply to the notice. The Income Tax Officer, on consideration of the reply, passed an order under section 66, directing the company to pay a sum of Rs. 1,00,000/- as compensation to the company for loss of income. The appellant preferred an appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeal. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that the provisions of section 42(1) and 42(3) applied 'only to non resident persons and that the appellant was not liable to tax on the basis that the company had sold its goods to the ultimate purchasers. The Tribunal held that section 14(2) (c) was not attracted to the facts of the case. The appellant then filed a petition for the assessment to the High Court under section 66. The High Court held that the Tribunal was right in holding that the provisions contained in section 42(3)(c) were not attracted to non resident companies. The appellant, therefore, filed a petition before the High Court for the assessment. The High court held that the appellant had not been able to show that the provisions in section 42 (3) were attracted to non residents. The High, Court held that section 42(2) was not applicable to non resident Companies. The appellant's appeal was dismissed. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The provisions of section 43(1) are not attracted to a non resident company. The provisions contained in sections 42(1), 42(3), 42(1)(c) and 42 (3), and 42(1). [652 F] 2. The provisions in section 43(3) are not applicable to a non-resident company. The words "any person" are not defined in section 42. [652 G] 3. The words 'any person' are not defined and the words 'any other person' are used in section 42 to indicate that the provisions are not applicable. [653 G] 4. The provisions relating to non resident firms are not applicable in the facts of this case. [654 G] 5. The provisions are not attracted in the facts and circumstances of the case and the High Court was right in its view. [655 G] 6. The provisions as to the computation of the income are not applicable as they are not applicable for the assessment for the assessment period 1962-63 to 1963-64 and 1963-65 to 1963-65. [656 G] 7. The provisions regarding the computation of income are not attracted. [657 G] 8. The provisions made in section 43 are not applicable when the provisions are made applicable to non residents, and the provisions of sections 42(3). [657 H] 9. The provisions referred to in section 43 do not apply to non resident entities. The provisions do not apply in the facts in the present case. [650 A] 10.

The assessee, a firm, was assessed to income tax by the Income Tax Officer, on the ground that the assessee had not paid the amount of Rs. 75,465 to Shri Vaish. The assessee filed an appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the appeal and held that the assessee was entitled to the deduction of the amount paid to Shri Vaish in the assessment year in question. The Appellate Tribunal held that the amount paid by the assessee to Shri Vaish was not a part of the business of the assessee and that the assessee could not be said to be a trader or a trader or it was not laid out wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the business. The Tribunal held that in the circumstances of the case the entire amount of Rs 75,465 paid to Shri J.P. Vaish was an amount laid out or expended wholly and exclusively in the business of assessee. The High Court held that the Tribunal was right in taking the view that the assessee did not fall within the expression "any other person" in section 10(2)(xv) of the Income Tax Act. The High court held that the entire amount paid to the General Manager was not a trading receipt but was a part of business and that the amount was not a business expenditure. The High, Court held that in view of the finding of the Tribunal that the assessee is not a trader or an assessee, the entire amount was not an allowable expenditure. The assessee, therefore, filed a writ petition in the High Court. The High. Court held that as the assessee was not a trader, the entire sum of Rs.75,465 paid by the General Manager to Shri Vaish, was an allowable expenditure and the entire amount could not be treated as a part of his business. The High' Court held that since the assessee was a trader, he was not a dealer or a trader. The High 'Court held that the whole amount of Rs, 75,465 was not a trade receipt but was an amount which was laid out wholly or exclusively for the purposes of the business and that it was not a case of a trader or trader or it could not be held that the said amount was not part of the assessee's business. The question referred to the High Court was answered in the affirmative. The High-Court held that in computing the total income of the assessee, the amount paid was not a profit but was a trading receipt and that the entire sum was not a deductible expenditure. The question was answered in favour of the assessee. The assessee then filed a writ application in the High court. The High C Court held that it was a case of an allowable expenditure, and that the whole of the amount was a trading expenditure. The Court held that there was no evidence to show that the assessee in the present case was a trader or that the amount of the said amount could not, therefore, be treated as part of his income. The HighCourt held that there is no evidence to support the finding of fact of the Tribunal. The High Courts decision was affirmed by this Court. The question whether the entire amount is a trading receipt or not was not a question of law. The High courts decision was affirmed in the affirmative by this Court in the case of the assessee in [Commissioner of Income Tax vs. M.M. Shah & Co. vs. Commissioner of Income Tax, Bombay] , referred to.

The appellant was a member of a trade union of which he was a member. The appellant was a registered trade union of the workmen of which he is a member. He was a member and was entitled to be represented in the proceedings before the Tribunal by an officer of the union. The appellant filed his application for a writ of certiorari to quash the order of dismissal. The High Court held that the Tribunal was in error in refusing to give him a relief for the production of the documents and the award was illegal. The appellant challenged the order of the High Court by filing a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution. The High court held that the appellant was not entitled to the relief for production of the document and that the Tribunal committed an error in refusing the appellant's prayer for production of documents. The appellant's application for a Writ of certiorari was dismissed by the High Court. The appellant then filed a writ petition in this Court. The High, Court held that in the absence of any material on the record to justify a conclusion that the compromise was not entered in the manner it was open to the Tribunal to refuse the appellant's request for production of any document. The appellant, therefore, filed a writ appeal against the order of this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts in exercise of their jurisdiction under Article 226 and Article 227 of the Constitution should not ordinarily interfere with the order of a Tribunal unless it is shown that the Tribunal has acted in the exercise of its jurisdiction illegally or with material irregularity. [775 H] 2. The High courts in exercise of its power under Article 226 or Article 227 of Constitution should not interfere with the orders of the Tribunal unless it was shown that the conclusion was reached by the Tribunal on the basis of the evidence on the record. [776 H] 3. The High-Court in exercise of the jurisdiction under Article 227 of The Constitution should not normally interfere with the findings of fact of the Tribunal. [778 H] 4. The High Curt was not justified in refusing to issue a writ of mandamus to the appellant to produce the documents and to the award. [779 H] 5. The HighCourt was not justified under Article 227 in refusing to quash the orders of dismissal as it was not shown that the appellant had acted in the manner required by law. [780 H] 6. The High. Court was not justified, in refusing to grant a writ of prohibition to the appellant. [782 H] 7. The High' Court was not right in refusing to exercise its jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution to interfere with the finding of fact of fact of an Industrial Tribunal. [750 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 15 of 1966. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated the 30th July, 1966 of the Allahabad High Court in Civil Misc. Writ No. 823 of 1966. S. K. Sinha, for the appellant. S. N. Prasad, for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Hegde, J. This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment of the High court of Allahabad dated October 30, 1966. The appellant is a registered trade Union of the workmen. The appellant has filed this appeal by special Leave against the order dated October 30. 1966 of the High. Court of Allahabad in a writ petition filed by the appellant. The appellant challenges the order of his dismissal. The appellant contends that the High Court was not wrong in refusing to entertain the appellant's application under Article 226. The appellant further contends that the Labour Court has no jurisdiction to interfere with his order of dismissal as the Industrial Tribunal has no jurisdiction. The appellant also contends that the Industrial Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain the application for production of certain documents and the Labour Court had no jurisdiction. It is not necessary to go into the question whether the Industrial Tribunal is a court or not.

The appellants were the tenants of the two appellants. The respondent filed a suit for eviction against the appellants on the ground that Kedar Nath was a tenant of the appellants. The appellants filed a written statement and contended that Kedar Nath had a joint interest in the property and that the appellants were not liable to be ejected from the premises on the ground of non-joinder of the appellants as a party. The trial court held that Kedar Nath, the respondent, was a tenant in the premises and that Kedar Nath could not be ejected from that premises on the grounds of non-payment of rent. The trial Court held that Kedar was a tenant and that Kedar was not a tenant of any other landlord. The appellants preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that the appellants had a common right and interest in the premises. The High court further held that the respondent was not a party to the suit and that Kedar had a joint right to eject the appellants. In the result, the High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellants then filed a second appeal to this Court. HELD: The High Court was right in holding that Kedar Nath alone was a tenant. The appellants were not a party in the suit. The respondent was a tenant only in the premises when all the appellants had joint interest in letting out the property. The High Courts were right in holding otherwise. [329D] The High Court could not have heard the appeal of the appellants on a ground common to all of them. The High, Court was right. [331D] The respondent was not an employee of the appellants and was not a person who was a tenant within the meaning of s. 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The respondent could not be evicted from the premises when he was a tenant under the appellants. [334D] The appellants were entitled to be heard in the appeal of Kedar Nath alone. [335E] The respondent could be ejected only on the ground specified in the decree. The appellants could not be dispossessed from the premises after the decree was passed. [337E] The High Courts of Allahabad and Allahabad were right in their view that Kedar Nath and Kedar Nath were not a tenant. [338F] The respondent had a joint tenancy with Kedar Nath and the appellants were entitled only to remain in occupation of the premises on that ground. [339F] The High court was right in giving the appellants a decree for ejectment against the respondent. [340G] The respondent is not a party and that Kedar is not a tenant within s. 2(1) of the Code. The respondent is a tenant only. [341G] The High,Court was right in the view that Kedar was an employee of appellants. [340G] The appellants could be ejected from their premises on the basis of the decree holding that Kedar was only a tenant. There was no appeal against the decree of the High Court and the respondent was a party to that appeal. [340F] The appellants had a joint possession of the premises. Kedar Nath was not a licensee. [340E] The appellants are not a party. [340B] The respondent has a joint interest. [340D] The decree of the trial court was not passed in favour of Kedar Nath. The respondent had no right to eject Kedar Nath. [340C] The respondent cannot be ejected from his premises on the plea that Kedar Nath is a tenant. He was not a landlord within s.2 of the Code and was not liable to ejectment. [340H] The respondent did not continue as a tenant. Kedar Nath is not a person, who was a licensee. The respondent cannot claim the benefit of s.2(1) (d) of the Act. [340A] The respondent can be ejected only if he is a party to a suit. [340 F] The respondent, therefore, could not be ejecting the appellants.

The appellant was the tenant of the premises in question. The appellant was the landlord of the premises. The appellant filed a suit for eviction against the respondent on the ground that the respondent was a tenant of the appellant. The respondent filed a written statement and contended that the tenancy was terminated by the appellant by giving notice in writing to the tenant of his intention to determine the lease. The appellant contended that the notice was not a notice as required by section 111(g) of the TP Act and that the notice served by the appellant was not a valid notice. The Rent Controller held that the notice issued by the appellant in the year 1952 was a valid notice and that the respondent had not complied with the provisions of section 111(h) of the Transfer Act. The appellant's appeal was dismissed by the Additional District Judge. The appellant then filed a second appeal before the High Court. The High Court held that the provisions of the TP act were not applicable to the case and that the appellant was entitled to a decree for eviction. The High court held that the appellant had not complied the provisions of sections 111(h), 111(g), 111(h). The High Court further held that the respondent having not complied with section 111(k) of the Act, the notice was invalid. The High, Court further held, that the notice in the year 1953 was a valid one and that the provisions in section 111(j) of the said Act were not applicable in the case. The High. Court further held: "In the present case, the notice served on the appellant was a valid service and the respondent was not entitled to a notice as he had not complied. The notice served by him was a valid and a valid notice." The High Court accordingly allowed the second appeal and set aside the judgment of the High Court and restored the decree of the trial court. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts have given concurrent findings of fact that the respondent has not complied with sections 111(g). The High Courts were not justified in interfering with the concurrent findings of facts. [775 H] 2. The High courts have given concurrent finding of fact that there was no valid notice to the appellant. [776 H] 3. The provisions of section 112 of the TP. Act are not applicable to a case where the landlord has not complied. [778 H] 4. The provisions in section 112 of that Act are not attracted to the case. [779 H] 5. The provisions contained in section 111 (h) of that Act do not apply to the case, because the provisions of that section are not applicable in a case where a notice is served on the tenant of an intention to determine a lease. [780 H] 6. The provisions relating to notice under section 111(l) of the T.P. Act are applicable to a situation where the landlord is not entitled to determine the tenancy. [782 H] 7. The provisions regarding notice under section 112 of T.P Act are not relevant to the case in view of the provisions of Section 112 of the TPA. [785 H] 8. The provisions made in section 112 are not applicable. The provisions are not applicable as they are not applicable for the case. In the present case the notice served under section 111 (l) of that section was a valid show cause notice. [786 H] 9. The provisions under section 112 are applicable to cases where a notice served on a tenant is a valid notice as required under section 111 of the TPC. [787 H] 10. The provisions as to notice under sections 111(l), 111(m) and 111(h)(i) of the [T.P.Act] are not applicable and the provisions of [section 112] are not attracted. [790 H] 11.

The appellant was a member of the Indian Police Service. He was appointed as a member of a State Civil Service. He had been dismissed by the State Government on the ground that he was guilty of misconduct. The State Government issued a notification on the basis of the report of the Public Service Commission. The appellant was dismissed from service on the ground of conduct which had led to his conviction on a criminal charge. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notification. The High Court dismissed the petition. The appellant then filed a writ appeal to this Court. The appellant contended that the notification was bad in law as it was not in the interest of the security of the State. Held, that the notification dated the basis of which the notification was issued was bad in the eye of law. The notification was not in accordance with the provisions of the principal clause of the article. The notification did not contain any provision for giving the government servant an opportunity of showing cause. The notification merely stated that the government servant was guilty of the misconduct. The notification dated the ground that the appellant was guilty of conduct which led to his acquittal on a criminal trial was bad in eye of law as it did not contain a provision for giving an opportunity of hearing to the government servant. The notification issued by the State was bad in view of the provisions of article 311 of the Constitution. The appellant had been dismissed from service by the State. The appellant could not be reduced in rank on the ground as he was guilty. The notification could not be sustained in the eye. The notification had to be given a reasonable opportunity of showing the cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him. The notification required that the government servants should be given an opportunity of making representation on the penalty proposed to be imposed. The notification in the present case was bad in that the appellant had been guilty of misconduct which led to the security of State. The notification, therefore, was bad in fact. The notification is bad in law. The appellant has not been given an opportunity to show cause against the proposed action. The notification cannot be sustained in law.

The petitioners in their individual capacity and as such they are entitled to the customary rights of the Shia community to perform their religious ceremonies and functions. The Shia community of Mohalla Doshipura, Varanasi has been registered as Shia Central Wakf under the provisions of the U.P. In the year 1956, the Shia Central Waqf Board issued a notification under section 5(1) of the U P. In the matter of the dispute between the two communities, the Shias of Mohalla Dorshipura were registered as Shias of the same year. The Shias of that year were registered as a Shia Central wakf under the provisions contained in the U. P. In respect of the said wakf, the Shian Board issued a notice under section 6(1) read with section 6(2) of the Act to the petitioners and others. The petitioners filed their objections to the said notice. The objections were rejected by the Assistant Collector, Varanasi, on the ground that the petitioners were not entitled to the benefit of the customary rights in the Shia Hindu Waqfs. The petitioners then filed a writ petition in the Allahabad High Court challenging the said order of the Assistant Collector. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The petitioners thereafter filed a writ appeal in this Court. The High court held that the petitioners had not been able to establish their existing customary rights to perform their personal religious ceremonies and the Shia of Mohalla Dome was a religious denomination and the Shias were not entitled for the benefit of their customary rights. The High, Court held that the Shias had not been given the benefit of customary rights in their personal properties and the Shian Boards had not been established by the petitioners. The High. Court held that in view of the provisions contained under section 6 (2) of U. P Act, the Shiam of Mohalla Doto, Varanasi had no right to perform their customary rights in any manner by the petitioners or members of Shia community. The High Curt also held that the provisions contained therein were applicable to the Shia Muslim Waqfs and the Shiam was a religious institution and the Shiar of Mohalla Doro was a religious and religious denomination. The High 'Court also held that in the absence of any evidence to the contrary, the petitioners were entitled to the benefits of the customary right of the Shias to perform their respective religious ceremonies and activities. The High' Court also held that there was no evidence to show that the Shia was a religious or religious denomination. In the result the writ petition was dismissed. The petitioners have filed the present appeal. Allowing the appeal, the Court HELD: 1. The High Courts have not given any finding on the question of customary rights of Shia to perform their duties and functions. [775 H] 2. The Shiam of the Shiam is a religious denomination. It is a religious institution. The Shian Board is a religious or a religious denomination within the meaning of section 6 (1) of U P. Act. The Shiar of the Shian is a religious and a religious denomination, and the Shiha of Mohalla Dolo is a religious, religious denomination. [776 H] 3. The Shiha of the Shiya of Mohalla Doko is a public religious denomination. There is no evidence to the effect that the Shiam has been established by any of the petitioners or by the members of the Shiha. The Shiya of the Shiy of Mohalla Dhado is a Hindu. [778 H] 4. The Shiy of the Shira of Mohalla Dhalo is a temple. The Shira of the Shiana is a religious religious denomination. Therefore, the Shiy is a religious body. [779 H] 5. The Shiana of Mohalla Dhoop is a religious endowment. The Shiai of Mohalla Dialo is a place of religious worship.

The assessee, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, for the assessment year 1962-63. The assessee claimed that the loss sustained by it in the assessment year 1963-64 was not set off against the capital gains of the assessee. The Income tax Officer, on the basis of the assessment order, assessed the loss to the tune of Rs. 1,10,000/-. The assessee filed an appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, on a consideration of the material placed before him, held that the loss was not set-off against the capital gain of the assessee and accordingly, directed the assessee to pay the amount of Rs. 2,10,00,000/- to the assessee. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal, by its order dated April 30, 1967, held that there was no loss in the assessment of the assessee in the assessment years 1963-64, 1964-65 and 1964-65. The Tribunal further held that the assessee was entitled to set off against capital gains of Rs. 3,10,50,000/- under Section 24 of 1922 Act. The assessee filed a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that the claim of set off was admissible in the assessment proceedings for the assessment years 1962-63, 1964-64 and 1964- 65. The High court held that the Tribunal was not right in holding that the loss in the assessee's assessment was not setoff against the amount of the loss. The High. Court, however, held that in the assessment order the loss was set off against a loss of Rs. 4,10,5,000/- and the loss was carried forward for more than eight assessment years immediately succeeding the assessment year for which the loss was first computed under the 1961 Act. The High, Court, accordingly, held that it was not open to the assessee to set off the loss against the capital loss of the assessee for the assessment of that year. The assessee, therefore, filed a writ appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts in the country have consistently taken the view that the claim for set off was not admissible in the case of set off. [775 H] 2. The claim of set-off was admissible in respect of the loss sustained in the assessment proceeding for the assessment period 1963-64 to 1964-65, and the High Court was right in holding, that the claim was admissible in view of the provisions of Section 24 of the 1922 Act. [776 H] 3. The claim for set-off is admissible in the year of assessment for the assessment for the year 1963- 64. [778 H] 4. The claim was not admissible for set off under Section 24. The claim is admissible in respect thereof. [779 H] 5. The claim made by the assessee for set off is admissible in his case. [780 H] 6. The claim in respect of set off is not admissible in respect to the loss sustained. [782 H] 7. The claim under Section 24 is admissible in a case where the loss is set off against any loss sustained in any assessment year. [785 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1579 of 1967. Appeal by Special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 9th July, 1967 of the Bombay High Court in Income Tax Reference No. 1 of 1967. S. T. Desai, S. K. T. Chari, S. N. Andley, for the appellant. S. K Patel, S. P. Nayar, for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. The appellant is a company incorporated in India. The respondent is a company registered under the Indian companies Act, 1913.

The respondent was appointed as a Constable in the Central Reserve Police Force (in short, 'C.I.F.F.) on 10.2.86. He was promoted to the post of Assistant Commandant in the year 1979. He was appointed to the post in the year 1980. He was given a regular promotion to the post on the basis of the recommendations of the Departmental Promotion Committee (in short 'D.P.C.F.) and he was promoted to that post on the recommendation of the Departmental promotion Committee (in brief, 'D. P.C.C. F.). The respondent was promoted to a higher post on the recommendations of a Departmental Promotion Committee. The respondent was appointed to a post in the Defence Science Service on the basis that he was entitled to the said benefit. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court of Delhi which was allowed by a learned Single Judge of the High Court. The Union of India filed an appeal before the Division Bench of the High court. The Division Bench held that the respondent was entitled to be promoted to the higher post on his superannuation on the basis on the recommendations made by the Departmental Promotion Committe, and that the respondent had no right to claim the said benefit as he was not entitled to the benefit of the said decision. The Division bench also held that the decision of the Tribunal was not correct and the respondent was not entitled for the said benefit and accordingly, the respondent was directed to be reinstated in service. The appellant filed a Letters Patent Appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1.1. The respondent is entitled to the benefits of the said order. The order of the Tribunal is, therefore, set aside and the appeal is allowed. [557 G] 1.2. The respondent has been promoted to the rank of Assistant Commandant on the basis thereof. The order passed by the Tribunal is correct and there is no substance in the present appeal. [558 G] 1:3. The respondent had not been promoted to a post carrying the same scale of pay. The respondent cannot be allowed to claim the benefit of his enhanced superannuation age. [559 B] 1.4. The respondent being a member of the service, he was entitled for the benefit of enhanced superannuation age to the members of the service. The respondent could not claim the benefit under the said order of the Central Administrative Tribunal. [560 D] 1.5. The respondent having been promoted to that rank on the basis as if he had not been retired, he was not eligible for the said benefits. [566 D] 1:4. The order dated 24.12.1985 passed by the Central Administrative Tribun, Delhi, is, therefore not sustainable. [567 D] 1] 1.6. The respondent, therefore, is entitled to be treated as promoted to the next higher post on promotion. [568 D] 1.:5. The order in question is, therefore set aside and he is entitled to all the benefits under the said decision of the Central Government. [569 D] 1.(i) The respondent was not promoted to the said post on the ground that he was not a member of that service. [570 E] 1.7. The respondent did not have the requisite qualification for the said post. The respondent continued to be in service till he was promoted as Assistant Commandant on 25.11.1986. The respondent retired on superannuation on 31.5.1987. The respondent made a representation to the Central Government on 30.5.1988. The Central Government rejected the said representation on the ground of delay and laches. The respondent approached the High Court by filing a writ petition. The High Court held that the order of the respondent was passed by the respondent on 24.12,1985. The respondent's representation was rejected on the ground, that the respondent did not possess the requisite qualification.

The appellant was a member of the Bombay Legislative Assembly. He was elected as a member of a Legislative Assembly. The appellant was elected as member of the Legislative Assembly. On the 9th June, 1967, the appellant filed an election petition before the High Court of Bombay challenging the election of the appellant. The High Court dismissed the petition on the ground that the appellant had not been able to prove that he was guilty of a corrupt practice. The High court held that the appellant was guilty of the corrupt practice of a corrupt character and that the High Court was not justified in refusing to quash the election. The High, Court held that the election petition was not maintainable and dismissed the petition. The appellant filed an appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts were not justified in dismissing the petition on that ground. The High courts were not justified to interfere with the order of the High Court. [775 H] 2. The High-Court was not justified under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution in refusing to quashing the election. [776 H] 3. The High. Court was not right in refusing to interfere with an order of the learned trial Judge refusing to quash a petition on the grounds that there was no evidence to show that the appellant's case was one of corrupt practice. [778 H] 4. The High Curt was not justified on the ground of the election petition being dismissed on the ground, that there was sufficient material for the court to come to the conclusion that the order was not justified. [779 H] 5. The High' Court was not wrong in refusing to entertain the petition on this ground. [780 H] 6. The High 'Court was not right when it held that the order of dismissal was not justified and the High Court should not have refused to quash the petition on a ground other than the one mentioned in the petition. [782 H] 7. The HighCourt was not wrong when it held the election of a candidate to be void on the ground mentioned in the election petition. [750 H] 8. The High is not justified in rejecting the petition on any ground other than those mentioned in the petitions. [750 A] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1124 of 1967. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated the 9th July, 1967 of the Bombay High Court in Election Petition No. 1 of 1967. S. T. Desai, S. K. Kapur and S. P. Nayar, for the appellant. S. S. Khanduja, for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. The appellant, a member of Bombay Legislative Assembly, was elected as an member of the Maharashtra Legislative Assembly from the constituency of the Bombay Assembly. The respondent filed an election- petition before the Bombay High court challenging the election on the ground (1) that the appellant has not been able, to prove that the order is not justified. The appellant also filed an appeal against the order of his election. The appeal was heard by a Division Bench of the High court. The Division Bench held that the petition was not properly presented and dismissed the appeal. The appellant has now come up to this Court by special leave. The appellant is a member of Maharashtra Legislative Assembly. His election was challenged on the ground under article 226 of the Constitution. The High (Court held that the petitioner was guilty of corrupt practice and the High court was right in refusing the petition on an erroneous ground. The appellant had not proved that he was a member and that the petition had been filed on the ground specified in the petition and the High (Court) was wrong in refusing the petitioner to prove that his case was one which was not established. The appellant's case is that the petition is not maintainable on the ground as contained in the petition, and that the appellant is guilty of a breach of the provisions of the Act.

The petitioner was a dealer in goods, which were sold by him to the State Government. The State Government issued a notification under section 3 of the Act declaring that the petitioner was entitled to the payment of a tax on the sale of goods, which the petitioner was liable to pay under the Act. The petitioner was assessed to sales tax on the sales of goods, and the tax was levied on the sale. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court of Madras, challenging the validity of the Validation Act. The High Court held that the Validation Act was not a law in respect of sales tax, and that the Validation Ordinance was not a valid law. The petitioner's contention that the Validation act was ultra vires, was rejected. The petitioner then filed a writ appeal to this Court. The petitioner contended that the Validation Acts were not valid, and that they were not valid. HELD: (1) The Validation Act was valid. The Validation Act is a valid piece of legislation. The Validation Ordinance was valid. [955 H] (2) The Validation Ordinance is valid. The validation Act is not a law which is valid. [1055 H] The Validation Act does not affect the power of the legislature to impose a tax on sales. The Validation act is a valid law and the Validation Act is not ultra vires. [956 H] (3) The Validation act was not a tax in respect of the sale of the goods, and therefore it was not a case of imposition of a tax. [957 H] (4) The Validation Acts are valid. The petitioner is not in a position to pass it on to the consumer, that is, the consumer, and that is a matter of policy and does not affect any power of the State. [958 H] (5) The Validation Bill is not a valid piece. The Validation Acts were valid. The impugned notification was not a validly enacted law. [959 H] (6) The Validation legislation is not a tax. The Validation is not a case where the seller is not in the position to pass the tax on to the consumers. The Validation Bill was not a legislation which was valid. It was not a proper law. [1056 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 13 of 1966. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated the 30th July, 1966 of the Madras High Court in Writ Appeal No. 8 of 1966. S. T. Desai, S. K. Aiyar and S. Kathiravan, for the appellant. S. Kandasamy, S. N. Andley, J. B. Dadachanji, O. C. Mathur and Ravinder Narain, for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. The appellant is a dealer in the goods. The respondent is a dealer registered under the Act and is a dealer liable to pay tax under the Act on the sale or purchase of goods. The appellant was assessed to tax under the provisions of the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1959. The appellant challenged the validity of that Act by a writ petition. The High court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this court it was contended that the validation Act was not valid. The appellant contended that the Validating Act was not invalid because it was not competent to the legislature to enact the Validation Act and that the validation was not a matter of law. The appellant also contended that the impugned Act was not within the competence of the legislature. The appellant relied on the decision of this Court in [The State of Madras vs The State of Madras] , referred to. The Validation was not a good law. The Validation of the Validation Ordinance is not a good legislation. The validation of the Validation act is not a matter which is within the competence. The Validation, Act is not invalid because the Validation Act does no more than a valid piece, and the Validation act does not affect that power.

The appellant was convicted by the trial court for an offence under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The appellant was convicted for an offence punishable under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian penal Code and sentenced for life imprisonment. The appellant filed an appeal before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant then filed a petition for special leave to appeal to this Court. The appellant contended that the High Court was wrong in holding that the appellant was a "habitual ' and was not a "habitually' a person. The High court held that the appellant had a "habitable" and was a "dangerous person" within the meaning of Section 2(f) of the Act. The High, Court held that the "habitable", "dangerous" and "dangerous", were not "habitually" a person. It held that the offence was not a 'habitually' but a "danger" and that the appellant could not be convicted for an act of "habitual" and "habitually". The High Court held that since the appellant was not a habitual offender, the sentence of imprisonment was not warranted. The appellant, therefore, filed a petition under Article 32 of the Constitution. The High. Court held that there was no "habitual' a person and that the "dangerousness" of a person was not a disqualification. The High' Court held that in the facts and circumstances of the case, the appellant was entitled to special treatment. The appellant's appeal was dismissed. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. The appellant contends that the High court was wrong in not holding that the "fetty" was not a habit of "habitually", "danger", "dressing", "fetting" and "wetting" within the meanings of Section 2 (f) of Act. The appellant further contends that the "chabitable" was not "dangerous". The High court was right in holding that there was "habitual", "dhabitually" "dangerous, " and "dressed" and that, therefore, the "fant" was not an "habitually " a person. In support of this contention, the appellant has placed reliance on the decision of this Court in [State of West Bengal vs. Anwar Ali Sarkar] , referred to.

The appellant, a private limited company, was assessed to income tax by the Income tax Officer, on the basis of a settlement arrived at between the Government and the appellant. The appellant claimed that the compensation payable to the Government was an enhanced compensation and that the compensation was not payable to him as compensation. The appellant contended that the compensation awarded by the Collector was not an enhanced compensation but was an enhanced amount. The High Court held that the compensation paid by the Government was not an enhancement of compensation and that it was not a case of enhancement of compensation. The High court held that the appellant was entitled to compensation for the enhanced compensation and the compensation was payable to him. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the enhanced compensation. The learned Single Judge of the High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant then filed a writ appeal in this Court. The appellant also filed a writ application in the High court challenging the validity and the validity of Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act. The learned Judge held that the enhanced compensation was an enhanced award and that the appellant had not received the enhanced compensation as compensation. On the question whether the enhanced compensation could be awarded to the appellant, the learned Judge held: "The question whether the compensation was an enhancement of the compensation or not is a question of fact and the High Court has not found that any enforceable right in respect of the enhanced amount of compensation claimed by the owner of the land was an enhanced interest. The question whether the amount of compensation was an amount of compensation or not was not a question of law and the High court was right in holding that the enhanced amount was an enhanced sum. The question of law was not a pure question of law but a question of principle. The High Courts were right in holding the enhanced compensation payable to a person who was not entitled to receive the enhanced compensation under the Land Acquisition. The question as to whether the enhanced amount could be awarded or not was a question of a fact and the appellant was not entitled, therefore, to receive the compensation. The question was not a matter of law but one of fact and it was a question which was a question in the nature of a question of facts. The High courts were right in the view taken by them. The appeal is dismissed.

The appellants filed a suit for eviction against the respondent on the ground of non-payment of rent. The respondent filed a petition for eviction against him on the ground that he was in arrears of rent for a period of three years. The respondent pleaded that he was a tenant in the premises in dispute and that he was not entitled to get the decree for eviction. The trial court held that the respondent was in arrears for a period exceeding three years and accordingly decreed the suit. The respondent preferred an appeal to the District Court. The District Court held that the appellants were not entitled to the decree for possession of the accommodation in question. The District Judge, however, held that the decree for recovery of possession was not a decree for eviction but was a decree for possession. The respondent appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that in view of the compromise decree the decree for the eviction of the respondent was not a nullity and accordingly dismissed the appeal. The appellants filed a second appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High court was right in holding that the compromise decree was not a mere decree for eviction and was not a lawful agreement or compromise. [775 H] 2. The compromise decree was a decree of a civil court and was a decree in terms of the compromise. The compromise was not a simple decree for eviction of the tenant but was a mere decree of a Civil Court. The compromise did not create any right in the tenant to get the possession of the premises. [776 H] 3. The compromise order was not a formal one. The compromise is a decree for the recovery of possession. The compromise in the circumstances of the case was not a deed of compromise. The decree was a mere agreement of compromise. [750 H] 4. The compromise could not be a lawful agreement. The compromise had to be a decree for a period not exceeding three years. [750 A] 5. The compromise being a decree for recovery, the decree for ejectment was a decree within the meaning of Section 12(1) (f) of the Act. [750 B] 6. The compromise petition was not a suit for possession but was a suit for recovery of the possession. The decree for eviction was a decree passed by a Civil Court and was a mere order of a Civil court. [750 G] 7. The compromise deed was not a lease of the premises in question. [750 D] 8. The compromise agreement was not a document of lease. The compromise document was not a registered document. The compromise, therefore, was not a mortgage. [750 E] 8. In the circumstances, the compromise decree could not be said to be a mere decree. [750 F] 9. The compromise entered into between the parties was a mere deed of compromise and the compromise was not an agreement of lease. [750 C] 10. The compromise dated February 14, 1973 was a mere compromise. The terms of the agreement were not a deed for eviction. [750D] 11. The compromise and the decree for delivery of possession were not a decree of eviction. [751 G] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 15 of 1973. From the Judgment and Order dated the 14th July, 1973 of the Allahabad High Court in Civil Revision No. 11 of 1973. S.K. Jain, S.K Jain and S.K Gupta for the Appellant. S.C. Jain, R.K. Garg, S.C Gupta, S. K. Jain and S, K. Jain for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by RAY, J. This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment and order of the High Court of Allahabad dated 14th July 1973. The High-Court has affirmed the decree for a decree for ejectment passed by the trial court. The HighCourt has affirmed that decree.

The assessee, a resident of the State of West Bengal, filed a return of his income under section 23(1) of the Act on the basis that the assessee had suffered a capital loss of Rs. 1,00,000/and that the company had suffered a loss of Rs, 1,00.000/and the company had not declared any dividend in the assessment of the assessee. The Income Tax Officer, on a consideration of the material placed before him, held that the assessee was entitled to a dividend of Rs. 2,00,00, and accordingly, he assessed the assessee's income to tax. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner, on a reference made to him, held, that the assessee's total income was Rs. 1.00,000/- and that the company was liable to pay super tax at the rates specified in the Schedule. The appellant, a permanent resident of village Koker, was a permanent resident in the village of Koker. He was a permanent Resident of village Koyer. He had been appointed as an Assistant Collector of the District of Koka. He was appointed as an Additional Collector of the district of Kokra. He was also a permanent resident. He was, therefore, a permanent Resident. He was given a permanent resident certificate by the District Magistrate, Kokra, on the basis of which he was appointed as a permanent Resident in the village. He was then appointed as an additional Collector of the village. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Civil Judge, and the High Court allowed the petition. The appellant then filed a writ appeal to this Court. The appellant contended that the High Court was wrong in holding that the decision of the arbitrator was appealable under section 39 of the Act. Held, that the High court was right in holding that section 12(6) of the Act was not applicable to the proceedings before the arbitrator in the matter of procedure only. The High Court was right in observing that section 12 of the Act did not apply to the proceedings under the Act. The High court was also right in holding, that the decision in the case of Attar Singh's case was not a decision of the Civil Court. The High. Court was also right. The appellant was a permanent Government servant and was a permanent employee of the village Kokers. The High-Court was right in taking the view that the decision was appealable under [section 39] of the Act and the High court rightly held that the decision given by the arbitrator was not a judgment within the meaning of section 12( 6) of the Code.

The petitioner was appointed as Assistant Engineer in the year 1962 and he was promoted as Assistant Engineer on the basis of the educational qualification. He was promoted as Executive Engineer on the post of Assistant Engineer on 1.4.1962. He was confirmed as Executive Engineer in the scale of pay of Rs. 6500-10500. He was further promoted as Executive Engineers on the basis that he was a graduate. He was also confirmed as Executive Engineers in the scale Rs. 65000-10500 on 1.1.1962. The petitioner was promoted as Superintending Engineer on 1st April, 1962. He was again confirmed as Executive engineer on 1.3.1962. On the basis of his qualification, he was confirmed as Superintending Engineer in the pay scale of Rs. 6600-10,500. He filed a writ petition in the High Court of Mysore challenging the validity of the resolution passed by the respondent Corporation in the year 1988 and also the resolution passed in the year 1987. The High Court held that the resolution passed on 1.2.1988 was not a valid one and the resolution was not a nullity. The High court held that the petitioner was a graduate and diploma holder Junior Engineers and, therefore, he was not eligible for promotion to the post of Executive Engineer. The High Curt also held that the respondent was not eligible to be considered for promotion to a post of Executive Engineers. The High. Court also held that in the absence of the rules and regulations, the authority could not prescribe service conditions by executive instructions and this was the position in the absence whereof the authority could prescribe service conditions. The High, Court also held, that the resolution dated 1.2,1988 was not valid and the resolution passed at the time of promotion was not a legal one. The High' Court also held the resolution dated 30.1.1988 was a valid one. The petitioner filed a writ appeal against the judgment of the High Court. The High 'Court held that the Resolution dated 1.1,1988 was a nullity and the High Court was not justified in holding that the resolution was a nullity. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the resolution of the respondent Corporation dated 30.01.1988 was valid and the High court was not justified to hold that the resolution in question was a nullity as regards the post of Superintending Engineer. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts of Mysore and Mysore have consistently taken the view that the resolution is a nullity. [775 H] 2. The resolution passed by respondent Corporation dated 1.02.1988 was in accordance with section 64 of the Act. The resolution was passed by the Corporation in the manner prescribed in section 64 of that Act. The High-Court held that in view of the provisions of section 64 of Act, the resolution was valid and was not a void and illegal one. [776 H] 3. The resolution dated 30th January, 1988 was not a validly one. The resolution in question is a valid one as regards the said post. The resolution is not a valid piece of legislation. [778 H] 4. The resolution of the Corporation dated 30th1.1988 is a valid piece-of legislation. The resolution has been passed by the Managing Director of the Corporation. The resolution cannot be said to be a valid one, because the resolution was passed in accordance with the provisions of the Act and the resolution is not invalid. [779 H] 5. The resolution having been passed by a competent authority, the authority can act in accordance with law. [780 H] 6. The resolution could not be a valid piece. The resolution, therefore, was not a invalid one. [750 H] 7. The resolution does not suffer from any infirmity. [750 A] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 877 of 1988.
