The appellant, a retired Judge of the High Court of Delhi, was appointed as a Judge of the Delhi High Court on the recommendation of the Chief Justice of India. The Chief Justice of the High court, by his order dated December 14, 1966, appointed a retired Judge as a Judge to the Delhi High court. The appellant was appointed as an Additional Judge of the said High court on the recommendation made by the Chief Justice. The appellant filed a writ petition in the Delhi High, Court praying for a writ of mandamus directing the Chief Justice to make a fresh look at the two 460 questions and to appoint a Judge of that High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition by a judgment dated December 14. 1967. The appellant then filed a writ appeal in the Delhi high Court which was dismissed by a judgment and order dated December 15, 1967. The High court held that the Chief Justice was not a constitutional functionary having a consultative role and the power of appointment was not justiciable. The appellant, therefore, filed a writ of certiorari quashing the order of the Chief Judge and also the order of appointment of the appellant as a Judge. The High, Court, however, dismissed the writ appeal. The appellant thereafter filed a writ application in the Delhi Court in the year 1967. The Delhi High Court dismissed that writ petition by its judgment and order. The appellant thereupon filed a writ in the year 1968 in the High Court. On December 14, 1967, the High Court dismissed his writ petition. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. The appellant contended that the Chief justice of India was not a Constitutional functionary having a consulted the Chief Justice and the view of the majority in S.P. Gupta's case was not correct. The appellant further contended that the High Court was not a Court of law and the Chief Justice, the Chief Justice or the Chief Justice could not be said to be a constitutional functionary. The appellant also contended that the appointment of the Chief Justices of the High Courts was not a judicial act. The High Courts were not constituted. The High-Court was not a court of law. The High. Court was not an administrative body having a consultatory role. The High' Court was not competent to appoint a judge of the High' Court. The appellant therefore contended that the order of appointments of the appellant was not a judgment in the eye of law. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The High 'Court was not an authority competent to appoint an Judge of the Court. The Chief justice of the High 'Court is a constitutional functionary and the power to appoint a person to the superior judiciary is not a judicial function. [775 H] 2. The Chief Justices of India are not constitutional functionaries having a consultee. The Chief Judge of the high Court is a constitutional functionaries having consult the Chief Justice as a constitutional functionary, and the power is not a constitutional authority having a consultatio-tion. [776 H] 3. The ChiefJustice of India is a constitutional authority. The Chief of the High-Court is a Constitutional functionary. The Chief-Judge of the High. Court is a Constitutional authority. [778 H] 4. The appointment of the Judge of the Supreme Court is not a legislative act. The appointment is not a matter of law. [779 H] 5. The appointment by the Chief Justices is not a statutory functionary. The appointment was not a matter for the High Court and the Chief Justices were not a constitutional functionaries. [780 H] 6. The appointment and appointment of the High, Court is not an administrative act. The Chief Judicial Magistrate is a constitutional Authority. [782 H] 7. The appointment or appointment of the judge of the Supreme court is not a law. The appointment, appointment or appointment is not an executive act. [785 H] 8. The appointment/appointment of the Chief justice is not a nullity. [786 H] 9.

The respondent was a member of the Bihar State Electricity Board. He was appointed as a Junior Engineer in the Bihar State Electrical Corporation Ltd. He was promoted to the post of Assistant Engineer in the year 1962. He was confirmed in the post of Junior Engineer in July, 1962. On his retirement, he was re-employed as a Junior Assistant Engineer in a new establishment. On his re-employment, he was promoted as Assistant Engineer in July 1962. On the basis of the order of his re-appointment, he was appointed as Assistant Engineer on probation for a period of two years. On his appointment as Assistant Engineer, he was confirmed in his post as Assistant Engineer. On his superannuation, he was paid his salary and allowances. On his resignation, he was allowed to continue in service till the date of his retirement. On his reinstatement, he was given a second chance to join the new establishment. The respondent was re-appointed as a Junior engineer in the year 1963. On his return to the new establishment, he was again re-employed in the new establishment as a Junior Executive Engineer. On the same date, he was also re-employed. On his voluntary retirement, he filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order dated December 14, 1963. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The order of the High Court was not illegal. The order of dismissal was passed by the President of India and the order of the President of the India State Electricity Board was not illegal and void. [775 H] (ii) The order passed by the High Court is not illegal. [776 H] (iii) The order was passed by an authority competent to do so. The order was not illegal because the order was passed in violation of the provisions of the Act. [778 H] (iv) The order dated December 13, 1963 was passed by a competent authority. The order dated January 14, 1963 was not illegal as the order was not passed by an officer competent to do it. [779 H] (v) The order is not illegal because it was passed by any authority competent to make it. The order is illegal because it is passed by an authorised officer. [780 H] (vi) The order cannot be sustained because the order is illegal. [750 H] (vii) The order in question was passed by one of the members of the Bihar Public Electricity Board. The order passed was illegal because the respondent was not given an opportunity to join the duty. [750 A] (viii) The order could not be sustained because it was not passed in violation or in violation of any provisions of the statute. [750 B] (ix) The order having been passed by an incompetent authority, the order was illegal. [751 H] (ix)(a) The order must be quashed because it was illegal because it did not amount to an order passed by an administrative authority. [751 G] (b) The order being illegal, it was not illegal since it was passed in breach of the provisions contained in the Act. The order could be passed by an authorized officer. [751 A] (c) The order should be quashed because the order passed by a person competent to do the same was illegal. The respondent could not be allowed to continue to work in the new establishments as a Junior Engineers. [751 B] (x) The order did not amount either to an order of dismissal or removal from service. [751 D] (xi) The order, therefore, was not illegal on the ground that it was passed without jurisdiction. [751 E] (xii) The order does not suffer from any infirmity. [751 F] (xiii) The order has been passed by the authority competent to pass it. [751 C] (xiii)(a) In the instant case, the order is not passed by the competent authority.

The appellant was the owner of a plot of land measuring about 7,000 sq. ft. in the area of the plot of land. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court of Delhi challenging the validity of the order of the Commissioner rejecting the application of the appellant for the erection of a building on the ground that the proposed building was not in conformity with the Master Plan. The High Court held that the appellant was entitled to the erection of the building on the plot of the plot and that the appellant had to establish that the proposed construction was in conformity with section 14 of the Development Act. The High court held that the proposed structure was in conformity of the Master Plan and that the Commissioner had no jurisdiction to reject the application of appellant for the construction of a building. The High. Court held that in the absence of any indication in the Master Plan, the procedure indicated in section 10 of the Development act was not applicable. The High, Court further held that the Commissioner was not competent to reject the appellant's application for the erection on the ground of violation of section 14 of Development Act. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in holding that the Commissioner acted in contravention of section 14(2) of the Development, Act and that the High court was in error. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts were not competent to interfere with the validity of a notification under section 14 of a Development Act. [775 H] 2. The High-Court was in error when it held that the provisions of section 14 were not applicable. [776 H] 3. The HighCourt was in a wrong view. [778 H] 3(i) The High Court was not competent under section 14 to reject the request for the erection. [779 H] (ii) The High- Court was in a correct view. [750 H] (iii) The High court was not competent. [750 A] (iv) The High Courts had no jurisdiction. [750 B] (v) The High.Court was in wrong view in error in rejecting the appellant's request for the construction. [750 G] (vi) The High,Court was in fact in error in interfering with the validity or the validity of an order rejecting the appellant for a construction of a particular kind. [750 D] (vii) The High C Court was in fact right in holding that section 14 was not applicable to the case. [750 F] (viii) The High' Court was in the error in holding the appellant to be entitled to the construction of the building. [750 E] (ix) The High 'Court was in the wrong view in interfering with an order rejecting an application for the construction on the ground on which the appellant was not permitted to use the land. [750 C] (x) The HighCourt had no jurisdiction under section 14. [750D] (xi) The High T Court was in no way in error in refusing to consider the appellant's case. [751 G] (xii) The High F.C.I.R. was not competent in law to reject the petitioner's application for erection on the basis of the building in question. [751 H] (xiii) The High courts were in error in not considering the appellant's prayer for the construction in accordance with section 14. The High C.I.T. was in error by not considering the petitioner's request for erection of the buildings on the plot. [751 A] (xiv) The High Cou rt was in error, in interfering with a finding of fact recorded by the Commissioner. [751 B] (xv) The High LC. was in fact competent to reject an application for erection of a new building on the same plot of land and the building in the new building.

The appellant No. 1 was convicted by the trial court and sentenced to death by the trial Court and the High Court. The appellant No. 2 was convicted by a criminal court and sentenced by the trial Magistrate to death by a judgment of the trial court. The appellant was convicted by that court and sentenced in the alternative to death by his judgment and order dated January 12, 1971. The appellant filed an appeal to the High Court against the judgment and order of the trial Magistrate. The High Court dismissed the appeal of the appellant No. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. The appellant's case was that the appellant No 1 was a member of the judiciary and was a member and was a leader of the judiciary. The appellant had been convicted by the High Court and sentenced to imprisonment for life by the trial Judge. The appellant also filed an appeal against the judgment of the High Court which was dismissed by this Court. The High court held that the appellant was a member in the judiciary and the appellant was not a member of any other judiciary and that the appellant had been rightly convicted by the Sessions Court and sentenced in his favour. The appellant then filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the conviction and sentence. The High, Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant thereafter filed a writ appeal in this Court. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The appellant is a member of a judiciary and is a member and is a leader of a judiciary. [775 H] 2. The appellant cannot be said to be a member of another judiciary. The High Courts have failed to appreciate that the appellant has been convicted by a competent court of law and sentenced to life by the High court. [776 H] 3. The appellant could not be convicted by a court of law. The appellant should have been convicted by that Court and sentenced him to imprisonment for a period of one year. [778 H] 4. The appellant must be held to be a person who is a member in a judicial service and is a person who has been convicted of an offence under section 161 of the Indian Penal Code. [779 H] 5. The appellant can be convicted by the court of law only if he is a member or a member of that judiciary. [750 H] 6. The appellant, therefore, cannot be convicted by any court of law unless he is a person in the judicial service. [750 A] 7. The appellant being a member of judiciary is a member. [750 B] 8. The appellant having been convicted by this Court and sentenced by that Court to imprisonment for one year by the trial of the appellant, the appellant cannot be convicted for the offence of criminal breach of trust. [750 D] 9. The appellant would be liable to be convicted by an appropriate court of law if he is not a member or member of the judicial service and was a person who was a member or an officer of the judicial Service. [750 G] 10. The appellant did not hold any judicial service. The appellant does not hold any Judicial Service. [751 G] 11. The appellant will be liable to suffer imprisonment for a term of one year by reason of his conviction and sentence by the trial magistrate. [751 H] 12. The appellant shall be liable to pay a fine of Rs. 500/- in addition to the fine of Rs 500/- which was imposed by the trial judge.

The appellant was appointed as a Constable in the Punjab Police on the basis of a written report submitted by one of the constables of the Punjab Police. The appellant was a constable in the Punjab police. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he had failed to make a written report to the police. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of dismissal. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant then filed a writ appeal in this Court. The appellant contended that the order of the High Court dismissing the writ petition was illegal and that the High Court should have set aside the order of his dismissal. The appellant also contended that the High court should not have set aside his order of dismissal because the order of punishment was passed by an authority not competent to pass the order of removal. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High court was right in holding that the order passed by the District Magistrate was illegal. [775 H] 2. The order of dismissal passed by an officer not competent to do so is a nullity. [776 H] 3. The order passed by an Officer not competent to impose any punishment on the appellant was a nullity. The order was passed by the officer not competent. [778 H] 4. The order is not a nullity. It is a nullity and the High Court was right in setting aside the order. [779 H] 5. The order dated December 14, 1968 was passed by a competent authority. The order in question was passed by another officer not competent and therefore, the order of termination was not a nullity and was liable to be set aside. [780 H] 6. The order terminating the services of the appellant was passed by one authority competent to pass it. The order did not suffer from any infirmity. [782 H] 7. The order dismissing the appellant was not a valid order. The order does not suffer from the vice of any irregularity. [785 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 15 of 1971. Appeal by Special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 14th July, 1971 of the Punjab and Haryana High Court in Civil Writ Petition No. 12 of 1968. S.K. Jain, for the appellant. S.N. Prasad, for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by P.B.R.L. Iyengar, J. This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment of the High court of Punjab and Haryana dated April 14, 1971. The appellant is a constable in Punjab Police. He was appointed as Constable in the State Police on the recommendation of the Punjab Public Service Commission. The appellant had passed the departmental examination for the post of Constable in the Haryana Police. The result of the examination was declared on December 14, 1967. The appellant challenged the validity of the order of her appointment by filing a writ petition before the High Court. The High, Court dismissed the petition. The High. Court held that the order was illegal and was liable for dismissal. The order has been passed by the High Court in a mechanical manner. The appellant has not challenged the order of appointment. The High-Court has held that the appellant was appointed by the Punjab Police as a Constable and therefore, she was not entitled to be paid salary for the period of her absence from duty. The High' Court has held that in the absence of a written order of the Government, the order was not a legal order. The appellant's contention that the order terminating the service of the appellant is illegal and that she was not given any opportunity to file a written statement was rejected. The High C.A. 15 of 1972 has been filed by the appellant challenging the order passed against her. The appellant contends that the order is illegal and is liable to be quashed. The appellant further contends that the High-Court should not have interfered with the order of reinstatement.

The respondent was a dealer in the goods in question. The respondent purchased the goods from the appellant. The goods were delivered to the appellant. On the basis of the purchase price, the appellant sold the goods to the respondent. The respondent filed a return of the goods in the prescribed form. The return was accepted by the assessing authority. The respondent paid the tax on the sale of the goods. The respondent then filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the assessment. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the assessment. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Explanation to sec. 30 of the Contract Act is not relevant for the purpose of determining the question whether the transaction was a speculative transaction. The Explanation to the Explanation is not relevant in the present case. The Explanation is not to be read in a restricted sense. It is not to give a meaning which would be more appropriate to the Explanation. [675 H] (2) The Explanation is in the nature of an exception to the general provision. The Explanation does not give a restricted meaning to the Explanation and the Explanation is to be read as a whole. [682 H] (3) The Explanation does give a restricted interpretation to the Explanation to secs. 30 and 24(1) of the Act. [683 H] (4) The Explanation applies to a case where the goods are not delivered to the buyer but only to the seller. [684 H] (5) The Explanation cannot be read in the manner suggested by the assessee. The Explanation cannot operate in the same manner as the Explanation. The Explanation applies only to a case of sale where the goods were not physically delivered by the seller to the buyer. [685 H] (6) The Explanation merely provides that if there is no actual delivery of the commodity or the scrips have been delivered, the loss in speculative business against the assessee must be a loss in a speculative business. [686 H] (7) The Explanation in the Explanation is merely to give a restricted construction to the Explanation, and does not give the Explanation any restricted meaning to a Explanation. [650 H] (8) The Explanation must be read as an exception to sec.30 of the Act and the Explanation does not make it a case of a speculative transaction which could be allowed to be set off against a profit in a speculative transaction, for the purpose for which the Explanation is attracted. [650 A] (9) The Explanation has to be read with the Explanation and it is not to make it a mere device to give a wider meaning to the explanation. [650 D] (10) The Explanation makes it clear that the Explanation applies to cases where the goods have been delivered to the buyers and the price is not the same as the Explanation and that the loss in a speculation business is a loss in the speculative business. The Explanation merely makes a restricted construction of the Explanation to the explanation and does not make the Explanation applicable to a case which could be said to be a speculative transaction and the Explanation applies only in a case where a trading transaction is not completed by actual delivery. [650 C] (11) The Explanation, therefore, does not give any restricted meaning. [650 F] (12) The Explanation only provides that if the goods are delivered to the seller, the loss of the goods must be a profit in the speculative transaction. [650 G] (13) The Explanation provides that if a transaction is a speculative transaction the loss in the speculation business against the person who has sold the goods. [650 E] (14) The Explanation also does not give an absolute meaning to the expression 'a trading transaction' and does not create a fiction in the Explanation. It only provides that where the goods in respect of which the loss in speculation business is not delivered to a buyer, the loss is a loss of the speculation business.

The appellant, a candidate for election to the Legislative Assembly of the State of Bombay, filed an election petition challenging the election of the appellant, the respondent, and the appellant, alleging that the appellant had committed a breach of the provisions of section 33 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The appellant contended that the respondent had not complied with the provisions of the Act and that the Returning Officer had not acted in accordance with the provisions contained in section 33 of that Act. The High Court held that the Returning officer had failed to consider the provisions of Section 33 of the Act. The appellant filed an appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions of section 36 of the Representation Of the People Act are mandatory and the Returning Officer is to make an enquiry into the objections. The Returning Officer is not to reject any nomination paper on the ground of any technical defect which is not of a substantial character. [675 H] 2. The provisions contained in the Representation of People Act are directory and not mandatory. The provisions in the Representation Of People Act are not mandatory. [676 H] 3. The provisions relating to the filing of nomination papers are mandatory and they are mandatory. The Returning officer is to see that the requirements of the Act are complied with. The provisions are mandatory. [776 H] 4. The provisions regarding the filing of the nomination paper are mandatory and not directory. [778 H] 5. The provisions for filing of nomination paper are directory. The provisions made in the Representation OF the People Act must be complied with. [775 H] 6. The provisions as to the filing and proof of the nomination papers are directory. [750 H] 7. The provisions under the Representation of The People Act are procedural in nature and are directory in nature. The provisions have to be complied with in the proper sense. [750 A] 8. The provisions referred to in section 36 of that Act are mandatory. If the Returning Officer has failed to comply with the provisions relating to a defect in the nomination paper, the provisions of sub-section (2) of section 36 are mandatory and are not mandatory and the provisions of law are directory. If the provisions of this Act are not complied with, the provisions are mandatory and if the provisions of a law are not mandatory, the provisions have to comply with them. [750 B] 9. The provisions prescribed in section 36 are directory and the provisions are directory. Section 36 is mandatory and not mandatory and it is mandatory. [750 G] 10. The provisions mentioned in section 36 have to be strictly complied with. If the requirements of section 36 have not been complied with, it is mandatory and the provision is mandatory. The provision is mandatory and is directory. [751 H] 11. The provisions, as to the deposit of the requisite amount, are mandatory and do not require the compliance of the provisions relating thereto. [751 G] 12. The provisions which are mandatory are mandatory and it cannot be said that the provisions are not mandatory in nature. [751 A] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1566 of 1987. From the Judgment and Order dated the 10th May, 1987 of the Bombay High Court in Election Petition No. 1 of 1987. S. N. Prasad, for the appellant. S. K. Bagga, for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by K. J. Kathi Raning Rawat, J. This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment and order dated October 10, 1987 of a Division Bench of the High Court of Bombay in Election Petition Nos. 1 of 1988 and 1 of 1988. The appellant, who was the candidate for the election to the House of the People's Legislative Assembly, was declared elected to the House by the Returning Officer. The appellant was declared elected. The appellant challenged the election of respondent No.

The appellants were appointed as workmen of the Company on October 22, 1972 and were confirmed in their services on October 22. 1972. On October 22, 1973, the appellants were appointed on October 22 and October 22, 1974. On October 23, 1973, they were confirmed in the services of the Company. On October 24, 1973, a notice was issued by the Company to the appellants calling upon them to show cause why their services should not be terminated. On October 25, 1973, an order was passed by the Company under Section 10(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (hereinafter referred to as the Act) directing the appellants to reinstate the appellants in service with effect from October 22,1973. On October 27, 1973, another notice was issued to the appellants asking them to show-cause why their services be not terminated. On November 27, 1973 the appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court of Delhi challenging the validity of the notice. The High Court dismissed the writ petition on the ground that the appellants had not filed any appeal against the order of the Company passed on October 27,1973. The appellants filed a special leave petition in this Court. On September 28, 1973, this Court dismissed the special leave petition. On September 29, 1973, on the application of the appellants, the High Court dismissed their writ petition. On October 29, 1973 the Company filed a writ application in the High court of Delhi challenging an order of the Labour Court dated October 27, 1974. The High court dismissed the writ application on the ground of delay and laches. On October 30, 1973, after the dismissal of the writ petition, the appellants filed an application for review of the order dated October 27. 1973. The High, Court dismissed the review application on the following grounds: (1) The order of the High Court dated October 29, 1974 was not challenged by the appellants before this Court and, therefore, the writ petition was not maintainable. (2) The order dated October 29. 1973 was passed by this Court in the special leave Petition filed by the appellants. (3) The order passed by the High Court on October 27. 1974 was not assailed by the appellants in the writ petition. (4) The order was passed in the special appeal filed by the Company on September 29, 1974. (5) The order in the special civil application was passed by a learned Single Judge of the High court on October 27 and the order was passed on October 29, 1976. (6) The order under Section 10 of the Act was passed by an Industrial Tribunal in the year 1973 and the order under Section 11 of the Act passed by the Labour Court was passed in a writ petition filed by the appellant. (7) The order dismissing the writ petition is not challenged by any of the appellants in this Court and the writ petition has been rightly dismissed by the High court. (8) The order impugned in the writ application was passed in pursuance of the order passed by this court on October 29. 1974. (9) The order is not challenged in the writ appeal. (10) The order does not disclose any reason for the High Court to interfere with the order of dismissal passed by the appellants on the ground mentioned in the order. (11) The order has been passed by the learned Single Judge on October 27 in the writ proceedings. (12) The order cannot be challenged by the Company in the writ proceeding. (13) The order, therefore, is not challenged. (14) The order suffers from a serious infirmity. (15) The appeal is without merit and is dismissed.

The appellant, a member of the Bombay Public Service Commission, was appointed as a District Judge in the State of Bombay. He was appointed as District Judge in a State Civil Court. He was confirmed in that court by the High Court of Bombay. On his appointment he was appointed as an Additional District Judge in that court. On his return to the State of Maharashtra he was appointed a District Judge. On his re-appointment he was confirmed in the State Civil Court and was confirmed in his place. On his being re-appointed he was appointed an Additional District and Sessions Judge in the High Court. On his failure to join the duties as an Additional Sessions Judge he was re-appointed as an Additional Judge in the Chief Justice's Court. On the same day he was reappointed as an additional District Judge in another State. On his resignation he was re appointed as an additional Sessions Judge in another state. On his reinstatement he was reelected as an Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate in the State. On the basis of the decision of the High Court, he was reallocated as an Additional Judicial Magistrate in another State in the State in which he was appointed. On his reversion to the State Civil Courts he was reemployed as an Additional Public Prosecutor in the State Government. On his retirement he was re employed as an Additional Special Public Prosecutor in another State and was reappointed to the State Judicial Service in the State on a reference made by the Chief Justice. On his having been reappointed as Additional District and Session Judge in another place he was re reappointed as a District and Sessions judge in the State and was confirmed as an Additional, Sessions Judge in other States. On his becoming a member of a District and Session Court, he became a member of that District and was re appointed an Additional Sessions judge in another State on a re-appointment as an Additional district and Sessions Judge. On the re-appointment of the Additional Sessions judge, he was confirmed as Additional District & Sessions Judge in a state Civil Court. On appeal, the High Court held that the earlier decision of the Chief Justice of the High court was erroneous and that the earlier decisions of the High Courts were not binding on the Chief Justice and that the subsequent decision of the Full Bench of the High, Court was not binding on him. On the question of the validity of the earlier decision, the High court held that the previous decision of the Court of the Chief Judge was not binding upon the Chief Justice, and that the previous decisions of the Court were not binding upon him. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The previous decision of a Court of the highest or a highest Court in a State, was not binding as between the parties to the litigation. [557 D] (2) The previous decisions of a Court, whether of a Division Bench or of a single Judge, are not binding on a Division Bench of the same Court. [558 D] (3) The previous orders of the Court in the present case were not binding. [559 F] (4) The previous order of the Court was not a judgment of a Division Court. The previous orders were not binding as they were not binding in the present proceedings. [560 D] (5) The previous judgment of the Court is not binding on any of the parties to a litigation. [660 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 15 of 1972. Appeal by Special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 10th July, 1972 of the Bombay High Court in Special Civil Application No. 15/72. S. N. Andley, for the appellant. S. S. Khanduja, for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court, was delivered by RAY, J. This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment of the High. Court of Bombay dated October 10, 1972 in Writ Petition No. 1567 of 1972.

The appellant was appointed as a temporary Assistant Engineer in the Public Works Department of the State of Tamil Nadu. He was promoted as a Junior Engineer in the year 1962. He was confirmed in the post of Junior Engineer in 1963. He was given a promotion as a Junior engineer in the year 1963. He retired from service on attaining the age of 55 years on 31.3.1965. He was granted a pension under the Pension Rules. He was retired from service in the year 1964. He was not given any pension under the Rules. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of retirement. The High Court held that Rule 2(2) of the Pension Rules was ultra vires Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India. The High court held that Rule 2046 was not ultra vires Articles14 and 16 of Constitution of India and the said Rule was void and inoperative. The High, Court held that the rule was ultra vires Article 14 and 16 and the said rule was void and ineffective. The appellant filed a writ appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The rule was valid and was valid. [675 H] 2. The rule is a rule of substantive law and is not a rule of law. The rule does not create any new right or liability. The rule merely provides that the power to retire under the Rules is in addition to the power already contained in the Pension Rules and the said rules are invalid. [676 H] 3. The rule in question was valid and did not create any right or liability in favour of the appellant. [678 H] 4. The rule did not create a new right or a liability in favour or the right of the appellant to retire under Rule 2(1) of the Rules. The rule only provided that the power of retirement under the Rules was in addition to that of Rule 2(s). [678 A] 5. The rule being a rule of procedure, the rule was not invalid. [650 D] 6. The rule cannot be said to create a new vested right or liability and the said provision was void and unenforceable. [650 A] 6. Rule 2046 is not a substantive rule. The rule provides that the powers to retire under this rule are in addition to those of Rule 2 of the Pension rules. [650 B] 7. The rule has been made under Article 309 of the Constitution and is not inconsistent with it. [650 C] 8. The rule, therefore, is not a law of substantive law. The said rule is not a statute of substantive law but is a rule for the purpose of Article 73 of the Constitution. [650 E] 9. The rule of substantive Law is not a statutory rule. The said rules are not inconsistent with the provisions of the Constitution or the said rules. [691 H] 10. The rule can be made by the President under Article 309 only if the rule is made under Article 73 of Constitution. [692 H] 11. The rule framed under Article 309 is a rule made under Article 77 of the Constitution which is not a part of Article 73. The rule made under [Article 77] is a rule framed under the proviso to Article 77 of Constitution. The rule making power is not a delegated legislation. [693 H] 12. The rule which is not inconsistent in the Constitution is not a provision of substantive law, but is a substantive law. [694 H] 13. The rule as it is not a mere rule of substantive legislation is not a matter of substantive law or substantive law. It is a rule which is inconsistent with the Constitution. The said Rule is not a Rule of substantive law; it is a rule to be made under Article 162 of the Constitution, and is not an amendment of the said rule. [695 H] 13(i) The rule is not an exception to the general rule of substantive laws.

The assessee, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, on the income of the company from the assessment year 1943-44. The Income Tax Officer, on the basis of the assessment order, assessed the company to income tax. The assessee filed a petition under section 66 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 for the assessment year 1944-45. The Income tax Officer, on a consideration of the material facts, held that the assessee was entitled to the benefit of the provisions of section 5 of the Act. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Tribunal, on a reference, held that since the assessee was not entitled to the exemption under section 5 of that Act, the assessee was liable to pay tax on the profits of the company. The Tribunal, however, held that as the assessee was a registered firm, the profits of which were not assessed to excess profits tax under the third proviso to section 5 of Act, must be computed on the basis that the assessee had carried on business at Raichur and that the profits of a part of the business, the manufacturing activity was not part of his business within the meaning of the third proviso. The Tribunal held that since in the assessment order the assessee was held to be entitled to the benefits of section 5, the assessee could not be said to have been entitled to the relief under section 5. The Tribunal also held that the excess profits tax was not payable by the assessee. The Tribunal accordingly, held that in the assessment year 1945-46, the assessee had not claimed the benefit of section 5 and that the excess profit tax was not liable to be deducted from the profits of that year. The Tribunal further held that the profits earned by the assessee were not assessed as profits of the business and that the assessee could be said to be entitled only to the benefit under section 5 and not to the benefit conferred by section 5. In the result, the Tribunal held that the loss of the assessee was assessable to excess profits Tax under section 5, and that the loss was not assessed to the excess profits Tax. The Tribunal then referred the following question to the High Court under section 66(1) of the Act: "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the assessee is entitled to the deduction of the excess profits of the year under section 5?" The High Court answered the question in the affirmative and against the assessee. Hence, this appeal by special leave. The question is whether the assessee is liable to pay the excess profits. The assessee is a registered firm and the assessment order was passed on the basis thereof. The assessee was assessed to excess profit tax under section 5 on the basis, of the standard profits. The Tribunal found that the assessee did not claim the benefit of Section 5. The High Court held that the Tribunal was right in holding that the assessee is not entitled to claim the benefit under Section 5. In this appeal, it is contended by the Revenue that the assessee has not claimed the relief under Section 5 and that, therefore, the assessee has no right to claim the relief under [section 5] and that the High Court was wrong in holding that in the case of the assessee, the profits earned during the chargeable accounting period were not assessed. The High court held that the claim of the assessee for the benefit under [section5] was not barred by section 5 and the assessee was, therefore, not entitled to any relief under section 115 of the Act, and that, in any event, the assessee cannot claim the benefit thereunder. The High,Court, however, took the view that the assessee cannot be said to claim the benefits under section 5 in the case, and that in the present case, the profits derived by the assessee from the business at Raichur were not assessed at the rate of Rs. 1,000 per cent.

The petitioner applied for the said post. The Board published a list of selected candidates in the prescribed form. The petitioner challenged the validity of that list by filing a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution. The High court held that the petitioner was entitled to exercise his option and then take his turn according to his rank in the common list prepared by the Public Service Commission. The High, Court held that the said list was not a valid one and the petitioner was not entitled to exercise the option and then the said list, was quashed. The High. Court held that in view of the fact that the petitioner had exercised his option in terms of Section 4 of Act, the petitioner was eligible to exercise his options and then take the turn according to the rank list. The petitioner's writ petition was dismissed. The petitioner has filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts and the Public Service Commissions are under a constitutional obligation to prepare a common list. The expression "the common list" in Section 4 of The Act is a mandatory requirement. The expression 'the common list' in Section 4(1) of the Act is a directory one. [775 H] 2. The expression used in Section 4 is "the common List" and not "the common lists". [775 G] 3. The expression in Section 4 means the common list. [776 H] 4. The expression is a mandatory one. The expression has to be construed in the context of the facts of the case. [778 H] 5. The expression, "the common reserve" in Section 5 is a mandatory provision. The expression does not mean that the common list is a mandatory condition. [779 H] 6. The expression must be construed in accordance with the facts of a case. [750 H] 7. The expression cannot be construed in a narrow sense. The expression means the common reserve. [750 A] 7. In the instant case, the petitioner did not exercise his option in the prescribed manner. [750 B] 8. The expression was not a mandatory one and the expression used in the Act is not a mandatory requirement and the petitioner did exercise his option. [750 D] 9. The expression meant the common list and not the common list' and the expression 'the Common List' in Section 5 means the common List. [750 G] 10. The expression should be construed in that context. [750 E] 11. The expression would be construed in terms of the facts and circumstances of the case and the said expression would include the common list or the common list'. [750 G-H] 12. The expression as used in Section 5 of the Act means the common lists. [750 F] 13. The expression not being a mandatory one, the petitioner is not entitled to invoke the said expression. [750 C] 14. The expression of the expression ' the common list', in Section 4, is a mandatory and not a mandatory condition and the said provision is mandatory. [750D] 15. The expression employed in Section 4 has to be interpreted in the context in which the expression has been used. [750E] 16. The expression which is not a directory one has to be read in the context and the facts of each case. [751F] 17.

The plaintiff, a partnership firm, was carrying on business in the name and style of M/s. M/s M/s S.K.M. & Sons, a partnership concern. The Tribunal held that the firm was entitled to the value of the assets of the firm and accordingly, the Income Tax officer assessed the firm. The Income tax officer, however, held that the partnership was not liable to pay tax. The Income-tax officer, however. held that the plaintiff was entitled to a tentative valuation of the suit. The plaintiff filed an appeal before the Income Tax Tribunal. The Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal. The High Court held that the valuation put by the plaintiff was arbitrary and unreasonable. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in holding that the valuation of the firm was arbitrary and that the valuation was arbitrary. The valuation placed by the plaintiff on the plaint was arbitrary and the court was not justified in rejecting the valuation. [750 H] 7. The valuation as made by the appellant was arbitrary and was not arbitrary and unreasonable in the sense that it was arbitrary. [750 A] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 15 of 1979. From the Judgment and Order dated the 14th September, 1979 of the Delhi High Court in Civil Revision No. 8 of 1979. The notification dated 1st April, 1981 exempted the industries specified in the Schedule to the notification from the operation of the notification. The exemption was granted by the notification dated 1.4.1981. The exemption granted by the Notification dated 1.3.1981 was in respect of the industries specified therein. The exemption under the notification was in respect to the industries specified by it. The exemption from the operation was in respect only to the industries mentioned in the Schedule. The exemption provided by the notification was not in respect of any of the industries mentioned therein. The notification did not set out the conditions on which, and the procedure for the grant of exemption. The exemption conferred by the notification did not apply to the industries in question. The exemption given by the notification of 1.3,1981 was in the nature of a conditional exemption. The notification was issued in respect of industries specified in rule 14. The exemption in respect of those industries was in respect in the nature and extent of exemption. In the case of the industries in the State of Madhya Pradesh, the exemption was in respect both to the industries and the exemption was not in the nature or extent of an exemption. The State Government had not issued any exemption under the Notification dated 31.3.1982. The exemption did not apply in respect of a particular industry. The exemption contained in the notification was only in respect of certain industries mentioned in rule 14 and not in respect to any other industry. The notification dated 1,3,1981 did not set forth the conditions on the basis of which, and did not set up the industry. The State Legislature did not make any provision for exemption in respect to industries specified in rules 14 and 15. The exemption is in respect of an industry specified in rule14. The exemption does not apply to a particular industry, but to a particular industries. The exemption cannot be said to be in respect of other industries. The notification issued under it did not set apart the exemption from the purview of the notification and did not apply for the exemption. The question whether the exemption was available to a particular industrial unit or not was not considered by the Full Bench. The Full Bench held that the exemption was granted in respect of industrial units specified in rule 15 and not in the case of industries specified therein and that the exemption contained in rule 14 was in respect not in respect in respect of that industry. The Full bench held that the notification dated 31.03.1982 did not set aside the exemption granted by it. In the result, the Full Bench held, the exemption granted to the industries was in the form of exemption from the provisions of the notification dated 01.03.1981.

The petitioners were appointed to the post of Additional District and Sessions Judges on the basis of selection by the High Court. The petitioners were appointed as Additional District and Session Judges on the recommendation of the High Court on the basis that they were appointed to temporary posts of Additional District & Sessions Judges on a temporary basis. The petitioners, who were appointed to officiate as Additional District & Session Judges on a regular basis, were appointed to a temporary post of Additional Sessions Judge on the basis on the recommendation made by the High court. The petitioners filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the appointment of the petitioners as Additional District Judges on the ground that the rules of continuous officiation in the cadre post did not provide for a quota of 1/3rd for direct recruits. The High Court dismissed the petition. The petitioners then filed a writ appeal to this Court. The Court held that the rules were not applicable to the petitioners as they were appointed by promotion on the basis thereof. The Court, however, held that the petitioners were appointed on the basis, of selection from amongst the members of the Delhi Judicial Service and that the rules did not provide that the appointments were to be made on the basis only of selection from among the members of Delhi Judicial Service. The Court further held that the Rules did not provide any quota for direct recruits and that the petitioners could not be treated as senior to the promotees. The Court also held that the appointments of the petitioners were made on the recommendation by the High, Court and appointments were made on merit cum seniority basis so that persons found not fit for promotion were ignored as in the case of Shri C.D. Summary: The petitioners were promoted to officiate as District and Sessions Judge on a regular scale of pay. The petitioners challenged the validity of Rule 7(a) and (b) of the said Rules. The Court rejected the contention that the rules violated the quota rule. The Court observed that the rules had not provided for a quota for direct recruitment and that the Rules were not applicable in the case. The Court accordingly held that the provisions of Rule 7 were not applicable. The Court then held that the seniority of the petitioners was to be governed by the rules of the Delhi Higher Judicial Service. In the result, the Court held that Rule 7(b) was not applicable to them. The Court directed that the petitioners should be considered for promotion on the post of District and Sessions and Sessions Judge. The Court was of the view that the petitioners had been appointed to officiate in a substantive capacity on a regular post and that the appointments could be made on merit-cum seniority basis so as to be placed in such a way that persons found unfit for promotion were considered as senior to a person as a District and Sessions judge. The Court therefore held that the quota rule was not applicable in their case. The petitioners thereafter filed a writ application in the High court challenging the validity and the validity of rule 7(a). The Court held, relying on the decision of the Constitution Bench in the case referred to above, that the quota for direct recruit was not prescribed in the rules. The Court dismissed the writ petition. The Court found that the quota prescribed in the Rules was not applicable. In the appeal to this court, it was held that the rule was not attracted to the petitioners. The Court finally held that the reservation for direct recruits was not applicable and that the quota was not prescribed for direct recruits in the case and that the rule did not provide a quota for promotees. The petitioners' challenge to the validity of Article 14 was rejected. The Court however held that the provision of the quota rule did not prescribe any quota for promotees and that the provisions were not applicable for direct recruits, the petitioners were not entitled to be considered for appointment on the post. The Court declared that the quota is not applicable to direct recruits.

The appellant, Debi Parshad, was a member of the family of Debi Parshad. He was a member in the family of the appellant. He was assessed to income tax on the income of the Ambala Flour Mills. The Income tax Officer assessed the income of Debi Parfshad to tax on the basis of the income of his family. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the income of a family of which the appellant was a member was liable to be assessed to tax on that basis. The Appellate Tribunal held that the Income tax Officer was competent to make the impugned direction. The High Court held that the Appellate Assistant Commissioner was competent to direct the Income tax officer to assess the income of an association of persons under section 31(3)(c) of the Income tax Act. The High court held that the order of the Appellate Assistant Commission was not a valid order. The High. Court held that there was no valid order of the Income Tax Officer. The High, Court held that in the absence of any finding that the income in the hands of the family was liable to tax, the Appellate Assistant Commisioner was competent to pass the impugned direction and directed that the income should be assessed in the hands or the family of a member. The High Curt held that the Tribunal was competent to issue a direction to the Income tax authorities to assess the Income tax payable by the appellant. The High' Court held that if the Income tax authority was competent to assess the assessee, the Income tax was not payable by the assessee. The High 'Court held that the assessee was not entitled to the relief of assessment. The High-Court held that there is no valid order passed by the Appellate Assistant-Commissioner. The HighCourt held that in view of the finding of the Appellate Tribunal that the income was liable to income tax, the High Court was competent to set aside the direction to assess the appellant. In the result, the High.Court allowed the appeal and set aside the order of assessment. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in holding that the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal was competent under section 28(1) of the Act to direct the income tax authorities to make the assessment. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts of the State of Uttar Pradesh and the Commissioner of Income tax, U.P. vs Kanpur Flour Mills, ; referred to. 2. The High courts of the State were competent to issue the impugned direction to the income tax authority. The High (Court was competent to give the direction. [605 C] 3. The High [Court] was competent to decide the question referred to it. [606 D] 3.1 The High Court was not competent to issue any direction to the authorities to assess or reassess the income of any association of persons. [607 D] 3:2. The High T. Court was competent under the Act to issue a mandamus to the Income Tax authorities to assess and reassess the income. [608 D] 3(i) The High Court erred. [609 D] 3.(ii) The High [court] was competent under [section 28(1)] to direct the authorities to make assessment and reassess the assessee. [610 D] 3 (iii) The High Courts were competent to give direction to the assessee to assess and assess the income. The High] Court erred in giving the direction. The order of the High Court is not a valid one. [611 D] 3rd May, 1966, the date of the order of this Court in Kanpur Flour Mills was the date of assessment. [612 E] 3.2 The High Court had no jurisdiction to direct the assessing authority to assess and re assess the income in question. [613 G] 3.3 The High Court could not have directed the assessing authority not to reassess the income in dispute.

The appellant was the owner of a house situated in the city of Madras. He was the owner in respect of the house situated in his house. He was a tenant in the house. He had two sons, namely, the appellant and the respondent. The respondent filed a suit for partition of the house in the City Civil Court, Madras, and the appellant filed a written statement. The trial court held that the appellant was entitled to a decree for partition of his house and the respondent was entitled to get the decree for partition. The appellant filed an appeal against the decree. The appellate court held that in view of the provisions of section 7(iv)(b) of the Act, the appellant was not entitled to a share in the house in question. The appellate Court held that the respondent was not entitled for a share in his house in the house and that the appellant had not valued the suit for the purpose of court fee. The respondent then filed an appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that in the plaint the appellant was claiming a share in a house in the city Civil Court, and that the valuation for the purpose for court fee was Rs. 1,000. The High court further held that the valuation of the suit for partition was Rs. 2,000. In the result the High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant then filed a second appeal to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court held that section 7(v) of the Suits Valuation Act postulates that the plaintiff must first value his claim for the purpose o the court fee and that the court fee was payable on the plaint. The Supreme court held that section 8 of the Suits valuation Act postulates that where the plaintiff is entitled to a sum of money for the purpose specified in the section, he is entitled to value of the suit. The Supreme Courts held that in a suit for the relief of partition, the plaintiff is not entitled to any share in the property in question. In the present case the appellant was the tenant in the suit house in the year 1953. The appellant was the landlord of the house. The appellant had valued the suit in the year 1955. The appellant claimed that he was entitled to the decree for the partition of the suit house. The trial Court held that as the appellant was a tenant, he was entitled for a sum of Rs. 2.000. The appellant preferred an appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The appellant is entitled to the value of the house as the value of his claim for partition. [775 H] 2. The appellant has not valued the house in dispute for the purpose to be taken for the purpose. The valuation for the purposes of court fee is the value of a suit for money. [776 H] 3. The appellant cannot be allowed to amend his plaint in the year 1962. The appellant could not have valued the suit as the value for the purpose in the plaint. [778 H] 4. The appellant should have valued the house for the purpose mentioned in the plaint and the value of court fee should have been taken as the valuation for purpose of court fees. [779 H] 5. The appellant must be allowed to add a sum of rupees one hundred to the value for court fee. [780 H] 6. The appellant would be entitled to a half share in the suit property. [782 H] 7. The appellant can be allowed to make a correction in the plaint if he is able to prove that the valuation made by the appellant is correct. [785 H] 8. The appellant, having valued the suit, should have valued it for the purpose indicated in the plaint, and should have valued court fee. It is not open to the appellant to amend his claim for a share of the suit property in the plaint in the manner provided in the Code of Civil Procedure. [786 H] 9.

The plaintiff, a partnership firm, was carrying on business in the name and style of "M/s. Hindustan Lever Ltd., and the business of the firm was taken over by the partners. The firm was dissolved on March 31, 1946. The firm filed a suit for partition and separate possession of the motor business in the Court of the Civil Judge, Delhi, and for recovery of the amount due to the firm. The firm claimed that the motor business was being run by the partners of the firm and that the partnership was dissolved on the death of the partners. It was contended that the partnership firm was dissolved by the death of one of the partners and the partnership was not dissolved by the firm. Held, that the partnership in the present case was dissolved by a death of the partner and the partnership continued to be in existence till the death of a partner. The partnership was dissolved by an order of the Court and the firm was dissolved. The partnership continued to subsist till the death or death of the partnership. The partnership could not be dissolved by the Court. The partnership in the instant case was dissolved on a dissolution of the partnership by the death or the death of any of the partners, and the partnership could not continue thereafter. The partnership had not been dissolved by the partnership. Held, further, that the firm was not dissolved on the dissolution of the firm by the death, of the partner. The firm could not be continued thereafter. The firm continued to be dissolved by an application under Order II, rule 2, C.P.C. and the suit was not barred under Order II rule 2, CPC. The suit was not maintainable. The partnership firm was not a dissolved firm. The partnership did not continue to subsist till a dissolution of that firm. The plaintiff was bound by the terms of the compromise decree. The plaintiff could not be permitted to continue the partnership after the death of his partner. The suit in the present suit was not governed by the compromise decree and the suit is not barred under the provisions of Order II, Rule 2, C..P.C., and the suit must be dismissed.

The respondent was appointed as a Tailoring Instructor in the Department of Technical Education in the year 1955. He was confirmed in the post of Assistant Engineer in the Department. He was promoted as Assistant Engineer in December, 1949. He was reverted to the post of Deputy Director of Technical Education, by an order dated December 12, 1949, and he was absorbed permanently in the Department in the year 1964. He was absorbed permanently on November 28, 1949, in the Department, in the grade of Assistant Engineer, on the basis of the order of the Government of Mysore, dated December 12. 1949. He joined the Department on November 28. The respondent was confirmed in that post on November 28 and he was confirmed in his post on November 29. The respondent continued to work in the Department till November 28, 1950, when he was absorbed in the Department on December 12, 1950. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court of Mysore, which was allowed by a learned Single Judge, and the order of dismissal was quashed. The State Government preferred an appeal to the Division Bench of the High Court. The Division Bench allowed the appeal and held that the respondent was entitled to the relief, which he was entitled to, on the date on which he was absorbed. The State of Mysore filed an appeal to this Court. The Court held that the order of confirmation of the respondent was not passed in accordance with the provisions of the Mysore Service Rules, and that the order was not passed by the Government of the State of Mysore, and that it was not necessary to pass an order of absorption in the Department and that the respondent could not be treated as a break in his service. The Court further held that the State Government had evolved a principle "that if a person was deputed to the Department of Engineering, he stayed on in that other department for a reasonable long time, his absorption in the department was not ordered owing to any fault of the respondent. In the present case, the respondent was absorbed permanently, in the department, in the year 1949, and the respondent was confirmed permanently in the post. The Court also held that the Government of India had evolved a rule "that if the person was deputed permanently, he was not suitable or qualified to hold the post of Tailoring Instructor. The Court accordingly held that the impugned order was not in accordance with law and the High Court was not justified in holding that the respondent's absorption was not ordered because he was not a regular employee of the Department of the State Government. The Court, therefore, held that the High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order of termination of the respondent, and that in the circumstances of this case, the order of his absorption was not passed on the basis that the respondent had stayed in the Department for a reasonable period. The Court then held that the appellant was entitled to relief under the writ petition. The Court observed that the respondent having been absorbed permanently, he could not be denied the relief. The Court directed the State Government to absorb the respondent in the Department as a Tailor in the Department with effect from November 28, 1955, and to pay him the salary and allowances for the period he was not absorbed permanently. The Court was of the opinion that the respondent should be given the relief, if he was not appointed on deputation permanently. The respondent, therefore, filed a writ appeal to this court. The Court allowed the appeal, and directed the State of the State to absorb the appellant in the Department by an order of the Court. The State filed an appeal against the order of this Court. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The respondent could not have been absorbed permanently in a post in the Department without the order of appointment of the State. [775 H] 2. The respondent had been absorbed permanently. He was not a direct recruit. He was appointed permanently. He could not be absorbed permanently. [776 H] 3.

The appellant, a foreigner, filed an application for guardianship of his child before the court of the District Judge, Delhi, on the ground that he was a foreigner and that he was not a foreigner. The court of the district judge, Delhi, held that the appellant was a foreigner. On appeal, the High Court of Delhi set aside the order of the District judge, Delhi and directed the appellant to be given in adoption. The appellant filed an appeal to this Court. The High Court held that the child was a foreigner within the meaning of Section 2(1)(a) of the Act and that the appellant had not been able to satisfy the court that he was entitled to be given the child in adoption. On the question of the appellant's right to be given to the child, the High court held that the father of the child was not a citizen of India and that he had not been given in adoption by the foreigner. The High court held, that the appellant could not be given in the adoption in view of the provisions of Section 2 (1)(a), (b) and (c) of the said Act. On the basis of the findings of the High Court, the appellant was directed to be given a child in adoption by a recognised social or child welfare agency. The appellant was directed by the High Court to be given an opportunity to the appellant to make a representation as to why he should be given the said child in adoption and after considering the representation, the court of district judge, New Delhi, was of the view that the appellant should be given in his favour. The appellant, therefore, filed an appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellant was a citizen of the country and he was a citizen. [775 H] 1.2 The appellant was not a resident of India and he was not entitled to be treated as a foreigner. [776 H] 1:2. The appellant had not made any representation as required by Section 2(a) of Act of the Act. The appellant could not have been given in the application for guardianship. [778 H] 1.:3. The appellant has not been able even to satisfy the Court that he was also entitled to be considered for adoption by the recognised social or the child welfare agency processing the application for the child. [779 H] 1] 1:3. The High Courts were not justified in holding that the appellant did not have the requisite qualification for being given in adoption and that he could not be denied the benefit of being given in the same manner as he was entitled. [780 H] 1a. The appellant is a foreigner and he was entitled for being given the child as a foreigner and the child was entitled to get the benefit of the Act as he was a resident of the country. [782 H] 1b. The appellant cannot be denied the right to be treated in the same way as he was not treated in the adoption. [785 H] 1c. The appellant should be treated as an Indian citizen. [750 H] 1o. The appellant having been given the child, he was entitled under Section 2(b) of the act to be given that child in adoption, and the appellant was entitled to the benefit of Section 2 of the Act, as he was also a foreigner. In the circumstances, the appellant is entitled to the benefits of the Act in the matter of his being given the benefit of a child in the same fashion as he was given in adoption in the same place. [750 A] 1c; 1d; 1e; 1e. The appellant must be given the benefit in the same terms as he was treated in the application filed by the appellant for guardianship. The appellant would be entitled to the same benefits as he was denied to be given. [750 B] 1c] 1d; 2:1.

The Company was an employee of the Company. The Company was an industrial undertaking. The Company had a permanent establishment in the State of Bihar. The Company has a permanent establishment. The Company is an industrial undertaking and the Company has a factory at the relevant time. The Company's factory is situated at a distance of about 50 kms. from the place of work. The Company owns a factory at a distance about 50 kms., and the Company is an industry. The Company, therefore, has a factory in the State. The Company also owns a factory in a nearby area. The Company maintains a factory at an average rate of Rs. 1,000 per month. The Company claims that the Company has paid the amount of Rs. 65,764 to the Company. It is not disputed that the Company is a registered company. The Company contends that the Company was an industry and the Company was not an industry. It is also not disputed that it is an industry and it is an industrial company. The Tribunal held that the Company had a factory at its factory at an amount of Rs, 65,76,410. The Tribunal also held that the workmen were not an industry and they were not an industrial undertaking within the meaning of the Act. The Tribunal further held that the payment of bonus to the Company was a payment made by the Company to induce the workmen to retire prematurely. The Tribunal accordingly held that the bonus payable to the Company is not an item of expenditure incurred by the Company on the ground of commercial expense in order to facilitate carrying on of the business. The Tribunal, however, held that the amount of bonus payable to be paid to the Company by the Company was Rs. 65.764. The Tribunal found that the Company did not pay the bonus to the workmen on the ground that the Company could claim bonus only in the sum of Rs. 64,764. On the basis of the Award of the Tribunal, the Company was directed to pay bonus to the extent of Rs. 66,794. The Tribunal directed that the bonus should be paid to be paid by the Company. In the appeal by the Company, the Tribunal held that it was an industry. In the second appeal, the Company contended that the Tribunal was not justified in rejecting the claim of the Company for bonus. The Tribunal observed that the Company's claim for bonus was not based on any commercial consideration and that the Company cannot claim bonus on the ground it was an industrial company within the meaning ofs. 2(f) of the Act, and that the Tribunal had not accepted the claim of Rs.65,764 as a deduction from the available surplus. The Tribunal rejected the claim of bonus. The Company filed a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that the Tribunal's finding that the Company should be paid bonus to the tune of Rs. 67,794 was not correct. The Tribunal then held that the claim of a workman for bonus was based on the ground on which the claim of an employer for bonus was rejected. The Tribunal was also of the view that the Company must be held to be an industry. On the question of bonus, the Tribunal observed that it was not disputed that in the case of the Company, it was an Industry. The Tribunal has held that the company was an industry, and the Company cannot be held to have a factory at any rate less than the one mentioned in the Act. In the result, the Tribunal rejected the claims of the Company and directed the Company to pay bonus. The High court held that the award of the Tribunal was erroneous. The Tribunal's finding was that the Company would be an industry and not an industry, but it was not a case of an industry. Accordingly, the Tribunal directed the Company's case to be treated as an industry. Hence, the appeal by special leave. The Tribunal considered the claim of Mr. S. N.

The appellant was a member of the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal, Madras. He was appointed as a Member of the Sales tax Appellate Tribunal, a former Judge of the High Court of Madras. He retired from service on November 29, 1974. The appellant was promoted as a Member, Sales Tax Appellate tribunal, a former Chief Justice of the High court of Madras. The appellant retired from service in the year 1974. The Government of Tamil Nadu issued a notification under section 4 of the Tamil Nadu General Sales Tax Act, 1959, (hereinafter referred to as the Act) on December 31, 1974, declaring that the appellant was eligible for promotion to the post of Deputy Commissioner of Commercial Taxes. The appellant challenged the said notification by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court quashed the notification and directed the Government to consider the case of the appellant in the light of the observations made in the judgment. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the notification. The High court held that the appellant had not been promoted as a Deputy Commissioner of Sales Tax and that the appellant's case was covered by the decision of this Court in the case of [The State of Tamil Nadu vs. The State of Tamil nadu] and that the said decision was not applicable to the facts of the case. The appellant, therefore, filed a writ appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The appellant is entitled to the benefit of the notification dated December 31, 1973. The appellant has been promoted as Deputy Commissioner of the Commercial Taxes Department. The appellant had been promoted as the Deputy Commissioner of a Sales Tax Appellate, Tribunal, Madras, on December 31. 1974. The said notification was issued on December 31 1974. The notification was issued under section 4(1) of the Act. The appellant could not be promoted as Deputy Commissioners of Commercial Taxes on the basis of the said notification. [775 H] 2. The appellant cannot be treated as a Government servant. The appellant's case is covered by the said notification and the appellant is entitled for the benefit of that notification. [750 H] 3. The appellant having been promoted as an Additional Commissioner of Commercial Tax, he cannot be treated to be a Government servant and he cannot be denied the benefit of promotion. [750 A] 4. The appellant being a Government servant, he cannot claim the benefit of any notification issued under section4 of the Act on December 31 of 1974. [750 B] 5. The appellant must be treated as an employee of the Department of Commercial Taxes and he cannot claim to be treated as Government servant. [750 D] 6. The appellant can be treated as the Government servant. He cannot be treated on par with the Government servant in the matter of promotion. The appellant should be treated as having been promoted to the post. [750 G] 7. The appellant would be entitled to the benefits of the notification under section4(1) and the notification under [section 4(1)] of the Act is quashed. [750 E] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1584 of 1988. From the Judgment and Order dated the 14th July, 1988 of the Madras High Court in W.P. No. 8 of 1988. V.S. Desai, S.K.
