The appellants were the owners of the buses in question. The State Transport Undertaking issued a scheme called the "Regional Transport Authority" for nationalisation of transport business in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The scheme was published in the official gazette on May 7, 1962. The scheme provided for nationalisation of the transport business in Andhra Pradesh. On the basis of the scheme the State Transport Undertaking was to be taken up for nationalisation. The scheme framed by the State Transport Authority was published in its official gazette on June 10, 1962. On the same day the scheme was published by the State Government in the official Gazette. The scheme under s. 68C was published in two newspapers on June 10 and 11, 1962. After the publication of the scheme in the official newspapers on June 11, 1962 the scheme was approved by the State of Hyderabad. On the application of the appellants the scheme was sanctioned by the State. The scheme, however, was not approved by the Government. On the other hand, the scheme was finally approved by the Regional Transport Authority. On the objection of the appellants that the scheme was not in conformity with the requirements of section 68C, the State Transport undertaking filed a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that the scheme framed by it was not in accordance with the requirements and the scheme was invalid. The appellants filed a writ appeal to this Court. The learned Judge held that the schemes were not in conformity of the requirements of the Act and the Rules made thereunder. The learned Single Judge held that there was no violation of section 68F(1) and the scheme framed was not in consonance with the requirements. The learned Judges held that the Scheme was not in conflict with the requirements laid down in section 68C and the Rules framed thereunder. The appellants then filed a writ application in the High court for quashing the scheme. The learned single Judge held that in view of the provisions of section 68D, the scheme framed under the Act was not in consistent with the requirements as laid down in the Act. The learned judge held that the appellants were entitled to the benefit of the scheme and the scheme could not be challenged on the ground that it was not consistent with the provisions of the Act. On the question of the validity of the scheme, the learned Judge held, that the scheme did not contravene the provisions of sections 68C and 68D. The learned judges held that the provisions of s. 68D were not in conflict and the scheme did no more than provide for the satisfaction of the requirements laid by the Act. In the result, the learned Judges held, that there was violation of section68F(1), and the scheme, therefore, was not in contravention of section 68E. The learned counsel for the appellants contended that the scheme is not in conformity or in conflict with section 68F and the scheme is invalid. The learned Attorney General for the State of Madras, who appeared for the appellants, contended that the schemes framed by the appellants were not in accordance or in accordance with law and the scheme cannot be challenged on that ground. The learned Additional Solicitor General, appearing for the appellants submitted that the scheme, as approved by the Central Government, was not consistent and in any event, the scheme could be challenged on any ground. The scheme is not inconsistent with the provisions contained in the Act and is not in conflict or inconsistent with the requirements set out in section 68F. The learned Solicitor General submitted that the schemes are not in conflict. The learned Counsel for the appellants also submitted that the learned Judge was right in holding that the scheme does not contravene the requirements of sections 68F and 68F. On the merits, the learned counsel for respondent No. 1 submitted that the appellants are entitled to the scheme. It was further submitted that the Scheme is not inconsistent and the scheme does no more than provides for the satisfaction that the requirements laid out in section68F and the Rules and the Rules are in conflict with it.

The appellant, a dealer in the goods, purchased a consignment of goods from the respondent, a dealer, in the State of Orissa, for the purpose of resale by him. The respondent purchased the goods from the appellant, a registered dealer, in respect of the goods, for the period from 1.4.1957 to 31.3.1957. The appellant purchased the goods, from the respondent. The respondent filed a return for the period 1.4,1957 to 31-3-1957, in respect to the goods purchased by him from the appellant. The respondent claimed that the goods purchased were not liable to tax under the Act. The appellant filed a return in respect of those goods, in respect thereof, in respect thereto, in respect whereof the respondent claimed exemption under the Act, and claimed that the said goods were liable to tax. The respondent, however, claimed that the appellant was entitled to exemption under the provisions of the Act. On the basis of the return filed by the respondent, the assessing authority, by its order dated 31.3,1957, assessed the appellant to tax the goods purchased from the appellant for the period commencing from 1.1.1957 to 30.4.1958. The respondent challenged the assessment order by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant then filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution in the High court. The High court held that the appellant had not made out a case for the exemption under the said provisions of the statute and the High Court was in error in holding that the appellant could not claim exemption under the provision of the Act, as he had not made a full and true disclosure of the facts. The appellant, therefore, filed a writ appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts were not justified in interfering with the assessment orders passed by the assessing authority. [532E] 2. The provisions of the Orissa Sales Tax Act, 1947, were not in the nature of an exception to the general rule of exemption. The exemption under the statute was not available to the dealer for the period prior to 1.4.'1957 to 31st March 1957. [533F] 3. The appellant was entitled, in law, to exemption under Section 5(2) (a)(ii) of the Act and the rules made thereunder. [534F] 4. The appellant had not furnished the correct information in respect of his sales tax returns. The appellant could not be permitted to claim exemption under Section 8(1)(a)(ii). [534G] 5. The appellant is entitled to exemption from tax under the provisions contained in the Act. [535G] 6. The appellant has not made out any case for the purpose. The appellant cannot claim exemption under section 5(2). [536F] 7. The appellant must be held to have made out a good case for the grant of exemption under the relevant provisions of the said Act. [546G] 8. The appellant should be held to be entitled to exemption. [546F] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1533 of 1968. Appeal by Special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 14th July, 1968 of the Orissa High Court in Misc. Case No. 11 of 1968. S. K. Bisaria, for the appellant. S. P. Sinha, for the respondent. S. N. Prasad, for the intervener. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Hegde, J. This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment of the High Court of Orissa dated April 14, 1968. The appellant obtained a certificate of fitness from the High Court under Article 133(1)(c) of the Constitution. The appellant applied for the certificate of fitness for appeal to this court.

The appellant was a member of the Bihar Police Service. He was convicted by the Magistrate of the first class of the State of Bihar and was sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of one year and to pay a fine of Rs. 500/- and in default of payment of fine to undergo rigorous rigorous imprisonment for one year. The appellant was convicted by a Magistrate of the First Class of the State and sentenced to undergo imprisonment for a further period of one month and to pay fine of Rs 500/- and on appeal by the State, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. The appellant filed an appeal to the High Court of Patna. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant then filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the Magistrate. The High court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant thereafter filed a writ appeal to this Court. The appellant contended that the High Court was wrong in holding that the appellant was guilty of the offence with which he was charged. The High, Court held that the appellant had been convicted by a Judicial Magistrate of the second class and sentenced to pay a sum of Rs. 1,000/- and to pay Rs. 500/and in default of the payment of fine, the Magistrate was not justified in holding that he was guilty of an offence with which the appellant was charged. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts were wrong in holding the appellant guilty of an alleged offence with which they were charged. [775 H] 2. The High courts were wrong in not considering the question whether the appellant was liable to be convicted for an offence withwhich he was charged and whether he was guilty. [776 H] 3. The High. Courts were wrong. The appellant had been acquitted by the Magistrate. [778 H] 4. The appellant could not be convicted for the offence withwhich the appellant was convicted. [779 H] 5. The appellant is entitled to the benefit of the provisions of Article 21 and Article 21 of the Constitution. [780 H] 6. The appellant has been convicted by the Judicial Magistrate of first class of cases and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for two years and to pay an amount of Rs. 1000/- and to undergo rigorous sentence for a period three years. [782 H] 7. The appellant cannot be convicted for a second offence with which we are concerned. [785 H] 8. The appellant must be held guilty of an act with which he is charged. [750 H] 9. The appellant can be convicted for offences with which he has been charged. [751 H] 10. The appellant should be held guilty for an offence under Section 395 of the Indian Penal Code. [751 A] 11. The appellant, if he is convicted for an act withwhich he is charged, should be held liable to be punished for an offence which he is not charged with. [751 B] 12. The appellant's conviction for an offence is not illegal.

The appellant was a tenant of a building in the city of Bombay. He was a tenant in the city. He was in possession of the building. He was served with a notice under section 34(1) of the Bombay Tenancy Act, 1939, on the landlord. The landlord filed a suit for eviction against the tenant on the ground of non-payment of rent. The tenant pleaded that he was a tenant under the landlord and that the tenancy was terminated by the landlord by notice dated December 31, 1951. The trial court held that the notice was not given before the commencement of the Amending Act and that the landlord was not entitled to terminate the tenancy. The High Court held that the landlord had failed to prove that the notice dated December 30, 1951 was given before the Amending Act came into force. The High court held that in the absence of any evidence to the contrary, the notice was given before December 31, 1952 and therefore the landlord was entitled to terminate his tenancy. The appellant filed a second appeal to the High Court. The High, Court held that in view of the notice dated January 31, 1951, the landlord was bound to terminate the notice and that the notice must be given before the date of the termination of the tenancy. In the circumstances, the High Court held, the landlord had not proved that the notice of termination was given before January 31, 1952. The High. Court held that it was not open to the landlord to terminate the lease by giving notice before the commencement date and that the tenant was not entitled for possession. The High Curt also held that the tenant had failed to establish that the notice given by the landlord was given before March 31, 1952, and therefore the court had to see whether the notice was in accordance with the restrictions imposed by subs. (2A) on the date of notice. The High-Court held that the tenancy had terminated by the notice dated February 30, 1951. In the result, the High Curt held that the suit was not barred by res judicata. The appellant then filed a second suit for eviction on the ground that the notice issued by the landlord on December 30, 1952 was not given prior to the date of termination of the notice. The appellant also filed a second application for the same relief on the same grounds. The HighCourt held that in spite of the notice issued on January 31, 1950, the landlord did not prove that the tenancy has terminated by the first notice dated December 29, 1952. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the notice under section34(1) was not given after the commencement of that Act and therefore the suit was barred by resjudicata. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts were right in holding that the notice in question was given before February 30, 1952, when the tenancy was not terminated by the appellant. [557 C] 2. The notice dated December, 30, 1952 is not given before December 30, 1953, and therefore it is not open to a landlord to terminate his lease by giving a notice before the date on which the notice was issued. [558 D] 3. The notice was given after the date of its termination. The notice must be read in the context of the Act and the rules made thereunder. [559 D] 4. The notice given by a landlord on December 29, 1951, was given before May 30, 1952. It was given before April 30, 1952 and was given before that date. The notice under section 31 was given before June 30, 1952; it was given before July 30, 1952 but was given before August 30, 1952 when the tenancy had not terminated. [560 D] 5. The notice issued by a landlord under section 34 was given before November 30, 1952 which was given before September 30, 1952 because the tenancy had been terminated by the tenant. [566 D] 6.

The petitioners, who were the sons of the late Nawab Ali, filed a suit in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Delhi, against the respondents, for a declaration that the sale deed dated October 10, 1950, was null and void and for a decree for possession of the properties. The respondents filed an appeal to the District Court, Delhi, and the District Court held that the sale was null and ineffective and that the petitioners were entitled to the possession of the houses. The District Court held, that the sale in favour of the respondents was null and without jurisdiction and that the respondents were entitled to a decree for the possession of their houses. The respondents preferred an appeal to this Court. The Court held that in view of the provisions of section 12 of the Act, the petitioners were not entitled to the relief claimed in the petition. The petitioners filed an appeal against the order of the District Court. The District Judge, Delhi dismissed the appeal. The petitioners then filed a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that section 12 of this Act was not applicable to the petitioners. The High court held that section 13 of the Act was not attracted to the petitioners and that the sale of the houses was null and invalid. The petitioners, therefore, filed a writ appeal to this court. The petitioners contended that section 13 was not applicable in the case. The High, Court held that there was no valid sale in favourof the respondents and that the provisions of the Act were not applicable to them. The High. Court held that as the petitioners were the sons and the respondents were the sons, they were entitled to possession of the house. The High' Court held that since the petitioners were sons and the petitioners were also the sons of their father, they were not entitled for the relief claimed. The petitioners' appeal was dismissed. The petitioners have filed this petition under Article 136 of the Constitution. The petitioners are not entitled to any relief in the petition, as the petitioners are not the sons of any of the petitioners. In the result, the petition fails and is dismissed.

The assessee is a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The assessee is a limited company incorporated under section 10(2)(xv) of the Act. The assessee was a limited company. The assessee company was incorporated under the provisions of the Indian Companies' Act, 1913, and was registered under the Indian Registration Act, 1908. The assessee had a branch office at Bombay. The assessee's branch office was at Bombay. On the basis of the agreement between the assessee and the company, the assessee was to distribute the profits of the business of the assessee. The assessee, on the basis of an agreement between the company and the assessee, was to distribute profits of the assessee's business to the assessee. On the other hand, the assessee had to distribute the profit of the assessee to the assessee in the ordinary course of business. The assessee filed a return of the profits of his business on the basis that the assessee had not made any profit in the ordinary business. The Income Tax Officer, on the other hand. held that the assessee was not entitled to the deduction under section 10 (2)(xv). The assessee filed an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the agreement between it and the assessee was a contract for payment of a share of profits simpliciter and not a mere agreement for distribution of profits simpliciter. The Tribunal, however, held that the payment in question was not a mere arrangement of an agency but was a mere agreement of distribution of profits. The Tribunal further held that the alleged payment was not a loan transaction and the assessee had no right to make any profit. The Tribunal accordingly held that the payments in question were not a mere contract for payment but were made out wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the business. The High Court, however, dismissed the appeal filed by the Revenue. The Revenue filed a special leave petition in this Court. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1.1 The agreement between the parties was a contract of agency and not a contract for the purpose for the purpose. The agreement was a contract to pay the remuneration of the agents in the ordinary way. The agreement did not create any right in the assessee to make any profits. [775 H] 1.2 The agreement was not a contract of a mere agreement to distribute profits simpliciter. It was a mere arrangement for distribution of profit. [776 H] 1:3. The agreement between it was a contract which was not a merely agreement of distribution. [778 H] 1 Whether the agreement was a mere contract or a contract for distribution of the profits simpliciter is a question of fact. [779 H] 1a. The agreement is a contract for a purpose other than the business of a business. [780 H] 1b. The agreement does not create any rights in the assessee in respect of the profits. [750 H] 1c. The agreement merely provides for a right to distribute the income of the assessee in his ordinary course of the business and does not create a right in the respondent to make any such profit. [750 A] 1c; D] 1.3 The agreement was only a contract for an agency and not an agency. [750 B] 1.4 The agreement was an arrangement for distribution. The agreement provided that the assessee would distribute the profits and the profits of business to the extent of the surplus of the profits and gains of the business to the shareholders. [750 D] 1c] 1.5 The agreement was merely a arrangement for distribution and not a merely an agreement for distribution. [750 E] 1.6 The agreement was one for distribution of a profit. [751 H] 1d; D] 2.1 The question whether the agreement was one of a mere arrangement or an arrangement for distributing the profits of a business does not arise in the present case.

The appellant, a resident of Bombay, was assessed to income tax by the Income Tax Officer, Bombay, for the assessment year 1958-59. The Income Tax Officer assessed the appellant to income tax for the assessment years 1958-59 and 1959-60. The appellant filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court of Madras for quashing the order of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, Madras, and for a direction to the Income Tax officer to refer the second question to the High Court. The High Court held that the provisions of section 256(1) of the Income tax Act, 1961, were applicable to the case and the question whether the provision of Rs. 6,900 for dividend was applicable to the present case was not a question of law which was not referred by the Appellate Tribunal to the High court. The appellant, therefore, filed a petition before the High court under Article 226 for quashing the notice issued by the Income tax Officer, Bombay. The High court held that the provision of section 256 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 was applicable to a case where the provisions of the Income -tax Act, 1922, were applicable. The High, Court held that section 256(2) of the Act was applicable to cases where the provisions were not referred to the High, Court. The appellant then filed a petition for special leave to this Court. The question whether the provisions of Section 256(2)(a) of the Incometax Act, 1961 were applicable to a proceeding under the Income Tax Act, 1961 or not was not a matter of law which could be referred to the Court. The appeal was allowed by the High Court and the order of dismissal of the petition was set aside. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The provisions of section 257 of the IncomeTax Act, 1961 are applicable to a proceedings under the Income-Tax Act, 1922. The provisions in the Income Tax Rules, 1962, are applicable to cases of assessment. [775 H] 2. The provisions contained in section 256(l) of the Indian Income Tax Act are applicable to the cases of assessment of income tax. The provisions relating to the assessment of income-tax are applicable to proceedings under the Indian Income tax Act. The provisions are applicable to all proceedings under the Act. [776 H] 3. The provisions referred to in section 256 of that Act are applicable only to cases where there is a finding of fact as to the law which is applicable to the proceedings under the Incometax Act. The question of law referred to the court is not a question in the present case. [778 H] 4. The provisions made in section 256 (1) of that Act apply to cases where an order of the Appellate Tribunal is not a decision of the High Court under section 254. [779 H] 5. The provisions regarding the appeals are applicable to appeals under the Income tax law. The provisions for appeals are applicable only in cases where the provision is not a matter in the Income tax statute. [780 H] 6. The provisions as to appeals are applicable in cases where an appeal is not a proceeding under section 256 of this Act. [750 H] 7. The provisions under section 256(3) of the 1961 Act are applicable in the cases of appeals under the Incometax law. [750 A] 8. The provisions with regard to appeals are not applicable to cases under section 256. The provisions mentioned in section 256 are applicable to such cases. [750 B] 9. The provisions which are applicable to an appeal under the Income - tax Act, 1922 are applicable to other proceedings under the [Income-tax Act], 1961. [750 G] 10. The provisions applicable to appeals are in the Income- tax Act, 1962. [750 D] 11. The provisions to the extent they are applicable to pending proceedings under the 1922 Act are applicable. [750 E] 12.

The plaintiff, the predecessor of the defendants, filed a suit for a declaration that the defendants were in possession of the lands for a period of 20 years and that they were in possession for a period exceeding the statutory period. The trial court held that the defendants had been in possession for the last 20 years and the plaintiff was entitled to assessment of fair and equitable rent. The trial Court held that the plaintiff was in possession for more than 20 years and accordingly the plaintiff was held entitled to assessment. The defendants filed an appeal to the District Judge, who agreed with the District Judge that the plaintiff had not proved that he was in possession and that the plaintiff could not be said to be in possession for long over the statutory period and that the defendants could be said to have been in possession of land for a period not exceeding 20 years. The District Judge held that the suit lands were not in the possession of the defendants for a period less than 20 years. On appeal the District Judge held, that the plaintiff's possession was not in the actual possession of the land for a long time and that the possession of land was not referable to a grant by the owner. The District Court further held that the possession was referable to a lease by the defendants for 20 years and therefore the plaintiff was not entitled to assessment under the provisions of the Bengal Tenancy Act. On appeal, the District Judge confirmed the decision of the District Judge. The plaintiff filed a second appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that on the facts found, no rent was payable for a period more than 20 year and that the title of the Asthal had become extinguished by adverse possession for long. The High court held that on a proper construction of the provisions of law, the plaintiff was a trespasser and that the provisions of Section 6 of the Bengal Land Tenancy Act were not applicable to the facts of the case. The High, Court held that in the view of the District Court, the plaintiff could be said that he was entitled to assess the fair and equitable value of the land. The High. Court held that as the plaintiff was found to be in the possession for a long period of time, the plaintiff had become entitled to assessment, and that the right of the plaintiff was extinguished by adverse title. The High C Court held that since the plaintiff was claiming to be in occupation for a period beyond the statutory period, the plaintiff is not entitled to claim assessment under the Bengal Tenancy. The High' Court held that it was not open to the plaintiff to claim assessment on the basis of the provisions contained in the Bengal Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 1932. The High 'Court held that the provisions contained therein were not applicable in the facts of that case. The plaintiff was entitled, therefore, to assessment under Section 6 of Bengal Tenancy Act and the High Court held, that in the absence of any evidence to the contrary, the plaintiff's claim was not barred by limitation. The High-Court further held that in view of the provisions in the Bengal Land Revenue Act, the plaintiff cannot be said to hold under a tenancy for a period longer than 20 years, and that it was open to the defendants to claim assessment. The HighCourt further held, that as the defendants were not in possession for 20 years, the plaintiff must be deemed to be in adverse possession for a longer period. The High Courts decision was affirmed by this Court. The plaintiff has not challenged the findings of the High Court on the question of adverse possession. The High T Court held that under the Bengal Land revenue Act, the possession of a tenant for a period extending over a period of time was not adverse to the plaintiff. The High F.A.O. No. 8 of 1972 was dismissed. The plaintiff preferred a second appeal. The High R.S.A. No. 9 of 1972 was allowed by this Court on the ground that the plaintiff is entitled to assessment on the ground of adverse possession for the period of 20 year. The plaintiff is entitled, therefore.

The appellant filed a suit for specific performance of a contract for sale of agricultural land in the year 1964. The respondent filed a suit in the year 1965 for specific performance. The appellant filed a written statement in the suit. The trial Court decreed the suit. On appeal, the District Court confirmed the decree. On further appeal, the High Court reversed the decree. The High Court held that the trial Court was not competent to decide the issue in the suit and the suit was not maintainable. The High court held that the suit was maintainable. The appellant, therefore, filed a second appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts in India have concurrent jurisdiction to decide the question of law. [675B] 2. The High courts have concurrent jurisdiction. The High C.M.P. was not competent. [676D] 3. The High. Court was not right in holding that the trial court was competent to settle, decide or deal with the same. [678F] 4. The High-Court was not right when it held that the issue was an incidental issue in a properly constituted civil suit before a civil Court having jurisdiction to entertain the same. The High, Court was right in holding, that the trial of the suit was a nullity. [680F] 5. The High' Court was right when it said that the trial was not competent in the sense that the issue is an incidental issue. [682F] 6. The High 'Court was right in saying that the trial is not competent. The HighCourt was right when he held that the question of jurisdiction was not a question of law but a mixed question of law and fact. [683F] 7. The High T.A.C. has concurrent jurisdiction to settle, decided, decide or dealt with the same and upon the reference made by the competent authority under the Tenancy Act, the jurisdiction of the civil Court is barred. [684G] 8. The High [Court] was right when the trial was held to be a nullity. The High F.A.F. was right in observing that the trial has not been properly conducted. [685G] 9. The High Civil Court was right. [686G] 10. The High] Court was right, in holding that in view of the provisions contained in section 63 of the Tenancy Act the jurisdiction of civil Court is not barred. [650B] 11. The High A Court has concurrent jurisdiction. [650D] 12. The High[Court] was not right. [650E] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1367 of 1987. From the Judgment and Order dated 11.8.1987 of the Bombay High Court in Second Appeal No. 8 of 1987. V.M. Tarkunde, S.K. Bagga, S.N. Bagga and S.K Jain for the Appellant. V.S. Desai, S.S. Khanduja, S.D. Agarwal, S.R. Khanduja and S.N Sharma for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by K.J. Shah, J. This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment and order of the High Court of Bombay dated 11th August, 1987. The appellant is a tenant of the land in question. The appellant was the tenant of the respondent. The respondent was the tenant in respect of the land. The respondent had filed a suit against the appellant for specific performance and the suit filed by the respondent was decreed. The respondent challenged the decree in the suit filed under section 11 of the Tenancy and Act. The respondent also filed an appeal against the decree in which the suit was dismissed. The respondent then filed a second suit for specific Performance of the tenancy. The appellant also filed an application for amendment of the plaint. The trial court dismissed the suit.

The assessee, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling articles in the State of Bombay. The assessee was a new industrial undertaking which was being carried on by the assessee. The assessee, a new industrial unit, was formed by the reconstruction of the business already in existence. The assessee started a new industrial business in the State. The assessee's new industrial undertaking was being carried out by the new industrial undertaking. The new industrial undertaking, which was being run by the assessee, was being carried by the new business. The new undertaking was being run in the name of the new industrial unit. The new business was being carried in the name and style of the new business of the assessee. On the basis of the new undertaking, the assessee was formed by reconstruction of the old business. The assessee filed a return of income under section 15C of the Act on the basis of its new business. On the same basis, the assessee filed a petition under section 15D of the Act for the assessment of the new company. The High Court held that the new industrial business was being run for the purpose of the new commercial undertaking and the new industrial activity was not a new industrial activity. The High court held that the old industrial undertaking was not formed by the new undertaking and the assessee was not entitled to the benefit under section 15 C. The High. Court held that in order to be entitled to the benefits under section 15B, the new industrial concern must be a new industrial concern and the new undertaking must be a newly started one. In the present case, the new undertaking was formed by a new industrial company which was being wound up by the assessee and the new business was carried on by it. The High, Court held that it was not a case of the new industry and the new company was not formed for the purpose. The High' Court held that there was no bar to an assessee carrying on a new business on the ground that it was formed by it. In the result, the High Court held, that the new undertaking is not a new undertaking and that the new business is not a newly started business. The High 'Court held that the newly started business was not a newly established business and the new commercial business was not being carried on in the new business and the newly started new business was not formed. The High-Court held that in the present case the new industrial company was formed by an reconstruction of the new new business and that the old business was being conducted by the new company and the new new industrial undertaking is not formed by it and the new concern is not a separate industrial concern. In the view of the High Court, the High.Court was not right in holding that the new commercial venture was not a fresh industrial undertaking. In the circumstances, the High' Court was not right. The High C.A. No. 8 of 1972 filed by the assessee was dismissed.

The inam lands were granted to the inamdar for the performance of services connected therewith. The inamdar was granted a lease of the inam lands for a period of five years. The inamdars were granted a lease for a period exceeding five years. On the expiry of the lease, the inamdar was entitled to resume the lands. The inam lands were resumed under section 44 B(2)(a)(i) and the inamdar continued to be in possession of the lands. On the death of the inamdar, the inamdars were entitled to the kudiwaram rights in the lands. In the year 1934, the inam lands were resumable under section 44B(2)(b) and the inams were resumted under section 44 C(2)(c). The inamdar continued in possession of these lands. On a petition filed by the inamdar under section 44C(2)(i) the Assistant Collector, the District Collector, the Collector, the Deputy Commissioner, the Collector and the District Collector issued a notice to the inamdars to show cause why the inam lands should not be resumed. The inam was resumed under section 43 B(2) (a) (i) and (ii) of the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908. The inam land was resumed under the provisions of section 44 B (2)(a) (ii) and (iii) of the Act. The inam properties were resumited under section 44 A(2)(d) and the tenants were evicted. The inam were resumced under section 44 D(2)(e) and the lands were resuscitated under section 44D(2)(f). The inamdars filed a suit for possession of the inam land and the suit was decreed. The inam village was resumed under Section 44 B(1) and the land was resumed. The plaintiffs filed an appeal against the order of the Assistant Collector. The District Collector, after hearing the parties, confirmed the order of resumption. On further appeal, the High Court held that the inam lands had been resumed under section44 B(2). The High Court held, that the inam land was resumable and the inam lands could not be resumed under section 45 B(2), as the inam lands did not belong to the inam. The High Court, therefore, held that the lands were resumed by the Assistant Collector under section 44-B(2) and the order of eviction was passed. The High court held that the order of possession was not a nullity. The High, Court held that there was no infirmity in the order of remand and the High Court was not satisfied that the order passed by the Assistant Commissioner was in accordance with law. The High. Court held that in the absence of any provision in the Act or in the rules made thereunder, the inam land could not be resumable. The High C Court held that as the inam land had been resumed by the Government under section 44 F(2)(1) and was resumited, the inam properties were rightly resumed under section 47 B(2); and that the inamdar had no right to resume the inam lands. The High' Court held that section 44- B(2)-(i) was applicable to the inam lands and the inam land should be resumited. The High-Court held that the grant of the inam was not a regrant under section 44(B) (2) and that the order was not in accordance with the law. The appellants filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution for a writ of mandamus directing the Assistant Collector to resume the land. The High 'Court held that section 47-B(1) was applicable only to the inam land. The appellants' contention that the inam was resumted by the Assistant, Collector was rejected. The HighCourt held that there is no infirmity in this order. The High Courts decision in the cases of the inam villages was not challenged before us.

The appellant Corporation was assessed to tax on the gross annual letting value of the lands and buildings in the State of Madhya Pradesh. The appellant Corporation was served with a notice under section 80 of the Act on the basis of the gross annual rent of the lands. The appellant was served with the notice on the basis that the gross annual value of the land was Rs. 1,000 per annum. The appellant challenged the notice on various grounds. The High Court held that the gross return of the appellant Corporation was not liable to be taxed under the Act and that the appellant Corporation had not adopted the said assessment list for the two assessment years 1953 54 and 1954 55. The High court held that the appellant was entitled to demand the tax at the rate of 7% of the gross return. The High. Court held that in view of the provisions of section 73 of the Act the appellant Corporation could not be held to be entitled to demand tax at the rates specified in the said section. The High, Court held that as the appellant Corporation did not adopt the said assessment for the two years 1953 54, 1954 and 1954 55, the appellant Corporation is not entitled to demand any tax at the said rate. The appellant is, therefore, entitled to demand a tax at the same rate as the gross return for the two periods 1953 54 and 1955 55. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. The appellant-Corporation is a public limited company. The appellant had filed a return of income for the two year 1953 54 and 1956 55 for the two previous years 1953 54 to 1956 55. The return was filed on the basis for the two subsequent years 1953 54 & 1955 55. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the gross returns for the two earlier years were not liable to tax under the Act. The High 'Court held that the tax was not leviable on the basis thereof. The High' Court held that since the appellant Corporation has not adopted the assessment list prepared for the two different years 1953 54 or 1954 55, under the 1954 Act it cannot be said that the appellant had adopted the said assessments for the two later years 1953 54. The appellant cannot be allowed to raise the plea that the gross income of the appellant was not liable for tax under the 1954. The High C.A. No. 10 of 1972 filed by the appellant Corporation against the judgment and order of the High Court is dismissed.

The assessee Company was carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling chemicals and raw materials and was carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of chemicals and raw material. The assessee Company was a dealer in chemicals and rawmaterials and was carrying the same business. The assessee company was carrying on a business of manufacturing chemicals and rawmaterial. The assessee was carrying on its business of manufacturing chemical and raw materials. The assessee purchased chemicals and raw goods from the selling company and sold them to the selling company. The selling company sold the chemicals and raw products to the selling Company. The selling Company sold the chemicals to the selling and the selling company, and the selling and selling company sold them to its selling company. On the basis of the sale price, the selling and purchasing company sold the chemical and raw material to the selling, and the sale price was determined by the selling and buying company. The assessee filed a petition under s. 66 of the Act before the High Court of Madras praying for a writ of mandamus directing the selling and supplying company to the selling of chemicals and the selling of the chemicals and the sale of the chemicals to it. The High Court dismissed the petition. The assessee's appeal to this Court was, however, dismissed. The assessee contended that the selling and manufacturing company was not a dealer in the chemicals and that the selling company was not liable to tax. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The selling and selling companies were not dealers in chemicals and the sales were not in the course of business. The selling companies were carrying on a trading activity and were carrying on business. [557 C] 2. The selling of chemicals or raw materials were not goods within the meaning of s. 2(f) of the Act. The selling or selling companies were, therefore, not dealers in the chemicals or raw material. [558 D] 3. The selling, selling and selling of chemicals are not dealers in chemical and rawmaterials. The selling is only incidental to the manufacturing activity. The selling activity is incidental to the manufacture of the chemicals. [559 D] 4. The selling was not a business. The purchasing and selling companies are not dealers. The selling are not dealers but only dealers. The purchasing is only incidental. [560 D] 5. The selling in the course or the sale of chemicals is not a dealer. The selling. company is not a manufacturer. The selling can only be a dealer. [566 D] 6. The selling cannot be considered as a dealer. It is only a dealer who is carrying on a trade, which alone would have attracted tax. [567 D] 7. The selling has to be incidental to the business. The manufacturing activity is incidental. The selling may be incidental to manufacture. [568 D] 8. The selling must be incidental to manufacturing activity. [569 E] 9. The selling does not constitute a dealer. There is no element of sale in the sale of chemical and rawmaterial and the selling is incidental to manufacturing. [570 G] 10. The selling takes place in the course and in the course. of business. [500 G] 11. The selling by the selling is not incidental to the sale of any chemical and raw-material. [500 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1320 of 1966. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated the 9th July, 1966 of the Madras High Court in Writ Petition No. 11 of 1966. S. T. Desai, S. T.. Desai and S. S. Desai, for the appellant. S.T. Desai, R. N. Sachthey and S. P. Nayar, for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Hegde, J. The appellant is a dealer in chemical and the selling. company was carrying its business of manufacture and sale. The selling business was not incidental to manufacturing activities.
